article_title: Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction.
citation: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329
title: Form collaborative learning groups around learners' common interests and goals
description: The guide recommends forming collaborative learning groups by examining intake results, goal setting, and conversations with learners to find shared interests. It advises that "the facilitator or site coordinator can look at common interests among those who are willing to work in groups," giving examples such as parenting skills, job search, and health careers. A shared theme supplies many possible topics for reading, writing, critical reflection, and collective analysis, and groups formed by convenient time or location can instead generate themes in the first weeks of class.
requirements: Initial intake interviews, goal-setting formats, and conversations that surface learners' interests and willingness to work in groups
constraints: Some centers are constrained to hold classes based on a convenient time, day, and location rather than a shared theme
target_learners: Adult literacy and basic education learners
target_learning_goals: Basic academic skills, GED preparation, and employment-related goals
examples: In Scenario 1, a coordinator invites learners interested in health care professions to form a group meeting for three months
key_sources: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329

article_title: Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 2 Report: Changing Education Agencies from the Inside Out
citation: Kristin Hallgren, Alyson Burnett. (2014). Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 2 Report: Changing Education Agencies from the Inside Out. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Four-section structure for documenting agency data-use partnerships
description: Each profile follows a recurring four-part structure: background and context for data use; working with SDP/EP fellows; data analysis and reporting; and challenges encountered and lessons learned. The document states that "Each profile contains the following information" and lists these sections, giving a reusable template for describing how an education agency builds data-use capacity through an embedded fellowship. An organizational chart in each profile displays the path from the fellow's position to agency leadership.
requirements: Site visit interview data from the agency
An organizational chart showing the fellow's positioning within the organization
constraints: Structure reflects the SDP/EP fellowship partnership context and the 2013–14 school year
target_learners: Education agency staff and leaders hosting data fellows
target_learning_goals: Organizational data use
Data analysis and reporting practice
examples: The challenges-and-lessons-learned section reviews difficulties encountered during the agency's partnership with SDP or EP
key_sources: Kristin Hallgren, Alyson Burnett. (2014). Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 2 Report: Changing Education Agencies from the Inside Out. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/companion-document-for-the-strategic-data-project-and-education-pioneers-year-2-report

article_title: Professional Communities and Instructional Improvement Practices
citation: Stevens, W. D., with Kahne, J. (2006). Professional Communities and Instructional Improvement Practices: A study of small high schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Support teacher professional communities by making instructional discussion a regular, formally led part of meetings
description: The report recommends that schools create common meeting time and then go beyond it: "teacher teams need to make instructional discussions a regular and formal part of their meetings," with routines and processes ensuring sustained and systematic attention to instructional practices. Meeting time alone is described as necessary but insufficient, since daily pressures can easily distract teachers from instructional improvement issues. The report also calls for identifying administrative and teacher leaders responsible for directing attention to systematic improvement of core instructional practices.
requirements: Common meeting time must be paired with formalized instructional discussion routines and identified leadership, since regular meeting times alone do not eliminate the pressures that distract teachers
constraints: Creating common meeting time is a necessary, but insufficient, step toward helping teachers work together on instruction
target_learners: High school teachers in small schools
target_learning_goals: Sustained collective improvement of core instructional practices
examples: In school C, the principal and lead teacher initiated recurring professional development workshops around developing a standards-based curriculum, which prompted sustained collective discussions about instruction
key_sources: Stevens, W. D., with Kahne, J. (2006). Professional Communities and Instructional Improvement Practices: A study of small high schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/professional-communities-and-instructional-improvement-practices-study-small-high

article_title: Using Data to Improve Schools
citation: Elaine Allensworth. (2025). Using Data to Improve Schools. Corwin. https://www.corwin.com
title: Focus improvement effort on high-impact metrics rather than overwhelming or irrelevant data
description: The article argues that educators are often "inundated with data that feels overwhelming, irrelevant, or unhelpful" and that improvement efforts should instead concentrate on identifying high-impact metrics. It states that schools can improve key performance areas by identifying such metrics and fostering a collaborative culture of improvement, countering common myths and assumptions that divert attention from the data that matter most.
requirements: Educators must be able to distinguish high-impact metrics from overwhelming or unhelpful data
constraints: Common myths and assumptions can divert attention from the data that matter most, per the article
target_learning_goals: improving attendance, test scores, and graduation rates through data-informed improvement
examples: The guide addresses common myths and assumptions that divert attention from the data that matter most
key_sources: Elaine Allensworth. (2025). Using Data to Improve Schools. Corwin. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/using-data-to-improve-schools

article_title: Does Four Equal Five? Implementation and Outcomes of the Four-Day School Week
citation: M. Rebecca Kilburn, Andrea Phillips, Celia Gomez, Louis Mariano, Christopher Doss, Wendy Troxel, Emily Morton, Kevin Estes. (2021). Does four equal five? Implementation and outcomes of the four-day school week. NWEA Research report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Communities should weigh mixed four-day-week evidence against their own goals and local context when deciding on adoption
description: Because the study's findings on the four-day school week are mixed — small cost savings, no quantitative attendance evidence, qualitative support for teacher recruitment, high stakeholder satisfaction, but lower ELA and math scores over time — the report concludes that "communities are likely to make different choices about the 4dsw depending on their goals and the local context." Adoption decisions should therefore weigh the academic tradeoff against the non-academic benefits stakeholders value.
requirements: Decision-makers need local information on their own goals (e.g., teacher recruitment, family time, cost) and context, since the evidence does not point uniformly in one direction.
constraints: The academic evidence points to lower ELA and math scores over time on the 4dsw, which any adoption decision must confront.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts considering a four-day school week, especially rural districts in the western United States
target_learning_goals: Maintaining student academic achievement in English language arts and math while managing costs, attendance, and teacher recruitment and retention
examples: The study compared 4dsw and 5dsw districts in Idaho, New Mexico, and Oklahoma using original qualitative data and administrative data from these and other states.
key_sources: M. Rebecca Kilburn, Andrea Phillips, Celia Gomez, Louis Mariano, Christopher Doss, Wendy Troxel, Emily Morton, Kevin Estes. (2021). Does four equal five? Implementation and outcomes of the four-day school week. NWEA Research report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/does-four-equal-five-implementation-and-outcomes-of-the-four-day-school-week/

article_title: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency content guide
citation: NWEA. (2025). Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Content Guide. https://www.nwea.org
title: Assess oral reading with rate, accuracy, prosody, and comprehension rather than WCPM alone
description: The guide argues one-minute WCPM-only assessment loses the instructional value of accuracy scores and can equate faster reading with better reading. Citing Valencia et al. (2010), it states that "four types of scores each contribute to a best prediction of general passage comprehension: rate, accuracy, prosody, and comprehension," and that "MAP Reading Fluency is modeled by this more robust approach" of reading a complete passage aloud and answering comprehension questions.
requirements: Audio recording and playback so teachers can rate prosody and consider dialect or pronunciation nuances
passage comprehension items accompanying oral reading passages
constraints: With oral reading, complex comprehension tasks are typically a poor fit since they often require revisiting text; the guide instead raises text complexity to gauge growth
target_learners: Primary-grade students still building passage comprehension skills
target_learning_goals: oral reading fluency
passage comprehension
examples: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency scores SWCPM, decoding accuracy, and passage comprehension automatically, with prosody rated by teachers via audio playback
key_sources: NWEA. (2025). Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Content Guide. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-reading-fluency-content-guide/

article_title: Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are
citation: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Four dimensions for reaching all learners: level, pacing, voice and choice, and supports
description: The paper organizes personalized learning practice around four dimensions that address learner variability. Level means adjusting tasks to the most productive difficulty, drawing on game-design calibration; pacing means mastery-based progression; voice and choice means extended experiences where students select or modify topics and products; supports means tailoring academic, college and career planning, and family supports. As the paper states, "Four dimensions that address learner variability are discussed below: Level Pacing Voice and Choice Supports."
requirements: Requires teachers and tools able to differentiate tasks, assess mastery frequently, and offer structured choices
constraints: The paper describes these dimensions as design commitments for personalized environments, not as tested interventions
target_learners: K-12 students in diverse classrooms, including learners with disabilities, English language learners, and gifted learners
target_learning_goals: Mastering content and skills at productive levels of challenge; developing learner agency and ownership
examples: Adaptive systems such as DreamBox, i-Ready, Istation, and A2I calibrate work automatically; Challenge Based Learning connects student projects to real-world challenges; advisory systems provide a sustained adult relationship at the secondary level
key_sources: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
grain_size: lesson/unit-level organization of personalized learning environments

article_title: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning
citation: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Four categories of factors influencing learner variability
description: The article organizes research on learner variability into four categories of factors: content area skills, social and emotional skills, cognitive skills, and background, environment, and experiences. It stresses that "while each of these categories individually affects learning, no single factor acts independently" and that understanding how the factors combine is critical. The pattern frames Learner Models and personalization decisions: a struggling decoder, for example, must also be understood through working memory. It calls for continued research on combinations of factors.
requirements: Research must continue into how these factors affect learning in various combinations
constraints: Current research is described as insufficient on how factors interact; no single factor acts independently
target_learners: All K-12 learners, given the growing diversity of U.S. classrooms
target_learning_goals: Improving the accuracy and precision of personalization across academic, cognitive, and social-emotional domains
examples: The article illustrates the pattern with decoding supported by multisensory strategies when working memory is low
key_sources: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity
citation: Angevine, C., Cator, K., Liberman, B., Smith, K., & Young, V. (2019). Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Four cross-cutting practices keep equity at the center of the R&D process at all times
description: The framework holds that engagement, capacity building, reflection, and recognition must run through every stage of the innovation process. Engagement builds trusting, mutually beneficial relationships with each stakeholder group; capacity building treats community members as true co-experts whose lived experience is honored; reflection uses recurring facilitated mutuality checks; and recognition sustains energy and broadens participation. The paper states these four cross-cutting practices keep equity at the center of the process at all times.
requirements: Recurring facilitated mutuality checks so that the assets, expertise, and needs of marginalized communities do not get exploited or re-marginalized
Resources, training, and mentorships to develop community members' capacity to lead and engage in education R&D
target_learners: Community members, practitioners, researchers, and developers collaborating on education R&D
target_learning_goals: Sustaining equitable partnerships and continuous improvement across all stages of innovation
examples: Reflection is operationalized as regular check-ins supporting shared meaning-making, alignment to project goals, and continuous improvement
key_sources: Angevine, C., Cator, K., Liberman, B., Smith, K., & Young, V. (2019). Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/d6db3e76-2dc9-4ea6-ae68-49814c88e6b6

article_title: Rubrics for Examining Historical Thinking Skills in High School World History Activities and Student Work
citation: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E., Means, B., & Seylar, J. (2023). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work. Digital Promise. (Original work published 2021). https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/111
title: Four-level developmental scale from absence to rigorous presence for scoring historical thinking
description: Each rubric dimension uses a common four-level structure: generally 0 indicates the absence of a historical thinking practice in the activity or student work, 1 indicates emergence, 2 indicates presence, and 3 indicates rigorous presence. Level 1 typically captures selecting, listing, or stating; Level 2 brief explanation or analysis; Level 3 extended explanation or analysis. This grain-size makes the rubrics usable to profile opportunities and performance across assignments.
requirements: Scorers judge the complexity rather than length of arguments in student work; in assignments, formative vs. summative purpose, expected evidence, and expected time or length help determine whether a brief or extended response is called for.
constraints: Almost every dimension calls for an extended argument to be scored at the highest level.
target_learning_goals: historical thinking skills
examples: A1 Level 3 requires an extended explanation of a claim, reason, or evaluation, such as integrating evidence from multiple sources and addressing counterarguments.
key_sources: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E., Means, B., & Seylar, J. (2023). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work. Digital Promise. (Original work published 2021). https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/111

article_title: Funding Coaching is Not Enough: The Role of the District Administrator in Coaching
citation: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Foster a non-evaluative culture of coaching in which coaching is framed as continuous improvement, not evaluation
description: The report recommends that districts build a coaching culture in which teachers understand that reflection, practice, and feedback opportunities exist "without any evaluative purpose." Suggested actions include consistently communicating that coaching is for continuous improvement rather than evaluation, recognizing participating teachers, and celebrating bright spots and sharing teacher testimonials.
requirements: Districts must consistently communicate that the purpose of coaching is continuous improvement, not evaluation
Leaders must be willing to model vulnerability and take personal responsibility for shortcomings
target_learning_goals: teacher participation in coaching
continuous improvement of teaching practice
examples: One district hosted monthly breakfasts on each campus where all teachers who had been coached during the year shared ideas and strategies, which the report says removed misconceptions that coaching was punitive or only for novice teachers.
key_sources: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/89f20796-22b4-44c1-889c-cc2fd46a19a2

article_title: Integrating Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/
title: Four learning mindsets—belonging, success expectancy, growth mindset, and value—support academic behaviors and persistence
description: The guide identifies four student mindsets that underpin academic behavior, persistence, and performance, expressed from the student's point of view: "I belong in this learning community," "I can succeed at this," "My ability and competence grow with my effort (also known as a 'growth mindset')," and "This work has value for me." These mindsets are presented as the motivational foundation schools should cultivate through relationships, purposeful learning, and student agency. The guide ties them to the claim that learning is a social process requiring connection to peers, teachers, and adults.
requirements: Students need to feel connected to and supported by peers, teachers, and other adults in the building
target_learning_goals: Academic behaviors, persistence, and performance on academic tasks
examples: Teachers foster purpose by connecting discussions to issues students care about and selecting texts reflecting students' identities, cultures, and interests
key_sources: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Four-stage data strategy cycle — understand, collect, transform, socialize — carried by a data strategist working with a team leader
description: This pattern describes how school-based data work is organized in NCS partner high schools. A data strategist moves through four stages: understand (know the research, the data systems, and which teams need what data), collect (find and download the needed data), transform (clean, merge, and build graphs, rosters, tables, and reports that spur teams to action), and socialize (bring data to teams, plan meetings, and help individuals understand what the data means). The paper stresses that generating the data and driving the conversation are two sides of the same coin, requiring a skilled data strategist and a team leader who collaboratively brings data to life in team meetings. Figure 3 applies the same four stages to attendance data, from reviewing attendance research to supporting the Care Team's follow-up with chronically absent students.
requirements: A data strategist with analytic skills and fluency in data analysis applications, and a team leader skilled in facilitating data-driven discussions
Data strategists benefit from district-provided professional development on school-facing data systems and from professional learning communities for sharing tools
constraints: The paper notes the strategist role varies across contexts and is more often played by an educator already on a team than a stand-alone position
target_learning_goals: analyzing student outcome data to guide practice
planning productive data conversations that lead to action
examples: Figure 3 applies the stages to attendance data: downloading period-level attendance files, merging variables into one spreadsheet, building an attendance-by-on-track graph for the Freshman Success Team, and creating a roster of chronically absent students for the Care Team
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Design data systems for practice: streamline data, keep displays simple, consolidate systems, and separate improvement data from accountability reporting
description: The paper gives data system designers four guidelines for focusing and aligning data systems while avoiding common mistakes. First, streamline the amount of data, asking what questions practitioners must answer and providing only the data needed, since educators drown in data when everything is included. Second, show data in ways that are easy to understand — users on the ground prefer something clean and simple, and basic stacked bar and line graphs are often best. Third, consolidate data into one system, because disconnected interfaces force front-line users to integrate data themselves and signal that improvement work is unrelated. Fourth, design data systems for practice, not accountability reporting, since compliance-driven collection creates fatigue and mistrust and often gives educators no mechanism to review the data for their own inquiry.
requirements: Placing the most important practitioner questions at the top of any data set or display
Building data infrastructure that connects data points and products across systems
Clear evidence that a new display format's benefits outweigh the learning curve for practitioners
constraints: The paper notes schools still require flexibility in day-to-day data monitoring to meet immediate practice needs, with simplicity reserved for big-picture views
target_learners: school-based educators who use district data systems
target_learning_goals: quickly answering priority questions about student outcomes
moving efficiently from data display to improvement conversation
examples: Figure 6's To&Through graph illustrates the guidelines: it opens with a framing question, uses a simple stacked line graph, disaggregates by moderately qualified graduates, and integrates high school and college data from different sources
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: College Readiness for All
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://www.futureofchildren.org
title: Four-pillar framework of college readiness skills
description: Drawing particularly on David Conley's work, the article defines college readiness through "four main areas of skill development that are critical in shaping college readiness: content knowledge and basic skills, core academic skills, non-cognitive skills and norms of performance, and 'college knowledge.'" Content knowledge is subject-specific; core academic skills such as writing and analytic thinking transfer across disciplines and are the areas where high school-college skill demands differ most; non-cognitive skills cover self-monitoring behaviors like study skills and time management; and college knowledge is the social-capital-based capacity to navigate admissions and financial aid. The article argues high schools must stress all four.
requirements: High schools must attend to all four skill areas rather than only the two commonly recognized ones
Schools must be explicit about which skills shape college access and how to measure them
constraints: The framework is developed for improving college access and readiness for low-income and minority students in urban high schools
target_learners: High school students, particularly low-income and minority students in urban high schools
target_learning_goals: College readiness across content knowledge, core academic skills, non-cognitive skills, and college knowledge
examples: The article distinguishes core academic skills from content knowledge using the American Diploma Project's English standards, which include writing, research, oral communication, and analytic thinking
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-readiness-all-challenge-urban-high-schools

article_title: The Essential Playbook for Family Engagement in Middle School
citation: Wallace, M., & Paredes, M. (2024). The essential playbook for family engagement in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Four-element framework for family engagement: Capacity, Process, Infrastructure, and Outcomes
description: The playbook organizes family engagement improvement around four interrelated elements. Capacity "develop[s] skills, confidence, and disposition for authentic home and school partnerships" through professional learning; Process covers selecting and implementing evidence-based practices; Infrastructure allocates time, resources, staff, and policies; Outcomes monitor, evaluate, and report progress. The elements form "a dynamic cycle of continuous improvement" and are presented through illustrative tables populated from needs-assessment findings.
requirements: A needs assessment identifies key areas requiring focused attention and resources before strategies are selected
constraints: The framework is developed for the middle school context and school and district leaders implementing family engagement plans
target_learners: middle school students and their families
target_learning_goals: strengthening school-family partnerships to support student attendance, social-emotional development, and academic outcomes
examples: Illustrative Tables 1-4 populate all four elements for one scenario: families feeling uninformed and disconnected, using professional development, phone scripts, tracking systems, and surveys
key_sources: Wallace, M., & Paredes, M. (2024). The essential playbook for family engagement in middle school. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED663740

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: A four-routine instructional sequence—explicit instruction, modeling, practice opportunities, and feedback—builds student capacity to self-assess
description: The brief describes a series of intentional instructional routines for building student capacity to self-assess. Explicit instruction provides clear, direct guidance as an early-stage strategy; modeling demonstrates self-assessment, including think-alouds and examples of both exemplary and less optimal practices; structured low-stakes practice opportunities allow improvement with regular and repeated practice; and feedback, such as probing questions, supports students reviewing work against success criteria and setting goals.
requirements: Teachers and students benefit from keeping a growth mindset, understanding that they are emergent learners who will improve with regular and repeated practice in low-stakes settings.
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment against success criteria and goal setting
examples: Models can come from other sources, for example, videos of other students using success criteria in their self-assessment.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Formative assessment as a planned ongoing process and feedback loop
description: The brief defines formative assessment as "a planned ongoing process of inquiry that teachers and students participate in together to understand the current status of learning". It is not a set of stand-alone tools but a sensemaking process of noticing and responding to what students say, do, make, or write. The feedback loop (Figure 1) includes setting learning goals and success criteria, planning evidence-embedding experiences, attending to and making sense of evidence, and responding to advance learning.
requirements: A collaborative and respectful classroom environment embedding clarifying goals, eliciting evidence, self-assessment and peer feedback, actionable feedback, and using evidence to move learning forward
constraints: It is not a set of stand-alone tools, strategies, or tests
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning and improved understanding of disciplinary learning outcomes
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673605

article_title: Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons from Innovative State Approaches under ESSA
citation: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper.
title: Four Key Tensions in Implementing Innovative Accountability Approaches
description: From case-study interviews and document review, the paper distills four tensions states navigate when implementing innovative accountability approaches: general versus targeted use of the system; accessible versus complex information; normative versus criterion-based approaches; and statewide requirements versus local flexibilities. The authors state, "Based on our interviews and document review conducted in the case studies, we distilled four key tensions as states attempted to implement innovative accountability approaches." Tensions operate across all levels of the hierarchy and manifest differently at each level.
requirements: Addressing these tensions in meaningful ways moves a system closer to improving integration within the education ecosystem
constraints: The tensions were distilled within the context of the four examined cases; a lack of clarity around these points can create additional challenges in achieving system goals
target_learning_goals: designing and refining statewide accountability systems that support school improvement
examples: Utah's bottom-25-percent indicator is presented as a normative approach example; proficiency measures as the most common criterion-based form; summative school ratings as an accessibility-versus-complexity example
key_sources: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677595

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments: Evaluation Final Report
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Four-step formative assessment cycle: create assignments, assist students through immediate feedback, assess class performance, analyze answers together
description: The report organizes the intervention around a "4-step formative assessment process (Heritage & Popham, 2013) that is integrated throughout the ASSISTments platform": (1) create assignments aligned with grade-level standards using OERs or Skill Builders; (2) assist students through immediate feedback, hints, and explanations; (3) assess class performance by reviewing reports to identify needs; and (4) analyze answers together by projecting anonymized reports for whole-class discussion of misconceptions. The vPLC embedded this cycle across its session content.
requirements: Teachers must review performance reports to identify student needs and inform future instruction, and project anonymized reports for whole-class review.
constraints: The cycle's ultimate goal, as stated, is to improve student math achievement; sessions 2 through 6 each highlighted different report features to build teachers' instructional toolkit over time.
target_learners: Middle school math teachers and their grade 6-8 students
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment practice and improved student math achievement
examples: Session 7 focused on the fourth step, analyzing answers together, including strategically sequencing and sharing student work leveraging ASSISTments open responses.
key_sources: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677852

article_title: Free to Fail or On-Track to College
citation: Stevens, W. D., Allensworth, E. M., Pareja, A. S., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J. A., Rosenkranz, T., & Sebastian, J. (2014). Free to Fail or On-Track to College: An Introduction to the UChicago CCSR Research Series. UChicago CCSR Research Brief. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Focus on Freshmen Study
description: The Focus on Freshmen Study is a UChicago CCSR research project examining the transition to high school and the school practices that contribute to ninth-grade performance. It followed a cohort "as they moved from eighth grade in spring 2008, through the ninth grade year (2008-09) and into tenth grade in 2009-10," including about 22,000 students. It combined district-wide records, student and teacher surveys, longitudinal in-depth interviews of 55 students and their teachers, and classroom observations in English and math.
requirements: District-wide student records, student and teacher surveys, longitudinal interviews, and classroom observations in eighth and ninth grade
target_learners: Ninth-grade high school students in Chicago Public Schools
target_learning_goals: Student engagement in coursework, course performance, and graduation readiness
examples: The study examined how teacher support, classroom instruction, and school practices lead students to be engaged in their work and earn good grades
key_sources: Stevens, W. D., Allensworth, E. M., Pareja, A. S., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J. A., Rosenkranz, T., & Sebastian, J. (2014). Free to Fail or On-Track to College: An Introduction to the UChicago CCSR Research Series. UChicago CCSR Research Brief. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/free-fail-or-track-college

article_title: Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego
citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: Four CAC-developed STEM pathway solution concepts (Inspire to Aspire, CIELO, ATGC, STEM SD Partner Exchange)
description: In the Design & Develop phase, advisors "voted to select four solution concepts and self-selected into subgroups based on their interest areas and expertise". Table 1 presents the concepts: Inspire to Aspire (career-connected professional learning for preschool–elementary educators to build student math and science confidence), CIELO (after-school STEM programs co-developed with families facing housing insecurity), ALL TOGETHER Get Connected (a place-based South Bay pilot spanning middle school STEM identity, high school career exploration, and paid college internships), and STEM SD Partner Exchange (an online repository of inclusive STEM pathway partners and resources).
requirements: Subgroup work guided by the Innovating a Solution: A Design-to-Action Plan, including generating ideas and identifying existing community resources
constraints: Concepts were developed in early 2025 and had not yet been tested; members will move to testing throughout the year
target_learners: Preschool through elementary students, middle and high school students, college students, families facing housing insecurity, and homeless and foster youth in the San Diego region
target_learning_goals: STEM interest, confidence, identity, career exploration, college exposure, and credit transfer toward STEM careers
examples: ATGC will pilot in South Bay leveraging Southwestern College innovations, combining expanded and work-based learning, early college credit, alternative assessments, and transfer pathways
key_sources: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254

article_title: Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity
citation: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185
title: Four showcased LER technologies introduced via onboarding videos
description: The study introduced participant-advisors to four LER technologies: "Teacher Wallet (RANDA Solutions), MilGears (SOLID Inc), LearnCard (LEF), and Career Wallet (Velocity Network)." Each technology partner delivered a 30-45-minute product walk-through to the research team and created a five-minute introductory onboarding video shown during the first co-design workshop, so learners and workers unfamiliar with digital and verifiable credentials could react to the designs and practical functionality for people experiencing transitions. These reflections fed the perceived challenges, opportunities, and wishlist findings.
requirements: Introductory videos were needed because many participants had never heard of digital and verifiable credentials, LER, or digital wallet technologies
constraints: Participants reflected on showcased technologies via video rather than hands-on use
target_learners: HSE adult learners and workers with varying digital fluency and LER awareness
target_learning_goals: understanding and evaluating LER technologies for transition support
examples: Workshop groups responded to each video by discussing promotive or inhibitory factors of each LER design for individuals experiencing transitions
key_sources: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185

article_title: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies
citation: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://forourbabies.org/wp/
title: For Our Babies platform of supports organized around four pillars tracking development from pre-conception to age three
description: The For Our Babies campaign outlines a comprehensive platform of services and supports for infants, toddlers, and their families. The article states it is "focused around four pillars that track babies' developmental trajectory from pre-conception to age three: prenatal care, paid leave; screening and follow-up services and well-baby care; and high-quality, affordable infant/toddler care." The initiative combines a book, multimedia website, public events, and outreach to families, educators, the press, and policymakers to spur local action and national policy change.
requirements: Supports must span the full developmental trajectory from pre-conception through age three, addressing prenatal care, paid leave, screening and well-baby care, and infant/toddler care together
constraints: The article presents this platform as an advocacy position for the U.S. context, not as an evaluated intervention
target_learners: infants and toddlers from conception to age three
target_learning_goals: healthy early development supporting later success in school and life
examples: The campaign includes Lally's book For Our Babies: Ending the Invisible Neglect of America's Infants, a multimedia website, virtual and in-person public events, and strategic outreach
key_sources: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://forourbabies.org/wp/

article_title: Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options
citation: Linquanti, R., & Cook, H. G. (2013). Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options. Council of Chief State School Officers. http://www.ccsso.org
title: Four-stage framework for a common English learner definition: identify, classify, establish an English-proficient standard, and reclassify
description: The paper organizes the entire EL definitional process around four stages adapted from a National Research Council panel report: "1) identify a student as a potential English learner; 2) classify (confirm/disconfirm) a student as an English learner; 3) establish an 'English-language proficient' performance standard on the state/consortium English language proficiency (ELP) test"; and 4) reclassify to former-EL status through multiple exit criteria. The framework is intended to help consortium member states "systematically review and document existing practices" and align instruments, policies, and practices within states, across states within a consortium, and across consortia.
requirements: Consortium member states must explicitly define their approaches to the four key steps and establish mechanisms to move toward sufficient convergence or alignment over time
constraints: The framework is adapted from an NRC (2011) panel report on comparability of state procedures for identifying, classifying, and reclassifying English learners
Fulfilling the common definition requirement is described as presenting substantial challenges requiring a carefully coordinated, multiyear effort proceeding in stages
target_learners: K-12 students potentially or actually classified as English learners
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency sufficient to access academic content instruction and participate fully in society
examples: Figure 2 presents the framework graphically, adapted from NRC 2011, p. 78
key_sources: Linquanti, R., & Cook, H. G. (2013). Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565753

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Four-domain framework for leading NGSS implementation
description: The Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation answers the question of what leaders need to know and be able to do to lead NGSS implementation. It comprises four domains: Leadership Knowledge (six knowledge areas), Critical Actions (eleven actions), Impacting NGSS Teaching and Learning (classroom interactions among teachers, NGSS, and students surrounded by six system drivers), and Sustaining Implementation of NGSS. The article states it "provides a vision of the four major domains that leaders focus on as they lead the implementation of the NGSS." Domains interact through a continuous improvement cycle connecting leaders' actions to classroom impact.
requirements: Leaders must develop and use new knowledge unique to the NGSS; the framework assumes possessing this leadership knowledge is necessary for carrying out the critical actions.
constraints: Developed for NGSS or closely aligned state science standards implementation in K-12 systems in the United States.
target_learners: Science education leaders at state, district, regional, school, and teacher-leader levels
target_learning_goals: Leading standards implementation
Planning and sustaining NGSS-aligned science education reform
examples: Used as a self-assessment for leaders to identify knowledge gaps and as a planning guide for critical actions.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Formative Assessment and Agency as Drivers of Instructional Transformation
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum brief: Formative assessment and agency as drivers of instructional transformation. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: Formative assessment feedback loop (Heritage & Gerzon, 2015)
description: Figure 1 of the brief reproduces the formative assessment feedback loop (Source: Heritage & Gerzon, 2015), which became "the central core of instructional practice" in Sunnyside School District. The loop is organized around three questions — Where am I going? Where am I now? Where to next? — and includes steps: determine learning goals, develop success criteria, elicit evidence of learning, interpret evidence, take responsive action, close the gap, and create building blocks.
requirements: Teachers eliciting student thinking rather than only checking for understanding, within a districtwide coherent focus on the instructional core
target_learning_goals: Eliciting and using evidence of learning to close gaps toward disciplinary learning outcomes and support self-directed learners
examples: Sunnyside made the feedback loop the central core of instructional practice, with constant messaging, principal meetings, walk-throughs, real-time coaching, and WestEd-sponsored teacher courses
key_sources: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum brief: Formative assessment and agency as drivers of instructional transformation. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED592990

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Formative Assessment and Agency as Drivers of Instructional Transformation
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum brief: Formative assessment and agency as drivers of instructional transformation. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: Formative assessment as a planned, ongoing process making student learning visible
description: The brief adopts the FAST SCASS (2018) definition: formative assessment is "a planned, ongoing process used by teachers and students during learning to elicit and use evidence to improve student understanding of disciplinary learning outcomes and support students in becoming self-directed learners." It draws a parallel to adult professional learning: formative assessment makes student learning visible in collaborative settings through self-reflection, structured and rigorous dialogue, and formative peer feedback, mirroring the high-effect-size features of teacher learning (discussion, feedback, self-assessment, reflection).
requirements: Planned, ongoing use during learning; eliciting and using evidence of learning; opportunities for student self-reflection, dialogue, and peer feedback
target_learning_goals: Improving student understanding of disciplinary learning outcomes
Developing self-directed learners
examples: ADE and Sunnyside used this shared definition as the foundation of statewide and districtwide implementation, with constant and consistent messaging around the definition and expectations for formative assessment
key_sources: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum brief: Formative assessment and agency as drivers of instructional transformation. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED592990

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Formative assessment as shared use of evidence of student learning to guide ongoing teaching and learning
description: The brief defines formative assessment as "the educational approach of engendering learning by having teacher and students alike assess students' current knowledge and understanding — based on what students say, do, make, or write — and then use that evidence to guide ongoing teaching and learning efforts." It repositions students as active agents who set goals, create self-oriented feedback loops, and adapt strategies, and notes teachers shift from "delivering" a subject to facilitating learning. Classroom culture changes are described as required for implementation.
requirements: Teachers and students share responsibility for learning; evidence of learning is used as a foundational practice
constraints: Requires changes in classroom culture and in traditional teacher and student roles
target_learning_goals: students learning how to learn; teachers using evidence of learning to guide instruction
examples: Teachers practicing formative assessment listen, observe, question, and review student work to determine what each student needs to move forward
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies
citation: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Focus organizational review on the system rather than individuals to create psychological safety for honest inquiry
description: Because looking inward can be challenging and staff may fear being singled out, R15CC emphasizes that the Systems Review is about analyzing the complete system and the results it produces. The report states that "the emphasis on the system, rather than anyone within it, contributes to a climate of safety, enabling teams to engage in honest and sometimes difficult conversations that build towards shared goals and improved results." This principle underpins the working agreements and the entire review stance.
requirements: Significant upfront time and recurring touchpoints reinforcing the systems framing with SEA teams
target_learners: SEA division and department staff undergoing a Systems Review
target_learning_goals: Honest engagement in systems analysis and shared goal-setting for improvement
examples: R15CC spends significant time at the beginning of the process, and as a touchpoint throughout, emphasizing the system-level focus
key_sources: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628329

article_title: Moving toward Instructional Coherence: How Four Popular Student-Centered Approaches Deepen Identity, Agency, Equity, and Community
citation: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Formative assessment as eliciting, interpreting, and using evidence of learning during learning to build metacognition and self-regulation
description: The paper defines formative assessment using Bell and Cowie's definition as 'the process used by teachers and students to notice, recognize, and respond to student learning in order to enhance that learning, during the learning.' It prioritizes learning how to learn and metacognition: teachers explicitly teach students to elicit, interpret, and use evidence of learning during instruction, gradually shifting power to students who learn to self-monitor independently and with peers. Daily routines such as student discourse, peer feedback, and self-assessment, supported by shared success criteria, are the operational core.
requirements: Teachers explicitly teach daily routines and practices such as student discourse, peer feedback, and self-assessment
Teachers and students share a conception of what learning will look like through the use of success criteria
constraints: Requires teachers to move away from a traditional teacher-directed instructional model
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Metacognition
self-regulation of learning
use of evidence of learning to guide next steps
examples: Students can say 'This is where I am in my learning, this is how I know, and these are next steps I can take' as evidence of self-regulation
key_sources: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655925

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: Choose accountability indicators using four questions: actionability, intended use, reliability, and differentiation
description: The report offers four questions for policymakers choosing an indicator: what the indicator measures and whether data are actionable; for what use the measure was designed and how data might be distorted by high stakes; whether the measure generates consistent, reliable data; and whether it meaningfully differentiates between schools and subgroups. It invokes Campbell's law, noting the more a measure is used for decisions with negative consequences, the more likely it is to be misunderstood or distorted.
requirements: An indicator should have strong construct validity, and schools should be held accountable for outcomes they can reasonably affect
constraints: Surveys designed for one-on-one settings may not produce valid data when administered en masse; indicators lacking sufficient variability may be publicly reported but not used to rank schools
target_learning_goals: sound indicator selection for accountability and continuous improvement systems
examples: The report notes students used to greater supports may be more critical of a condition, rendering comparable ratings objectively unequal
key_sources: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability

article_title: Educating the Whole Child: Improving School Climate to Support Student Success
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child
title: Four-domain framework for whole child education
description: The report organizes its school implications around four major domains that research suggests schools should attend to: supportive environmental conditions, social and emotional learning, productive instructional strategies, and individualized supports. The framework states that "research suggests that schools should attend to four major domains," each elaborated with concrete practices: positive school climate and strong relationships; explicit SEL instruction, infusion, and restorative approaches; meaningful, inquiry-based, collaborative, mastery-oriented instruction with metacognitive opportunities; and integrated services, extended learning, and multi-tiered systems of support. It functions as the report's central explanatory structure linking the science of learning and development to school design.
requirements: Accomplishing the work requires an intensive focus on adult development and support so educators can design for and enact the practices
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Social and emotional skills
Healthy development
examples: The report elaborates each domain with practices such as looping, advisory systems, explicit SEL instruction, performance assessments, and multi-tiered systems of academic, health, and social supports.
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child

article_title: Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity through the Every Student Succeeds Act
citation: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa
title: Four Pillars of Opportunity framework for leveraging ESSA toward equity
description: The report organizes its analysis of ESSA around four pillars of opportunity: "(1) access to learning opportunities focused on higher-order thinking skills; (2) multiple measures of equity; (3) resource equity; and (4) evidence-based interventions." The framework is presented as a bridge from an inequitable "factory model" of schooling relying on rote thinking and memorization toward a 21st-century model offering deeper learning. Each pillar is treated in a dedicated section with policy provisions and state and district examples.
requirements: Thoughtful regulation and implementation of ESSA provisions by federal, state, district, and school actors
constraints: The report notes concerns that ESSA's emphasis on state control of accountability systems may lead states to overlook the needs of low-performing schools
target_learners: students who are homeless or in foster care
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking skills
deeper learning
equitable access to college- and career-ready curriculum
examples: Figure 1 depicts the four pillars bridging the factory model to a 21st-century model of education
key_sources: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Four models for integrating performance assessment into state systems
description: The paper organizes state performance assessment options into four models: "Performance items or tasks as part of traditional 'sit-down' tests", curriculum-embedded tasks implemented during the school year, "Portfolios or collections of evidence that aggregate multiple tasks", and comprehensive assessment systems combining all of these, "each serving distinctive complementary purposes". The models "can also be combined in various ways" and all "have been used successfully at scale in states and nations around the world". The paper describes design, implementation, and scoring for each.
requirements: States must manage task selection and scoring to assure validity, reliability, and comparability
constraints: Under ESSA, states must assess students annually in ELA and math in grades 3-8 and once in high school, and at least once in each grade span in science
target_learners: K-12 students in state assessment systems
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking skills and understanding
application of knowledge to complex problems
examples: New York Regents tests, GCSE through-course assessments, New Hampshire's comprehensive system, and the Performance Assessment Resource Bank
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Improving Education the New Mexico Way: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Oakes, J., Espinoza, D., Darling-Hammond, L., Gonzales, C., DePaoli, J., Kini, T., Hoachlander, G., Burns, D., Griffith, M., & Leung, M. (2020). Improving education the New Mexico way: An evidence-based approach. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way
title: Four domains central to meaningful learning goals
description: The report defines meaningful 21st century learning goals through four domains: "Both research and local knowledge suggest four specific domains that are central to meaningful learning" — high-level cognitive skills in core academic disciplines; culturally and linguistically responsive curriculum and instruction; social and emotional learning developing self-regulation, collaboration, problem-solving, conflict resolution, perseverance, and resilience; and pathways integrating college and career preparation. It recommends a whole-child approach that improves academic opportunities, affirms cultural and linguistic identities, supports well-being, and redesigns high schools through integrated pathways.
requirements: Adequate attention and funding for cultural and linguistic diversity statutes, which the report says have had inadequate attention and funding
constraints: The report finds New Mexico has not adequately pursued social and emotional learning and trauma-informed practices despite high rates of adverse childhood experiences
target_learners: K-12 students in New Mexico, including English learners and Native American students
target_learning_goals: Higher-order thinking and deeper learning in the disciplines, culturally and linguistically responsive learning, social and emotional competencies, and college and career readiness
key_sources: Oakes, J., Espinoza, D., Darling-Hammond, L., Gonzales, C., DePaoli, J., Kini, T., Hoachlander, G., Burns, D., Griffith, M., & Leung, M. (2020). Improving education the New Mexico way: An evidence-based approach. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way

article_title: Engaging First: Supporting Young Learners through Family Engagement
citation: Morgan, I., Gillispie, C., & Waller, A. (2024). Supporting Young Learners Through Family Engagement: Engaging First. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Four facets of meaningful and effective family engagement
description: The report organizes its analysis of effective family engagement around four facets: "communication; shared decision-making; connections, trust, and mutual respect; and cultural inclusiveness." It holds that authentic engagement is a collaboration that "involves shared decision-making, trust, mutual respect, and should be asset based and culturally responsive," and that engagement strategies mainly bringing parents into the school building tend to be less effective than programs linking families to children's learning at home. The report uses these facets to structure its survey findings and recommendations.
requirements: Schools must build relationships and share decision-making, particularly with families from groups marginalized by the education system
constraints: One-off activities such as open houses, conferences, volunteering, and chaperoning are not sufficient to improve outcomes and may conflict with work schedules or pose logistical hurdles
target_learners: families and schools of first and second grade students
target_learning_goals: meaningful family engagement that supports student learning and well-being
examples: The report's Findings section is structured by these facets: communication, shared decision-making, connections with parents and school staff, and cultural inclusiveness
key_sources: Morgan, I., Gillispie, C., & Waller, A. (2024). Supporting Young Learners Through Family Engagement: Engaging First. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658182

article_title: Keeping Schools Safe? The Research on Behavioral Threat Assessments
citation: DePaoli, J. L., & Loewe, S. B. (2025). Keeping schools safe? The research on behavioral threat assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/808.437
title: Four major school-based behavioral threat assessment models (FBI, NTAC, CSTAG, Salem-Keizer)
description: The report organizes school-based behavioral threat assessment into four major models that states adopt or reference in legislation and policy: "federal models from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and from the National Threat Assessment Center (NTAC), the Comprehensive School Threat Assessment Guidelines (CSTAG) model, and the Salem-Keizer model." All models define serious threats, establish multidisciplinary teams, guide threat handling, and require team training. The FBI model uses threat categorization and a four-pronged assessment; NTAC provides site-level guidance with an eight-step process; CSTAG uses a five-step decision tree distinguishing transient from substantive threats; Salem-Keizer begins with screening questions and can extend to a communitywide team.
requirements: Each model identifies appropriate threat assessment training as a key component of high-quality implementation, including training for all adults, students, and parents on the reporting and assessment process
constraints: Many districts and schools adopt BTA practices that do not follow any of these specific models; the Salem-Keizer model has only one published research study on its implementation or outcomes
target_learning_goals: preventing school violence
responding appropriately to student threats of violence
examples: Virginia created its own model policies based on NTAC guidance; Florida adopted CSTAG as its statewide BTA system
key_sources: DePaoli, J. L., & Loewe, S. B. (2025). Keeping schools safe? The research on behavioral threat assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/808.437

article_title: Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System
citation: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/
title: Four cornerstones of a fair and effective school funding system: adequacy, equity, transparency, and responsibility
description: Developed by EdBuild and summarized in this report, the framework holds that a fair school funding system rests on four cornerstones. "ADEQUACY: The school funding allocated through the state formula should be sufficient to support a rigorous, high-quality education program for all students." EQUITY requires targeting funds to districts according to students' greater needs; TRANSPARENCY requires spending reporting that creates a feedback loop between state decisions and district needs; RESPONSIBILITY treats district and school leaders as accountable, flexible decision-makers. The report uses the framework to evaluate Michigan's system and propose reforms.
requirements: Expenditure reporting is required for general per-pupil funding and for every student need category so spending reflects state intentions and reaches intended students.
constraints: The report presents these as policy cornerstones based on EdBuild national research and lessons from strong funding systems, not as empirically tested interventions.
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly low-income students, English Learners, students with disabilities, and students in high-poverty and rural districts
target_learning_goals: Ensuring sufficient and equitably distributed educational resources so all students can achieve at high levels and access post-secondary opportunity
examples: The report evaluates Michigan against each cornerstone, finding regressive district funding, very low equity weights, weak fiscal transparency, and inadequate accountability for equity-targeted dollars.
key_sources: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/

article_title: Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators
citation: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Typology of four assessment types: statewide summative, diagnostic, formative, and interim
description: The report's sidebar defines the four assessment types schools use. Statewide summative assessments are year-end tests administered to all students across a state, and "provide insights on the extent to which students have mastered grade-level content that is aligned to state college and career readiness academic standards." Diagnostic assessments are administered near the beginning of the year to identify skills, strengths, and weaknesses; formative assessments are classroom-based checks such as exit tickets, quizzes, and unit tests; interim assessments are administered a few times per year to track progress toward grade-level mastery and monitor interventions. The report argues the four types should ideally form a coherent, aligned picture of student achievement.
requirements: Each assessment should be aligned with a high-quality curriculum and state standards, and stakeholders empowered to use each for its intended purpose
constraints: The report notes different assessments are not always aligned with one another, state standards, and/or the curriculum
target_learners: K-12 students in grades 3-8 and high school
target_learning_goals: mastery of grade-level content aligned to state college and career readiness standards
examples: Federal law requires math and ELA summative assessments in grades 3-8 and once in high school, and science assessments once in grades 3-5, 6-9, and 10-12

article_title: Strategies and Suggestions for Local Education Agencies Using the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement Framework
citation: The Center for School Turnaround and Improvement. (2025). Strategies and suggestions for local education agencies using the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement framework. WestEd. https://csti.wested.org/

The framework names four domains — Turnaround Leadership, Talent Development, Instructional Transformation, and Culture Shift — each with three practices (12 practices total), and this guide supplies LEA-level strategies, desired future states, and reflection questions for each practice.

target_learning_goals: System-level school improvement planning and turnaround leadership
examples: The guide devotes one chapter to each of the 12 practices, each opening with a practice description and an LEA-based example, then practice items with strategies and reflection questions

article_title: Leading Inclusive, Coherent, and Effective Assessment Systems: Closing Opportunity and Outcome Gaps for Students with Disabilities
citation: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Leaders should foster a culture of inclusion and high expectations for students with disabilities before or alongside technical assessment improvements
description: The brief argues that technical assessment improvements alone will fail without a culture of inclusion and high expectations. Focus group experts recommended three moves: championing inclusion (students with disabilities are "general education students first"), recognizing intersectional student identities, and employing asset-based approaches such as reframing the IEP "from a deficit-repair tool to a learning resource." Leaders set a shared communitywide vision that explicitly includes students with disabilities.

constraints: Technical improvements to assessment practices alone will likely not have a positive impact if low-expectation culture persists

access to general education curriculum
examples: Focus group experts recommended reframing the IEP from a deficit-repair tool to a learning resource, shifting educators' approaches to intervention, instruction, and assessment.

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Four positive classroom conditions framework for engaged math learning
description: The report organizes its findings around four classroom conditions under which, drawing on the science of learning and development and the authors' prior research synthesis, students learn math best: positive relationships with teachers and peers, a strong sense of classroom and mathematics belonging, support in adopting a growth mindset, and opportunities to engage with high-quality instruction. Figure 1 depicts these conditions, together with data access and use and school and district practices, as system factors supporting students' engagement in learning math. The framework holds that these conditions "can occur simultaneously with and reinforce high-quality instruction" and particularly matter for students from historically marginalized groups and during the middle school years.
requirements: System factors—data access and use, and school and district practices—that enable teachers to cultivate the conditions
constraints: Evidence base summarized from neuroscience, psychology, and developmental and learning sciences syntheses; classroom illustrations drawn from 10 case-study teachers
target_learning_goals: engaged math learning
positive math mindsets
reduced math anxiety
examples: The study documents how 10 teachers fostered each condition, e.g., routines such as welcoming students at the door, structuring daily group work, and creating a space of learning without fear of ridicule or shame.
