article_title: Evolution of AI in Education: Agentic Workflows
citation: Kamalov, F., Santandreu Calonge, D., Smail, L., Azizov, D., Thadani, D. R., Kwong, T., Atif, A. (2025). Evolution of AI in Education: Agentic Workflows. https://github.com/AzizovDilshod/Multi-agent-System-for-Essay-Assessment/tree/main
title: Four-paradigm taxonomy of agentic workflows in education: reflection, planning, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration
description: The article proposes a technological taxonomy that categorizes agentic workflows in education into four major design paradigms. As the article states, "Four major paradigms underpin many current agentic approaches" — 1) reflection, where the agent analyzes past actions to refine future behavior; 2) planning, where the agent creates and follows a sequence of steps or sub-goals; 3) tool use, where the agent leverages external resources such as calculators, code execution, web search, and APIs; and 4) multi-agent collaboration, where multiple specialized agents coordinate toward a common goal. The review applies this framework to map technical capabilities onto pedagogical affordances.
requirements: An LLM-based agent layer that orchestrates reasoning, tools, and coordination around a goal
constraints: The paradigms are distinct but often complementary strategies; implementations vary in degree of agenticness
target_learners: educators and instructional designers building agentic tools
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating AI-agent-based educational systems
examples: The review dedicates a subsection of Section 4 to each paradigm, synthesizing educational applications, advantages, and challenges

article_title: Teaching the Way Students Learn Best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School
citation: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale
title: A framework of four principles for whole child education derived from the science of learning and development
description: The report organizes its case around four principles for educational practice drawn from syntheses of neuroscience, cognitive science, and the developmental sciences: (1) environmental conditions supporting positive, trusting relationships, safety, and belonging; (2) intentional development of social, emotional, and cognitive skills, mindsets, and habits, with "supports for behavior should be educative and restorative"; (3) curricular designs and instructional strategies featuring "well-scaffolded instruction and ongoing formative assessment"; and (4) multi-tiered systems of support based on a shared developmental framework. Figure 1 presents these as a Framework for Whole Child Education, and Appendix B maps Bronxdale practices onto the principles.

constraints: The report presents the framework as derived from recently published research syntheses rather than testing it empirically in this case study.
target_learners: K–12 students, especially diverse learners and students experiencing adversity
target_learning_goals: Academic capacity, competence, motivation, metacognitive skills, social-emotional skills, and resilience
examples: The report uses the framework to structure its account of Bronxdale's culture, SEL teaching, instruction, and systems of support, with a mapping table in Appendix B.

article_title: Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, so Why Are University Faculties so White?
citation: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Four-metric faculty equity grading framework (diversity relative to students, hiring equity, tenure equity, change over time)
description: The report develops a four-metric framework for auditing faculty racial equity at individual institutions. Metrics 1-3 produce 0-100 scores converted to letter grades: faculty diversity relative to student diversity, equity in tenure-track versus contingent hiring, and equity in tenure distribution. Metric 4 measures percentage point change in faculty representation between 2005 and 2020. The framework is designed so advocates can "use these metrics and findings to see what's happening at institutions and push for change."

constraints: The diversity metric "does not take their appointment status — i.e., whether they are contingent or tenure track — into account"; IPEDS data limits analysis of other faculty of color groups
target_learning_goals: increasing Black and Latino faculty representation
improving college completion for students of color
examples: Bluefield State College scored 99 (A) on Black faculty diversity because 9.5% of faculty were Black versus 9.6% of students; Ball State scored 105 (A) on Latino hiring equity

article_title: Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human-AI co-regulation in learning
citation: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258
title: Four roles of AI in cognitive regulation: scaffolding, metacognitive support, memory augmentation, and decision assistance
description: The proposed co-regulation model distinguishes four primary roles through which AI participates in cognition. As a scaffold, AI enables performance beyond independent capability; as metacognitive support, it prompts reflection and strategy evaluation; as external memory, it stores and generates content that offloads internal processing; as decision partner, it offers recommendations that shape action. The article states: "The model highlights four primary roles of AI in cognitive regulation: scaffolding, metacognitive support, memory augmentation, and decision assistance."

constraints: The nature and intensity of AI involvement vary across developmental stages, becoming more prominent in later stages where metacognitive capacities are more developed

metacognitive monitoring
memory and reasoning support
decision making
examples: Figure 1 presents the conceptual model showing co-regulated cognition, temporary cognitive performance, and long-term developmental effects

article_title: The AI Adaptation Gap in Higher Education: Students, Faculty, and Administrative Staff
citation: Braun, Y. S., & Khafizov, S. M. (2026). The AI Adaptation Gap in Higher Education: Students, Faculty, and Administrative Staff: AI Use, Trust, and Institutional Policy at a University Specializing in Teacher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25063
title: Four-domain account of university AI adaptation: perceived usefulness, self-reported competence, academic integrity concerns, and institutional policy clarity
description: The study is guided by the premise that "patterns of AI use and trust are associated not with any single variable but with a combination of four domains: perceived usefulness, self-reported competence, academic integrity concerns, and institutional policy clarity". Usefulness is understood as a subjective assessment that AI makes educational or administrative activity more efficient, effective, or convenient; policy clarity is treated as a potential resource for institutional governance; and responsible use entails checking accuracy, understanding model limitations, following local rules, and maintaining reflective control. The framework treats AI as embedded in university assignments, communication, planning, assessment, and administrative processes rather than as a single tool.
requirements: Role-adapted measurement of each domain, since the same AI functions may be evaluated differently by students, faculty, and administrative staff
constraints: The cross-sectional design cannot establish the direction of causal influence; the propositions are interpretations of observed associations, not evidence of a causal pathway
target_learning_goals: understanding and governing AI adoption and responsible use in higher education
examples: Pooled OLS models on N = 1254 estimated associations of the four domains with trust and current AI-use intensity

article_title: A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion
citation: Reed Orchinik, David Rand. (2026). A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16432
title: Inform users of AI's persuasive potential before AI conversations to confer targeted protection without general distrust
description: Because recognizing a counter-party's persuasive intent creates resistance (the article's persuasion knowledge theory motivation), designers should present a brief warning that LLMs can be prompted to persuade and may present information selectively before users converse with AI on contested topics. The article's evidence shows this roughly halves persuasion while leaving general trust in generative AI intact, suggesting protection is targeted rather than blanket skepticism.
requirements: The warning must be shown before or at the start of the AI conversation; wording must convey that models can be prompted to persuade or manipulate
constraints: Does not entirely eliminate AI's persuasive effects; tested on political attitude topics, and the authors state effectiveness may differ for factual beliefs such as conspiracy theories
target_learners: Adult users of conversational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Resistance to manipulative AI persuasion while preserving the benefit of accurate AI
examples: Two experiments randomized U.S. participants to warning or no-warning control before conversations with GPT-4.1 (Study 1) or Grok 4.5 (Study 2) instructed to shift their political views

article_title: Evidence of a Cognitive Shift in AI Education: How Students Are Rethinking Human Intelligence?
citation: Islem Rekik. (2026). Evidence of a Cognitive Shift in AI Education: How Students Are Rethinking Human Intelligence? Published as a conference paper at ICLR HCAIR Workshop 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16292
title: Four hypothesized phases of student perception of intelligence: Hype, Distrust, Trust, and Dependency
description: The article proposes four conceptual lenses for organizing how students' valuation of human versus artificial intelligence shifts as experience with AI deepens: Hype (HI < AI), Distrust (HI > AI), Trust (HI ~ AI), and Dependency (HI >> AI). The phases are explicitly "not proposed as universal or sequential psychological stages, but as conceptual lenses for organizing these shifts, which may overlap or reoccur." In the Trust phase AI serves as a cognitive scaffold while responsibility for evaluation remains with the learner; in Dependency, generation and organization are partially externalized to the system.
requirements: Interprets longitudinal poll data from sustained, hands-on student experience with AI systems in AI-focused courses
constraints: The phases are not universal or sequential psychological stages and may overlap or reoccur
Derived from a single forced-choice question to classroom cohorts, not a population-level estimate
target_learners: MSc and undergraduate computer science students in AI-focused courses
target_learning_goals: Calibrated valuation of human versus artificial intelligence
Metacognitive regulation of AI use
examples: The article annotates Fig. 1's 2020–2026 poll trend with the four phase braces and maps each phase to a preference pattern (HI < AI, HI > AI, HI ~ AI, HI >> AI).

citation: Daniele Verí. (2026). Beyond AI Literacy: A Structured Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis of Measures for Competent Generative-AI Use. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15624
title: Four-domain framework for competent generative-AI use measurement: knowledge and use, epistemic oversight, reliance calibration, and operational control of tool-using agents
description: The review organizes validated instruments into four domains ordered by proximity to operational work: knowledge and use, epistemic oversight, reliance calibration, and operational control of tool-using agents. The domains are "complementary measurement targets, not a single proficiency continuum": a person may know much about AI yet rely on it poorly, verify diligently without technical depth, or manage an agent safely through a familiar workflow without explaining model architecture. The framework is cut by measurement claim rather than curricular content, distinguishing it from curricular frameworks such as the AI Literacy Heptagon.
requirements: Training placement needs the distinctions between domains; domains should not be collapsed into one continuum without evidence.
constraints: The coverage map is the author's interpretive classification with no independent duplicate coding or inter-rater agreement; coverage describes measurement target, not validation quality.
target_learners: adults using generative AI in work and education
target_learning_goals: competent generative-AI use including verification, reliance calibration, and supervision of tool-using agents
examples: The review maps 22 focal instruments into Table 1 coverage ratings (Strong, Partial, Weak, None) across the four domains.

article_title: Shaping Responsible GenAI Use in Research Through AI Literacy-Oriented Guidelines: Insights From Postgraduate Students
citation: Wei Dai and Cecilia Ka Yuk Chan. (2026). Shaping responsible GenAI use in research through AI literacy-oriented guidelines: insights from postgraduate students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00609-6
title: Ng et al.'s four-dimensional AI literacy framework as a lens for researchers' responsible GenAI use
description: The study draws on Ng et al.'s framework conceptualising AI literacy as an integrated set of knowledge, practical, evaluative, and ethical capacities: "Know & Understand AI", "Use & Apply AI", "Evaluate & Create AI", and "AI Ethics". In the research context, the dimensions denote awareness of GenAI's capabilities, limitations and risks; appropriate employment across research tasks; judging the accuracy, originality and scholarly value of AI-mediated outputs; and reasoning about authorship, originality, privacy, accountability and over-reliance. The study uses the framework to analyse PGR students' practices and to structure its proposed guidelines.
requirements: Guidelines must address each of the four dimensions across diverse research tasks rather than principles alone.
constraints: The article states AI literacy had not yet been sufficiently defined or contextualised in relation to research practice prior to this study.
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of GenAI in research
AI literacy development across knowledge, application, evaluation and ethical dimensions
examples: The study mapped focus-group findings onto the dimensions: capability awareness to Know & Understand, discipline-specific applications to Use & Apply, ethical boundaries to Evaluate & Create, and concerns about accuracy, originality, privacy and skill degradation to AI Ethics.
key_sources: Wei Dai and Cecilia Ka Yuk Chan. (2026). Shaping responsible GenAI use in research through AI literacy-oriented guidelines: insights from postgraduate students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00609-6

article_title: Epistemic Dependence in AI-Mediated Learning
citation: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
title: Four-pathway model linking AI affordances and institutional conditions to configurations of epistemic dependence
description: The review's central analysis specifies four parallel pathways — fluent authority, frictionless delegation, opaque synthesis and institutionalised dependence — linking contextual conditions to configurations of epistemic reliance. A pathway is explicitly not a deterministic causal chain: "Educational consequences are attached only to harmful configurations, while design, pedagogical and governance responses may intervene at more than one point in the model." The framework distinguishes direct educational evidence from adjacent-domain evidence treated as hypotheses.
requirements: Assessment of each pathway configuration through the six diagnostic criteria before attributing educational consequences
constraints: Pathways are plausible relations to be investigated, not established causal effects; adjacent-domain evidence from search, smartphones, medicine or aviation does not prove equivalent educational effects
target_learners: Learners, teachers and institutions using or provisioning generative AI in education
target_learning_goals: Preserving verification, evaluative and disciplinary judgement under AI mediation
examples: Pathway 1 treats fluent authority and personalised social presence; Pathway 2 treats delegation compressed into a single request-response cycle; Pathway 3 treats synthesis that hides evidential structure; Pathway 4 treats institutional procurement and platform integration
key_sources: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1

article_title: EduZone: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Safety for K-12 Students and Teachers
citation: Park, J., Han, J., Yoo, H., Ahn, S.-Y., Yoon, J., & Oh, A. (2026). EduZone: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Safety for K-12 Students and Teachers. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02024
title: Four-level response safety classification (refusal, safe answer, risky with warning, fully risky) for evaluating educational LLM safety
description: EduZone grades every model response into one of four ordered safety levels rather than a binary safe/unsafe decision. A Level 3 response is one where "The model provides content that fulfills the hidden intent, but also includes explicit safety warnings, disclaimers, or guidance", whereas a Level 4 response fulfills the intent without any warning. Levels distinguish refusal (L1), safe redirection (L2), and the two risky grades, capturing differences in mitigation strategy across models.
requirements: A defined hidden intent or risk per interaction so responses can be judged against the four levels
A classification model validated against human annotators (Cohen's κ of 0.83 and 0.82 reported)
constraints: Refusals are safest but the article notes they offer limited utility compared with safe redirections that preserve pedagogical utility
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether LLM responses in educational interactions are safe, refuse safely, or provide risky assistance
examples: The classifier Gemini-3.5-Flash assigned responses to levels with justification and, for L3 or L4, extracted a short supporting quote demonstrating the risky behavior
key_sources: Park, J., Han, J., Yoo, H., Ahn, S.-Y., Yoon, J., & Oh, A. (2026). EduZone: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Safety for K-12 Students and Teachers. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02024

article_title: ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models
citation: Yilin Jiang, Xiaorong Zhu, Fei Tan, Zicheng Zhang, Kaiyi Huang, Yang Yu, Zexuan Fei, Yiming Luo, Keqian Li, Hao Hao, Guangtao Zhai, Aimin Zhou. (2026). ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09548
title: Four-requirement framework for education-facing LLMs: general capability, safety and trustworthiness, basic teaching ability, and high-level educational cultivation
description: The article organizes evaluation around four requirements an education-facing model should jointly satisfy, drawn from the learning-sciences literature (Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, Bloom's tutoring ideal, and AI-in-education ethics frameworks). As the article prints them: "These are general capability, the subject mastery that teaching presupposes; safety and trustworthiness, robust and age-appropriate behavior under sensitive and adversarial prompts; basic teaching ability, the production of usable instructional behavior; and high-level educational cultivation, the pedagogical judgment a domain expert exercises." ELBench operationalizes these as its four modules, and the evaluation shows the requirements are related but not interchangeable, since safety and teaching behave as competing objectives.
requirements: Evaluation must place all four requirements on the same models under a common measurement protocol so trade-offs among them become observable
constraints: High-level educational judgment has no agreed definition of the right response and no reward model to optimize against
target_learners: Students interacting with education-facing LLMs, including minors in K-12 settings
target_learning_goals: Subject mastery
Safe and age-appropriate behavior
Usable instructional output
Professional-level pedagogical judgment
examples: ELBench's Basic Education module draws on pedagogical content knowledge and scores multi-turn tutoring transcripts for instructional quality, not only final correctness
key_sources: Yilin Jiang, Xiaorong Zhu, Fei Tan, Zicheng Zhang, Kaiyi Huang, Yang Yu, Zexuan Fei, Yiming Luo, Keqian Li, Hao Hao, Guangtao Zhai, Aimin Zhou. (2026). ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09548

article_title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Four educational design objectives for course-specific AI support: course-specificity, independent learning, transparency and trust, and complementing existing teaching
description: The article organises Beacon's educational design around four objectives: providing course-specific academic support aligned with module outcomes; supporting independent learning through explanations and guidance rather than complete solutions; promoting transparency and trust so students can verify where information originates; and complementing existing teaching practices by enhancing rather than replacing lecturer and tutor interaction. The authors state "RAGwasthereforeadoptednotsimplyasatechnicalsolution,butas aneducationaldesignchoicethatenablesAI‐generatedsupporttore maintransparent,contextuallyrelevant,andalignedwithinstitutional teachingpractices." These objectives informed each stage of development, from knowledge-base construction to interface design.
requirements: Approved teaching materials are treated as the authoritative foundation for all responses, with the LLM functioning as the conversational interface rather than the primary source of knowledge.
target_learners: higher education students in computing modules
target_learning_goals: module-aligned academic guidance
independent learning
trust and verification of AI-generated explanations
examples: Objective 3 states students should be able to verify explanations, for example by the system stating the material was from a specific session presentation and slide, or from a handout.
key_sources: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Four-stage learner-controlled workflow: concept check, guided application, guided feedback, and guided Q&A
description: The deployed workflow implements graduated prompting under learner control in an ERD editor. "The deployed workflow follows graduated prompting under learner control [3, 11, 33]. Each accessed stage consumes one feedback credit." Stage 1 uses an educator-authored question pool the LLM selects from without modifying; Stage 2 fills template slots from the selected ERD component and evaluates responses against a reference rubric; Stage 3 gives concise artifact-grounded feedback while withholding the localized correction; Stage 4 supports multi-turn requirement-grounded clarification without generating the complete ERD. After every interaction, students may revise the ERD or request more explicit assistance, so each stage can be a stopping point.
requirements: Educator-defined stage sequence, question pools, templates with reference rubrics, and feedback credits; the diagnostic pipeline from a prior requirement-grounded ERD feedback system
constraints: Progression is learner-controlled rather than automatic; the agent does not modify the ERD; each accessed stage consumes one credit
target_learners: Undergraduate database systems students revising ER diagrams
target_learning_goals: Applying modeling concepts such as identifying relationships, weak entities, cardinality, and participation constraints to specific requirements
examples: Stage 2 template "Do you think [Relationship] is identifying?" instantiated for the relationship under review, with the LLM evaluating the written response against the rubric
key_sources: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870

article_title: Critical AI Tutors: Empower or Enslave?
citation: Favero, L., Pérez-Ortiz, J. A., Käser, T., & Oliver, N. (2025). Do AI tutors empower or enslave learners? Toward a critical use of AI in education. Applications of Generative AI to support teaching and learning in Higher Education, co-located with AIED 2025, Palermo, Italy.
title: Four-area framework of AI-in-education risks: cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics
description: The paper organizes the risks of AI integration in education into four key areas of the learning process: cognition, emotion, ethics and agency. On the cognition side it identifies cognitive offloading, mental laziness, and limited creativity; on agency, dependency, outsource decision-making, passivity, and over-trusting; on emotion, AI guilt, damaged self-efficacy, stress and anxiety, and social isolation; on ethics, lack of privacy, surveillance, data exploitation, and academic integrity. The framework is summarized in Figure 1, which pairs each challenge with interventions such as AI literacy, scaffolding, stimulating thinking, and strong ethical frameworks and policy. It serves as the paper's organizing structure, with one section devoted to each area.
requirements: The framework is a position-paper synthesis drawing on cognitive science and pedagogy literature rather than a tested model
constraints: The paper states the risks are not inherent to the tools themselves but lie in how they are utilized
target_learners: students in education using AI chatbots, particularly higher education
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
learner autonomy
emotional well-being
academic integrity
examples: Figure 1 maps challenges such as cognitive offloading, dependency, AI guilt, and lack of privacy to interventions including AI literacy, scaffolding, and strong ethical frameworks and policy
key_sources: Favero, L., Pérez-Ortiz, J. A., Käser, T., & Oliver, N. (2025). Do AI tutors empower or enslave learners? Toward a critical use of AI in education. Applications of Generative AI to support teaching and learning in Higher Education, co-located with AIED 2025, Palermo, Italy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06878

article_title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
citation: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271
title: FOXGLOVE: a parallel dataset of sentence-anchored, goal-labeled instructor and LLM writing feedback with urgency rankings and expert quality ratings
description: FOXGLOVE is a dataset of 2,340 feedback comments on 69 twelfth-grade argumentative essays from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus: 696 comments from 14 trained writing instructors and 1,644 from four LLMs (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen3-Next 80B) produced under a shared protocol. It is, per the article, a dataset collected with "anchored, goal-labeled feedback comments" from trained human instructors and models. It adds expert quality ratings on 105 comments across seven dimensions (1,430 ratings), urgency rankings, and reusable annotation protocols for instructors, LLMs, and raters.
requirements: Feedback must follow the shared schema: sentence-anchored comments addressing one of five argumentative goals, an urgency ranking of the three most important comments, and one global comment per essay
constraints: The schema privileges feedback organized around predefined argumentative moves and may underrepresent feedback such as encouragement and praise
Feedback was collected for the study rather than drawn from authentic instructional settings, without an ongoing relationship with the writer
target_learners: writing instructors and LLM feedback system evaluators
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing revision through goal-oriented, anchored, prioritized feedback
examples: Each essay was independently annotated by two instructors via Google Docs, with comments anchored to sentences, goal labels recorded, and the top three comments ranked for urgency
key_sources: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271

article_title: Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio
citation: Suleiman, A. D., DeWaters, J., Shepherd, D. C., Korkmaz, T., Hussain, F., Liu, Y., & Hou, D. (2026). Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11129
title: FORAP: a framework organizing computing PjBL projects as coordinated adoption-ready packages
description: FORAP (Framework for Organizing Reusable and Adaptable PjBL Projects) organizes each project as a coordinated package centered on aligned learning objectives, described through project attributes, and supported by three coordinated support packages: instructor, student, and assessment. Project attributes (greenfield vs. brownfield, scope and duration, technical complexity, domain, and optional competency specification such as CC2020 mapping) let instructors judge course fit and plan adaptation. The framework was used to package a 14-project portfolio and is grounded in PjBL principles of authentic, collaborative, and self-directed learning.
requirements: Aligned learning objectives as the organizing anchor for project packaging
Modular, flexible packaging that supports reuse across offerings and adaptation to different course contexts
Support materials addressing instructor adoption barriers and common student technical challenges
Structured milestones, checkpoints, and aligned assessment artifacts for formative and summative assessment
constraints: Successful implementation still depended on instructor preparation, TA readiness, class size, and platform or environment constraints
Materials require ongoing maintenance as dependencies, software versions, platforms, and technologies change
Adoption is not plug-and-play; instructors still make local decisions about scope, pacing, tooling, and support
target_learning_goals: computing course learning objectives across software engineering, cybersecurity, machine learning, databases, and related domains
examples: The Touchalytics project package illustrates the framework: four phased tasks, instructor notes and sample solutions, installation guidelines and labs, and phased milestones with transfer-oriented design problems and a detailed rubric
key_sources: Suleiman, A. D., DeWaters, J., Shepherd, D. C., Korkmaz, T., Hussain, F., Liu, Y., & Hou, D. (2026). Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11129

article_title: Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio
citation: Suleiman, A. D., DeWaters, J., Shepherd, D. C., Korkmaz, T., Hussain, F., Liu, Y., & Hou, D. (2026). Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11129
title: Multi-scale portfolio of 14 adoption-ready computing PjBL project packages
description: The paper contributes a multi-scale portfolio of 14 computing PjBL projects packaged using FORAP, developed over multiple years from instructor course needs, faculty expertise, research by-products, open-source projects, and prior student project ideas. Projects vary in scope and duration (from about four weeks to a full semester), technical complexity, codebase context (greenfield and brownfield), and domain, spanning software engineering, cybersecurity, systems, machine learning, databases, behavioral biometrics, web, and mobile development. Table I summarizes attributes and classroom trial counts per project, and the portfolio is available at the project's documentation site.
requirements: All 14 projects were organized using the FORAP package structure, including instructor, student, and assessment support, with project-specific artifacts tailored to each project
constraints: Project types are not equally easy to adopt: more self-contained and shorter projects provide lower-barrier entry points, whereas brownfield and more technically complex projects typically require additional scaffolding, support, and careful scoping
target_learning_goals: course-specific computing competencies such as implementing authentication workflows, applying machine learning to behavioral data, and modifying open-source systems
examples: Touchalytics: an Android authentication application using swipe behavior as a biometric signal with cloud storage and a Python machine learning backend; Moodle and Xfig as brownfield high-complexity projects; RSA and Breached! as low-complexity short modules

article_title: From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools
citation: Ofek Levy, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein, and Yossi Ben-Zion. (2026). From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22From+Prompt+to+Embodied+Simulation%22
title: Four-element prompt structure for generating embodied AR physics simulations
description: A reusable prompt template whose fixed elements are the tools (libraries and camera handling), the display (objects drawn over the camera image and what each represents), the hand controls (which finger motion controls which quantity), and optimization requirements that prevent jumps and jitter. The article states "The elements are fixed; only their content changes from one simulation to the next," and shows that "The same four elements produce very different simulations, and in all of them the physics appears in the learner's own environment." Each simulation runs as a single HTML file in an ordinary browser with no installation.
requirements: A common LLM tool with a code-running canvas mode (or copying the code into an .html file), a camera, and the MediaPipe Hands library plus a transparent drawing layer, with Three.js for 3D scenes
constraints: In tools such as ChatGPT and Claude the built-in preview window may not have access to the camera, requiring saving the code as an .html file and opening it in the browser
A first prompt is almost never perfect and AR simulations are sensitive to edge cases, so iterative refinement is expected
target_learning_goals: physics concepts represented spatially, such as amplitude, wavelength, electric fields, and the right-hand rule
examples: The wave-and-lamp simulation, a single charge with its 3D field grid, two charges with a combined field, and the right-hand rule drawn on the student's own hand, all built from the same four elements
key_sources: Ofek Levy, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein, and Yossi Ben-Zion. (2026). From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22From+Prompt+to+Embodied+Simulation%22

article_title: Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios
citation: Leman Figen Gül, Burak Delikanlı, Oğulcan Üneşi, Ertuğrul Ömer Gül. (2025). Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios. ITU A|Z • Vol 22 No 3 • November 2025 • 751-774. https://doi.org/10.58278/0.2025.109
title: Four approaches to leveraging GenAI in the architectural design process: exploring the unknown problem space, solution space enhancement, framing and rephrasing, and design externalization
description: The article organizes students' observed GenAI use into four approaches mapped to Boden's creativity types: 'exploring unknown problem space' for concept development and inspiration in early design, 'solution space enhancement' for generating alternatives, 'framing and rephrasing' where LLMs and prompts become central to the design process, and 'a tool for design externalization' after design decisions, analogous to a rendering engine. The article states "A central limitation shared by these four approaches to leveraging GenAI is the inherently subjective nature of creativity, which resists objective evaluation."
requirements: Students need competencies and discernment to differentiate between GenAI models and use them effectively to avoid design fixation
constraints: The article acknowledges that further research is necessary to substantiate the framing-and-rephrasing approach
creativity is context-dependent and resists objective evaluation
target_learning_goals: design creativity
design process exploration and ideation
examples: A student based her entire design methodology on transforming GenAI visuals into virtual spaces, using LLMs to describe spaces, generating 2D images, and converting them into 3D models for plans and sections

article_title: Who Acts, Who Knows, Who Answers? A Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis of Agency, Epistemic Responsibility, and Accountability in Generative AI Higher Education Research
citation: Poudyal, B. (2026). Who Acts, Who Knows, Who Answers? A Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis of Agency, Epistemic Responsibility, and Accountability in Generative AI Higher Education Research. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7210-5480
title: Four-part conceptual distinction: grammatical activation, functional agency, epistemic authority, and normative accountability
description: The article proposes a four-part conceptual distinction drawn from its empirical observations: "grammatical activation, functional agency, epistemic authority, and normative accountability". Grammatical activation makes an actor identifiable in a clause; functional agency refers to performance that produces consequences; authority is a warranted capacity to judge and endorse; accountability is an obligation to justify and bear consequences. The categories relate but are not equivalent, and the distinction explains how the literature gives AI functional agency while retaining human answerability without drawing the boundary clearly.
requirements: Users must keep the difference between performing an action, holding authority over an action, and being accountable for an action clearly in view when describing AI in educational writing.
constraints: The distinction was derived from titles and abstracts only, which the article states carry far less information about method and joint authorship than full texts.
target_learners: higher education researchers and scholars writing about GenAI
target_learning_goals: distinguishing functional agency from epistemic authority and normative accountability in discourse about AI in education
examples: The corpus analysis showing AI grammatically active in 447 predicate associations yet never assigned a strictly responsible predicate illustrates the distinction.
key_sources: Poudyal, B. (2026). Who Acts, Who Knows, Who Answers? A Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis of Agency, Epistemic Responsibility, and Accountability in Generative AI Higher Education Research. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7210-5480

article_title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
citation: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w
title: Four-category functional classification of student GenAI use (Learning, Formatting, Doing Task, Feedback) with SAMR mapping
description: A descriptive coding framework developed inductively from students' mandatory GenAI-use declarations in the physics unit, classifying the "clearly stated pedagogical function of each reported GenAI use" into four themes: Learning (researching, understanding, conceptualising, refining understanding), Formatting (structure, organisation, admin tasks), Doing Task (calculations), and Feedback (clarification, feedback, verification, checking results). Each category was mapped to SAMR levels: Learning to Substitution→Augmentation, Formatting to Substitution, Doing Task to Modification→Redefinition, and Feedback across all levels. Frequencies per assessment provided the primary evidence for evaluating student GenAI use.
requirements: Mandatory student declarations stating tools and purposes of GenAI use
Collaborative coding by two academics with consensus decisions
constraints: The SAMR mapping was interpretive and context-dependent rather than a fixed classification; declarations were self-reported and may be incomplete or strategically framed
target_learning_goals: understanding what students use GenAI for in assessment work
examples: 23 unique GenAI uses were reported across the three assessments and coded into the four themes
key_sources: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w

article_title: Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education
citation: Thomas, D.R., Borchers, C., Vanacore, K.P., Koedinger, K.R., & Kizilcec, R.F. (2026). Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29141
title: Four shifts for establishing ground truth in AIED: diagnostic IRR, transparent reporting, LLM risk mitigation, and validity-first evidence
description: The article's central framework proposes four practical shifts for establishing ground truth in AIED labeling: (1) treat IRR as "a diagnostic signal to localize disagreement and refine constructs rather than a mechanical acceptance threshold"; (2) require transparent reporting of rater expertise, codebook development, reconciliation procedures, and segmentation rules; (3) mitigate risks in LLM annotation through bias audits and verification workflows; and (4) complement agreement statistics with validity and effectiveness evidence, including uncertainty-aware labeling, criterion-related checks, and close-the-loop evaluations. The framework is grounded in the distinction between noise and bias and illustrated through multimodal tutoring case studies.
requirements: Reporting must cover rater characteristics, codebook evolution, and conflict resolution for the transparency shift to function as described.
constraints: The framework targets AIED settings with high-inference constructs, skewed label distributions, and temporally segmented multimodal data; the authors state the goal is not to replace established psychometric frameworks but to translate and extend them.
target_learners: AIED researchers and dataset builders annotating educational interaction data
target_learning_goals: Improving reliability and validity of labeled educational datasets used to train and evaluate AI tutoring and assessment systems
examples: The paper uses a running example of multimodal tutoring data in which a student's verbal confusion is paired with visual cues and processed into a transcribed, timestamped interaction.
key_sources: Thomas, D.R., Borchers, C., Vanacore, K.P., Koedinger, K.R., & Kizilcec, R.F. (2026). Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29141

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence and the marginalization of minoritized knowledges in higher education
citation: Fatiha TALI OTMANI. (2025). L'intelligence artificielle générative et la marginalisation des savoirs minoritaires dans l'enseignement supérieur. Le cas du handicap. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22marginalisation+des+savoirs+minoritaires+dans+l%27enseignement+sup%C3%A9rieur%22
title: Les quatre modes d'usage de l'IA dans la recherche (Oracle, Surrogate, Quant, Arbiter) et l'« illusion d'exploration scientifique »
description: La revue mobilise la taxonomie de Messeri et Crockett (2024) de quatre modes d'usage de l'IA dans la recherche, « porteurs chacun d'un risque pour la diversité épistémique ». Comme Oracle, l'IA synthétise la littérature mais ne traite que les corpus accessibles, marginalisant les travaux non anglophones ou non textuels ; comme Surrogate, elle produit des données de substitution reconduisant les biais des populations surreprésentées ; comme Quant, elle risque de contourner les cadres théoriques au profit du calcul ; comme Arbiter, elle s'invite dans le peer review. Ces modes convergent pour produire une « illusion d'exploration scientifique » : les chercheurs croient parcourir l'ensemble des questions possibles alors qu'ils n'examinent qu'un sous-ensemble compatible avec les capacités des outils.
requirements: Les quatre modes supposent que les chercheurs reconnaissent que chaque mode ne traite qu'un sous-ensemble des questions et corpus, afin d'éviter l'illusion d'exhaustivité que l'article nomme « illusion d'exploration scientifique ».
constraints: L'article précise que la performance des agents-Surrogate « suppose toutefois que les participants modélisés appartiennent aux populations les mieux documentées » (Park et al., 2024).
target_learners: enseignants-chercheurs et chercheurs en enseignement supérieur
target_learning_goals: maintien de la diversité épistémique dans les pratiques de recherche
usage critique des outils d'IA dans la production scientifique
examples: Park et coll. (2024) : des agents reproduisent à 85 % les réponses humaines à l'Enquête Sociale Générale, performance limitée aux populations les mieux documentées.

article_title: Guardrails or Roadblocks? Effects of Pedagogical Style and Context Awareness in AI Teaching Assistants for Programming

title: Four GPT-4o-backed AI TA configurations with pedagogical guardrails on a web-based coding platform
description: The study's artifact is a set of four AI teaching assistants backed by the OpenAI GPT-4o LLM, deployed on a web-based coding platform with a split-screen interface showing the problem statement, submission history, and chatbot beside an embedded editor. The four configurations varied only in system prompts and contextual information: "AI TAs were backed by the OpenAI GPT-4o LLM and returned responses to student queries based on custom prompts" with pedagogical guardrails similar to CodeHelp. Direct conditions gave brief responses without complete code solutions; Socratic conditions guided exclusively through targeted questions.

A web-based coding platform hosting the programming tasks and chat interface
constraints: The four configurations differed only in system prompts and contextual information; the interface was otherwise identical
Guardrails withhold complete code solutions rather than providing them

target_learning_goals: code-writing and debugging tasks involving lists, loops, and conditionals
examples: 132 students were randomly assigned across Direct + Full Context, Direct + No Context, Socratic + Full Context, and Socratic + No Context conditions while completing one code-writing and two debugging tasks

citation: Kenzhebayeva Z, Matayev B, Sarsembayeva E, Kolyukh O, Assenova N and Ospanova A (2026) Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists. title: Four-role rotation cycle: Case Constructor, Research Analyst, Practitioner-Interventionist, and Reflective Researcher
description: The pattern assigns four successive professional roles within each case-based learning cycle. The Case Constructor focuses on "contextual problem framing"; the Research Analyst evaluates evidence and compares AI-generated information with psychological theories; the Practitioner-Interventionist adapts recommendations to specific educational contexts and justifies strategies; and the Reflective Researcher critically examines AI-generated outputs and collaborative decisions. Explicit role descriptions and facilitation, since participants reported uncertainty in unfamiliar roles
constraints: The Reflective Researcher role was most frequently described as challenging; the Case Constructor role was generally perceived as more accessible

Analytical reasoning and evidence evaluation
Intervention planning
Critical reflection on professional decisions

article_title: Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation
citation: Lo S, Lea T, Mavromoustakos A, Joseph B, Yii M, Exintaris B, Karunaratne N, Pearson DL, Ritchie T, Yuriev E and Pyun J (2026) Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation. Front. Educ. 11:1818781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1818781
title: Four-phase iterative cGPT co-creation process with SPAR reflective logging
description: The article describes a reusable co-creation pattern with four construction phases: Creation (writing the system prompt and selecting knowledge-base files), Refinement (iterative testing, prompt editing, and SPAR reflections), Consolidation (finalising prompts and merging versions), and Evaluation (scoring responses to ten evaluation questions). Throughout, students wrote SPAR reflections — "Stimulus (Prompt sent to GPT), Processing (GPT's response), Analysis (Evaluation of GPT response based on design principles) and Reflection (Next steps based on GPT response)" — which informed system prompt adjustment until satisfactory accuracy and instruction adherence were reached.
requirements: Regular student-academic team meetings (weekly to twice weekly) for testing and refinement, and design principles focused on clear, accurate and consistent responses
constraints: The overall process from construction to implementation lasted two to six weeks, depending on the cGPT's topic, students' prior experience, and availability of resources such as system prompt templates
target_learners: undergraduate students without extensive prior research experience
target_learning_goals: AI literacy, teamwork, and project management
iterative design and evaluative judgment
examples: SPAR reflections were written individually prior to peer discussion to reduce groupthink and retrospective smoothing, and evaluation scored twenty generated responses per evaluation question on accuracy, concision and relevance

article_title: Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review
citation: Jennifer Lock, Soraya Arteaga, Carol Johnson. (2025). Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review. International Journal on Innovations in Online Education, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1615/IntJInnovOnlineEdu.2026060433
title: Four-theme framework for AI integration in online higher education
description: The review's organizing framework groups the literature on AI in online higher education into four interrelated themes: "(i) Types and purpose of AI integration; (ii) pedagogical approaches (e.g., use of AI literacy); (iii) benefits of using AI in online learning; and (iv) challenges of using AI in online learning." article_title: MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing
citation: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535
title: Four-level taxonomy of co-writing interaction paradigms (L0-L3)
description: The article organizes co-writing systems into four paradigms that differ in initiative distribution, contextual signals for intent inference, and adaptivity. It states: "We organize co-writing systems into four interaction paradigms, as summarized in Table 3." L0 is user-initiated collaboration reacting to explicit intent; L1 is stateless proactive collaboration predicting intent from local context; L2 is stateful proactive collaboration conditioning on interaction history; L3 is adaptive proactive collaboration with adaptive intent modeling. The taxonomy provides a unified lens for analyzing user acceptance and editing behavior.
requirements: Quantitative comparison requires paradigms where interaction events are well-defined and directly comparable, which the article states holds for L1 and L2.
constraints: L3 is treated as an analysis-driven paradigm whose evaluation is reserved for downstream system design and user studies, not the controlled quantitative comparison.
target_learners: adult writers using LLM writing assistants
target_learning_goals: aligning assistant initiative with user intent during writing
examples: The user study instantiated all four interaction paradigms with a unified LLM backend (GPT-5.1) in an online interactive writing system.

citation: Guo, Q., Tang, J., Huang, X., Lin, H.-Y., Zhong, Y., & Zhuang, X. (2026). LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29672
title: Four binding constraints on low-cost, personalized, equitable language education (C1-C4)
description: The article distills its evidence review into four constraints that have bound low-cost, personalized, equitable language education: "C1: the human oral provision is intrinsically expensive"; C2, that technological substitutes presuppose connectivity and recurring payment; C3, that substitute content has been fixed and cannot ingest the learner's own documents; and C4, that capable software has never run on cheap hardware. Each row of its Table 1 taxonomy is an instance of one constraint. The scheme of the paper is built on the claimed dissolution of C4, which it argues makes C2 and C3 unnecessary and bypasses rather than solves C1.
requirements: The constraints are derived from the article's evidence review of learner needs and prior technologies; using the taxonomy requires the published evidence base it assembles.
constraints: The article states C1 is a fact about humans and will not change, while C2 and C3 are design choices and C4 was, until recently, a fact about software.
target_learners: self-directed second-language learners in resource-constrained households
target_learning_goals: second-language listening, reading, speaking, and writing as one bound skill
examples: Table 1 maps eight difficulties of second-language acquisition under resource scarcity onto the four constraints, each with a prior technological answer and its documented limit.

article_title: Preservice mathematics teachers’ noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping
citation: Selen Galiç, Mathias Tejera, Sebastián Parodi, Markus Hohenwarter, Zsolt Lavicza. (2026). Preservice mathematics teachers' noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping. ZDM – Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01805-4
title: Four-phase weekly cycle for AI-based noticing practice: video, chatbot interaction, reflection, mentor feedback
description: The implementation was organised as a repeating weekly structure in which "each week consisting of four phases". In phase one preservice teachers watched videos depicting a student's equal-sign misconception; in phase two they interacted with the student chatbot at their own pace; in phase three they reflected on the conversation using three guiding questions and documented reflections with comments linked to chat responses; in phase four they received mentor chatbot feedback. This cycle repeated across three weeks with a different virtual student each week.
requirements: Weekly materials assigned with completion within one week; reflection prompts designed to examine noticing; conversation transcripts copied into a separate file with linked comments
constraints: The article notes the tasks used may have influenced noticing transitions, and the three-week design does not permit conclusions about the durability of noticing practices

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: Four-layer model of pedagogical safety for educational RL (structural, progress, behavioral, alignment) with the RHSI severity metric
description: The article formalizes pedagogical safety as four constraint classes: "Structural Safety (C1):Prerequisites are architecturally enforced via action masking", progress safety (C2, windowed mastery gain), behavioral safety (C3, minimum cognitive demand), and alignment safety (C4, engagement coupled to mastery). A policy is pedagogically safe if it simultaneously satisfies C1–C4, with an ε-relaxed weighted-norm version for practice. The Reward Hacking Severity Index quantifies the degree to which a policy simultaneously achieves high return and high violation, bounded in [0,1]. The authors argue via informal propositions that no proper subset of the four constraints implies the full set.
requirements: Constraint thresholds must be calibrated to the specific domain (e.g., εprog from a mastery-only baseline's per-window progress distribution; δmin=0.4 set at the ICAP passive/active boundary)
constraints: C1 is enforced architecturally and excluded from the aggregate violation vector (v1≡0 by convention)
The framework's safety guarantees hold with respect to estimated mastery, not necessarily true mastery
Constraint independence arguments are informal sufficiency arguments rather than formal proofs
target_learners: Learners in intelligent tutoring systems, simulated here as struggling, average, and advanced programming-education profiles
target_learning_goals: Genuine mastery of domain concepts (27 Python concepts) rather than proxy engagement maximization
examples: SmartTutor enforces C1 via action masking and C3 via an action selection module online; C2 and C4 are evaluated as offline safety metrics from session logs
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading
citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: Four-domain mapping of AI-associated cognitive offloading (D1-D4)
description: The article defines AI-associated cognitive offloading as the pattern where "what gets delegated is the thinking itself: reasoning through a problem, generating ideas, learning new material, or communicating with other people". It organises reflection around four domains grounded in the 2023-2026 literature: reasoning and critical thinking, creativity and originality, research and learning, and social and communicative capacity. Each domain is treated as a continuum on which self-reported behavioural patterns indicate offloading depth, not underlying ability. The author states these are "a working vocabulary grounded in the literature, not a tested factor structure".
requirements: Domains are read as indicators of self-reported offloading patterns, not measures of underlying ability
constraints: The four-domain structure is a working organisation, not a confirmed factor structure
Scope is limited to consumer-facing LLM-class tools, excluding recommender systems and embodied AI
The emotional strand (anxiety, AI guilt, emotional dependence) falls outside the current scope
target_learners: Adult LLM users (researchers, creatives, students, knowledge workers, software engineers)
target_learning_goals: Maintaining reasoning, creativity, learning, and social-communicative capacities while using generative AI
examples: Figure 1 maps the four domains D1-D4 onto distinct strands of the 2023-2026 empirical literature feeding into the self-check

article_title: Governing generative AI in higher education: Emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. universities
citation: Qian, Y. (2026). Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. Universities. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00233-x
title: Four-pillar framework for GenAI-era academic integrity: accountability, transparency, equity, and privacy
description: The article proposes that academic integrity when GenAI is permitted under stated conditions is organized by "a four-pillar framework for GenAI-era integrity: accountability, transparency, equity, and privacy." Accountability frames human agency in collaboration, with users expected to steer, critique, verify, and revise AI outputs rather than defer to them. Transparency operates through disclosure and attribution as a design principle reducing ambiguity before submission. Equity holds that integrity expectations are fair only when students have comparable opportunities to access and understand tools and norms. Privacy is treated as an integrity condition because inappropriate data sharing can undermine fairness and erode trust. Together the pillars define the conditions under which AI-assisted academic work can remain legitimate.
requirements: Integrity expectations must be paired with comparable student access to tools and norms for the equity pillar to hold
constraints: The framework is derived from document analysis of 50 innovation-oriented U.S. universities and is offered as analytically transferable insight, not statistical generalizability
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of generative AI in academic work
academic integrity under AI-permitted conditions
examples: Arizona State's syllabus toolkit characterizes AI tools as partners in work while emphasizing that humans must iterate on AI outputs
Yale's guidance instructs community members not to enter confidential, legally restricted, or moderate/high-risk data into AI tools
key_sources: Qian, Y. (2026). Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. Universities. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00233-x

article_title: Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs
citation: Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano. (2026). Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06669
title: Four-layer defense-in-depth architecture for educational LLM guardrails
description: The article describes a "defense-in-depth mechanism comprising four distinct layers": deterministic lexical pattern filters (Layer 1), structural output validation (Layer 2), contextual sandboxing with explicit delimiters (Layer 3), and session-level behavioral heuristics (Layer 4). It is "designed as a progressive filter", starting with high-speed deterministic checks and escalating to structural, contextual, and session-level behavioral analysis, with each layer targeting a specific class of attack vectors while minimizing false positives on benign educational queries.
requirements: Layer 1 requires curated language-specific regex patterns; Layer 4 requires temporal metadata and repeated variations from real session traces to function
constraints: Layer 4 blocks zero attacks in the offline single-turn benchmark and is relevant only for online multi-turn enforcement; indirect injection is explicitly out of scope
target_learners: students in programming education tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: preventing answer extraction while permitting legitimate clarification, hint-seeking, and debugging help
examples: Layer 1 uses 30 curated regular expression patterns grouped into English jailbreak, Portuguese, and educational extraction families; Layer 2 enforces JSON-structure constraints and scans for HTML/XSS-like patterns

article_title: Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation
citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: Four-stage windowed pipeline architecture for deck-level question generation
description: The article's organizing architecture is a multi-pass generative pipeline: a Window Planner that "Analyzes overlapping windows of slides, creating a contact sheet image to infer titles, summaries, modalities, roles, and a provisional question budget"; a Deck Synthesis phase merging window analyses into one coherent deck plan; a Slide Annotator generating questions per slide using deck context; and a Reconciliation phase evaluating the full-deck annotation for redundancies and unbalanced coverage. The windowed design is intended to mitigate LLM context limits while preserving the presentation's narrative flow.
requirements: All outputs must conform to strongly typed JSON schemas (Pydantic models SlidePlan, SlideAnnotationModel, ReconciliationModel) to ensure data integrity
constraints: The multi-pass architecture incurs substantial LLM inference latency and API costs on large decks
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in technical lecture courses
target_learning_goals: deck-level pedagogical scaffolding of comprehension questions across a full presentation
examples: The reconciliation phase re-runs annotation with adjusted budgets when actions such as rewrite, expand, or reduce are needed

article_title: Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation
citation: Walkington, C., Beauchamp, T., Ikram, F., Koçyiğit Gürbüz, M., Xia, F., Lee, M., Lan, A. (2025). Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation.
title: Four specialized evaluation agents for LLM-generated problems
description: The system employs four agents that each evaluate a different dimension of generated problems: an Authenticity agent evaluating whether the context is age-appropriate and likely to be relatable for middle school learners; a Realism agent evaluating whether quantities, units, and contextual details are plausible for the chosen topic; a Reading-level agent evaluating whether vocabulary and sentence complexity match the intended reading level; and a Hallucination agent evaluating whether the problem is mathematically consistent with the original. Each agent returns a binary pass/fail decision, and failed cases return identified issues that are combined and provided to a refinement agent.
requirements: Each agent has a specified role and prompt; issues from failed cases are combined and provided to a refinement agent
constraints: Each agent returns a binary pass/fail decision rather than a graded assessment

article_title: The University AI Didn''t Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era
citation: Binkowski, K. P., & Hopkins, A. (2026). The University AI Didn't Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era. Macquarie University. https://www.mq.edu.au/
title: Four-level framework of institutional AI adoption in universities, from defensive containment to AI-embedded transformation
description: The article names and substantively describes a four-level framework of institutional response to generative AI: "ranging from defensive restriction to full integration of AI into educational systems, with many institutions presently operating around Level 0 or Level 1". Level 0 treats AI as an integrity threat and restricts it; Level 1 is informal, individual-educator experimentation without institutional recognition; Level 2 is strategic integration into policy and curriculum; Level 3 embeds AI in core infrastructure with learning reorganised around AI-supported reasoning. A 2x2 matrix (Figure 1) maps levels by degree of AI integration and institutional recognition.
requirements: Institutional recognition and structural alignment, including policies, workload models, and promotion frameworks, to move beyond Level 1
constraints: The framework is a descriptive summary of institutional response stages, not a tested model; the authors note it is not completely clear whether exemplar institutions are genuinely at the strategic adoption stage
target_learners: university students in AI-rich higher education environments
target_learning_goals: AI-supported reasoning, judgment, and responsible AI use
examples: The paper positions Macquarie University's case studies as illustrating movement from Level 1 informal innovation toward Level 2 strategic integration

article_title: Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education
citation: Germán Arroyo, Luis López, and Juan Carlos Torres. (2026). Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05929
title: Four-metric behavioral taxonomy for distinguishing authentic iterative coding from automated workflows
description: The article defines four analytical metrics derived from explicit API event logs to "differentiate authentic learning behaviors from automated or externally synthesized workflows": (a) a class rhythm heatmap of temporal interaction density, (b) cumulative platform engagement showing staircase-like growth, (c) session intensity defined as the ratio of recorded explicit actions to session duration, and (d) daily work volume aggregating events over 24-hour periods. Triangulated, these metrics anchor a behavioral profile distinguishing iterative human development—variable intensity, plateaus, diurnal rhythms—from rigid, unbroken automated patterns.
requirements: Centralized execution so all workloads run on managed infrastructure rather than local unmonitored machines
Explicit human-driven API interception instead of passive keep-alive telemetry, which fires approximately every 300 seconds regardless of human interaction
constraints: API-level event logs capture interaction patterns but not intent; the metrics cannot independently prove academic misconduct
target_learners: undergraduate and master's students in computer programming courses
target_learning_goals: monitoring authentic iterative development processes
detecting automated or AI-assisted code synthesis
examples: Applied to a pilot cohort of 19 students producing 1,880 discrete API events over approximately 57 active student-hours

citation: Heidi Taveter and Marina Lepp. (2026). From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using “Vibe Coding” to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24757
title: Four design goals for teacher-facing programming-process visualization: visibility, workflow support, formative feedback, and non-automated integrity clarification
description: The article organizes the tool's design around four stated goals: DG1 making students' programming processes visible to teachers through interpretable views; DG2 supporting teacher decision-making through workflows for both quick individual inspection and efficient review of larger log sets; DG3 supporting process-informed formative feedback; and DG4 supporting clarification of academic-integrity concerns without automating judgment. For DG3, the tool should help teachers "identify situations in which students may need support, such as repeated run-error cycles with limited progress, a late start of the program execution, or unusually long periods of inactivity." The framework translates prior programming-process research into teacher-facing views.
requirements: Underlying IDE activity logs must be available, since the views summarize signals such as runs, errors, debugs, pauses, and copy-paste behavior captured in Thonny logs
constraints: Integrity-related indicators are intended as warning signals rather than automated determinations, with interpretation left to teachers

timely formative feedback
academic-integrity case clarification

citation: Riichiro Mizoguchi, Tomoki Aburatani, Kento Koike, Machi Shimmei. (2026). Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering —Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI—. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05545
title: Four quadrants and four types of structural-gap origin: a vocabulary decomposing who synthesized and who analyzed
description: The framework superimposes the distinction between executing agents (human, AI) on the distinction between cognitive functions (Synthesis, Analysis), yielding quadrants Q1 (human Synthesis), Q2 (AI Synthesis), Q3 (human Analysis), and Q4 (AI Analysis). From these, four types of structural-gap origin are derived, with Type (IV) — Vibe Compiling — placing the gap "between the AI's output and the human's judgment." The authors argue the quadrants make describable what the single word "done" conflates: what the AI evaluated versus what the user could evaluate, and what the AI made versus what the user constructed.
requirements: Both the function distinction and the agent distinction must be drawn together for the design demand (reserve Q3 and purpose-setting Q1 to the human) to be statable
constraints: Agent columns name the side that principally carries each mapping, not an exclusive right to execute it
The internal thought process after a probe does not appear in the classificatory variables
target_learners: Researchers and designers of AI-supported learning and research systems
target_learning_goals: Protecting and driving human metacognition and epistemic agency under AI assistance
examples: Draft V1 of the paper is cited as an instance of Type (II), where the type was almost fully satisfied while human content stayed empty
The vocabulary is proposed as a design question to put to any support system: against whose Synthesis or Analysis does it elicit a gap

Unlike prior ID-based benchmarks, it provides "complete question text for 3,400 mathematics problems" and records actual student responses, including which distractors students selected on multiple-choice items. citation: Agarwal, B., Urlings, C., van Lankveld, G., & Klemke, R. (2022). Identifying the Ethical Values and Norms of Artificial Intelligence in Education: a Systematic Literature Review. Open University of the Netherlands. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7347-8465

description: The review classifies the addressees of AIED ethical norms into four stakeholder sets, adopting Smuha's (2022) classification with one renaming. citation: Patricia D. Simon, Lily Min Zeng, Luke K. Fryer. (2026). A systematic review of student engagement research in adaptive learning platforms. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100360
title: Extended four-component student engagement framework (behavioral, affective, cognitive, agentic) applied to adaptive learning platforms
description: The review adopts an integrated framework combining Fredricks et al.'s three common engagement dimensions with Reeve and Tseng's extension. As the review states, "Reeve and Tseng [16] extended this framework and proposed a fourth component called agentic engagement." Behavioral engagement covers observable participation such as time and effort; affective engagement covers attitudes, motivation, confidence and persistence; cognitive engagement covers self-regulation and deep processing; agentic engagement covers students' constructive contribution into the flow of instruction, such as help-seeking. The framework guided deductive coding of the 44 included studies.
requirements: Operationalized definitions of each engagement component to code indicators consistently across studies
constraints: The review notes contentions in how the dimensions are conceptualized, with challenges regarding measurement and statistical methodology, and only moderate interrater reliability in categorizing engagement types
target_learners: Students across educational levels using adaptive learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Understanding and promoting student engagement in technology-mediated, adaptive learning environments
examples: The review coded presence or absence of engagement indicators in 44 articles using these operationalized definitions, with two rounds of interrater reliability checking
key_sources: Patricia D. Simon, Lily Min Zeng, Luke K. Fryer. (2026). A systematic review of student engagement research in adaptive learning platforms. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100360

article_title: Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning
citation: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457
title: Four design possibilities arising from the incommensurability of performance and learning
