description: The article proposes a 2x2 framework crossing short-term performance and longer-term learning outcomes, yielding four design possibilities. It states that "Exploiting the incommensurability between learning and performance results in four possibilities for design: productive success, productive failure, unproductive success, and unproductive failure." Productive success maximizes both; productive failure sacrifices initial performance for longer-term learning; unproductive success shows an "illusion of learning in initial high performance"; unproductive failure maximizes neither. The framework is used to reposition direct instruction and discovery learning as extremes of a larger design space.
requirements: The framework presupposes that conditions maximizing initial performance can be distinguished empirically from conditions maximizing longer-term learning
constraints: The categorization is explicitly relative: what seems productive success against one comparison can seem unproductive success against another
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students learning novel concepts
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
transfer
long-term retention
examples: Direct instruction is analyzed as a productive success relative to pure discovery learning but potentially an unproductive success relative to productive failure and productive success designs
key_sources: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457

article_title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
citation: Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266
title: Four-category framework for evaluating the generalizability of learning techniques
description: The monograph organizes each technique review around four categories of variables, inspired by Jenkins' (1979) model: "materials, learning conditions, student characteristics, and criterion tasks." Materials pertain to the content to be learned; learning conditions concern how and where the technique is implemented (e.g., dosage, group vs. individual); student characteristics include age, ability, prior knowledge, and motivation; criterion tasks range from cued recall to problem solving and essay writing. Each of the 10 technique reviews assesses generalizability across these categories before assigning a utility rating.
requirements: Sufficient empirical evidence must be available for each technique to permit a preliminary assessment of efficacy across the categories
constraints: The framework excludes techniques requiring advanced technologies or extensive teacher-prepared materials, per the monograph's selection criteria
target_learners: students and teachers selecting techniques for self-regulated learning across content domains
target_learning_goals: evaluating which learning techniques support retention, comprehension, and transfer
examples: Each of the 10 technique reviews is structured with sections on learning conditions, student characteristics, materials, criterion tasks, educational contexts, implementation, and overall assessment
key_sources: Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266

article_title: How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro
citation: Vibeke Normann Andersen and Kasper M. Hansen. (2007). How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro. European Journal of Political Research, Volume 46, Issue 4, pp. 531-556. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6765.2007.00699.x
title: Four-dimension framework for analyzing deliberative processes
description: The article organizes its analysis of the Deliberative Poll around four research questions that together form an evaluative framework for deliberative processes. As printed: "Four research questions regarding these deliberative processes are analyzed: openness and access, the quality of deliberation, efficiency and effectiveness, and publicity and accountability." Each dimension captures a distinct requirement a deliberative forum must meet — who may take part, how well the deliberation proceeds, whether it produces results, and whether it is publicly accountable — and the Danish euro Poll is assessed along all four.
requirements: A concrete deliberative forum (such as a Deliberative Poll) to which the four questions can be applied
constraints: The framework is applied here to one national Deliberative Poll on the single European currency
target_learners: Adult citizens participating in national deliberative forums
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the quality and democratic legitimacy of deliberative processes
examples: Analysis of the Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro along openness and access, quality of deliberation, efficiency and effectiveness, and publicity and accountability
key_sources: Vibeke Normann Andersen and Kasper M. Hansen. (2007). How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro. European Journal of Political Research, Volume 46, Issue 4, pp. 531-556. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6765.2007.00699.x

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Classroom Management Strategies and Classroom Management Programs on Students’ Academic, Behavioral, Emotional, and Motivational Outcomes
citation: Korpershoek, H., Harms, T., de Boer, H., van Kuijk, M., & Doolaard, S. (2016). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Classroom Management Strategies and Classroom Management Programs on Students' Academic, Behavioral, Emotional, and Motivational Outcomes. Review of Educational Research, 86(3), 643-680. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626799
title: Four-category taxonomy of classroom management strategy foci: teacher, student behavior, social-emotional development, and teacher–student relationships
description: The meta-analysis organizes classroom management programs by coding each included intervention for the presence or absence of four categories of strategies. As the article states, "Programs were coded for the presence/absence of four categories of strategies: focusing on the teacher, on student behavior, on students’ social-emotional development, and on teacher–student relationships." This taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the moderator analyses of which strategy foci drive intervention effectiveness in primary education.
requirements: Programs must be codable for presence/absence of each of the four strategy categories
constraints: Applied to primary education intervention studies published 2003–2013
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes
behavioral outcomes
social-emotional outcomes
motivational outcomes
examples: The 54 included programs were each coded for presence or absence of the four strategy categories and the codings were used in moderator analyses
key_sources: Korpershoek, H., Harms, T., de Boer, H., van Kuijk, M., & Doolaard, S. (2016). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Classroom Management Strategies and Classroom Management Programs on Students' Academic, Behavioral, Emotional, and Motivational Outcomes. Review of Educational Research, 86(3), 643-680. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626799

article_title: Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. [Aprendizaje cooperativo y rendimiento académico: ¿por qué funciona el trabajo en grupo?]
citation: Slavin, R. E. (2014). Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. Anales De Psicología, 30(3), 785–791. https://doi.org/10.6018/analesps.30.3.201201
title: Four theoretical perspectives on achievement effects of cooperative learning
description: The chapter organizes explanations for cooperative learning's achievement effects into four named perspectives: "Motivational, social cohesion, developmental, and cognitive elaboration." Each perspective offers a different account of why students working in small groups to help each other learn produces achievement gains, and the chapter reviews evidence for each before reconciling them.
requirements: Each perspective must be evaluated against evidence from practical classroom research on achievement effects
constraints: The perspectives concern achievement effects of cooperative learning specifically, not other outcomes
target_learners: students working in small groups in classrooms
target_learning_goals: academic achievement through cooperative learning
key_sources: Slavin, R. E. (2014). Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. Anales De Psicología, 30(3), 785–791. https://doi.org/10.6018/analesps.30.3.201201

article_title: Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course
citation: Breakstone, J., Smith, M., Connors, P., Ortega, T., Kerr, D., & Wineburg, S. (2021). Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course. Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) Misinformation Review. https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-56
title: Four one-hour course-embedded modules teaching fact checkers' evaluation strategies in an asynchronous nutrition course
description: The intervention consisted of four required, roughly hour-long weekly modules embedded in an asynchronous online nutrition course at a large state university. Each module combined three activity types: "videos provided direct instruction about evaluating the credibility of Internet sources" (Crash Course videos), guided evaluations of online sources tied to course content, and screencasts of a researcher modeling lateral reading, described as "cognitive modeling, an instructional approach that makes expert strategies visible to novice learners." Modules also addressed misconceptions such as trusting dot-org domains.
requirements: Modules were required course components with points awarded for completion, though module quality did not affect course grades
Examples tied to the course's subject matter (nutrition sources)
constraints: Instruction was delivered asynchronously via a learning management system; module quality did not affect course grades
target_learners: Undergraduate students in a required nutrition course, including majors and students fulfilling a general education requirement
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the credibility of online sources using fact checkers' strategies, especially lateral reading
examples: Module 2 introduced lateral reading with a Crash Course video, then students evaluated an American Council on Science and Health article and watched a screencast of a researcher applying lateral reading to it
key_sources: Breakstone, J., Smith, M., Connors, P., Ortega, T., Kerr, D., & Wineburg, S. (2021). Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course. Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) Misinformation Review. https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-56

article_title: Preventing social isolation and loneliness among older people: a systematic review of health promotion interventions
citation: MIMA CATTAN, MARTIN WHITE, JOHN BOND and ALISON LEARMOUTH. (2005). Preventing social isolation and loneliness among older people: a systematic review of health promotion interventions. Ageing & Society, Volume 25, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0144686X04002594
title: Four-category typology of health promotion interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness among older people
description: The review organises interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness among older people into four categories: "'group' (n=17); 'one-to-one' (n=10); 'service provision' (n=3); and 'community development' (n=1)". The typology sorts thirty quantitative outcome studies published between 1970 and 2002 by delivery format, enabling the review's comparison of effectiveness across intervention types. It underpins the review's finding that group activities with educational or support input predominated among effective interventions.
requirements: Quantitative outcome studies of health promotion interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness among older people, identified via electronic databases, journals, abstracts and key informants
constraints: Based on studies published between 1970 and 2002, most conducted in the USA and Canada
target_learning_goals: preventing and alleviating social isolation and loneliness
examples: The review categorised thirty identified studies: group (n=17), one-to-one (n=10), service provision (n=3) and community development (n=1).
key_sources: MIMA CATTAN, MARTIN WHITE, JOHN BOND and ALISON LEARMOUTH. (2005). Preventing social isolation and loneliness among older people: a systematic review of health promotion interventions. Ageing & Society, Volume 25, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0144686X04002594

article_title: Sense of Belonging as a Predictor of Intentions to Persist Among African American and White First-Year College Students
citation: Hausmann, L.R.M., Schofield, J.W. & Woods, R.L. (2007). Sense of Belonging as a Predictor of Intentions to Persist Among African American and White First-Year College Students. Research in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-007-9052-9
title: College retention programs should address students' sense of belonging, since belonging predicts persistence intentions and can be bolstered by intervention
description: The article argues that retention programming should incorporate students' sense of belonging to their university. Belonging predicted persistence intentions controlling for other predictors, and a randomized intervention to enhance belonging slowed the typical first-year decline. The authors state that "implications for the development of college retention programs and for existing models of student persistence are discussed," grounding the recommendation in both the predictive and the intervention findings.
requirements: Programs must be able to reach first-year students during the academic year, when belonging and persistence intentions decline.
constraints: The intervention evidence concerns slowing the decline in sense of belonging, not directly demonstrating improved retention.
target_learners: African American and white first-year college students
target_learning_goals: Persistence intentions and retention in higher education
examples: First-year students were randomly assigned to a belonging-enhancing intervention or one of two control groups and surveyed three times across the academic year.
key_sources: Hausmann, L.R.M., Schofield, J.W. & Woods, R.L. (2007). Sense of Belonging as a Predictor of Intentions to Persist Among African American and White First-Year College Students. Research in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-007-9052-9

article_title: Foreign and second language anxiety
citation: Elaine K. Horwitz. (2010). Foreign and second language anxiety. Language Teaching, Volume 43, Issue 2, April 2010, pp. 154-167. https://doi.org/10.1017/S026144480999036X
title: Foreign language anxiety (FLA) as a situation-specific anxiety construct
description: The article identifies foreign language anxiety (FLA) as a unique form of anxiety, identified in the mid-1980s, that some people experience in response to learning or using a second language. It is 'categorized as a situation-specific anxiety', comparable in kind to other familiar anxiety manifestations such as stage fright or test anxiety. This situation-specific conceptualization is what allowed language anxiety to be studied as a distinct construct rather than as generic anxiety.
requirements: Must be treated as distinct from trait, state, and achievement anxiety rather than as a generic anxiety measure
constraints: Applies specifically to anxiety experienced in response to learning and/or using an L2, not to anxiety in general
target_learning_goals: second language learning and production
examples: The article situates FLA's identification in the mid-1980s as a turning point after earlier mixed findings on anxiety and achievement
key_sources: Elaine K. Horwitz. (2010). Foreign and second language anxiety. Language Teaching, Volume 43, Issue 2, April 2010, pp. 154-167. https://doi.org/10.1017/S026144480999036X

article_title: Learning Simple and Complex Second Language Rules Under Implicit, Incidental, Rule-Search, and Instructed Conditions
citation: Peter Robinson. (1996). Learning Simple and Complex Second Language Rules Under Implicit, Incidental, Rule-Search, and Instructed Conditions. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 27-67. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100014674
title: Four-condition computerized training design for implicit, incidental, rule-search, and instructed L2 rule learning
description: A computerized training apparatus in which 104 adult ESL learners were randomly assigned to implicit, incidental, rule-search, or instructed conditions, then judged novel tokens of easy and hard rule sentence types. Speed and accuracy of these grammaticality judgments served as the dependent measures, allowing comparison of learning conditions across simple and complex rules in a single randomized design.
requirements: Random assignment of learners across the four training conditions and computerized presentation of training and judgment trials
constraints: Studied with adult learners of English as a second language in a computerized laboratory setting
target_learners: Adult learners of English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Acquiring simple and complex second language grammatical rules under different attentional and instructional conditions
examples: One hundred four adult learners randomly assigned to the four conditions; speed and accuracy of judgments of novel tokens used as dependent measures
key_sources: Peter Robinson. (1996). Learning Simple and Complex Second Language Rules Under Implicit, Incidental, Rule-Search, and Instructed Conditions. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 27-67. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100014674

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: A framework that supplies a rationale for formative assessment within theories of pedagogy and unifies the diverse set of practices described as formative.
description: The article proposes a framework whose purpose is twofold: to give formative assessment a rationale located within broader theories of pedagogy, and to unify the heterogeneous practices that have been called formative. The authors state that "This paper aims to offer such a rationale, within a framework which can also unify the diverse set of practices which have been described as formative." The framework is then used analytically to connect formative assessment with other pedagogic initiatives and with literatures on self-regulated learning and classroom discourse, and to guide teacher implementation work.
requirements: Serves as an organizing rationale for practices already described as formative; it presupposes the existing body of formative assessment practice it seeks to unify.
constraints: The article presents it as a rationale and unifying framework, not as an empirically tested model; the full text beyond the abstract was not accessible here.
target_learning_goals: Improving learning through formative assessment practices embedded in pedagogy
examples: The article states the framework is used to relate formative assessment to cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, self-regulated learning models, and classroom discourse.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Formative assessment is related to cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, models of self-regulated learning, and classroom discourse within the proposed framework.
description: A second organizing contribution of the article is a set of theoretical linkages: the framework connects formative assessment to neighbouring pedagogic initiatives and research literatures. The abstract states: "The analysis is used to relate formative assessment both to other pedagogic initiatives, notably cognitive acceleration and dynamic assessment, and to some of the existing literature on models of self-regulated learning and on classroom discourse." This positions formative assessment not as an isolated assessment technique but as continuous with pedagogies that regulate and accelerate learning, with dynamic assessment traditions, with self-regulation models, and with classroom dialogue research.
requirements: The linkages depend on the article's unifying framework for formative assessment within pedagogy.
constraints: The article presents these as relations established by theoretical analysis, not as empirically demonstrated equivalences.
target_learners: School students in classrooms served by formative, dialogic, and cognitive-acceleration pedagogies
target_learning_goals: Regulating and developing learning through assessment, dialogue, and cognitive acceleration
examples: The article's keywords list the linked constructs: formative assessment, assessment for learning, dynamic assessment, self-regulation, cognitive acceleration, and dialogue.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback
citation: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158
title: Four-type negative feedback manipulation contrasted with a no-feedback comparison group
description: The study operationalizes negative feedback as four distinct types assigned between groups. Upon an error, "Group A subjects were given explicit metalinguistic information about the generalization we hoped they would learn"; "Group B subjects were told that their response was wrong"; "Group C subjects were corrected when they erred, giving them a model of the response desired along with implicit negative evidence that their response was incorrect"; and "Group D subjects, having made an error, were asked if they were sure about their response." A comparison group received no feedback. This taxonomy separates explicit metalinguistic, explicit rejection, model-plus-implicit-negative-evidence, and elicit-confirmation feedback types.
requirements: Learners must first be trained on the target structure so that errors can be elicited and feedback delivered upon error
constraints: Feedback was delivered in response to errors on a single trained structure, the English dative alternation, with adult Spanish-speaking ESL learners
target_learners: Adult Spanish-speaking learners of English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Learning abstract constraints on the English dative alternation
examples: Subjects were divided into groups according to the type of feedback they received when they made an error, with a no-feedback comparison group
key_sources: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158

article_title: Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI ‐generated feedback
citation: Er, Erkan; Akçapınar, Gökhan; Bayazıt, Alper; Noroozi, Omid; Banihashem, Seyyed Kazem. (2024). Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13558
title: Four-dimension feedback perception framework: usefulness, fairness, developmental value and encouragement
description: The study organises student perceptions of feedback into four constructs: usefulness (how easy feedback is to understand and apply), fairness, developmental value (feedback's capacity to guide improvement) and encouragement (positive comments acknowledging effort). It operationalises these with subscales adapted from Strijbos et al. (2010) and Lizzio and Wilson (2008), noting that "these perceptions influence whether and how students engage with and utilise feedback."
requirements: Validated perception subscales; students must have received feedback to rate
constraints: Perceptions may not always relate to desired learning outcomes, as the article notes some studies show perceptions can deviate from actual learning gains
target_learning_goals: understanding student engagement with feedback
examples: The study measured all four dimensions with 5-point Likert subscales and compared them between instructor- and AI-feedback conditions
key_sources: Er, Erkan; Akçapınar, Gökhan; Bayazıt, Alper; Noroozi, Omid; Banihashem, Seyyed Kazem. (2024). Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13558

article_title: Sequential effects of high and low instructional guidance on children’s acquisition of experimentation skills: Is it all in the timing?
citation: Matlen, B.J., Klahr, D. (2013). Sequential effects of high and low instructional guidance on children's acquisition of experimentation skills: Is it all in the timing?. Instructional Science, 41, 621–634. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9248-z
title: Four-sequence high/low guidance intervention for teaching CVS to third graders
description: An instructional intervention in which third-grade children received instruction in the control of variables strategy (CVS) under one of four orderings of guidance: "high followed by high (HH), high followed by low (HL), low followed by high (LH), and low followed by low (LL)". High guidance combined direct instruction with inquiry questions, while low guidance used only inquiry questions. The design allowed timing of guidance to be isolated as the manipulated factor.
requirements: Instruction in CVS delivered via the two guidance types: high guidance combining direct instruction and inquiry questions, low guidance using only inquiry questions
constraints: Studied with third-grade children learning simple experimental design procedures and concepts (CVS)
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the control of variables strategy (CVS) for designing experiments
long-term transfer of experimentation skills
examples: Children were assigned to HH, HL, LH, or LL sequences; after dropout, group sizes were HH = 14, HL = 11, LH = 14, LL = 13
key_sources: Matlen, B.J., Klahr, D. (2013). Sequential effects of high and low instructional guidance on children's acquisition of experimentation skills: Is it all in the timing?. Instructional Science, 41, 621–634. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9248-z

article_title: IDENTIFYING THE IMPACT OF NEGATIVE FEEDBACK AND LEARNERS' RESPONSES ON ESL QUESTION DEVELOPMENT
citation: Kim McDonough. (2005). IDENTIFYING THE IMPACT OF NEGATIVE FEEDBACK AND LEARNERS' RESPONSES ON ESL QUESTION DEVELOPMENT. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 27, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263105050047
title: Four-condition communicative task treatment contrasting negative feedback and modified output opportunities
description: The treatment consisted of a series of communicative tasks carried out with native English speakers under four conditions that differed in the negative feedback and modified output opportunities they provided. Sixty Thai EFL learners completed these tasks and four oral production tests over an 8-week period, allowing the study to separate the contribution of feedback provision from learners' production of modified output.
requirements: Native-speaker interlocutors during communicative tasks and repeated oral production tests to measure change.
constraints: Findings pertain to Thai EFL learners interacting with native English speakers on these tasks over 8 weeks.
target_learning_goals: ESL question development
examples: Learners carried out communicative tasks with native English speakers in four conditions and completed four oral production tests over 8 weeks.
key_sources: Kim McDonough. (2005). IDENTIFYING THE IMPACT OF NEGATIVE FEEDBACK AND LEARNERS' RESPONSES ON ESL QUESTION DEVELOPMENT. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 27, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263105050047

article_title: Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges
citation: Frederick L. Oswald and Luke Plonsky. (2010). Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, Volume 30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190510000115
title: Four-stage model of conducting a meta-analysis in SLA research
description: The review organizes the conduct of a meta-analysis in second language acquisition research into four typical stages: "defining the research domain," "developing a reliable coding scheme," "analyzing data," and "interpreting results." The model frames meta-analysis as a staged process in which each stage requires choices, and the article uses it to structure its discussion of the benefits and challenges that inform those decisions in SLA meta-analyses.
requirements: Each stage requires deliberate decisions by the researcher; the coding scheme must be developed to be reliable for the results to be meaningful
constraints: The model is presented as describing typical stages of meta-analysis in SLA research specifically
target_learners: second language acquisition researchers conducting syntheses
target_learning_goals: systematic quantitative synthesis of L2 research findings
examples: The review describes typical stages of a meta-analysis in second language acquisition (SLA) research across four numbered steps
key_sources: Frederick L. Oswald and Luke Plonsky. (2010). Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, Volume 30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190510000115

article_title: Effects of a formative assessment script on how vocational students generate formative feedback to a peer’s or their own performance
citation: Peters, O., Körndle, H. & Narciss, S. (2018). Effects of a formative assessment script on how vocational students generate formative feedback to a peer's or their own performance. Eur J Psychol Educ, 33, 117–143. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-017-0344-y
title: Formative Assessment Script (FAS) for generating formative peer and internal feedback
description: The FAS is a collaboration-script instructional support designed to scaffold vocational students in generating formative feedback, in separate versions for feedback to a peer's performance and to one's own performance. The study investigated "effects of a formative assessment script (FAS) that was designed to support vocational students in generating feedback to (1) a peer's and (2) their own performance." It was applied during a technical planning task in which students first produced individual drafts and then gave feedback on a fictitious erroneous peer draft and on their own drafts.
requirements: Students work on a performance product (a draft) that can be evaluated against criteria, so that feedback comments, detected errors, and improvement suggestions can be generated.
constraints: Benefits for internal feedback are partial: no gains in detecting missing information or generating improvement suggestions for one's own draft.
target_learning_goals: generating formative feedback to a peer's performance
generating internal feedback to one's own performance
examples: Students produced individual drafts for a technical planning task, then gave peer feedback on a fictitious erroneous peer draft and subsequently on their own drafts, with or without FAS support.
key_sources: Peters, O., Körndle, H. & Narciss, S. (2018). Effects of a formative assessment script on how vocational students generate formative feedback to a peer's or their own performance. Eur J Psychol Educ, 33, 117–143. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-017-0344-y

article_title: Four Ways of Considering Emotion in Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Plass, J. L., & Kalyuga, S. (2019). Four Ways of Considering Emotion in Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 339–359. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09473-5
title: Four-perspective taxonomy of emotion–cognitive load relationships understood through an interval view of cognitive load
description: The article organizes the relationship between emotion and cognitive load theory into four perspectives: emotion as extraneous load, emotion's direct effects on encoding, storage, and retrieval, emotion as part of intrinsic load, and emotion's effect on motivation and mental effort. The authors state that "These four ways of considering emotion as part of CLT are best understood when taking an interval view of cognitive load." The taxonomy serves as a framework for integrating emotion into cognitive load theory rather than treating emotion as a single undifferentiated factor.
requirements: Cognitive load theory must be interpreted through an interval view of cognitive load for the four perspectives to be coherent
constraints: The framework is theoretical; the article presents it as a discussion of perspectives rather than an empirically tested model
target_learning_goals: understanding how emotion interacts with cognitive load during learning
key_sources: Plass, J. L., & Kalyuga, S. (2019). Four Ways of Considering Emotion in Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 339–359. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09473-5

article_title: Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning
citation: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5
title: Four-constraint framework for when prompted self-explanation aids learning
description: The article proposes that self-explanation's effectiveness is bounded by four constraints: the target outcomes and domain, what is being explained, the design of explanation prompts, and effectiveness relative to alternative instructional techniques. As the authors state, the constraints "will facilitate a priori predictions of whether prompted self-explanation will improve learning in a particular context." The framework is grounded in the processes of knowledge integration and knowledge generalization that self-explanation is thought to support.
requirements: Learners must generate explanations that are inferences going beyond the given information, generated by and for the learner
constraints: The constraints address prompted self-explanation, defined by condition, not spontaneous self-explanation, because control-condition learners may self-explain spontaneously
target_learners: learners across a range of age groups, from preschool children to adults
target_learning_goals: comprehension
transfer
retention of new information
examples: The authors synthesized experimentally manipulated self-explanation studies identified via PsychInfo and ERIC searches and citation checking
key_sources: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5

article_title: Form-Focussed Instruction and Second Language Acquisition: A Review of Classroom and Laboratory Research
citation: Nina Spada. (1997). Form-Focussed Instruction and Second Language Acquisition: A Review of Classroom and Laboratory Research. Language Teaching, Volume 30, Issue 2, pp. 73-87. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261444800012799
title: Form-focused instruction is an organizing framework for reviewing second language acquisition research across classroom and laboratory settings
description: The article is a state-of-the-art review organized around form-focused instruction as its central construct, examining its relationship to second language acquisition. Its title announces the scope as "A Review of Classroom and Laboratory Research", indicating that the framework is applied to studies conducted both in classrooms and in laboratory settings. The review appears in Language Teaching as a survey of this research area rather than a primary experimental study.
requirements: Access to the full review text to apply the framework's detailed findings
constraints: The supplied record prints only the title, metadata, and reference list; the review's internal taxonomy of form-focused instruction types is not recoverable from the accessible text
target_learners: second language learners in classroom and laboratory instructional settings
target_learning_goals: second language grammar and form learning
examples: Published as a State-of-the-Art Article in Language Teaching, Volume 30, Issue 2, April 1997, pp. 73-87
key_sources: Nina Spada. (1997). Form-Focussed Instruction and Second Language Acquisition: A Review of Classroom and Laboratory Research. Language Teaching, Volume 30, Issue 2, pp. 73-87. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261444800012799

article_title: The influence of retrieval on retention
citation: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03204076
title: After some learning is achieved, learners should be given forced retrievals without the target material present
description: The article draws a direct practical implication from its findings: "the optimal method of paired-associate learning should include a large number of test trials" and, after some degree of learning, the learner should face forced retrievals without the target material present. This follows from the four experiments showing that retrieval produced better retention than equivalent-time study. The authors note flashcards embody an implicit belief in test trials, but say the phenomenon is hardly mentioned in the educational literature and call for analysis of where test trials help.
requirements: Some degree of learning must already have been achieved before the forced-retrieval trials
constraints: The evidence comes from paired-associate rote learning with undergraduate subjects in controlled laboratory experiments
target_learners: learners of paired-associate or vocabulary material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned pairs
examples: In the TTST condition, subjects attempted to say the response term aloud during a 5-sec period in which only the stimulus term was present, before the response term appeared
key_sources: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03202713

article_title: Knowledge as a formative construct: A good alpha is not always better
citation: Stadler, Matthias, Michael Sailer, and Frank Fischer. 2021. “Knowledge as a formative construct: a good alpha is not always better.” New Ideas in Psychology 60: 100832. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.newideapsych.2020.100832.
title: Formative versus reflective measurement models as a framework for relating constructs to their indicators
description: The article distinguishes two measurement models. In reflective models, "manifest indicators can be the effects" of latent variables, as with general intelligence; in formative models, indicators "form a latent construct or cause the changes that occur in it", as with socioeconomic status. The article uses this framework, adapted from Bollen and Lennox, to argue that domain knowledge assessment usually misfits reflective assumptions.
requirements: Researchers must provide persuasive theoretical arguments for the merit of each formative indicator, since inclusion or exclusion of an indicator changes the construct.
constraints: The article frames this as an argument about construct conceptualization in structural equation modeling, not a tested empirical result.
target_learners: students whose domain knowledge is assessed in educational research
target_learning_goals: valid assessment and modeling of domain knowledge
examples: The article contrasts general intelligence as a reflective example with socioeconomic status, where income, education and occupational prestige form the construct.
key_sources: Stadler, Matthias, Michael Sailer, and Frank Fischer. 2021. “Knowledge as a formative construct: a good alpha is not always better.” New Ideas in Psychology 60: 100832. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.newideapsych.2020.100832.

article_title: Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project
citation: J. 't Gilde, M. Volman. (2021). Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project. Cambridge Journal of Education, 51(6), 673-692. https://doi.org/10.1080/0305764X.2021.1906845
title: Framework for finding students' funds of knowledge and categorising FoK/I-related teaching practices
description: A framework produced by the project's analyses that serves two functions: it "suggests ways to find students’ FoK" and it categorises FoK/I-related teaching practices along two dimensions — (1) individual students' resources vs. collective resources and (2) scope of the teaching activities. It is the article's central artifact for supporting teachers in superdiverse primary classrooms.
requirements: Teachers need ways to find students' funds of knowledge before FoK/I-related teaching practices can be categorised and used.
constraints: Developed within a collaborative action research project in superdiverse primary schools.
target_learners: primary school students in superdiverse classrooms
target_learning_goals: identifying and building on students' funds of knowledge/identity in teaching
examples: The framework emerged from analysis of pre-structured logbooks, teacher interviews and focus groups collected in the project.
key_sources: J. 't Gilde, M. Volman. (2021). Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project. Cambridge Journal of Education, 51(6), 673-692. https://doi.org/10.1080/0305764X.2021.1906845

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Four orientations of academics' conceptions of graduate attributes: precursory, complementary, translation and enabling
description: The paper presents Barrie's (2006) phenomenographic analysis identifying four distinct orientations academics hold toward graduate attributes: 'precursory, complementary, translation and enabling'. Precursory attributes are fundamental skills for learning; complementary skills sit alongside disciplinary knowledge; translation attributes apply disciplinary knowledge in real-world contexts; enabling attributes 'infuse and enable all scholarly learning' and transcend disciplinary boundaries. Each orientation implies a distinctly different focus for teaching, learning and assessment, and multiple conceptualisations may underpin one institution's practice.
requirements: Assessment design must be matched to the conception of the attribute being assessed
constraints: Students may encounter inconsistent or contradictory evidence requirements for similarly labelled attributes across courses in a single programme
target_learning_goals: graduate attributes including critical thinking and disciplinary application skills
examples: From a complementary perspective a standardised test such as the California Critical Thinking Skills Test may suffice, while an enabling perspective would require students to make and justify a claim to the attribute based on collected evidence
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: In vivo experiments on whether supporting metacognition in intelligent tutoring systems yields robust learning
citation: Koedinger, K., Aleven, V., Roll, I., & Baker, R. (2008). In vivo experiments on whether supporting metacognition in intelligent tutoring systems yields robust learning. https://learnlab.org/
title: Four-level framework of goals for metacognitive tutoring toward robust learning
description: The chapter organizes metacognitive tutoring research around four cumulative goals, depicted in Figure 1, in which "less ambitious and more proximal goals... support the more ambitious, ultimate goals above." As printed, "The first goal is for students to improve their metacognitive behavior within the learning environment while they receive metacognitive support," followed by better domain learning, internalization of the practices in subsequent instruction, and accelerated future domain learning. The authors state an ideal experiment measures all four levels, but their work has mainly addressed the first two, with the third addressed only in the help-seeking experiments and the fourth left for future work.
requirements: Experiments evaluating metacognitive support should measure behavior in the supported environment, domain learning, internalized metacognitive behavior, and future domain learning to test the full framework
constraints: So far the research program has focused mainly on the first two goals; the fourth goal remains for future work
target_learners: high-school and middle-school mathematics students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: metacognitive strategies such as self-explanation, error self-correction, help seeking, and avoiding gaming the system
examples: The self-explanation and error self-correction lines assessed domain learning only; the help-seeking experiments additionally assessed whether help-seeking behavior improved after the intervention
key_sources: Koedinger, K., Aleven, V., Roll, I., & Baker, R. (2008). In vivo experiments on whether supporting metacognition in intelligent tutoring systems yields robust learning. https://learnlab.org/

article_title: Illusions of competence during study can be remedied by manipulations that enhance learners’ sensitivity to retrieval conditions at test
citation: Koriat, A., & Bjork, R. A. (2006). Illusions of competence during study can be remedied by manipulations that enhance learners' sensitivity to retrieval conditions at test. Memory & Cognition, 34(5), 959-972. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03193694
title: The foresight bias account: overconfidence arises from the mismatch between study conditions, where the answer is present, and test conditions, where it is absent
description: The article proposes that judgments of learning made during study are inflated because the answer is present at study but absent, but solicited, at test. It distinguishes a priori association (the probability the cue alone brings the target to mind) from a posteriori association (the perceived association when both words are present), arguing that "a priori associations are the more critical for performance during cued recall" while a posteriori associations dominate predictions. When a posteriori associations are strong relative to a priori ones, learners fall prey to an illusion of competence; remediation requires conditions at study that sensitize learners to retrieval conditions at test.
requirements: Remediation requires creating conditions at study that sensitize learners to retrieval conditions at test, such as test experience or delayed, cue-alone JOLs.
constraints: Delayed JOLs reduced but did not eliminate the foresight bias in Experiment 4.
The account is developed for paired-associate learning with asymmetrically associated word pairs.
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of future recall
effective allocation of study time
examples: Backward-associated pairs such as cheese–cheddar, whose target-to-cue association is strong but cue-to-target association weak, induced inflated JOLs in Koriat and Bjork's (2005) experiments.
key_sources: Koriat, A., & Bjork, R. A. (2006). Illusions of competence during study can be remedied by manipulations that enhance learners' sensitivity to retrieval conditions at test. Memory & Cognition, 34(5), 959-972. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03193244

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Four-part framework for conceptualizing the tradeoffs of learning analytics methods: sampling, capturing, reduction, and pattern finding
description: The article proposes a framework for thinking about what LA methods add to the learning sciences method space. It states: "We suggest here a simple four-part framework to help us conceptualize this new space of tradeoffs: (a) sampling, (b) capturing, (c) reduction, and (d) pattern ﬁnding." Each part is a stage at which any method trades breadth against depth: sampling concerns which learning phenomena are studied, capturing which aspects are recorded, reduction how captured data are transformed, and pattern finding how patterns are discovered and confirmed. LA reshapes each tradeoff rather than eliminating it.
requirements: Researchers must articulate the learning sciences' fundamental assumptions about learning when selecting among methods, since "Any method that we might use has strengths and weaknesses."
constraints: The article notes that when applying LA, researchers "are more likely to restrict our study to learning activities that are conducted using computers (though, as we will see, this is not an absolute requirement)."
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers and educational researchers selecting research methods
target_learning_goals: Understanding methodological tradeoffs in studying learning processes with computational methods
examples: The framework is used to compare student written responses, video recordings, and computer log files as capture types, and to position LA between traditional quantitative and qualitative methods in reduction labor.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia
citation: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388
title: A three-foundations by three-sources framework for organizing research and theory on interactive multimedia
description: The article proposes a matrix framework for organizing research and theory relevant to interactive multimedia design. As printed, "The matrix shown in Table 1 organizes existing research and theory according to foundations--psychological, pedagogical, technological--and basic sources-general, component, primary." Foundations represent fundamental influences on learning-system design, while sources represent how generalizable the principles are, from media-independent psychological theory to capabilities of specific interactive multimedia technologies. The framework is used throughout the article to root each design principle in identifiable empirical and theoretical referents.
requirements: Design decisions must draw on multiple foundations together, since in practice the foundations and sources interact rather than being applied in isolation
constraints: The principles and implications derived are explicitly not all-inclusive, but represent the range of empirically referenced guidelines extractable from the framework
target_learners: designers and developers of interactive multimedia learning systems
target_learning_goals: grounding interactive multimedia design decisions in empirical research and theory
examples: Table 2 maps specific concepts and authors, such as schema theory, dual coding, anchored instruction, and disorientation, into the framework's cells
key_sources: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388

article_title: Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally
citation: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x
title: Four categories of cultural differences affecting cross-cultural online instructional design
description: The study organizes the cultural differences designers encountered into four categories: "general cultural and social expectations, teaching and learning expectations, differences in the use of language and symbols, and technological infrastructure and familiarity." These categories emerged from interviews rather than being imposed from prior frameworks such as Hofstede's, reflecting the study's grounded-theory approach. They serve as a map of where designers should probe learner contexts.
requirements: Designers must investigate each category for the specific learner population rather than assume group-level generalizations apply to individuals
constraints: Categories emerged from 12 practitioners' lived experience in an exploration study; the authors call for research on how each category can be expanded and better measured
target_learning_goals: Culturally responsive design of online instruction
examples: Mike described Tongan social protocols around rank affecting reception of distance learning; Ian described Australian indigenous oral traditions complicating literacy assumptions; Joey described unreliable internet access becoming "a barrier and an exclusion instead of an inclusion."
key_sources: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x

article_title: Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game
citation: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2016.05.047
title: Four-facet problem solving competency model grounded in rule acquisition and rule application
description: The article's competency model divides problem solving skill into four facets: "analyzing givens and constraints", "planning a solution pathway", "using tools and resources effectively and efficiently", and "monitoring and evaluating progress". The first facet maps to rule acquisition and the remaining three to rule application, following recent research distinguishing knowledge acquisition from knowledge application. The model was developed from a literature review and implemented in Bayesian networks, one per game level, to produce overall and facet-level estimates.
requirements: In-game indicators must be identified for each facet to supply evidence to the Bayes nets
constraints: The model was developed and calibrated for middle-school students playing Use Your Brainz; the article notes the need to verify results with a larger sample
target_learning_goals: problem solving skill, overall and on four facets
examples: The model was implemented in Use Your Brainz with 32 indicators distributed across the four facets and a unique Bayes net for each of 42 game levels
key_sources: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2016.05.047

article_title: Critical Ethical Reasoning and Role-Play
citation: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313
title: Four grounded categories of player preference and game features: effecting change, mirroring, social context, and significant decisions
description: From grounded-theory-informed analysis of the interview themes, the article proposes four categories encompassing both preference and fact themes: effecting change (desire for character actions to change the game world), mirroring (desire for emotional bond and for the game world to reflect the valence of the player's actions), social context (desire for a consistent, rich social environment), and significant decisions (desire to control the character's behavior through legitimate, experienced-as-important choices). When applied to the factual themes, the four categories explained them as well, which the authors take as partial validation of the scheme.
requirements: The categories were built up from preference themes and then applied to factual themes to partially check their validity
constraints: The authors caution that the sample is small when positing the validity of the categorization scheme
target_learners: game designers and researchers of role-play learning environments
target_learning_goals: fostering critical ethical reasoning through role-play
examples: The categories are used to derive four criteria for fostering ethical decision making in games, each illustrated with an interview excerpt such as Eileen's Oblivion account of suffering consequences like being bitten by a vampire
key_sources: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313

article_title: Critical Ethical Reasoning and Role-Play
citation: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313
title: Design games for ethical decision making by providing consequential choices, mirrored emotional valence, rich social context, and significant decisions
description: The article derives four design criteria for fostering ethical decision making within games from its four emergent categories. Player choices must have the potential to effect change in the game world; players must have the emotional valence of their choices mirrored back to them, typically through responses of other in-game characters; games must provide a sufficiently rich in-game social context to render actions significant beyond the individual level; and players must be given the opportunity to make significant decisions that let them inhabit their characters with their own game-related intentions, desires, and goals.
requirements: Choices must be legitimate rather than predetermined, since apparent choices where outcomes are identical undermine significance
constraints: The four categories are tightly intertwined and regularly overlap in practice; games vary greatly in how successfully they manage this effect
target_learning_goals: critical ethical decision making
empathy and perspective taking
examples: Eileen's Elder Scrolls: Oblivion account illustrates effecting change (no do-over, suffering consequences such as becoming a vampire); Robert's Final Fantasy VI account of Shadow's daughter illustrates mirroring; Fergus's Knights of the Old Republic 2 account of the Jedi's warning illustrates social context; Eileen's assassins guild choice illustrates significant decisions
key_sources: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313

article_title: Early predictors of middle school fraction knowledge
citation: Bailey Drew H., Siegler Robert S., Geary David C. (2014). Early Predictors of Middle School Fraction Knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12155
title: Focus elementary and middle school mathematics instruction on whole numbers and fractions
description: The article argues that longitudinal evidence lends support to the National Mathematics Advisory Panel's central recommendation that "mathematics instruction in elementary and middle school focus on promoting knowledge of whole numbers and fractions". First graders' whole number magnitude and arithmetic knowledge were uniquely predictive of middle school fraction knowledge, and fifth graders' fraction knowledge predicted tenth graders' mathematics achievement. The authors tie this to the trend toward focusing on fewer mathematical goals pursued in more depth.
requirements: Longitudinal evidence identifying which early strands uniquely contribute to later achievement
constraints: No data are yet available on whether early proficiency in geometry and data analysis/statistics uniquely contributes to later mathematics achievement
target_learning_goals: whole number magnitude knowledge
whole number arithmetic proficiency
fraction magnitude and arithmetic knowledge
examples: The authors note the Common Core State Standards Initiative embodies the trend toward focusing on fewer mathematical goals and pursuing them in more depth
key_sources: Bailey Drew H., Siegler Robert S., Geary David C. (2014). Early Predictors of Middle School Fraction Knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12155

article_title: Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school
citation: Lyn D English and Jane M Watson. (2015). Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school. International Journal of STEM Education (2015) 2:3. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-015-0016-x
title: Four-level developmental hierarchy of appreciation of variation (prerequisites, partial recognition, applications, critical aspects)
description: The article adopts, from Watson et al. (2003), a four-level hierarchy of increasing appreciation of variation used to frame its research questions and interpret student responses. Level 1 covers prerequisites such as interpreting context and simple graph reading; level 2, partial recognition, involves "putting ideas in context but focusing on single aspects and neglecting others"; level 3, applications, consolidates ideas in context with inconsistency on the most salient features; level 4, critical aspects, employs complex justification or critical reasoning. The study maps its three research questions to levels 2, 3 and 4 respectively.
requirements: Assessment of responses requires coding criteria that can distinguish descriptions, single-aspect focus, consolidation in context, and complex justification
constraints: The article states its assessment was more general than the Watson et al. survey and could only consider descriptively whether responses exhibited the type of thinking typical of the four levels
target_learners: elementary school students, with the hierarchy spanning grade levels 3 to 9 in its original development
target_learning_goals: understanding of variation in statistical investigations
statistical thinking and informal inference
examples: The study assumed all students had reached level 1, Prerequisites for Variation, and linked research question 1 to level 2, question 2 to level 3, and question 3 to level 4
key_sources: Lyn D English and Jane M Watson. (2015). Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school. International Journal of STEM Education (2015) 2:3. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-015-0016-x

article_title: Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood
citation: Hastings, E. C., & West, R. L. (2011). Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood. Neuropsychology, Development, and Cognition. Section B, Aging, Neuropsychology and Cognition, 18(4), 471-493. https://doi.org/10.1080/13825585.2011.575926
title: Foster learning goals and avoid performance-goal emphasis when supporting adult memory learners
description: Because dispositional learning goals were adaptive and performance goals maladaptive for memory self-efficacy in adulthood, instruction for adult memory learners should emphasize skill mastery and improvement over outcome evaluation. The article reports that "learning goals had a significant positive effect on memory self-efficacy, and that performance goals had a significant negative effect on self-efficacy", with effects on memory operating indirectly through self-efficacy. Framing memory tasks as opportunities to build mastery rather than as tests of fixed ability aligns with these findings.
requirements: Goal orientation must be measured or addressed alongside domain-specific self-efficacy, since the goals' impact on memory occurred via memory self-efficacy
constraints: The study was cross-sectional; the memory task was an incidental word game that may not have engaged goal orientations, and the authors note a more challenging task might yield different results
target_learning_goals: memory performance
memory self-efficacy
examples: The study measured dispositional goal orientation with the GOQ and memory self-efficacy with the MSEQ-4, then assessed free and cued recall in a telephone word game
key_sources: Hastings, E. C., & West, R. L. (2011). Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood. Neuropsychology, Development, and Cognition. Section B, Aging, Neuropsychology and Cognition, 18(4), 471-493. https://doi.org/10.1080/13825585.2011.575926

article_title: Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops
citation: Martínez-Alcalá CI, Rosales-Lagarde A, Alonso-Lavernia MÁ, Ramírez-Salvador JÁ, Jiménez-Rodríguez B, Cepeda-Rebollar RM, López-Noguerola JS, Bautista-Díaz ML and Agis-Juárez RA (2018) Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops. Front. ICT 5:21. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2018.00021
title: Four-point educational model for older adults' digital literacy
description: The article proposes that the educational model toward digital literacy of the elderly should be based on 4 important points: "Usefulness of Learning", "Cooperativeness and collaboration", "Fostering social inclusion", and "Promoting autonomy". Learning should be personalized, cooperative, collaborative and meaningful, grounded in andragogy and the biological, psychological and social characteristics of older age. The workshops in this study instantiate this pattern, with tutors trained in andragogy and gerontology support staff providing personalized attention.
requirements: Content must be designed considering the learning styles, interests and expectations of the older individual; motivation should be the main factor in any educational program for this population
target_learners: older adults aged 60 and above with little or no ICT knowledge
target_learning_goals: digital competencies that respond to personal and social needs, social inclusion through the web, and learner autonomy
examples: The digital literacy workshops had a tutor with knowledge about andragogy, as well as support staff who were gerontology students
key_sources: Martínez-Alcalá CI, Rosales-Lagarde A, Alonso-Lavernia MÁ, Ramírez-Salvador JÁ, Jiménez-Rodríguez B, Cepeda-Rebollar RM, López-Noguerola JS, Bautista-Díaz ML and Agis-Juárez RA (2018) Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops. Front. ICT 5:21. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2018.00021

article_title: Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: an event‐related brain potential study
citation: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x
title: Foundational-skill hypothesis: atypical development of core neurocognitive systems (e.g., selective attention) has cascading consequences on later learning
description: The article proposes that academic underachievement among children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds "might be related most strongly to the development of certain foundational skills or neural systems," such that "atypical development of a foundational skill could have cascading consequences on later development and learning." The theory motivates identifying specific neurocognitive deficits early in development so that focused interventions can target these systems. The present ERP study instantiates this framework by tracing the SES-linked attention difference to a specific early mechanism, distractor suppression within 100 msec, and by arguing that difficulty filtering distracting sounds could render typical environments, including classrooms, poorly suited for learning.
requirements: Interventions informed by this framework depend on identifying specific neurocognitive deficits "early in development" so they can target the systems most in need
constraints: The article states the present study "was not designed to answer causal questions about the relationship between the neural mechanisms of selective attention and skill in other domains"; poor spatial resolution of ERPs prevents strong conclusions about which neural networks are involved
target_learners: children aged 3–8 years from diverse socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: founding academic skills including selective attention, language, and reading
examples: The article links poor suppression to potential reading difficulty: readers must suppress prepotent responses to similar learned words (e.g., encountering cot without reading it as cat), and letter-focus training interventions are associated with improved decoding skill
key_sources: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x

article_title: “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children's metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities
citation: Ebru Aydın, Çağlayan Dinçer. (2022). “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children’s metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities. Thinking Skills and Creativity 45 (2022) 101104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101104
title: Four-category coding framework for young children's metacognitive knowledge: knowledge of self, others, universal properties of cognition, and task-specific strategies
description: The study develops a coding system for analyzing young children's metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in mathematical measurement activities. Building on Whitebread et al.'s (2009, 2010) framework and prior research with young children, the authors devised four category codes: "(a) knowledge of self, (b) knowledge of others, (c) knowledge of universal properties of cognition, and (d) knowledge of task-specific strategies." These four metacognitive knowledge variables were used as category codes to code the children's interactions in video transcripts and observation forms. The framework treats knowledge of tasks and strategies together in a task-specific way, since activities included certain mathematical tasks/goals so children's cognitive strategies could be considered in a task-specific way.
requirements: Activities must include certain mathematical tasks/goals so children's cognitive strategies can be considered in a task-specific way
Video recordings and observation forms of peer interactions are needed as data sources
constraints: Developed from and applied to two 5-year-old children in one kindergarten class over 16 measurement activities
The framework was mapped according to but not limited by Whitebread et al.'s (2009, 2010) framework for young children's metacognitive knowledge
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive knowledge in mathematical measurement activities
examples: Applied to 28 hours of video recording transcripts of 16 activities; inter-coder agreement of %84.2 on a randomly selected activity
key_sources: Ebru Aydın, Çağlayan Dinçer. (2022). “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children’s metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities. Thinking Skills and Creativity 45 (2022) 101104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101104

article_title: Efficacy of Learning Strategies Instruction in Adult Education
citation: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291
title: Four-phase modified SIM explicit instruction model for adult learners
description: The article describes a modified Strategic Instruction Model (SIM) instructional method adapted for adult-to-adult interaction in four phases: Phase 1 addresses learning readiness, goal setting and commitment; Phase 2 reviews and builds fundamental skills needed for the target strategy; Phase 3 is when "students are expected to master the target strategy"; Phase 4 is a generalization process applying strategies to different text types in academic, employment, and other settings. Within Phases 2 and 3, instructors guide learners through a four-step acquisition process of describe, model, scaffolded practice and feedback, and progress or mastery checks, with scaffolding incrementally removed and progress graphed to keep learners motivated.
requirements: Instructors trained in the scripted strategy and instructional method
Audio or video recording of sessions for fidelity review
constraints: The method was designed for explicit, intensive delivery, which the authors found elusive in adult education settings with typical attendance patterns
target_learners: Adult basic education learners with low literacy or limited educational attainment
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and reading-related subskills
Acquisition and generalization of learning strategies
examples: Instructors modeled strategies by vocalizing their own thinking processes, and learner practice moved from verbal to guided, partner, and independent practice
key_sources: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291

article_title: Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish‐learning children
citation: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/
title: Four measures of maternal child-directed speech coded from play-session transcripts
description: The study quantified caregiver input using four measures of maternal speech coded from video-recorded 12-minute play sessions transcribed under CHILDES protocols: number of utterances, number of word tokens, number of word types, and mean length of utterance (MLU, in words per utterance for romance languages). The first two estimate amount of talk during a fixed-length session, word types index lexical diversity, and MLU indexes grammatical complexity. Each maternal word was coded for word root, part of speech, tense, number and person using the Spanish-language mor utility in CHILDES.
requirements: Video- and audio-recorded mother–child play sessions with age-appropriate toys
Transcription by trained native Spanish-speakers following CHILDES protocols
Double-checking of transcripts and codings for accuracy
constraints: Transcripts were reduced to 12 minutes based on the shortest play session, beginning 2 minutes after participants were comfortably engaged
target_learners: Mothers of children aged 18 months in Spanish-speaking, primarily low-SES immigrant families
target_learning_goals: Characterizing quantity, diversity, and grammatical complexity of child-directed speech as predictors of children's lexical development
examples: Mean values at 18 months: 210.6 utterances, 609.1 word tokens, 110.5 word types, MLU 2.9 words (Table 2)
key_sources: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/

article_title: A review study about creativity in adolescence: Where is the social context?
citation: van der Zanden, P. J. A. C.; Meijer, P. C.; Beghetto, R. A. (2020). A review study about creativity in adolescence: Where is the social context? Thinking Skills and Creativity, 38, article 100702. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100702
title: Four-category classification of factors in adolescent creativity: individual, parental, educational, and social contextual
