description: The review organizes findings from 65 studies on adolescent creativity into a four-category framework: individual factors (demographics, personality and affect, motivation, academic achievement), parental factors (parental support, parental involvement), educational factors (freedom and structure, teacher-student relationship, collaborative learning, playful activities, tools), and social contextual factors. The authors state: "We classified supportive and inhibiting factors into four categories: individual factors, parental factors, educational factors, and social contextual factors." They acknowledge the categories may be interrelated rather than discrete, noting that from a sociocultural standpoint it would be problematic to view the factors as clearly distinguishable.
requirements: Studies must report relationships between specific variables and creativity in adolescents aged 12-19 to be classified within the framework
constraints: The authors acknowledge the categories may be conceptualized as interrelated rather than fixed or discrete, and different researchers may conceptualize them differently
target_learning_goals: Creativity development in adolescence
examples: The review mapped each of the 65 sampled studies to Tables 1-3 by which factor category prevailed, and Fig. 1 illustrates the factors as interrelated with bi-directional arrows
key_sources: van der Zanden, P. J. A. C.; Meijer, P. C.; Beghetto, R. A. (2020). A review study about creativity in adolescence: Where is the social context? Thinking Skills and Creativity, 38, article 100702. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100702

article_title: Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity
citation: Petersen, I. T., Hoyniak, C. P., McQuillan, M. E., Bates, J. E., & Staples, A. D. (2016). Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity. Developmental Review, 40, 25-71. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.02.001
title: Four-cluster taxonomy of complex inhibitory control task demands: perceptual, performance, association, and motivational inhibition
description: The review groups complex inhibitory control tasks into four a priori clusters by task demand: "perceptual inhibition, performance inhibition, association inhibition, and motivational inhibition". Perceptual tasks inhibit perceptual information (e.g., Baby Stroop, Spatial Conflict); performance tasks use a cue to signal when to inhibit on a subset of trials (Bear/Dragon, Simon Says); association tasks require inhibition plus a competing response on all trials (Day/Night, Hand Game); motivational or 'hot' tasks add a motivational component (Less is More, Tower). The authors note this distinction between performance and association inhibition is one they believe no other group has made, and call it speculative but possibly useful.
requirements: Tasks must be classifiable by their demand structure; the authors caution the clusters are not mutually exclusive because all measures tap multiple aspects of inhibitory control
constraints: The authors describe the grouping as an oversimplification and the performance/association distinction as speculative
target_learners: typically-developing children under 8 years of age
target_learning_goals: measuring the development of inhibitory control as a component of self-regulation
key_sources: Petersen, I. T., Hoyniak, C. P., McQuillan, M. E., Bates, J. E., & Staples, A. D. (2016). Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity. Developmental Review, 40, 25-71. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.02.001

article_title: Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity
citation: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/
title: Four-C developmental model of creativity (mini-C, little-C, Pro-C, Big-C) with evolving metacognition across levels
description: The article reviews Kaufman and Beghetto's (2009) four-level developmental model of creativity. Mini-C involves creative insights during learning, represented by emerging mental constructions; little-C involves products triggering positive assessment from peers or teachers; Pro-C involves professional contributions deemed original and appropriate by gatekeepers of a field; Big-C involves eminent creativity producing an entire body of work that has made a difference in a cultural field. The author complements this model by arguing that spontaneous cognition dominates at mini-C and little-C levels, while controlled cognition and metacognitive assessment become increasingly important at Pro-C and Big-C levels, where "Metacognitive judgments are not self-generated" but incorporate field standards.
requirements: Distinguishes four levels of creativity with different sources of evaluation
constraints: The authors do not think it is necessary to pass through each level to become an eminent creator
target_learning_goals: understanding developmental trajectories of creativity
understanding how metacognition evolves with creative expertise
examples: Table 1 summarizes how metacognition evolves at the four levels, from exploration and improvisation at mini-C to developing networks of enterprise at Big-C
key_sources: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/

article_title: Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective
citation: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816
title: Four categories of neighborhood-effect mechanisms, all involving a temporal dimension of exposure
description: The article organizes theoretical mechanisms linking disadvantaged neighborhoods to educational attainment into four families: "those based on social isolation, social organization, neighborhood resources, and the physical environment." Social isolation theories emphasize role models and cultural repertoires; social organization theories emphasize collective supervision of youth; resource theories emphasize schools and institutions; environmental theories emphasize pollution and housing hazards. The article argues each requires sustained exposure for effects to accumulate or internalize.
requirements: Estimating duration-dependent effects requires measuring neighborhood context repeatedly over childhood rather than at a single point in time
constraints: The article presents these as theoretical mechanisms whose temporal implications motivate the empirical analysis, not as individually tested pathways
target_learners: children and adolescents growing up in disadvantaged neighborhoods
target_learning_goals: high school graduation and progression through school
key_sources: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816

article_title: Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented
citation: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298
title: Four-characteristic model of national historical master narratives
description: The article presents a model distinguishing four characteristics of national historical master narratives: the historical subject established by inclusion and exclusion, identification processes attaching affect and value judgments, historical events simplified around one common narrative theme, and a romantic and essentialist concept of the nation. The model was developed as a unit of analysis for studying how students consume master narratives, and the study applies it to Argentine students' narratives about May 25, 1810. The authors state it 'could be applied to master narratives in other countries, for example, on the American continent.'
requirements: Narratives about a nation's own history that can be analyzed against the four characteristics and their more historical alternatives
constraints: Developed and illustrated with the Argentine myth of origin; contextualization of the specific national narrative is needed because cultural tools are known to be context-specific
target_learning_goals: historical understanding of the national past
critical historical thinking about master narratives
examples: Applied to 38 Argentine students' semistructured interview narratives about May 25, 1810, coded per characteristic with two independent judges agreeing on over 94.5% of a random 30% sample
key_sources: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Four paradigms of shared knowledge span individual representations, shared objects, shared situations, and shared communities
description: The editorial organizes CSCL analyses of shared knowledge into four paradigms spanning a range from individual to community levels. It states that "Studies of CSCL each tend to focus on a certain form of knowledge and assume a certain way of sharing this knowledge," with choices depending on the study's theoretical position. The paradigms are offered as a lens for reading the issue's four technology-design articles, and the authors note it "may be possible to select the most appropriate paradigm for any given study."
requirements: Studies must make their assumptions about the form of knowledge and mode of sharing explicit
constraints: The question of how the paradigms might fit together is deferred, as "a topic for another time"
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers of collaborative learning technologies
target_learning_goals: Understanding and analyzing how knowledge is shared in collaborative learning
examples: The editorial maps each of the issue's four articles (wikis, virtual reality, PowerPoint, group formation software) to a different paradigm of shared knowledge
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: An international research community
citation: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y
title: Four-factor scripting approach for blended learning: space, pedagogical method, participants, and history
description: The final article in the issue, by Mar Pérez-Sanagustín, Patricia Santos, Davinia Hernández-Leo, and Josep Blat, proposes and illustrates a scripting approach the editors describe as "focused on four factors: the space, the pedagogical method, the participants, and the history." The emphasis on space relates to a blended learning geography course that uses mobile and other technologies to support teams of students exploring the urban environment in Barcelona.
requirements: A blended learning setting in which collaboration can be scripted along the four factors
constraints: Illustrated in a geography course using mobile technologies for urban exploration in Barcelona
target_learners: student teams in blended higher-education courses
target_learning_goals: structuring collaboration in blended learning activities
examples: Teams of students exploring the urban environment in Barcelona with mobile and other technologies.
key_sources: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y

article_title: Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design
citation: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y
title: Design CSCL learning environments and tasks so that targeted group practices actually emerge
description: The editorial derives from all five papers a shared design focus: necessary group practices for productive collaboration "do not happen automatically" and must be fostered by "the design of the learning environment, including the learning technology and the learning task(s), as well as the instructor facilitation." Analysis of social interaction and group practices should "systematically inform the design, testing, and refinement of CSCL environments and practices."
requirements: Task design, technology design and instructor facilitation must jointly support the emergence of the targeted group practices; analysis of interaction should feed design iterations
constraints: The editorial notes coupling levels, technologies and venues differed greatly across contexts, so targeted practices must be matched to the specific context and domain
target_learners: student teams, museum visitors, children, and interprofessional student groups
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative learning and domain-specific collaboration practices
examples: Role assignment on wikis shaped venues; tabletop exhibits were designed for loosely-coupled interactions; instructors facilitated third-person reflection in debriefings
key_sources: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y

article_title: Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods
citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Rose, C., Law, N., & Ludvigsen, S. (2018). Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 235–240. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9284-z
title: Four-stage framework of coupling minds across levels of information processing
description: The authors organize CSCL research on coupling individual minds into social systems around four stages of information processing: attention, core cognition, metacognition, and activities. They write that 'The coupling processes themselves can take place at different stages of information processing' and map one paper in the issue to each level, noting each level requires different tools and analysis methods. The framework links theories of joint attention, knowledge integration, socially shared regulation, and collaborative writing activity.
requirements: Each level of coupling needs its own specific tools and methods of data capture and analysis, as the editorial states for the four papers
constraints: The framework is presented as an organizing scheme for the four papers in this special issue, not as a tested model
target_learners: collaboratively learning students across K-12 and higher education as studied in the four papers
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
regulation of collaborative learning
examples: The editorial assigns Schneider et al. to joint visual attention, Matuk and Linn to cognition and thinking, Hadwin et al. to metacognition, and Heimbuch et al. to writing activities
key_sources: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Rose, C., Law, N., & Ludvigsen, S. (2018). Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 235–240. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9284-z

article_title: The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2023). The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09385-1
title: Four sequential session types of online PBL interaction: argumentation-triggered, information-triggered, socially-triggered, and facilitated discussions
description: Differential sequence mining with agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the longest common prefix, validated by average silhouette width and R-squared, grouped students' interaction sessions into four types. "The best number of clusters according to ASW and R-squared was four." The Argumentation triggered cluster "contains sessions that always begin with Argue", the Information triggered cluster begins with Share and is short and less argumentative, the Socially triggered cluster begins with social gestures, and Facilitated discussions has a considerable teacher presence. Sessions start most often as Information triggered (39%) and transition freely between types.
requirements: Time-stamped, qualitatively coded interaction data from an online forum so interactions can be ordered and session epochs defined
constraints: Derived from one blended medical PBL course (four offerings) at a single university; session epochs defined by a 20-minute inactivity threshold
target_learners: first-year medical students in blended online PBL
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving and knowledge construction in problem-based learning
examples: Cluster sizes as reported: Argumentation triggered n = 709, Information triggered n = 423, Socially triggered n = 398, Facilitated discussions n = 883
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2023). The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09385-1

article_title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
citation: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x
title: Four modalities of embodied collaboration in shared VR environments
description: The article integrates theories of embodied cognition with distributed and extended cognition to focus on four modalities for embodied collaboration in shared VR: actions on virtual objects, gesture, body movement, and speech. These modalities are the semiotic resources learners orchestrate simultaneously or in sequence to build shared geometric understanding. The framework treats the group, not the individual, as the interactional unit of analysis.
requirements: A shared VR environment in which multiple learners can simultaneously manipulate the same virtual object and see each other's avatars and actions in real time
target_learning_goals: collaborative geometric reasoning and embodied mathematical knowledge construction
key_sources: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Formalise theories with computational models (e.g., Bayesian framework) to counter epistemic fragmentation in CSCL
description: The authors recommend striving for a unified language, such as a formalisation strategy, in which different CSCL theories can be expressed, proposing the Bayesian framework as a formal language within reach for CSCL researchers. Formal modelling "makes us think deeply about our theories", highlights gaps and lack of clarity, contributes to open theorising by making assumptions explicit, and yields compact, easily exchanged theories.
requirements: Willingness to specify background knowledge and how it is connected in inferences; Bayesian method basics can be learned in a couple of weeks and are supported by software tools including several R packages
constraints: The authors acknowledge the possibility that CSCL is a research area where formalisation and simulation do not add value (the pitfall of reductionism), comparing it to social psychology's absence of formalized theory
target_learning_goals: theory building and unification in CSCL; modelling collaborative sense-making and regulation
examples: The authors formalise shared meaning-making as Bayesian inference of P(concept | utterance), and suggest Bayesian modelling of metacognitive regulation as rational choice of learning activities providing a yardstick of optimal performance.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
citation: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x
title: Four types of collaborative learning process data for analyzing individual participation
description: The review synthesizes the process data used to analyze individual participation into four categories: oral conversational data (N = 28 studies, mostly co-located), textual input data (N = 18, almost all online), log data from CSCL platforms (N = 20, the most common in online settings), and nonverbal physical data (N = 14) including gestures, eye gazing, touch, and electrodermal activity. Fourteen studies employed multimodal data, most combining oral conversation data and nonverbal physical data, which the review says captured "a more comprehensive view of participation." The mapping of data types to participation forms is summarized in the study's Fig. 3.
requirements: Nonverbal physical data were often used together with other process data such as oral communication data to interpret students' physical actions in co-located collaborative learning
constraints: Log data was rarely used to analyze participation forms other than solo active participation and cognitive interactions "owing to its limitations for capturing emotional nuances and the learning processes occurring beyond the collaborative learning platform"
target_learners: students in higher education and K-12 collaborative learning contexts
target_learning_goals: measuring individual participation across cognitive, metacognitive, socioemotional, coordinative, solo active, and passive forms
examples: Törmänen et al. (2022) combined oral conversational data and electrodermal activity data to analyze individual socioemotional participation; Nguyen et al. (2023) used log data frequency and duration of logged behaviors
key_sources: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x

article_title: Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers’ video analysis
citation: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Focused self-explanation prompts with an interactive strategy diagram
description: Focused prompts in this training operationalized principle-based self-explanation after video viewing. "The focused prompts presented the summary diagram from the introductory text (see Fig. 2a). This diagram version was interactive and participants were instructed to click on a particular tutoring strategy for each event they remembered from the video". After selecting a strategy, a text box instructed participants to describe and interpret that noticed strategy, with at least four comments per video; the open-prompt control condition provided only an empty text box without the diagram.
requirements: a pre-training introductory text whose tutoring strategies the diagram connects to
constraints: the article distinguishes focused prompts from open-ended prompts, which "have few restrictions on learners' explanations"
target_learning_goals: knowledge integration between theoretical tutoring principles and noticed practice events
examples: Seventy-one participants were assigned to focused prompts and 59 to the open-prompt condition.
key_sources: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y

article_title: Refuting student teachers’ misconceptions about multimedia learning
citation: Anja Prinz, Julia Kollmer, Lisa Flick, Alexander Renkl, Alexander Eitel. (2022). Refuting student teachers' misconceptions about multimedia learning. Instructional Science, 50, 89–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09568-z
title: Four common misconceptions about multimedia learning
description: The article organizes multimedia-learning misconceptions into four named types: the learning-styles misconception (matching material to visualizer/verbalizer styles), the hemispheric-isolation misconception (presenting text and pictures to activate both brain hemispheres), the naïve-summation misconception (more media and modalities yield better retention), and the motivation-primacy misconception (multimedia works mainly by raising motivation). It states "there are four common multimedia misconceptions" and explains the scientifically correct account for each, such as that "the extent of active processing and successful integration with prior knowledge rather than the mere number of media used to present information predicts retention".
requirements: Learners or teachers must hold the misconception for a refutation intervention targeting it to be relevant
target_learning_goals: correct knowledge about effective multimedia material design
examples: The experiment's texts and questionnaire items each addressed one of the four misconceptions: learning styles, hemispheric isolation, naïve summation, and motivation primacy.
key_sources: Anja Prinz, Julia Kollmer, Lisa Flick, Alexander Renkl, Alexander Eitel. (2022). Refuting student teachers' misconceptions about multimedia learning. Instructional Science, 50, 89–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09568-z

article_title: Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity
citation: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x
title: Use flexible, adaptive formative assessment during learning to provide information on results for regulation
description: The article argues regulation of teaching requires valid and timely information on results, and that end-of-term tests have minimal feedback value due to timing. Instead, "More ﬂexible, adaptive, formative (self) assessment methods applied during learning can identify the gap between goals stated and present status, and suggest resources to teachers and learners for remediation."
requirements: Valid and timely measures, preferably of process as well as outcomes
constraints: Many teachers see tests as indicators of students' success and failure, not their own
target_learning_goals: monitoring progress toward goals
remediation of learning gaps
examples: Furtak et al.'s three-year study of teachers developing formative assessment skills, in which better information on results led to better student learning
key_sources: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x

article_title: Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning
citation: Piia Näykki, Tiina Törmänen, Jaana Isohätälä, Hanna Järvenoja, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09815-1
title: Four observable group-level emotion regulation strategies: task structuring, encouragement, social reinforcement, and awareness raising
description: The article distinguishes four qualitatively different, socially observable emotion regulation strategies used by groups during collaborative tasks. Task structuring is "a cognitively oriented strategy" used to restore on-task behaviour when members are unfocused; encouragement involves praising or supporting a member lacking confidence; social reinforcement aims to "reinforce a stable, safe or positive socio-emotional atmosphere"; and increasing awareness involves verbalizing and addressing each other's affective states so the group can jointly explain and reduce negative feelings. The categories were developed from prior emotion regulation research and reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.79.
requirements: Coding relies on socially observable, verbal or nonverbal regulation attempts in group interaction, since purely mental self-regulatory processes are not visible in video analysis
constraints: Only social-level indicators of observable attempts at emotion regulation were categorized
target_learners: teacher education students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: managing emotional challenges during collaborative learning
maintaining a productive socioemotional climate for group work
examples: Table 1 illustrates each strategy with transcribed interaction, e.g. a member asking "Does it bother you?" to raise awareness of frustration with fraction divisions
key_sources: Piia Näykki, Tiina Törmänen, Jaana Isohätälä, Hanna Järvenoja, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09815-1

article_title: Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school
citation: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8
title: Four-step heuristic worked example model for mathematical modeling with dialogical fictitious-student examples
description: The article advances a four-step account of mathematical modeling linked to Polya's steps: "(1) understand the problem, (2) mathematize it, (3) work mathematically, and (4) explain the result." Heuristic worked examples are built on this structure, presenting dialogues between two fictitious students who negotiate solutions across the four phases, make realistic attempts, "go a little wrong sometimes, discuss their detours and mistakes, but ultimately demonstrate adequate strategies." This erroneous-elements design is intended to support active processing and sensitize students to pitfalls, while the dialogue simulates expert modeling and scaffolds the problem-solving process.
requirements: Worked examples segmented into the four modeling sections with a standard strategic scheme across varying surface characteristics
Fictitious students must ultimately solve the problem adequately, since erroneous examples benefited only high-prior-knowledge learners in the cited work
constraints: The study operationalized the model on concrete content areas (basic numeracy, plane geometry, linear functions), so results must be interpreted against those domains
Intervention duration was a single 45-minute period, so effects reflect initial learning rather than comprehensive competency
target_learners: lower secondary school students in Grades 5 and 7
target_learning_goals: mathematical modeling competency for reality-based tasks
modeling-specific strategy knowledge and metacognitive self-regulation
examples: The 'Mohawk' worked example has fictitious students Paul and Sara identify the needed information, estimate the head height by measuring, and derive 125 cm for the hairdo height
key_sources: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8

article_title: Investigating Students’ Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks
citation: Parks, T., Shehab, S., & Mercier, E. (2026). Investigating Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09816-0
title: Four-process framework for collaborative problem solving in ill-structured STEM tasks (P1–P4)
description: The article operationalizes Ge and Land's four problem-solving processes for ill-structured engineering tasks: P1 (exploring and representing the problem, including joint FBD construction), P2 (planning how to solve, considering multiple approaches), P3 (attempting to solve with justifications), and P4 (evaluating the solution and considering alternatives). The framework holds that "Quality verbal interactions in collaborative problem solving can trigger these four essential processes that engage groups in more effective problem solving." An idealized distribution (0.5 P3, 0.25 P4, 0.125 each P1/P2) is proposed as a target for group engagement.
requirements: All four processes must be engaged for complete problem solving
Groups are the unit of analysis; verbal interactions are coded to identify process engagement
constraints: The optimal distribution of time across processes is unknown; the proposed ratios were iterated from prior-semester observations and literature
Novice designers tend to skip P1 and P2 and proceed directly to P3 without scaffolding
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students working in small groups on ill-structured tasks
target_learning_goals: engagement in all four collaborative problem-solving processes during ill-structured engineering tasks
examples: Turns were coded into P1–P4 categories (e.g., a P1 example: students discussing whether to account for the weight of the wood), and thematic episodes were used to construct video graphs of each group's progress
key_sources: Parks, T., Shehab, S., & Mercier, E. (2026). Investigating Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09816-0

article_title: Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning
citation: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5
title: Four-activity framework of online collaboration: task-related activities, social activities, regulation of task-related activities, and regulation of social activities
description: The article proposes that online collaboration comprises four types of activities: task-related activities in the content space (exchanging information, asking questions), social activities in the relational space (greetings, social support, grounding via shared understanding), regulation of task-related activities (planning, monitoring, evaluating task progress), and regulation of social activities (planning, monitoring, evaluating the collaboration). The authors argue that "to gain a complete picture of the nature of online collaboration, attention should be paid to all four activities," noting researchers usually address only one or two. The framework was operationalized in a 19-category coding scheme and validated by factor analysis.
requirements: A coding scheme distinguishing the four activity types applied to logged communication, aggregated to the group level
constraints: The study examined secondary education students working on history inquiry tasks in one CSCL environment; the authors note only correlations, not cause-effect relationships, could be established
target_learners: Secondary education students in the pre-university track, aged 15–18
target_learning_goals: Collaborative historical inquiry: reading, comprehending and synthesizing historical sources into group texts
examples: The coding scheme classified chat messages into 19 categories across the four scales, coded with the MEPA program with Cohen's Kappa between .86 and .94 across the three studies
key_sources: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5

article_title: Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning
citation: Nadine Melzner · Markus Dresel · Ingo Kollar. (2022). Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:813–836. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09316-9
title: Four case vignettes systematically varying motivational and comprehension-related problems
description: The study's core instrument is a booklet of four case vignettes describing a study group preparing for an exam, arranged in a 2 × 2 within-subjects design: no problems ("high knowledge and high learning motivation"), only motivational problems, only comprehension-related problems, and both problems ("low knowledge and low learning motivation"). After each vignette participants indicated at three social levels whether they would "do something to ensure a high quality of learning" and wrote down open-ended strategy answers. A soccer-team example vignette familiarized participants with the level distinctions.
requirements: Participants able to imagine being a member of the described study group and to distinguish the three social levels of regulation, supported by the example vignette
constraints: The vignettes describe hypothetical rather than real group learning situations, and did not point to specific group members who might have more motivational or comprehension-related problems than others
target_learners: university students in an introductory Educational Science lecture
target_learning_goals: reporting conditional strategy knowledge for regulating motivational and comprehension-related problems at self, co and shared levels
examples: Vignettes were presented on paper in randomized order, each followed by three blank text fields, one per social level of regulation
key_sources: Nadine Melzner · Markus Dresel · Ingo Kollar. (2022). Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:813–836. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09316-9

article_title: Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review
citation: Élisabeth Bélanger, Marine Moyon, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Steve Masson. (2026). Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10198-5
title: Four recurring characteristics of competing automatisms in learning topics requiring inhibitory control
description: The review proposes four recurring characteristics of the automatisms that compete with correct responses in learning topics requiring inhibitory control: "strong perceptual salience, reliance on the “more A–more B” intuitive rule, susceptibility to whole-number bias, and frequent reinforcement through instruction and experience." These characteristics serve as initial conceptual landmarks intended to help identify other learning topics likely to involve similar automatisms and thus require inhibitory control, moving beyond a binary view of whether a topic requires inhibition.
requirements: Automatisms are rapidly and automatically activated, often without conscious awareness, and can interfere with task-relevant processing when not adequately inhibited
constraints: The characteristics are proposed as initial conceptual landmarks, not validated diagnostic criteria
target_learning_goals: overcoming interfering automatisms in mathematics, science and language topics
examples: Decimal comparison errors from the 'more digits, larger value' automatism; buoyancy errors from 'heavier objects sink more'
key_sources: Élisabeth Bélanger, Marine Moyon, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Steve Masson. (2026). Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10198-5

article_title: Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z
title: Four-dimensional model of learning engagement: behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic engagement
description: The article conceptualizes learning engagement as a multidimensional phenomenon in which students involve themselves in learning activities behaviorally, cognitively, emotionally, and agentically. It defines behavioral engagement as exert effort, cognitive engagement as absorbed in thought, emotional engagement as feel activated, and agentic engagement as the student's constructive contribution into the flow of instruction they receive, with operational indicators such as offering input, asking questions, and making suggestions. The paper argues agentic engagement is a fourth strategic approach a student might use to optimize and advance their learning, not just another way of involving oneself.
requirements: Measurement of each dimension separately, as in Table 1's conceptual and operational definitions
constraints: The article focuses narrowly on learning engagement in academic work, nested within the broader school engagement literature
target_learning_goals: active involvement in learning activities
examples: Table 1 provides conceptual and operational definitions for each type of engagement and each correlate
key_sources: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z

article_title: How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms
citation: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520
title: Foster internal regulation along with positive perceptions of instrumentality to make future goals motivate achievement in multicultural classrooms
description: The review's central design principle is that future goals motivate school achievement only under two conditions: students must perceive a clear positive connection between doing well in school and later success, and they must experience future goals as internally driven rather than externally imposed. As the authors state, "future goals will motivate achievement in multicultural classrooms, provided that schools and families succeed in fostering internal regulation along with positive perceptions of instrumentality." Schools and families are jointly addressed as the agents fostering these conditions.
requirements: Students must perceive a clear positive connection between doing well in school and success later in life
Future goals must be experienced as internally driven or self-set rather than externally controlled or imposed
constraints: The principle is derived from a review of largely correlational cross-cultural evidence, not from an intervention test
target_learners: minority and migrant students in multicultural classrooms
target_learning_goals: school engagement and achievement motivation
examples: The review draws on questionnaire studies measuring future goals, perceived instrumentality, and regulation among Turkish, Moroccan, and native students in Dutch high schools
key_sources: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520

article_title: Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education
citation: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6
title: Cross-theoretical integration of four motivational theories of teacher influence on engagement
description: The article synthesises four theories of how teachers improve student engagement: self-determination theory, achievement goal theory, growth mindset theory, and transformational leadership theory. SDT hypothesises three basic psychological needs — competence, autonomy, and relatedness — whose fulfilment leads to optimal motivation and engagement. Achievement goal theory holds that "students with mastery goals... will be more engaged than those who have performance goals". Growth mindset theory recommends praising effort and improvement rather than ability, and transformational leadership theory describes leaders who empower followers beyond their own self-interests. The framework treats these as overlapping and competing sources of behavioural predictions to be assessed simultaneously.
requirements: A mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive list of theory-recommended behaviours so each theory's predictions can be assessed simultaneously
constraints: The theories overlap — all four emphasise improvement-oriented specific feedback — creating empirical redundancy and jingle-jangle problems the integration must manage
target_learners: Year 7 secondary school students in low socio-economic status schools
target_learning_goals: student engagement (affective, behavioural, cognitive) in physical education
examples: Behaviours were classified under each theory by four authors, e.g. using achievement goal theory's TARGET framework
key_sources: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6

article_title: Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students’ Experiences of Belonging at School
citation: Alexander S. Browman. (2025). Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students' Experiences of Belonging at School. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10009-3
title: Four-fit model of students' experiences of belonging in school (social, self-concept, goal, and resource fit)
description: The article proposes that when students report feeling they do or do not belong at school, their experience hinges on four forms of person-environment fit: "social fit", "goal fit", "self-concept fit", and "resource fit". The model extends Schmader and Sedikides' State Authenticity as Fit to Environment (SAFE) model, adding resource fit as a fourth form. Belonging is framed as the cumulative result of whether students currently experience the four associated fluencies in that environment, and the model is illustrated in Figure 1.
requirements: The model presupposes students have a clear sense of their true self-concept, since the article notes a metacognitive prerequisite of authentic self-awareness for experiencing fit or non-fit
constraints: The article states the model focuses on state (versus trait) authenticity, and does not extensively explore the distinction between social fit with peers versus with teachers
target_learners: students at all levels of education, especially those from historically under-researched or marginalized backgrounds
target_learning_goals: students' sense of belonging at school and its relation to academic motivation and performance
key_sources: Alexander S. Browman. (2025). Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students' Experiences of Belonging at School. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10009-3

article_title: Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students’ Experiences of Belonging at School
citation: Alexander S. Browman. (2025). Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students' Experiences of Belonging at School. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10009-3
title: Four fluency experiences (interpersonal, motivational, being-cognition, need-cognition) as precursors of belonging
description: Building on the SAFE model, the article proposes that each form of fit promotes its own unique experience of fluency: social fit yields interpersonal fluency, goal fit yields motivational fluency, self-concept fit yields being-cognition fluency, and the newly proposed resource fit yields need-cognition fluency, in which students can devote mental and temporal bandwidth to schoolwork without tending to unmet needs. These fluencies are proposed to be "precursors to a more gestalt sense of being authentic", and the article argues they cumulatively constitute students' phenomenological experience of belonging.
requirements: Each fluency is proposed to arise only when the corresponding form of fit is experienced in the academic environment
constraints: The fluency mechanisms are proposed theoretically; the article notes psychological research on belonging has generally not examined the majority of these proposed factors
target_learning_goals: academic motivation, effort investment, and performance
key_sources: Alexander S. Browman. (2025). Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students' Experiences of Belonging at School. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10009-3

article_title: Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students’ Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study
citation: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10137-4
title: Foster beliefs in the positive interdependence of mathematical and verbal abilities and in the changeability of abilities to mitigate dimensional contrast effects and support balanced self-concept development
description: The article recommends targeting the beliefs that moderate comparison effects rather than the comparisons alone. As the authors put it, "fostering a belief in the positive interdependence of mathematical and verbal abilities as well as a growth mindset may help mitigate dimensional contrast effects and support more balanced self-concept development across domains." The COMPASS intervention operationalizes this by educating students that mathematical and verbal abilities are not mutually exclusive and that abilities are changeable, pairing belief change with reflection exercises.
requirements: Students receive education about comparison effects plus exercises and discussions that let them apply the beliefs to their own performance histories
constraints: Effects were demonstrated in math and, per the abstract, English in academic-track secondary schools; the pilot study's modules did not enhance German self-concept
target_learners: Secondary school students in subjects where they perform relatively worse
target_learning_goals: Balanced academic self-concept development across domains
Sustainable belief change about ability interdependence and changeability
examples: In the COMPASS intervention, students reflected on whether they were a math or a language type and chose behaviors they could transfer from other subjects to the intervention subject
key_sources: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. article_title: Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025)
citation: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2
title: The FoRe-Squares model: effective instruction requires both focus support and reward
description: The FoRe-Squares model is a 2×2 framework in which instruction is characterized by two predictor constructs: focus support (cognitive guidance and stimulation) and reward (motivational support). The model postulates that effective instruction requires both factors to enable and energize active goal-directed processing: "we expect instruction to be effective when it provides at least medium levels of both focus support and reward." Only the top-right square (both medium-to-high) is expected to yield good learning outcomes; the other three squares, where either factor or both are lacking, are expected to yield lower outcomes. The model builds on CTML and CLT for its cognitive techniques and on SEVT for its value facets.
requirements: Instruction must provide at least medium levels of both focus support and reward simultaneously for active goal-directed processing to occur
constraints: The model does not (yet) address the dynamic interactions between instructional design and individual learner characteristics, unlike CLT and CTML
target_learners: students in technology-augmented and multimedia instruction
target_learning_goals: learning outcomes from instruction
examples: The model's main prediction is illustrated in a 2×2 figure where the combination of medium to high focus support and reward is hypothesized to stimulate active goal-directed processing and good learning outcomes
key_sources: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2

article_title: Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025)
citation: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2
title: Focus support as an instruction-level predictor construct
description: Focus support is defined in the FoRe-Squares model as "the overall degree of (meta-)cognitive guidance and stimulation for students to focus their processing on the crucial elements of instruction." It is a construct at the level of instruction, distinct from CLT's cognitive loads and CTML's processing types, which are mediator-level consequences of instruction. Cognitive techniques such as signaling, coherence, and testing are concrete instantiations of focus support, and the construct builds on CTML and CLT assumptions about stimulating active processing and reducing unnecessary processing in limited working memory.
requirements: Element interactivity should not be excessive for the target learner group for focus support to be high
target_learners: students in multimedia and technology-augmented instruction
target_learning_goals: focusing cognitive processing on the crucial elements of instruction
examples: Signaling, coherence, and testing are named as cognitive techniques that instantiate focus support in instruction
key_sources: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2

article_title: Assessing Writing Motivation: a Systematic Review of K-5 Students' Self-Reports
citation: Alves‑Wold, A., Walgermo, B. R., McTigue, E., & Uppstad, P. H. (2023). Assessing Writing Motivation: a Systematic Review of K‑5 Students’ Self‑Reports. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09732-6
title: Four‑component framework of writing motivation (self‑efficacy, goal orientations, interest/value, outcome attributions)
description: The review adopts Troia et al.’s (2012) account that writing motivation comprises four broad components: self‑efficacy beliefs, goal orientations, task interest and value, and outcome attributions, with associated constructs such as domain self‑concept and task utility. The review uses this schema to systematize the 32 motivational constructs identified across the 56 studies (Table 4). The review notes that some links, such as the causal pathways between self‑efficacy, interest, and value, remain unclear, and that the schema’s authors invite combining methods such as classroom observation and students’ self‑reports to test these connections.
requirements: Motivation constructs must be clearly defined for the framework to guide accurate measurement of students’ voices
constraints: Some causal pathways between components (self‑efficacy, interest, value) are stated by the source review to remain unclear
target_learners: K‑5 elementary students in mainstream classrooms
target_learning_goals: Assessing and understanding students’ motivation to write
examples: The review categorized the 32 identified constructs into the four theorized components plus associated constructs, with interest and value (n = 39) and self‑beliefs (n = 28) most frequent
key_sources: Alves‑Wold, A., Walgermo, B. R., McTigue, E., & Uppstad, P. H. (2023). Assessing Writing Motivation: a Systematic Review of K‑5 Students’ Self‑Reports. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09732-6

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Four levels of learning analytics (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive) map onto the three stages of formative assessment
description: The review organizes learning analytics into four levels — descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive — and argues they align with formative assessment's three processes. It states: "These levels of analytics seem to be well-aligned with formative assessment practices as they provide insights into the main three stages of formative assessment (Black & Wiliam, 2009), including where the learner is going (for this purpose, learning analytics at the predictive level could serve), where the learner is now (descriptive and diagnostic analytics tend to be appropriate learning analytics levels for supporting this stage of formative assessment), and how to get there (prescriptive analytics could serve this stage)." This mapping structured the review's coding scheme (levels C1–C7).
requirements: A combined coding category was added because several studies used learning analytics at multiple levels rather than in a unimodal way
constraints: The alignment is the authors' conceptual mapping, not an empirically tested result
target_learning_goals: connecting analytics outputs to formative assessment stages
examples: Descriptive analytics answers 'What has happened?' via dashboards; predictive analytics provides early warnings for at-risk students; prescriptive analytics suggests task-specific strategies
key_sources: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Four characteristics underpin the validity of formative assessment, which learning analytics can strengthen through rich multimodal evidence
description: The review presents validity as a matter of degree and identifies characteristics that underpin valid formative assessment. It states: "According to Gikandi et al. (2011), four characteristics underpin the validity of formative assessment: (1) authenticity of assessment activities, (2) effective formative feedback, (3) inclusion of multidimensional perspectives, and (4) robust learner support." It further argues that learning analytics strengthens the validity argument by "capturing, analyzing, and reporting rich, multimodal evidence of student learning progress," and cites Divjak et al. (2023) on using analytics to compare ideal learning-objective priorities, assessment weights, and achievement data.
requirements: Valid formative assessment must provide sufficient evidence that inferences about student learning are accurate and aligned with intended learning outcomes
constraints: The validity framework is attributed to Gikandi et al. (2011) and Divjak et al. (2023); the review does not empirically test it
target_learning_goals: valid evidence-based formative assessment
examples: Divjak et al.'s model uses clustering and trace data analysis to support constructive alignment between learning outcomes and assessment

article_title: Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature
citation: Oliveira, T., Nada, C., & Magalhães, A. (2024). Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231226336
title: Four-theme framework of academic careers under marketization: individual project, surviving the game, emotionality, and inclusion/exclusion
description: The review organizes its answer to how marketization affects academic careers into four inductively derived themes: "academic careers as an individual project," "surviving the academic career “game,”" "academic careers influenced by emotionality," and "academic environments as places of inclusion and exclusion." The framework maps how neoliberal dynamics individualize career projects, frame careers as competitive games governed by audit metrics, embed emotional narratives that normalize exploitation, and produce inclusion and exclusion in academic environments. It was derived via thematic analysis of 54 documents in NVivo.
requirements: A corpus of literature on academic careers amenable to inductive thematic analysis, as the review conducted with NVivo-supported coding
constraints: The review states it is a partial expression located geographically, overrepresented by English-language countries, with no article from Scielo remaining after selection
target_learners: Academics and early career academics in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how marketization shapes academic career development and professional pathways
examples: The review's findings section presents the four themes in sequence, each supported by documents from the 54-article corpus marked with an asterisk in the reference list.

article_title: A Systematic Review of International Higher Education Scholarships for Students From the Global South
citation: Anne C. Campbell and Emelye Neff. (2020). A Systematic Review of International Higher Education Scholarships for Students From the Global South. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320947783
title: Proposed four-criteria definition of international scholarship programs
description: The article proposes a definition of international scholarships built from prior scholars' conceptualizations, with four criteria: recipients study at the higher education level outside their home country with a mobility component; recipients work toward a degree at an accredited institution; the award is part of a program with uniform selection criteria, centralized administration, and open competitive advertisement; and "The award must cover the majority (over 50%) of the study, travel, and other expenses associated with international study." The definition responds to the field's lack of consensus, noting scholarships have been "typically identified by example rather than definition."
requirements: Awards must be part of a program: more than one scholarship with the same purpose, uniform selection criteria, centralized administration, and an open, competitive process
constraints: The definition excludes visiting-scholar-style schemes where students access only seminars or campus facilities, and refugee students need not cross borders at the same time as their studies
target_learners: international scholarship recipients from Global South countries
target_learning_goals: distinguishing international scholarship programs from other mobility and funding schemes for research and evaluation purposes
examples: The criteria were used to screen approximately 450 items down to the 105 included in the review

article_title: Computer-assisted word reading intervention effects throughout the primary grades: A meta-analysis
citation: Verhoeven, L.T.W.; Voeten, M.J.M.; Segers, P.C.J. (2022). Computer-assisted word reading intervention effects throughout the primary grades: A meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 37, article 100486. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100486
title: Four-type taxonomy of computer-assisted word reading interventions
description: The article organizes computer-supported word reading interventions into four program types: foundational (comprehensive) reading instruction, supplementary alphabetics, reading fluency programs, and remedial reading programs for at-risk students in higher grades. It states "A distinction can be made between programs focusing on basic phonics instruction, supplementary alphabetic skills, reading fluency programs, and remedial reading interventions", and compares these four types on accuracy and speed of processing letters, phonological units, words, pseudowords, passages, and spelling. Comprehensive programs teach grapheme-phoneme correspondences explicitly in incremental sets; supplementary programs add phonological awareness and letter training; fluency programs build speeded word recognition; remedial programs give individualized or small-group tutoring.
requirements: Studies must report experimental comparisons between experimental and control conditions with a pre-test and post-test on the same outcome measure
constraints: Specific treatments focused solely on spelling or reading comprehension were left out for reasons of parsimony
target_learners: primary school children in grades 1 to 6
children at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: word reading accuracy
word reading speed and fluency
phonological awareness
letter knowledge
spelling
examples: The meta-analysis compared the four treatment types on accuracy and speed outcomes across 67 studies

article_title: Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001
title: Four-challenge framework for designing blended learning environments
description: The article presents a framework organizing blended learning design around four key challenges: incorporating flexibility, stimulating interaction, facilitating students' learning processes, and fostering an affective learning climate. The authors state: "This study presents a framework that is based on four key challenges to the design of blended learning: incorporating flexibility, stimulating interaction, facilitating students' learning processes, and fostering an affective learning climate." The framework was derived from a comparison of influential blended learning studies and used as the coding scheme for the systematic review. It can help designers create, communicate about, and evaluate blended learning designs.
requirements: Studies must define blended learning as a combination of face-to-face and online interventions and take an instructional, course-level design point of view
constraints: The framework excludes other dimensions such as which educational objectives are targeted in the online or face-to-face component
target_learning_goals: course-level design of blended learning environments
examples: The authors applied the framework as a coding scheme to 20 selected studies, with two coders reaching 74-95% percent agreement across 18 variables

article_title: Self-regulated learning strategies in continuing education: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Yvonne M. Hemmler, Dirk Ifenthaler. (2024). Self-regulated learning strategies in continuing education: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100629
title: Four-category framework of factors associated with SRL strategies in continuing education
description: The article organizes the factors associated with learners' use of SRL strategies in continuing education into four inductively derived categories. Factors were "inductively extracted from the primary studies and assigned to one of the following four main categories: learning process-related, learner-related, CE-related, or work-related factors." Learning process-related factors cover behavior, motivational states, and performance during a CE activity; learner-related factors cover general dispositions and beliefs; CE-related factors cover instructional characteristics and learner perceptions; work-related factors cover job characteristics and the work environment. The framework structures both the narrative synthesis and the meta-analyses.
requirements: Empirical primary studies that report an empirical measure of SRL strategies in relation to other variables in a CE context
constraints: Learners with disabilities were excluded from the evidence base
Only studies published in English in peer-reviewed journals were included
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use in continuing education
key_sources: Yvonne M. Hemmler, Dirk Ifenthaler. (2024). Self-regulated learning strategies in continuing education: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100629

article_title: The connection between the social network perspective and teacher professional development: A systematic literature review
citation: Coppe, T., Thomas, L., Strijbos, J.-W., & Vanderlinde, R. (2026). The connection between the social network perspective and teacher professional development: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100818
title: Integrated conceptual model of four rationales connecting the social network perspective and teacher professional development
description: The review proposes an integrated conceptual model organizing how empirical studies connect the social network perspective and TPD. From 51 studies, thematic analysis yielded "four distinct rationales for connecting the social network perspective and TPD": the network as a source of TPD, as a catalyst for enactment and sustainability of reforms with TPD, as purposefully (re)shaped by professional development initiatives, and as a (latent) school capacity for teacher and school development. The model gives researchers "conceptual clarity to situate their own work within the different theoretical rationales" and helps practitioners and policy-makers understand the different roles teacher networks can play.
requirements: Empirical studies using a social network perspective in relation to TPD, restricted to on-site primary and secondary school teacher networks
constraints: Excludes online/digital social networks, higher education, and conceptual or review studies; covers publications 2000–2024
target_learning_goals: teacher professional development understood as growth in work-related knowledge, skills and attitudes through formal or informal dynamics
examples: The model was built from a two-stage analysis: a 12-item data extraction table followed by iterative deductive and inductive thematic coding of the 51 included studies
key_sources: Coppe, T., Thomas, L., Strijbos, J.-W., & Vanderlinde, R. (2026). The connection between the social network perspective and teacher professional development: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100818

article_title: Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review
citation: Andreas Widmann, Regina H. Mulder. (2025). Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review. Educational Research Review 49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100736
title: Four-type taxonomy of behavioural change in team learning behaviours: dynamics, pattern, development, and minor change
description: The review defines four types of change in team learning behaviours, distinguished by the shape of the sequence of increases and decreases. Dynamics is "a sequence of increases and/or decreases in frequency, duration, intensity, or quality of team learning behaviours in a chaotic way without any regularity". Patterns are repetitive sequences, development is a sequence of major increases possibly with minor decreases, and minor change is a sequence of minor increases and/or decreases. The taxonomy was built from the theoretical framework and used to categorise the findings of the 15 included studies.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measurement of team learning behaviours to distinguish the types of change
constraints: Precise definitions and clear distinctions were largely lacking in prior research, so the definitions are the review's own alignment
target_learners: members of natural work teams in organisations
target_learning_goals: understanding and fostering change in team learning behaviours over time
examples: The review classified the results of eight quantitative and seven qualitative studies into the four change categories
key_sources: Andreas Widmann, Regina H. Mulder. (2025). Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review. Educational Research Review 49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100736

article_title: Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research
citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Four macro strands of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education: coping, training and studying, personal value, and critical engagement
description: To connect the themes produced by its analysis, the review discerns four thematic macro strands of DLE purpose: coping in data-intensive contexts, data-related training and studying, finding personal value in data, and critical engagement with data (fication). Each strand bundles themes positioned within and across Biesta's three domains; for example, data competencies can be ends in themselves or prerequisites for professional qualifications. The review notes that "Some themes may have additional relevance to others in intricate ways" and that not all relationships are theorized systematically.
requirements: Themes must first be produced by analysis of expressed educational purposes before being (re)positioned into macro strands
constraints: The authors state relationships among themes are not theorized systematically due to their potentially immense amount and nature
target_learning_goals: Understanding the range of educational purposes data literacy education can serve
examples: Fig. 3 depicts the macro strands as discerned from the themes and their relationships, e.g., reaching personal goals may involve acquiring professional qualifications
