article_title: Exploring learning and fit in the transition from higher education to the labour market: A systematic review
citation: Grosemans, I., Coertjens, L., & Kyndt, E. (2017). Exploring learning and fit in the transition from higher education to the labour market: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 21, 67-84. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.03.001
title: Four types of fit distinguish the higher-education-to-labour-market transition: vertical, horizontal, competence, and person-environment fit
description: The review organises the fit construct in the transition from higher education to the labour market as a four-part taxonomy. As the review states, "four types of fit are distinguished: vertical, horizontal, competence, and person-environment fit." This taxonomy structures how congruence between graduates' education and their work context is analysed in the reviewed literature, and it connects to findings that background characteristics influence fit and that fit relates to outcomes such as career progress.
requirements: The taxonomy presupposes a transition context in which a graduate's educational background can be compared with characteristics of the work context.
constraints: The supplied text presents the taxonomy as the review's organising distinction without printing definitions of each fit type.
target_learners: higher education students and recent graduates entering the labour market
target_learning_goals: understanding person-context congruence during the school-to-work transition

article_title: The impacts of open inquiry on students’ learning in science: A systematic literature review
citation: Muhamad Dah, N., Mat Noor, M. S. A., Kamarudin, M. Z., & Syed Abdul Azziz, S. S. (2024). The impacts of open inquiry on students' learning in science: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 43. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100601
title: Four-level model of inquiry teaching (confirmation, structured, guided, open)
description: The review organises inquiry-based science teaching around a four-level model established by Rezba et al. (2007), drawing on Schwab (1958) and Herron (1971). The levels differ by how much is given to students: "questions, procedures, and solutions are offered (confirmation inquiry); questions and processes are given to students (structured inquiry); questions are merely provided to students (guided inquiry); and students develop questions, procedures, and solutions (open inquiry)". Open inquiry is the fourth and highest level, in which students generate their own questions and design investigations, most closely following the work of actual scientists.
requirements: Requires students to develop their own questions, procedures, and solutions, with teacher support and classroom management
constraints: The review notes open inquiry is not a popular pedagogical practice due to challenges in relation to time and resources, and has rarely been implemented
target_learning_goals: Scientific inquiry skills
Conceptual understanding of science
examples: The review located 24 empirical studies of open inquiry across elementary, middle and high school levels, with high school students (ages 15–19) in 14 cases

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Four-phase model of interest development: from triggered situational interest to well-developed individual interest
description: The four-phase model describes how interest develops over time from a temporary response to features of the task and context into an integrated aspect of identity. The article states the model "includes four phases: triggered situational interest, maintained situational interest, emerging individual interest, and well-developed individual interest." Each phase has affective and cognitive components; earlier phases are relatively more affective, later phases more cognitive, requiring ongoing development of knowledge and value.
requirements: Support through interactions with educators and peers and the design of the environment can trigger and develop interest at any age
constraints: How interest connects to learning and how it should be supported depends on the phase of the students' interest
target_learners: students at any age developing interest in course topics
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and reengagement with topics and domains
examples: In earlier phases learners respond to triggers encouraging meaningful connections to related content; in later phases learners generate questions that go beyond what they are assigned

article_title: Epistemic Beliefs in Science—A Systematic Integration of Evidence From Multiple Studies
citation: Julia Schiefer, Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Andrea Bernholt, Nele Kampa, Andreas Nehring. (2022). Epistemic Beliefs in Science—A Systematic Integration of Evidence From Multiple Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09661-w
title: Four-dimensional model of epistemic beliefs in science (Conley et al., 2004)
description: The model conceptualizes epistemic beliefs in science along four dimensions: certainty (stability of scientific knowledge), development (science as an evolving discipline), source (whether knowledge resides in external authorities or can be generated through one's own thinking), and justification (the role of experiments and evidence in evaluating claims). According to the article, 'central epistemic beliefs in the domain of science include beliefs about the certainty, development, source, and justification of knowledge.' Each dimension ranges from naïve to sophisticated stances, with the sophisticated end valuing change, critical evaluation, and evidence-based reasoning.
requirements: Assessment instruments must cover all four dimensions to enable profile identification
constraints: The model was originally developed for students in Grade 5, and Likert-scale assessment may work best when instruments are adapted to specific age groups, particularly for younger participants
target_learners: Elementary to upper secondary school students (Grades 3–12) in science education
target_learning_goals: Development of sophisticated epistemic beliefs about the source, certainty, development, and justification of scientific knowledge
examples: The six integrated studies administered the 26-item Conley et al. (2004) instrument (German version by Urhahne & Hopf, 2004) with subscales for source (5 items), certainty (6 items), development (6 items), and justification (9 items)

article_title: Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dicke, T., Ferber, K., Devine, E., Collie, R., Granziera, H., Parker, P., Guo, J., Marsh, H., et al. (2026). Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10216-6
title: Four-domain taxonomy of teacher well-being and ill-being indicators
description: The review organizes heterogeneous teacher functioning constructs into four theory-informed domains: self-efficacy, teacher motivation, job satisfaction and commitment, and psychological functioning. The authors "grouped individual constructs into four broader categories that reflect common distinctions in the literature". Psychological functioning is defined by a positive criterion — teachers' experienced affective and health-related states and adaptive capacities — and is split into well-being indicators (positive affect, enjoyment, vitality, coping, resilience) and ill-being indicators (stress, burnout, adverse emotional experiences, mental health difficulties), reflecting the view that positive functioning and distress are related but distinct dimensions rather than opposite ends of one continuum.
requirements: Constructs must be mappable to a domain via theoretical alignment and operationalization similarity, as coded in Table 1
constraints: The domains are theory-informed organizing categories rather than mutually exclusive theoretical constructs
The categorization was not preregistered and was derived after screening, so domain comparisons are post hoc
target_learning_goals: teacher functioning as a lever for student motivation and achievement
examples: Table 1 maps search terms such as burnout, self-efficacy, job satisfaction, and coping onto the four domains and the JD-R, Transactional Stress, PERMA, SDT, and Social Cognitive frameworks

article_title: Linking Language Attitudes to Proficiency Across Learning Contexts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Correlational Evidence
citation: Maria Adelina Ianos, Andrei Rusu, Ramona Paloş, Cristina Petreñas, Clara Sansó. (2026). Linking Language Attitudes to Proficiency Across Learning Contexts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Correlational Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10193-w
title: Four-object taxonomy of language attitudes (language, speakers, learning, learning situation)
description: The article organizes language attitudes as an umbrella term covering four distinct attitude objects: "attitudes toward the language itself, (2) attitudes toward its speakers, (3) attitudes toward learning the language, and (4) attitudes toward the language learning situation." Evaluations of a language concern its perceived value or aesthetic qualities, while evaluations of speakers involve social judgements tied to group identity; the language–culture discrepancy hypothesis supports their non-interchangeability. The meta-analysis is the first to test all four objects against proficiency systematically.
requirements: Attitude-object measures must specify which object is targeted, since the objects have often been conflated although they are not interchangeable
constraints: The learning-situation category contained only three effects from two clusters, precluding reliable subgroup inference in the meta-analysis
target_learners: language learners in foreign-language and local-language contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding how affective factors relate to language proficiency
designing language education policies that foster favorable language attitudes
examples: The meta-analysis decomposed 132 effect sizes by the four attitude objects, with attitudes toward the language (k = 93) the most studied category

article_title: How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples
citation: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4
title: Four-stage model of cognitive skill acquisition through the worked-example approach
description: The article describes the worked-example approach as a procedure that "usually involves four stages" of cognitive skill acquisition. In Stage 1 learners receive instructional explanations communicating basic knowledge of principles and concepts; in Stage 2 they study worked examples with self-explanation prompts; in Stage 3 they turn to initial problem-solving, which deepens understanding and can serve self-assessment; in Stage 4 they practice extensively to enhance problem-solving speed and accuracy. The first three stages correspond to the early and intermediate phases of skill acquisition, focused on understanding the rationale of solutions, while Stage 4 corresponds to the late phase focused on efficiency. The present study targets the transition out of Stage 3, where accurate self-assessment decides whether learners restudy examples or proceed.
requirements: Learners navigating the sequence in a self-regulated manner must accurately self-assess their level of understanding after initial problem-solving to decide whether to proceed to Stage 4.
constraints: The article states it is generally unclear how many problems learners need to solve at what times to effectively consolidate the acquired schemata in Stage 4.
target_learners: learners acquiring cognitive skills through example-based learning, such as university students learning mathematical urn model problems
target_learning_goals: understanding the rationale of solution procedures
enhancing speed and accuracy of problem-solving
examples: The experiments implemented Stages 1–3 with instructional explanations, four worked examples with self-explanation prompts, and four problems to solve before self-assessment.
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4

article_title: Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years’ Research
citation: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6
title: Four-c model of creativity: mini-c, little-c, pro-c, and big-c levels
description: The review adopts Kaufman and Beghetto's (2009) Four-c model as its framework for levels of creativity. "mini-c (…) encompass the creativity inherent in the learning process"; little-c is everyday amateur creativity; pro-c requires roughly ten years of daily professional effort; big-c creators revolutionize a field and must appear as geniuses to "the gatekeepers who comprise the field". The review uses these levels to scope its research question and notes that no researcher claims big-c or pro-c creativity is possible without lengthy training.
requirements: Distinguishing creativity levels requires judging novelty and appropriateness relative to a reference community (novice, amateur, professional, field gatekeepers)
constraints: The review's corpus only explores little-c creativity because participants are always students
target_learners: learners at all levels, from novices (mini-c) to professionals (pro-c)
target_learning_goals: understanding what level of creative performance a learner can attain
examples: The review defines the domain-general question separately for mini-c, little-c, pro-c and big-c
key_sources: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6

article_title: Developing the Mental Effort and Load–Translingual Scale (MEL-TS) as a Foundation for Translingual Research in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Tino Endres, Lisa Bender, Stoo Sepp, Shirong Zhang, Louise David, Melanie Trypke, et al. (2025). Developing the Mental Effort and Load–Translingual Scale (MEL‑TS) as a Foundation for Translingual Research in Self‑Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09978-8
title: Use four effort and load items within a reference point evaluation as best practice for translingual cognitive demand assessment
description: The article's closing recommendation is a best practice for measuring cognitive demand across languages: "As best practice, we recommend four items within a reference point evaluation." This means administering the validated four-item mental effort and four-item mental load subscales with a reference point so ratings are anchored to a comparable learning situation across languages and cultures. The recommendation follows from the scale's demonstrated criterion, convergent, and incremental validity in English, Chinese, and German samples.
requirements: Researchers should use the translated and validated MEL-TS items and embed them in a reference point evaluation so ratings are comparable across languages
constraints: The recommendation rests on validation in English, Mandarin Chinese, and German versions with first-language participants; the distinction may be less clear in Chinese participants' ratings

target_learning_goals: assessing mental effort and mental load comparably across languages and cultures
examples: The authors offer "a set of translated and validated items as a common foundation for translingual research" and provide the items on the Open Science Framework

article_title: Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm
citation: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3
title: Four-system architecture of the mind: specialized structural systems, representational capacity, inference, and consciousness
description: The article proposes that the mind is organized into interacting systems: specialized structural systems interfacing with environmental domains, a representational capacity system serving as the work space of the mind, an inference system connecting information toward the goal of the moment, and a consciousness system that monitors, controls, and regulates processing, including metarepresentation. The systems interact dynamically so that changes in each are related to changes in others.
requirements: Integration of psychometric, cognitive, and developmental research traditions into one account of understanding, problem solving, and learning
constraints: The essay focuses on cognitive processes, integrating motivational and emotional considerations only briefly
target_learning_goals: understanding, problem solving, and learning across domains
key_sources: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3

article_title: Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction
citation: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z
title: The FoRe-Squares model: instruction is effective when it provides both focus support and reward
description: The FoRe-Squares (Focus-Support-Reward-Squares) model is a teaching model, not a learning model, synthesizing cognitive and motivational theory for technology-augmented instruction. It postulates two continuous independent variables — focus support and reward — that drive the mediating variable of active goal-directed processing and thus learning outcomes. As the article states, "the combination of focus support (cognitive factor) and reward (motivational factor) predicts and fosters good learning outcomes." The model takes an augmentation perspective in which technology supports, but cannot replace, human teachers and learners, and aims to serve as "a parsimonious schema to explain many instructional design effects." It draws on situated expectancy-value theory for its reward factor, using the value component to explain what learners may find rewarding.
requirements: Both focus support and reward must be present at least at a medium degree for active goal-directed processing and good learning outcomes
constraints: The model is not a learning model but a teaching model; it specifies causal relations between independent, mediating, and dependent variables rather than replacing existing theories
target_learning_goals: recall and transfer of key terms, principles, and procedures
key_sources: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z

article_title: Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Amanda Vite, Erika A. Patall, Man Chen. (2024). Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09967-x
title: Four competing cultural hypotheses for the role of culture in psychological need effects
description: The article organizes debate about cultural universality of autonomy need effects as a continuum of four positions. As it states, "we review four competing hypotheses regarding the role of culture in psychological needs and outcomes including a strict universalist perspective (Ryan & Deci, 2000b), a compensatory perspective (Lee et al., 2023; Gewirtz & Baer, 1958), a cultural matching perspective (Schüler et al., 2013), and a strict cultural relativist perspective (Markus & Kitayama, 1991)." The strict universalist view expects no cultural variation; the compensatory view predicts stronger satisfaction effects where autonomy is inconsistently satisfied; cultural matching predicts stronger effects where autonomy is culturally embedded; the strict relativist view treats needs as entirely context-specific.
requirements: Testing these hypotheses requires studies spanning multiple cultural contexts with comparable autonomy and well(ill)-being measures
constraints: The article notes it could not examine variation in the definition of autonomy due to insufficient data, and SDT researchers distinguish autonomy-as-endorsement from independence and independent choice
target_learners: K-12 youth across cultural contexts worldwide
target_learning_goals: Understanding how cultural context moderates the relationship between autonomy experiences and well(ill)-being
examples: The meta-analysis framed its cultural moderator analyses against these four hypotheses, with the region findings described as in line with the compensatory hypothesis
key_sources: Amanda Vite, Erika A. Patall, Man Chen. (2024). Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09967-x

article_title: Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, David Williamson Shaffer, Nikol Rummel. (2022). Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1479–1516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09676-3
title: Taxonomy of four intentions of authenticity underlying authentic learning design
description: The review synthesizes five prior classifications of authenticity (Shaffer & Resnick 1999; Polman 2012; Strobel et al. 2013; Doyle 2000; Fougt et al. 2019) into four intentions: creating personally meaningful learning activities, emulating the work of professionals, connecting learners with a community of practitioners, and reflecting experiences from real/daily life. The review states it "extracted the fol- lowing four intentions of authenticity" and treats intentions as "the overarch- ing determination or definition of authenticity in learning settings" that determine how design elements are selected and implemented.
requirements: Design elements are selected and implemented in ways determined by the intended authenticity; certain elements are presumed more strongly linked to certain intentions
constraints: Authentic assessment and teacher authenticity are deliberately not treated as equivalent intentions of authenticity in this taxonomy
target_learners: Higher education and vocational learners as represented in the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: Contextualizing learning so learners recognize the value, utility, meaning, and functionality of the knowledge to be acquired
examples: The codebook example for community of practice: teacher candidates connected to professional learning communities and supervised by experienced teachers
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall, David Williamson Shaffer, Nikol Rummel. (2022). Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1479–1516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09676-3

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Forward and backward curiosity: a two-type taxonomy of state curiosity
description: The review proposes a conceptual distinction of state curiosity by its two primary determinants: "We refer to the curiosity elicited by unpredictability and incongruity as forward and backward curiosity, respectively." Forward curiosity (curiosity for what) requires minimal knowledge, involves no prediction or surprise, shows an inverted-U relationship with its cause, and serves knowledge acquisition. Backward curiosity (curiosity for why) requires moderate-to-high knowledge, involves prediction, surprise and confusion, scales linearly with incongruity, and serves knowledge revision through causal search.
requirements: Backward curiosity requires sufficient prior knowledge to make predictions and recognize incongruity
constraints: Not all unpredictability produces forward curiosity unless a discernable information gap is created
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing curiosity experiences to design curiosity-inducing instruction
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Four levels of functional specificity of theoretical propositions, from non-causal association to functionally specified causal effects
description: The article proposes that propositions differ in specificity, which determines their falsifiability. Table 1 depicts four levels: non-causal association, weak causal effect, moderate causal effect with specified direction, and strong causal effect with a defined functional form. The author notes that "almost all propositions of the motivation theories addressed are located on Levels 1–3" and argues that moving to Level 4 would make contradictions between theories and between theory and evidence easier to detect.
requirements: Precise theoretical propositions and precise measurement are needed, otherwise contradictions may not be detectable
constraints: Even specified Level 1 associations remain weak from a causal inference perspective
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
examples: The article classifies Martin's wheel factors being correlated as Level 1, feedback impacting engagement as Level 2, and teacher support positively affecting outcomes as Level 3
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation
citation: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8
title: Four lines of research on educational interventions against misinformation
description: The review's data-driven approach organizes the 107-article corpus into four distinct research lines, each with its own theoretical perspective, study designs, and intervention types: research on moderators of the misinformation effect (memory literature), lie detection trainings (deception literature), information-literacy trainings (curriculum and instruction), and fraud trainings at the intersection of human behavior and information technology, plus an "other" category for singular articles. The authors state that "The data-driven approach identified four distinct categories that examine educational interventions about misinformation from different angles." Comparing each line to an idealized model of educational interventions reveals research gaps such as missing delayed posttests and unmeasured prior knowledge.
requirements: Articles must describe a concrete implemented intervention with an empirical evaluation of misinformation susceptibility via pretest-to-posttest or control comparisons
constraints: Coding was limited to interventions targeting cognitive processes in individual learners; emotional, behavioral, and stable-factor interventions were excluded
target_learners: adults and children across lab and field studies, depending on the research line
target_learning_goals: recognizing and resisting misinformation
detecting deception
evaluating information credibility
examples: Forty of the 107 articles concerned moderators of the misinformation effect; 30 concerned lie detection trainings; 23 concerned information-literacy trainings
key_sources: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8

article_title: Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving
citation: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w
title: Foster mastery goals through autonomous rather than controlled motivators such as rewards
description: Because mastery aims appear strongly bound to autonomous reasons, educational practice seeking to foster mastery goals should rely on motivators aligned with autonomous regulation rather than external pressure. The article warns that if educators assume aims are equidistant to reasons, "such a practice could undermine autonomous reasons for goal striving in the sense of an overjustification effect and as a result effectively reduce mastery goal striving". Practice should therefore center on the primarily energizing reasons for the desired aim.
requirements: Knowledge of which reasons primarily energize the target aim in the given population
constraints: If an aim were genuinely equidistant to reasons, a broader range of motivators would be suitable; the evidence base for performance aims remains ambiguous
Large external pressure may in some conditions enforce bonds between controlled reasons and an aim
target_learning_goals: mastery goal adoption
autonomous motivation for learning
examples: The article's illustrative case of teachers using rewards for learning, which could backfire for mastery goals given their stronger bond to autonomous reasons
key_sources: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w

article_title: Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning
citation: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7
title: Four-phase model of interest development
description: The article follows Hidi and Renninger's model in which interest is "a cognitive and affective motivational variable that may develop." Development "is initiated by an initial triggering," which, if sustained, "continues to deepen in knowledge and value, and may continue to develop into a well-developed individual interest." Across populations and subject matters the developmental course is the same, yet individual pathways are idiosyncratic; the process may take a short time or extend over several years. The article uses this model to organize its review of interest's indicators, pedagogical supports, and relations to the other variables.
requirements: Sustained support after triggering, through interactions with people and/or environment design, for interest to deepen in knowledge and value
constraints: Students may not be fully aware of their interest, which may impact their ability to self-report it
target_learners: K-16 students in disciplinary classrooms, including science
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and re-engagement with disciplinary content
Development of individual interest in a discipline
examples: The pilot workshop designed NGSS-aligned modules on everyday phenomena so students with no formal science training could make connections and trigger interest
key_sources: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7

article_title: The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study
citation: Rosman, T., Mayer, A.-K., Kerwer, M., & Krampen, G. (2019). The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.01.006
title: Three-semester four-wave longitudinal design with multi-group growth modelling for parallel epistemic-belief processes
description: The study's methodological element is a "three-semester long four-wave study with 226 undergraduates" in which "Data were analysed by multi- group growth modelling for parallel processes." This design permits modelling of belief trajectories across disciplines in parallel, enabling the differential-development analysis that grounded the article's conclusions about epistemic sophistication.
requirements: Repeated measurement across four waves spanning three semesters to model belief trajectories.
constraints: Applied to undergraduates in computer science and psychology; findings reported for these two disciplines.
target_learning_goals: measuring change in epistemic beliefs about the nature of knowledge over time
examples: Hypotheses about discipline-specific belief trajectories were tested in this design.
key_sources: Rosman, T., Mayer, A.-K., Kerwer, M., & Krampen, G. (2019). The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.01.006

article_title: Teachers’ immigration attitudes and students’ performance
citation: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303
title: Foster inclusionary school diversity climates to promote the academic integration of first-generation immigrant students
description: The article's central design recommendation is that schools should cultivate inclusionary diversity climates—reflected in teachers' pro-immigration attitudes—because such climates are associated with higher first-generation immigrant students' performance and narrower achievement gaps. It states that "fostering inclusionary school climates may meaningfully improve first-generation students' achievement" given the observed effect sizes, and that interventions can target students, teachers, or structural features like leadership and policy, with results pointing especially to teacher-focused efforts.
requirements: Requires addressing teachers' explicit attitudes toward immigrant rights and opportunities, e.g., through professional development that reduces prejudice and builds multicultural competencies
constraints: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference; generalizability is constrained to public schools in OECD countries
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
reducing achievement disparities between immigrant and non-immigrant students
examples: In the PISA 2018 data, first-generation students in more inclusionary schools scored up to 29.18 points higher in reading than in more exclusionary schools
key_sources: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303

article_title: The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school
citation: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e
title: Four theoretical models of the interplay between behavioral problems and academic achievement
description: The article organizes prior theory, based on Hinshaw (1992) as described by Chen et al. (2022), into four models of how behavior and achievement interrelate: "The adjustment erosion model", the academic incompetence model, the reciprocal model, and the shared risk model. Each specifies a different direction of influence, including third-variable common antecedents. The study tests these against cross-lagged data and finds no clear preference for any single model across domains.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of both behavior and achievement to distinguish directional paths
constraints: The study's data gave no clear preference for any of the four models; support varied by achievement domain
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading, writing, and mathematics; behavioral development
examples: The study mapped domain-specific results onto the models: shared risk for reading, academic incompetence for writing, adjustment erosion and reciprocal for mathematics.
key_sources: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e

article_title: Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills
citation: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080
title: Formal math teaching activities at home can alleviate familial risk for children of parents with lower math skills
description: The study concludes that teaching activities at home have the potential to alleviate familial risk for children whose parents have lower math skills. For children at risk of developing math difficulties because of parental math difficulties, it was beneficial to support development via formal activities, "such as showing how objects are calculated or teaching how to count." The protective effect was strongest when formal activities occurred before school entry (ages 2 and 5).
requirements: Formal home math activities provided particularly before school entry, targeting children at higher familial risk
constraints: The protective effect of formal HME was smaller at school age; among lower-risk children, more formal HME was associated with worse performance
target_learners: Children at familial risk of math difficulties due to parental math difficulties, ages 2–9
target_learning_goals: Arithmetic fluency in early grades
examples: Higher-risk children with higher levels of formal HME before school entry had better arithmetic skills than higher-risk children with less formal HME
key_sources: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080

article_title: Supplemental Material for Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests
citation: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp
title: Select neuro-psychological measures against four explicit criteria before classroom EEG studies
description: The article proposes screening candidate neuro-psychological measures against four criteria: potential to add unique information about challenge and threat states, compatibility with portable EEG devices, a strong empirical and theoretical basis for inference from EEG data, and the ability to remain meaningful when aggregated over time in observational studies. Applying these criteria iteratively led to selecting alpha-based internal attention and theta-based working memory activity.
requirements: Candidate measures must have a plausible connection between the measured quantity and the cognitive states of interest, and must remain meaningful when averaged over extended periods
constraints: The criteria exclude measures needing precise brain signal localization, millisecond timing or relative phase, event-related potentials, and measures exceeding device frequency specifications
target_learners: high school science students in observational classroom studies
target_learning_goals: measuring cognitive processing and engagement during academic tasks
examples: The criteria excluded event-related potentials because the observational design involved no stimulus manipulation, and identified dominant brain rhythms such as alpha as having the greatest potential

citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: Use student and teacher teaching-effectiveness ratings formatively for reflection and professional learning, not summative evaluation
description: The article positions the SEEQ-S and TEEQ-S as formative diagnostic tools: they are "Designed for formative feedback and professional learning rather than summative evaluation", transforming multidimensional evidence into actionable feedback for reflective practice and targeted professional growth. Multidimensional evaluations suit this purpose because they offer fine-grained information about specific teaching behaviors that can guide instructional improvement over time.
requirements: Feedback must be tailored to individual strengths and growth areas using the 15-factor profile
Integration into routine school improvement cycles with ongoing, longitudinal feedback
constraints: The article states the present study did not directly test feedback interventions; the instruments were designed with this formative purpose in mind

examples: The TXcel initiative integrates SEEQ-S and TEEQ-S into feedback reports to inform goal setting and instructional planning

article_title: Reading comprehension on handheld devices versus on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators.
citation: Salmerón, L., Altamura, L., Delgado, P., Karagiorgi, A., & Vargas, C. (2023). Reading comprehension on handheld devices vs. on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000830
title: Foster print reading in schools while developing effective ways to incorporate handheld devices for reading
description: Based on their synthesis showing a small but significant comprehension advantage for print over handheld devices, the authors recommend that schools continue promoting print reading while also working out how handheld devices can be incorporated effectively for reading purposes. They state: "We discuss the need to continue fostering print reading in schools while developing effective ways to incorporate handheld devices for reading purposes." The educational impact statement adds that in-print reading can be considered an efficient way to promote students' text comprehension.
requirements: Requires recognition that the print advantage is small, so devices need not be excluded but integrated thoughtfully
constraints: The recommendation rests on a small pooled effect with high heterogeneity across studies
target_learners: school students who read on tablets and e-readers
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: The meta-analyses pooled 38 between-participants and 21 within-participants effect sizes comparing handheld-device and print reading comprehension.

article_title: Communications and discussions: The doctrine of formal discipline: two neglected instances of transfer of training.
citation: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Specific training can insure general training under certain limitations, supporting formal discipline
description: The article argues that recent experimental results offer cumulative evidence that the doctrine of formal discipline "is still good pedagogical doctrine under certain limitations," because "Specific training does, under certain conditions and in varying measure, insure general training." It presents transfer of training between analogous functions and corresponding organs as the basis for this position, offering its reversible-perspective instances as further evidence in favor of the doctrine.
requirements: Transfer occurs between analogous or similar functions and organs, under certain conditions and in varying measure
constraints: The author notes some cited experimental results are discrepant with this conclusion, and offers the instances with no attempt to further justify, limit and explain the doctrine
target_learners: learners in educational settings generally, as framed by the doctrine of formal discipline
target_learning_goals: general mental training arising from specific practice
transfer of trained ability to new situations
examples: The article cites practice transferring across hands, senses, school subjects such as neatness from geography to arithmetic, and verbal memorizing, plus its own reversible-perspective experiments.
key_sources: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: An experiment in learning an abstract subject.
citation: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072644
title: Four-factor account of what makes 'hard' subjects hard beyond abstractness, organization, rigor and precision
description: The article proposes that part of the greater difficulty of subjects like mathematics, Latin, or physics is due not only to abstractness, organization, rigor and precision, but to four additional factors: "the sheer unfamiliarity of the date, the greater amount to be learned per unit of time, the more subtle symbolism, and the larger number of missing links—facts that have to be read between the lines." In the experiment all four appeared: strange concepts, thirteen formulas in six hours, symbolism that is at first a burden, and many required inferences. The account reframes subject difficulty as partly incidental rather than intrinsic.
requirements: The account is offered as highly probable from the facts of this one experiment with adult learners of electricity and magnetism, not as a tested result.
constraints: The authors state the common view (abstractness, organization, rigor, precision) is true; the four factors are additions deserving consideration alongside it, not replacements.
target_learners: adult learners of novel abstract material
target_learning_goals: understanding elementary laws of electricity and magnetism
learning abstract, symbolically represented subject matter
examples: The authors illustrate with a half-page textbook passage on magnetic flux requiring multiple inferences, and with hypothetical ways unfamiliar data, symbols, and omitted statements would make history harder.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0065229

article_title: Inspector Winch's experiments on transfer.
citation: Locke, L. L. (1913). Inspector Winch's experiments on transfer. https://www.google.com/books/search?q=%22Inspector+Winch%27s+Experiments+on+Transfer%22
title: Formal discipline: the doctrine defending mathematics courses through transfer since Plato
description: The article names formal discipline as the long-standing doctrine that training in mathematics quickens and disciplines the mind generally. It observes that the doctrine 'has been invoked from Plato's time to the present as a defense of the courses in mathematics,' and treats Inspector Winch's experiment as preliminary research on whether accuracy in reasoning transfers from arithmetical to other situations.
requirements: The doctrine rests on the assumption that arithmetical training produces gains, in quickness at least, in other kinds of knowledge.
constraints: The article notes that the almost universal lay belief in transfer persists regardless of theoretical argument, so the doctrine's popularity does not depend on evidence.
target_learning_goals: transfer of accuracy in reasoning from arithmetical to other situations

article_title: Preliminary study of the relative efficiency of inductive and deductive teaching of logical reasoning.
citation: Felix Sachs. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Relative Efficiency of Inductive and Deductive Teaching of Logical Reasoning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsyc
title: Formal discipline as development of transferable patterns or forms of thought
description: The article frames its experiment within the doctrine of formal discipline as discussed by Meiklejohn, according to which training along a specific line develops patterns or forms of thought that may thereafter function in other and different activities. The study sought to see whether practice in detecting fallacies would build up inductively in observers' minds patterns of these fallacies that could be subsumed and ticketed when the fallacies recurred in other settings and material.
requirements: Access to observers skilled in introspection to study the formation and transfer of patterns, which the author recommends for future repetitions
constraints: The hoped-for introspective account of the genesis and nature of these forms was not realized, whether from error in method, incapacity of observers, or actual impossibility of the task
target_learning_goals: transfer of reasoning patterns to new material
examples: One tutored observer reported in several instances making a deliberate comparison of the test-example with the typical example used in his training

article_title: Reading for university or for myself? Effects of context and beliefs about science on college students’ document selection.
citation: Cornelia Schoor, Jean-François Rouet, and M. Anne Britt (2024). Reading for University or for Myself? Effects of Context and Beliefs about Science on College Students' Document Selection. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116 (3), pp.317-345. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000849
title: Foster both knowledge about how science works and positive beliefs about science in education to support expert-source selection
description: Based on both experiments' finding that more positive beliefs about science and greater knowledge about how science works predict fewer selections of personal-experiences sources, the article's educational impact statement concludes that "these findings indicate the importance of fostering both knowledge and beliefs about science in education". The principle holds that instruction should target not only scientific content knowledge but also learners' trust in and perceived utility of science, since these dispositions shape which sources students consider appropriate for further reading in both academic and personal reading situations.
requirements: Instruction must address both explicit knowledge about how science works and beliefs (trust in and utility of science)
constraints: The evidence base is document selection about science by university students in the studied contexts
target_learning_goals: selecting trustworthy, scientifically expert sources for further reading
examples: The experiments measured utility of science, trust in science, implicit associations, and scenario-based methodology knowledge as the belief and knowledge variables tied to selection behavior.

article_title: Using choice and utility value to promote interest: Stimulating situational interest in a lesson and fostering the development of interest in statistics.
citation: Asher, M. W., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2025). Using Choice and Utility Value to Promote Interest: Stimulating Situational Interest in a Lesson and Fostering the Development of Interest in Statistics. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000921
title: Hidi and Renninger four-phase model of interest development
description: The article organizes its seven experiments around the four-phase model of interest development, in which "interest is both a cognitive and affective state and a motivational variable" and is content specific. The model differentiates situational interest (phases 1 and 2: triggered and maintained) from individual interest (phases 3 and 4: emerging and well-developed), and holds that "individuals don't skip phases of interest development: interest must be triggered before it can be maintained." The authors use it to predict that choice targets triggered situational interest while utility value targets later phases.
requirements: Instructional practices must be matched to the phase of interest development being targeted
constraints: The model concerns interest in a particular topic or content area, not interest in general
target_learning_goals: developing situational and individual interest in academic content
examples: Seven experiments mapped manipulations onto phases: choice was expected to trigger situational interest; utility value to promote maintained situational and emerging individual interest, measured via voluntary resource requests.
key_sources: Asher, M. W., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2025). Using Choice and Utility Value to Promote Interest: Stimulating Situational Interest in a Lesson and Fostering the Development of Interest in Statistics. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000921

article_title: Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry.
citation: Minnick, J. H. (1925). Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Certain+Abilities+Fundamental+to+the+Study+of+Geometry
title: Four abilities fundamental to the formal demonstration of a geometry theorem
description: The article names and describes an explanatory framework of four abilities that it argues success in formal geometric demonstration depends upon: "The ability to draw a figure for the theorem", "The ability to state correctly and accurately the hypothesis and conclusion of the theorem", the ability to recall additional facts about a figure when some are given, and the ability to select from available facts those necessary for a proof and arrange them toward the conclusion. The framework organizes the four diagnostic tests and the diagnosis of class weaknesses.
requirements: Each ability must be measured separately by a test arranged to measure only that one ability, as the article designed Tests A-D to do
constraints: The investigation was limited to classes which had recently completed the first two books of geometry
target_learners: High school geometry students who have completed the first two books of geometry
target_learning_goals: Formal demonstration of geometry theorems
examples: Four tests, known as A, B, C, and D, were developed, each testing one of the abilities in question

article_title: Foil type modulates developmental changes in statistical learning across childhood to adulthood
citation: Liang, F., Zhu, Y., Li, R. & Fu, Q. (2026). Foil Type Modulates Developmental Changes in Statistical Learning Across Childhood to Adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00434-6
title: Include both nonword and partword foils when measuring developmental change in statistical learning
description: The article's own methodological lesson is that foil selection is critical when detecting age-related effects in statistical learning. Because the developmental pattern reversed across foil types — improvement within childhood for nonword foils but an adult advantage for partword foils — the authors state that "this crossover pattern reveals a developmental dissociation that would be obscured if foil types were collapsed." Assessments or studies that collapse foil types or use only one foil type risk missing genuine developmental change.
requirements: Use both nonword foils and partword foils in 2AFC recognition tests of statistical learning
constraints: Demonstrated for auditory statistical learning of trisyllabic nonsense words after brief exposure; the article notes broad child age ranges can also obscure age-related effects
target_learning_goals: auditory statistical learning and word segmentation
examples: In the study, partword foil accuracy was stable within childhood while nonword foil accuracy improved, and the reverse contrast appeared from late childhood to adulthood; collapsing foil types would have hidden both effects
key_sources: Liang, F., Zhu, Y., Li, R. & Fu, Q. (2026). Foil Type Modulates Developmental Changes in Statistical Learning Across Childhood to Adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00434-6

article_title: Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning
citation: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4
title: Four forms of relational reasoning: analogical, anomalous, antithetical, and antinomous
description: Drawing on reasoning, mathematical set theory, and philosophy literatures, the author's research program settled on four forms of relational reasoning encompassing key patterns of similarity and dissimilarity discernible in any informational stream. As printed, the forms "pertained to patterns of similarity (analogical reasoning), discrepancy (anomalous reasoning), opposition (antithetical reasoning), and exclusivity (antinomous reasoning)". Analogical reasoning has garnered the most empirical attention, and anomalous reasoning has focused largely on science and mathematics; antinomous and antithetical reasoning have grounding in ontological categories research and in persuasive-text and conceptual-change literatures.
requirements: Theoretical and empirical grounding within educational, psychological, and philosophical literatures
constraints: Other forms of relational reasoning likely exist beyond these four
target_learning_goals: discerning patterns of similarity, discrepancy, opposition, and exclusivity in informational streams
examples: Heraclitus's unity of opposites is cited as philosophical grounding for antithetical and antinomous reasoning
key_sources: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4

article_title: The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts
citation: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6
title: Four neurosemantic dimensions underlie the neural representation of advanced physics concepts in expert physicists
description: The article proposes that physics concepts in expert brains are organized along four underlying dimensions: "relating to a measurable magnitude", "relating to a mathematical formulation", "entailing a repeated systematic change over time as in periodicity or wave-related concepts", and "relating to classical physics as opposed to post-classical intangible but consilient ideas". These factors emerged from factor analysis of consistently activated voxels and constitute "an orthogonal set of dimensions that collectively underpinned the neural representations of all of the concepts". Independent faculty ratings of the concepts along each dimension converged with the brain-derived factor scores.
requirements: Concepts must be rated along the hypothesized dimensions by independent domain experts to validate the factor interpretations
constraints: Dimensions were derived from the first four seconds of thought about each concept, capturing first-order rather than extended associations
Factor interpretations were developed by one author based on concept ordering, then validated by ratings
target_learning_goals: representation of classical and post-classical physics concepts
examples: Concepts at the extremes of the measurable magnitude dimension included frequency, wavelength, acceleration, and torque at one end and dark matter, duality, cosmology, and multiverse at the other
key_sources: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6

article_title: The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts
citation: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6
title: Four cognitive processes characterize thinking about post-classical physics concepts, each linked to specific brain regions
description: The article proposes that post-classical concepts evoke four types of cognitive processes: "(1) Reasoning about intangibles, taking into account their separation from direct experience and their lack of direct observability; (2) Assessing consilience with other, ﬁrmer knowledge; (3) Causal reasoning about relations that are not apparent or observable ; and (4) Knowledge management of a large knowledge organization consisting of a multi-level structure of other concepts." Each process was linked to voxel clusters whose activation increased for post-classical concepts, with the process-location associations supported by independent ratings convergence, participants' reported properties, and the Neurosynth meta-analysis database. The article notes this reverse inference is uncertain on its own but is backed by converging evidence here.
requirements: Converging evidence beyond reverse inference: ratings convergence, reported concept properties, and meta-analytic location-process associations
constraints: The process attributions rest on reverse inference from activation locations, which the article calls an uncertain inferential method on its own
target_learning_goals: reasoning about intangible, post-classical scientific concepts
examples: The concept of multiverse evoked properties related to assessing consilience, such as "a hypothetical way to explain away … constants."
Thinking about a tachyon invokes a structured network of simpler concepts (mass, velocity, light, etc.), constituting a knowledge unit larger than a single concept
key_sources: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6

article_title: Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion
citation: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8
title: Four-category taxonomy of question types crossing open-closed with possibility-non-possibility dimensions
description: Building on Acar and colleagues' framework, the article proposes crossing two dimensions — open versus closed questions and possibility versus non-possibility thinking — to yield four categories: open non-possibility (O-NP), open possibility (O-P), closed non-possibility (C-NP), and closed possibility (C-P). The article states possibility thinking questions "explicitly invite speculation, imagination, or the consideration of alternatives via words such as '…might…' and '…could…'". Because the taxonomy is grounded in lexical features, it was implemented as an automated rule-based classifier with weighted F1 = 0.896 against human labeling of 1,807 sentences, enabling large-scale analysis of question-posing intent in naturalistic data.
requirements: Reliance on lexical cues in question starters, which the authors note does not fully capture nuances of intent and tone
constraints: Past question categorizations were limited to specific domains; this taxonomy is offered as working assumptions needing further validation with additional psychological measures
target_learning_goals: question-posing as curious behavior
information-seeking stance
examples: Applied to the SGExams corpus, sentences were classified by starter words and modals, e.g., open non-possibility questions begin with interrogatives without possibility modals, closed possibility questions start directly with modal verbs.
key_sources: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8

article_title: Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia
citation: B. Pedemonte, C. W. Pereira, V. Borghesani, M. Ebbert, I. E. Allen, P. Pinheiro-Chagas, J. De Leon, Z. Miller, B. L. Tee & M. L. Gorno-Tempini. (2024). Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00217-x
title: Four-domain taxonomy of mathematical cognition with distinct cognitive and neural correlates
description: The article organizes mathematical cognition into four domains — number processing, arithmetical procedures, arithmetic facts retrieval, and geometrical abilities — each grounded in a distinct body of cognitive and neuroscience research. It states that "These four domains, which affect mathematical cognition and differ in their cognitive and neural correlate s, can be differentially impacted by neurological processes and environmental factors." Number processing rests on subitizing and the approximate number system; procedures rely on fronto-parietal networks; facts retrieval on hippocampal and angular gyrus structures; geometry on occipito-temporal, temporo-parietal, and parietal visuospatial systems.
requirements: Assessment must cover each domain with dedicated subtests, including formats (digits, dots, words), timed and untimed calculation, and 2D/3D geometry tasks
constraints: The article presents this as a preliminary classification; e.g., transcoding and magnitude understanding may subdivide number-processing deficits further
target_learners: children in grades 2–8 with dyslexia or mathematical learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of mathematical cognitive deficits across number processing, calculation, fact retrieval, and geometry
key_sources: B. Pedemonte, C. W. Pereira, V. Borghesani, M. Ebbert, I. E. Allen, P. Pinheiro-Chagas, J. De Leon, Z. Miller, B. L. Tee & M. L. Gorno-Tempini. (2024). Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00217-x

article_title: Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries
citation: Madia, J. E., Gruijters, R. J., Raabe, I. J. & Hübner, N. (2025). Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00365-8
title: Four-way decomposition framework separating the total SES effect into controlled direct, reference interaction, mediated interaction, and pure indirect effects
description: The article applies VanderWeele's four-way decomposition within a counterfactual (potential outcomes) framework to disentangle mediation and interaction. The "TE is the sum of all four components": the Controlled Direct Effect (effect of SES net of mindset), the Reference Interaction (interaction when SES does not affect mindset), the Mediated Interaction (interaction operating through SES-influenced mindset), and the Pure Indirect Effect (SES operating through mindset). The authors argue this avoids overcontrolling bias and misleading coefficient comparisons that plague standard regression approaches in the mindset literature.
requirements: Assumes relationships between SES, growth mindset, and achievement are unconfounded and no reverse causality is present, per the article's stated assumptions
constraints: Estimates are upper bounds of the true causal effect because sequential ignorability may be violated in observational data
target_learners: 15-year-old students assessed in PISA 2022 across 73 countries
target_learning_goals: Mathematics, reading, and science achievement as measured by PISA test scores
examples: Applied to PISA 2022 data from 73 countries using the Stata Med4way package, with the mediator fixed at levels 0, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 plus a closing-gap specification
key_sources: Madia, J. E., Gruijters, R. J., Raabe, I. J. & Hübner, N. (2025). Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00365-8

article_title: The International Science and Evidence-based Education Assessment
citation: Duraiappah, A., van Atteveldt, N., Asah, S., Borst, G., Bugden, S., Buil, J. M., Ergas, O., Fraser, S., Mercier, J., Restrepo Mesa, J. F., Mizala, A., Mochizuki, Y., Okano, K., Piech, C., Pugh, K., Ramaswamy, R., Singh, N. C. & Vickers, E. (2021). The International Science and Evidence-based Education Assessment. npj Science of Learning 6:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00085-9
title: Four pillars of education as benchmarks for evaluating learning success
description: The framework adopts UNESCO's four pillars of education — Learning to Know, Learning to Do, Learning to Be, and Learning to Live Together — as benchmarks for evaluating learning success, which the article links to human flourishing and the Sustainable Development Goals. The article states: "Second, we will use the four pillars of education: (i) learning to Know, (ii) learning to Do, (iii) learning to Be, and learning to Live Together19 as benchmarks to analyze how contextual factors have in ﬂuenced and been in ﬂuenced by the educational aims and practices that these pillars encompass". The pillars are used in Box 4 of the conceptual framework.
requirements: Assessment of the inter-linkages between educational policies and practices (Box 3) and the What, Where, How and When of learning (Box 4)
constraints: Used as benchmarks within the ISEE Assessment's conceptual framework rather than as an independently validated measure
target_learners: learners across all levels and scales of education systems
target_learning_goals: knowing, doing, being, and living together as educational aims
examples: The assessment will analyze how contextual factors have influenced and been influenced by the educational aims and practices the pillars encompass

article_title: Enhancing learning and retrieval of new information: a review of the forward testing effect
citation: Chunliang Yang, Rosalind Potts and David R. Shanks. (2018). Enhancing learning and retrieval of new information: a review of the forward testing effect. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0024-y
title: Eight-mechanism theoretical framework for the forward testing effect, classified by locus (encoding vs retrieval) and motivational role
description: The review organizes candidate explanations of the forward testing effect along two dimensions: whether the mechanism acts at encoding or retrieval, and whether it is motivational. Non-motivational accounts are the release from PI, encoding reset, activation facilitation, encoding strategy, and retrieval strategy theories; motivational accounts are the test expectancy, failure-encoding-effort, and retrieval effort theories, the latter two attributing effort to "retrieval failures in prior interim tests" inducing dissatisfaction. Mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and may operate in parallel; which dominates depends on material, e.g. release from PI matters for single items while activation facilitation matters for complex materials.
requirements: Direct testing of key predictions made by different theoretical accounts, which the review says few have received
constraints: The review states most accounts are at a preliminary stage of development and few have been directly tested
Mechanisms need not be mutually exclusive and may produce overlapping forward testing effects
target_learners: College students and other learners studied in forward testing experiments
target_learning_goals: Learning and retrieval of new information following interim testing on prior material
examples: The review cites Yang et al.'s Experiment 3 measuring classification time as an index of retrieval effort, which affirmed the retrieval effort theory's prediction
Weinstein et al. had participants report test-expectancy before each list and found the Interim Test group's expectancy increased across lists while the Distractor group's decreased

article_title: Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling
citation: Nicole M. Hutchins & Gautam Biswas & Ningyu Zhang & Caitlin Snyder & Ákos Lédeczi & Miklós Maróti. (2020). Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00209-z
title: Four-step educational DSML design process mapping curriculum learning objectives to modeling-language constructs
description: The article implements its design principles as a four-step process: (1) domain analysis via evidence-centered design, (2) integrated domain maps connecting STEM, CT, and modeling constructs, (3) creation of DSML blocks based on evidence from the first two steps, and (4) implementation of system structures such as the Simulation Step and Initialization blocks. The authors state the framework "is implemented as a four-step process" and demonstrate it in Physics, Marine Biology, and Earth Science to show generality.
requirements: Each step depends on outputs of the previous ones: block creation (step 3) must follow from the domain analysis and integrated domain maps
constraints: Steps must be adjusted to the target audience's math proficiency, e.g., qualitative relations for middle school versus analytic equations for high school
target_learners: K-12 science students across elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: model building and problem solving in science
computational thinking practices
examples: In Physics, position and velocity mapped to variable initialization and updating blocks, while no acceleration-update block was included to match curriculum scope.
