article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: Four peer tutor help-giving skills as targets for adaptive support
description: APTA's adaptive support targets an enumerated set of tutor competencies: "our goal was to target four peer tutor skills that exemplify good help in our context." These are timely help (responding to tutee errors and help requests), appropriate help (prompting self-explanation and giving error feedback), conceptual help (explaining steps with domain concepts), and use of classifiers (accurately labeling utterances). Each skill maps to a subset of the production rules and to its own knowledge-traced skill estimate that drives feedback selection.
requirements: Sentence classifiers in the chat interface so classifier use can be assessed
Access to tutee problem-solving step evaluations from the domain tutor
constraints: The skill set is specific to the peer tutoring context and literal equation solving domain
target_learners: High school students acting as peer tutors
target_learning_goals: Giving timely, appropriate, and conceptual help during peer tutoring
examples: When a tutor gives an instrumental hint after a tutee error, the system may ask in chat, "Tutor, why do you say that? Can you explain more?"
key_sources: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9

article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: Four-valence production rule model of peer tutor help-giving with adapted knowledge tracing
description: APTA models peer tutoring with 19 production rules divided into four valence levels rather than correct/buggy: "rules were divided into four types: effective, somewhat effective, somewhat ineffective, and ineffective behaviors. These four levels allowed us to represent ambiguity in the model." Rules cover four skills (timely, appropriate, conceptual help, classifier use) and fire on tutor inaction as well as action. An algorithm based on Bayesian knowledge tracing maintains a mastery probability per skill, and rule firings update it; unmodeled behavior is treated as correct, as in constraint-based tutoring.
requirements: Multiple assessment channels: CTA step classifications, student self-classifications, and machine dialogue classifications
A configurable xml rule representation so the rule set can be modified without recompiling
constraints: The approach violates knowledge-tracing assumptions: a student can transfer from a learned to an unlearned state, and more than one skill maps to a given action
Skill estimates are tuned to trigger feedback rather than to accurately estimate collaborative skills
target_learners: High school peer tutors in algebra
target_learning_goals: Peer tutoring help-giving skills
examples: A tutor's nonconceptual next-step hint after a tutee error fired rules 2, 13, 15, and 16, raising timely-help and classifier estimates while lowering appropriate-help and conceptual-help estimates

article_title: Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies
citation: Sandra Schulz · Bruce M. McLaren · Niels Pinkwart. (2023). Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00305-2
title: Give robotics feedback through a four-layer escalation from general problem category to concrete solution
description: Feedback during robotics problem-solving should escalate through four layers: naming the main problem category, then the subcategory, then a situation-specific description of the problem without revealing the solution, and only in the fourth layer the concrete problem and a solution. Wizards “go[] always from the 1st layer to the 4th layer and only providing more detailed help if needed”, so students are led toward the solution without being handed it, and each new independent problem restarts at layer 1.
requirements: Wizards trained in the model and its feedback rules, with standardized wording, continuous observation of students' interaction, body language and progress, and support only when help is needed.
constraints: Wording on layers 3 and 4 may vary slightly by wizard; timing of further hints varies with students' motivation and self-efficacy; one wizard reported needing to jump directly to layer 4 when earlier layers were not understood.
target_learners: secondary school students (grades 7–11) working in pairs on robotics programming tasks
target_learning_goals: problem-solving, debugging, and troubleshooting strategy during robotics activities
examples: In the worked example, the wizard tells students the problem lies in the software (layer 1), in the program code (layer 2), that the robot should not drive so close to the box (layer 3), and finally to program the ultrasonic threshold to at least 15 cm (layer 4).
key_sources: Sandra Schulz · Bruce M. McLaren · Niels Pinkwart. (2023). Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00305-2

article_title: ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem
citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: Four-Loop User Adaptation model extends traditional ITS adaptation at grain sizes above the outer loop and below the inner loop
description: The article proposes a four-loop model of user adaptation built on VanLehn's (2006) inner loop/outer loop framing. Beyond macro-adaptivity (problem selection) and step-based adaptivity (hints and feedback), it adds meta-adaptivity, where "the system adapts to the user by shifting the learner to an entirely different ITS system," and micro-adaptivity, which fine-tunes interactions below the problem step level. The paper states: "This implies a four-loop model for user adaptation, as shown in Fig.1." It holds that system, activity, and step boundaries "are likely to remain key decision points for adaptive systems."
requirements: Adaptation loops at meta and micro grain sizes require sufficient user data and mature AIED technology to be feasible
constraints: The article notes other loops of interest may exist and that VanLehn (2015) framed ITS behavior more generally as regulatory loops
target_learners: learners using adaptive learning technologies in formal and self-directed settings
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of problems, feedback, systems, and event-level interactions matched to learner needs
examples: Fig. 1 depicts the four-loop model spanning system handoffs, problem selection, step-level help, and event-level optimization
key_sources: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8

article_title: Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches
citation: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1
title: Four-task architecture of difficulty prediction models: ground truth labelling, pre-processing, feature extraction, prediction
description: The review characterises difficulty prediction models as sharing four architectural components representing four fundamental tasks: "1) Ground truth labelling, 2) pre-processing, 3) feature extraction and 4) prediction." Ground truth is labelled via psychometric theories (CTT, IRT) or expert rating; pre-processing applies standard NLP techniques such as stemming, POS tagging and lemmatisation; feature extraction operates at syntactic (surface) or semantic levels; and prediction is overwhelmingly supervised. The review uses this structure to organise its findings sections.
requirements: A dataset of questions with ground-truth difficulty labels, obtained via psychometric testing theories or manual labelling
constraints: Feature extraction is limited in the review's scope to features intrinsically derived from item structure, not student performance data
target_learners: students taking pedagogical assessments in classroom, CAT, ITS and AQG settings
target_learning_goals: predicting question difficulty to support item calibration, item sequencing and evaluation of generated questions
examples: The review's subsections Ground Truth Labelling, Pre-processing, Feature Extraction and Prediction each treat one of the four tasks
key_sources: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1

article_title: Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students
citation: Josu Arruarte, Mikel Larrañaga, Ana Arruarte & Jon A. Elorriaga. (2021). Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 585–602. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00208-0
title: Four-aspect classification of metrics and statistics for measuring the quality of test-based exercises
description: The article classifies the metrics and statistics usable to measure the quality of test-based exercises from student performance data according to four aspects: whether the results of the exercise are consistent (CIC via Cronbach's alpha, True Weight), whether undesired situations can be inferred (mean, median, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis), whether the exercise meets the student's level of knowledge (Ease Index, Item Difficulty), and whether the exercise can determine the student's knowledge level (Error Ratio, Standard Error, Random Guess Score, Discrimination Index, Discrimination Efficiency, Item Discrimination Index). This classification, building on Peña (2014), structures both the tool and the evaluation questions.
requirements: The analysis assumes students have only one attempt to answer each question and that all the students have already answered.
constraints: Some metrics are valid only at the item level (e.g., CIC, true weight, error ratio, standard error), others only at the test level (e.g., standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis).
target_learners: teachers and developers of educational material
target_learning_goals: evaluating the quality and validity of test-based exercises and items
examples: TEA implements these metrics and statistics and presents them through visualizations and alerts.
key_sources: Josu Arruarte, Mikel Larrañaga, Ana Arruarte & Jon A. Elorriaga. (2021). Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 585–602. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00208-0

article_title: Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus
citation: Michael D. Mrazek, Dustyn S. Ransom, Amy R. Texter, Calvin V. Tower, Bryce A. Rutila, Thomas F. Kennedy, Elijah J. Woodson, Jonathan W. Schooler, Alissa J. Mrazek. (2026). Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10730-y
title: Focus Coach digital study tool
description: The Focus Coach is a no-cost, publicly available digital study tool that students keep open on their phone or computer while completing a separate academic assignment. It supports attention training through customizable sessions, real-time self-monitoring via periodic check-ins asking “Just then, how focused were you?”, and progress tracking via an end-of-session graph of focus. It occupies the full phone screen to block unrelated apps, offers curated ambient soundtracks, and lets teachers view engagement patterns while individual responses remain private. It complements a brief online course teaching anchoring, focusing, and releasing distractions.
requirements: Used during real academic work (independent work or homework), typically alongside the online attention-training course; students customize session duration, check-in frequency, check-in sound, and optional ambient soundtrack.
constraints: The article notes it is not possible to assess focus trajectories without the tool, and the tool and course were delivered together, so unique component effects cannot be disentangled.
target_learners: adolescent middle and high school students in public schools
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and self-regulating focus during academic work
examples: In Study 1 students completed an average of 6.4 Focus Coach sessions (SD = 3.9) averaging 20.4 minutes, answering 2.6 check-ins per session; in Study 2, 5.3 sessions averaging 16.3 minutes.
key_sources: Michael D. Mrazek, Dustyn S. Ransom, Amy R. Texter, Calvin V. Tower, Bryce A. Rutila, Thomas F. Kennedy, Elijah J. Woodson, Jonathan W. Schooler, Alissa J. Mrazek. (2026). Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10730-y

article_title: Critical events and pivotal factors as tools for analyzing the sustainability of online study programs
citation: Jarkko Suhonen · Erkki Sutinen. (2022). Critical events and pivotal factors as tools for analyzing the sustainability of online study programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10133-9
title: Four-pillar sustainability model for online study programs
description: The article applies a four-pillar sustainability model in which "The model consists of four sustainability pillars: economic, social, environmental, and ethical." The economic pillar covers resources and funding, the social pillar internal dynamics and community, the environmental pillar the physical, technical, cultural and psychological contexts, and the ethical pillar the values behind goals and working principles. The pillars are mutually interrelated and can be traded off; the authors use the model to analyze critical events and pivotal factors of an online doctoral program.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying pivotal factors connected to critical events from the perspective of each pillar
constraints: The authors note relying too heavily on a single pillar or even two could be potentially problematic for the sustainability of the program
target_learners: doctoral students in online study programs
target_learning_goals: sustainable design and continuation of online study programs
examples: The authors analyzed six critical events of the IMPDET online doctoral program using the model, labeling factors Eco+, Eco-, Env+, Env-, So+, So-, Et+, Et-.
key_sources: Jarkko Suhonen · Erkki Sutinen. (2022). Critical events and pivotal factors as tools for analyzing the sustainability of online study programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10133-9

article_title: A systematic review of using tablet games to promote early math learning in preschool settings: effectiveness and influencing factors
citation: Jing Chen. (2026). A systematic review of using tablet games to promote early math learning in preschool settings: effectiveness and influencing factors. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10626-x
title: Four-level model of factors influencing tablet-based DGBL effectiveness
description: The review organizes influencing factors, adapted from Outhwaite et al. (2020b), into four levels: "app-level factors, individual-level factors, school-level factors, and macro-level factors". App-level factors include self-adaptation, multi-level content, and a parental involvement module; individual-level factors include demographic, developmental, environmental, and experience-related variables; school-level factors cover time on task and integration mode; macro-level factors cover device accessibility and educational philosophy. The review concludes effectiveness "is not determined by a single factor but by the interplay among four-level factors", shifting focus from whether DGBL works to under what conditions it works.
requirements: Requires coding of intervention studies across all four levels to give a comprehensive picture of implementation conditions
constraints: Some identified factors may not show influences in the reviewed studies; macro-level factors' influence has not yet been explored
target_learning_goals: early mathematics learning (numeracy, shapes, spatial abilities, measurement)
examples: The review coded each included study's discussion sections against the four-level framework, producing Tables 8 and 9 of factors with example studies
key_sources: Jing Chen. (2026). A systematic review of using tablet games to promote early math learning in preschool settings: effectiveness and influencing factors. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10626-x

article_title: Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed?
citation: Hankeln, C., Kroehne, U., Voss, L., Gross, S., & Prediger, S. (2025). Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed? Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 1953–1973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10486-x
title: Four-step research-informed design process for topic-specific DFAs of deep conceptual understanding
description: The article suggests four steps to ensure the validity, relevance, and in-depth informativity of DFAs: Step 1, selection of relevant topics by identifying basic concepts; Step 2, unpacking selected basic concepts into concept elements, representations, language means, and valid indicators; Step 3, optimizing validity and in-depth informativity of DFA items; and Step 4, enhancing in-depth informativity by exploiting additional digital potentials such as log data and speech-to-text.
requirements: Steps 1 and 2 are purely subject-matter related, while Steps 3 and 4 have to take the digital environment into account
constraints: The four-step design process can help to identify technical limitations of digital platforms
target_learners: Grade 5–7 students who struggle in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding of abstract concepts
key_sources: Hankeln, C., Kroehne, U., Voss, L., Gross, S., & Prediger, S. (2025). Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed? Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 1953–1973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10486-x

article_title: Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas
citation: Zvereva, G., Guillén, G., Al-Msallam, S., Hamari, J., & Xi, N. (2026). Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10678-z
title: Four business ethics board games varying in ethical sense-making, social interaction modes, and themes
description: The study employed four business ethics board games adopted from prior research: LMX: The Game!, the Ethics Argumentation Game, Privacy by Design, and the Trading Trainers Game. They were "adopted from prior research and designed to vary in ethical sense-making, modes of social interaction, and themes", implemented as independent pedagogical tools without teacher facilitation, with printed materials and clear rules. Table 1 reports participants' evaluations of each game on a 1 (Very Poor) to 7 (Excellent) scale.
requirements: Games were new to participants, used printed materials, and were accompanied by clear rules
constraints: The games were implemented as independent pedagogical tools without any intended facilitation from teachers or instructors
target_learners: adults of diverse cultural, professional, and age backgrounds, aged 18-59
target_learning_goals: ethical sensitivity, ethical reasoning, ethical motivation, and ethical action in business contexts
examples: Games were played in randomized order, two per morning and two per afternoon, with participants randomly assigned to 2-3-member teams per game
key_sources: Zvereva, G., Guillén, G., Al-Msallam, S., Hamari, J., & Xi, N. (2026). Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10678-z

article_title: Implementing open educational resources in digital education
citation: Tang, H. (2021). Implementing open educational resources in digital education. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 389–392. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09879-x
title: Four perspectives—research, design, culture, practice—for implementing OER in digital education
description: The article organizes its special issue around four perspectives on implementing OER in digital education: research, design, culture, and practice. It states that the issue "presents four additional perspectives in research, design, culture, practice about implementing OER in digital education," extending Hilton's (2016) efficacy-focused synthesis. The framework treats implementation as requiring attention beyond efficacy alone.
requirements: Implementation of OER in digital education is considered alongside, not instead of, evidence of OER efficacy
constraints: The article text provided presents the framework as a framing for a special issue rather than substantiating each perspective
target_learners: K-12 learners in digital education contexts
target_learning_goals: effective learning with open educational resources in digital education
examples: The special issue extends Hilton's (2016) synthesized findings by presenting the four perspectives
key_sources: Tang, H. (2021). Implementing open educational resources in digital education. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 389–392. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09879-x

article_title: Everyone already has their community beyond the screen: reconceptualizing online learning and expanding boundaries
citation: Kyungmee Lee. (2018). Everyone already has their community beyond the screen: reconceptualizing online learning and expanding boundaries. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9613-y
title: Four-phase development of an internal course CoP paired with sequenced external CoP development tasks
description: In the double-layered CoP model, "an online course itself is nurtured and developed into an internal CoP through four interdependent learning phases; i.e., course preparation, foundation building, interactive learning, and knowledge transfer". In parallel, each student develops an existing community in their teaching context into an external CoP through sequenced sub-tasks: community selection, membership development, knowledge sharing, and collaborative practice. Students write CoP journal entries reflecting on these experiences and connecting course ideas to practice.
requirements: Course preparation must explicitly explain the double-layered CoP structure and emphasize the value of learning in CoPs before the course starts
constraints: The external CoP development task is described as rather challenging and needs to be structured as small sub-tasks in a sequence
target_learners: in-service teachers and adult professionals in online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: linking course knowledge to professional practice and facilitating knowledge transfer between internal and external CoPs
examples: Foundation building provides introductory CoP readings with the discussion question 'Is CoP a useful concept for learning?'
key_sources: Kyungmee Lee. (2018). Everyone already has their community beyond the screen: reconceptualizing online learning and expanding boundaries. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9613-y

article_title: What makes for readable writing and reading success
citation: Audio-Visual Communication Review, digest items abstracted by E. G. Sherburne, Jr. and Edmund Faison. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=audio-visual+communication+review
title: Use readability formulas as an aid to editorial judgment, not as a substitute for it
description: The readability survey recommends treating formula scores as one input to writing and editing decisions. Because the formulas "deal with stylistic qualities of prose rather than with its meaning", their results "may serve as an aid to the judgment of an editor or writer", while the content aspect of readability remains the province of a talented writer or competent editor.
requirements: A writer or editor must supply the content-side judgment of readability that the formulas do not measure
constraints: The formulas measure stylistic qualities rather than meaning, so scores do not capture content readability
target_learners: writers and editors of instructional printed material
target_learning_goals: producing readable instructional text
examples: The survey positions formula results as an aid to the judgment of an editor or writer, with content readability handled by the editor or writer themselves
key_sources: Audio-Visual Communication Review, digest items abstracted by E. G. Sherburne, Jr. and Edmund Faison. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=audio-visual+communication+review

article_title: “I don’t think that word means what you think it means”: A proposed framework for defining learning communities
citation: Richard E. West, Gregory S. Williams. (2017). 'I don't think that word means what you think it means': A proposed framework for defining learning communities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9535-0
title: Four-boundary framework for defining learning communities: access, relationships, vision, and function
description: The article proposes that learning communities be defined by four boundaries that serve as limits for what counts as a community: access (who is present physically or virtually), relationships (emotional ties), vision (shared purpose), and function (what members do together). The authors state that "learning community boundaries often defined in terms of participants' sense that they share access, relationships, vision, or function", and that these boundaries "sometimes overlap but often represent distinctive features". The framework is offered to guide research and practice.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners must specify which boundary or boundaries they use when defining or studying a learning community
constraints: The authors state the boundaries "are not finalized indicators" and recommend further research to verify or adapt the framework
target_learning_goals: understanding and cultivating learning communities
improving research on social learning
examples: The authors apply the boundary strategy to freshman learning communities, virtual communities, and classroom-based K-16 student communities identified in their literature review
key_sources: Richard E. West, Gregory S. Williams. (2017). 'I don't think that word means what you think it means': A proposed framework for defining learning communities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9535-0

article_title: Putting learning back into learning analytics: actions for policy makers, researchers, and practitioners
citation: Dirk Ifenthaler, David Gibson, Doreen Prasse, Atsushi Shimada, Masanori Yamada. (2021). Putting learning back into learning analytics: actions for policy makers, researchers, and practitioners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09909-8
title: Four themes of learning analytics challenges: data literacy, guiding principles and policies, ethical standards, and flexible user-centred design
description: The article organises the issues and challenges facing educators linked to learning analytics into four themes developed by an international expert panel. As printed, "The four themes are 1. development of data literacy in all stakeholders, 2. updating of guiding principles and policies of educational data, 3. standards needed for ethical practices with data quality assurance, and 4. flexible user-centred design for a variety of users of analytics, starting with learners and ensuring that learners and learning is not harmed." The themes frame both the Delphi findings and the research agenda.
requirements: The themes emerged from expert panel discussion and are offered as provocations to organise researcher, policymaker and practitioner dialogs
constraints: The themes are outcomes of expert panel discussion rather than tested empirical results
target_learning_goals: supporting learning processes and educational decision-making with learning analytics
ethical and effective use of educational data
examples: The expert panel agreed there is a widespread lack of knowledge and understanding regarding learning analytics and the need to select and use learning analytics systems to support learning, teaching and assessment
key_sources: Dirk Ifenthaler, David Gibson, Doreen Prasse, Atsushi Shimada, Masanori Yamada. (2021). Putting learning back into learning analytics: actions for policy makers, researchers, and practitioners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09909-8

article_title: Virtual virtuoso: a systematic literature review of immersive learning environments for psychomotor skill development
citation: Khaleel Asyraaf Mat Sanusi, Deniz Iren, Nardie Fanchamps, Mai Geisen, Roland Klemke. (2025). Virtual virtuoso: a systematic literature review of immersive learning environments for psychomotor skill development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10449-2
title: Four-dimension framework for analyzing ILEs for psychomotor skill training
description: The review organizes ILE-based psychomotor training research around four interconnected dimensions: "motor skills, ILE technologies, feedback components, and design characteristics of virtual environments". Each dimension is grounded in principles that can enhance training effectiveness, and synthesizing them "enables a comprehensive analysis of utilizing ILEs in the context of psychomotor skill training". The framework structures the review's research questions, frequency analysis, and correlation analysis.
requirements: Studies must address at least one of the four dimensions (motor skills, technologies, feedback, design characteristics) to be analyzed within the framework
constraints: The framework was applied to a corpus of 39 peer-reviewed studies published from 2013 onwards
target_learners: learners training psychomotor skills in immersive learning environments
target_learning_goals: psychomotor skill development and acquisition
examples: The review coded 39 articles with one-hot encoding across the four dimensions and ran frequency and Pearson correlation analyses on the resulting variables
key_sources: Khaleel Asyraaf Mat Sanusi, Deniz Iren, Nardie Fanchamps, Mai Geisen, Roland Klemke. (2025). Virtual virtuoso: a systematic literature review of immersive learning environments for psychomotor skill development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10449-2

article_title: Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic
citation: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6
title: Four-profile classification of creative intention versus effective solution in repeated tasks
description: The article classifies participants along two axes — creative versus conservative intention, and creative versus conservative effective solution — yielding four profiles: the creatives, the conservatives, the non-intentional creatives and the non-intentional conservatives. Non-intentional creatives intended to repeat their solution but failed and adopted a creative behavior, while non-intentional conservatives include participants whose creative intention collapsed into conservative behavior. This pattern lets an observer diagnose where in a repeated task creative pursuit is lost or accidentally achieved.
requirements: Video analysis of both task occurrences to code the first figure tested in activity 2 and the successful final figures
constraints: Profiles were identified in one educational robotic task with adult participants
target_learning_goals: diagnosing creative intention and persistence in repeated tasks
examples: A participant reproducing a train figure by only swapping two cubes was coded as the same figure; assembling the four cubes in a square was coded as a different figure.
key_sources: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6

article_title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
citation: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6
title: Four-domain conceptual framework for teachers' AI competency
description: The article proposes a new framework extending DigCompEdu, P21's framework, and Ng et al.'s four cognition domains model, organizing teachers' AI competency into four domains: "Teacher professional engagement", "Instructional design", "Content choices" across disciplines, and "Learning competencies". It frames AI competency as "a non-technical, critical and complex competency that young people need to learn to manipulate AI technologies ethically, safely and wisely", not merely technological skill. The framework is offered as a guide for instructional design and professional development in the post-pandemic context.
requirements: Teachers and school leaders must be aware of opportunities and challenges of employing AI systems before applying the framework
constraints: Conceptual paper using research examples as evidence; the framework is proposed rather than empirically validated
target_learning_goals: AI digital competencies
twenty-first century skills
AI literacy
key_sources: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6

article_title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
citation: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6
title: Four cognition domains of AI competency based on Bloom's taxonomy
description: Drawing on Ng et al. (2021b), the article describes a model categorizing AI competencies into four cognition domains: "know and understand; use and apply; evaluate and create; and ethical issues", ordered from lower to higher thinking skills and inspired by Bloom's Taxonomy. For example, recognizing and understanding AI maps to know and understand, critically interpreting data to evaluate and create, and societal impacts to ethical issues. The model helps teachers design instruction and assessment around students' AI competencies.
requirements: Educators design instructions and assessments around these competencies
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
AI knowledge from low to high thinking skills
key_sources: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6

article_title: Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning
citation: Lin Lin, Tristan Johnson. (2021). Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09960-z
title: Four-aspect commentary framework: Impact/Value, Application, Limitations and Constraints, Future Suggestions
description: The editors established review criteria asking responding authors to structure their commentary pieces around four aspects: 'Impact/Value', 'Application', 'Limitations and Constraints', and 'Future Suggestions'. Each aspect is phrased as a question the respondent answers from their own perspective, e.g., 'What impact or value does the paper have on "Shift to Digital" from your specific perspective?' This pattern turns a review of prior work into practice-oriented dialogue.
requirements: Respondent authors identify 2–3 manuscripts of interest and specify the perspective they will focus on
A defined context of need, here flexible learning, online learning, and learning disruptions with limited resources
constraints: Essays were 500–1000 words and situated the 17 previously published articles within COVID-19 learning needs
target_learning_goals: applying published research to rapid digital shifts
examples: Responding authors were asked to focus on Impact/Value, Application, Limitations and Constraints, and Future Suggestions when writing their commentary pieces
key_sources: Lin Lin, Tristan Johnson. (2021). Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09960-z

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Four dimensions of epistemic fluency for postdigital teaching
description: Drawing on Markauskaite and Goodyear (2017), the article identifies four key dimensions of fluency: "(1) combination and integration of different kinds of knowledge; (2) coordination and weaving different ways of knowing; (3) creating tools and assembling productive environments; and (4) constructing a conscientious and conscious self". These dimensions connect to postdigital pedagogies and underpin capabilities for teaching in hybrid environments, including knowing when to design, when to practise skills, when to learn from colleagues, and when to outsource decisions to learning analytics tools.
requirements: Teachers engaging in different kinds of expert practices, not explicit professional learning alone, to develop recognition of what makes teaching productive in a situation
constraints: The article states this recognition cannot be achieved through explicit professional learning alone
target_learning_goals: integrating diverse knowledge and ways of knowing in hybrid teaching
co-designing tools and environments
examples: The article describes empathic design of digital learning environments and engaging learners in co-design as practices connected to the third dimension
key_sources: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z

article_title: Designing research to inform sustainability and scalability of digital technology innovations
citation: Howard, S. K., Schrum, L., Voogt, J., & Sligte, H. (2021). Designing research to inform sustainability and scalability of digital technology innovations. Educational Technology Research and Development, 69(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09913-y
title: Four-loop causal model of technological innovation: Organization, Innovation, Research, New Contexts
description: The article presents an adapted causal loop model drawing on systems thinking, in which 'loops' represent components of a system of technology innovation in education and arrows represent effects between components. The four loops are Organization (L1) at the core, Innovation (L2), Research (L3), and New Contexts (L4). It was developed by a thematic working group of educational technology experts at EDUsummIT 2019 and refined against literature on educational change, and is used to analyze three international case studies.
requirements: Research must be led by participants and co-constructed with researchers, and outputs aimed at practitioners, for the Research loop to be meaningful
constraints: The authors state this is only an initial testing of the model and considerable work is needed to validate the key factors and relationships among the loops
target_learners: teachers and teacher educators involved in technology integration
target_learning_goals: understanding and designing sustainable and scalable technology innovations
examples: The model was applied as a coding structure to three case studies from the Netherlands, United States and Australia, with results mapped to the framework in Figs. 2, 3 and 4
key_sources: Howard, S. K., Schrum, L., Voogt, J., & Sligte, H. (2021). Designing research to inform sustainability and scalability of digital technology innovations. Educational Technology Research and Development, 69(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09913-y

article_title: Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions
citation: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x
title: Four participation styles in online instructional discussions: To Socialize/Connective, To Get Information/Analytical, To Discuss/Innovative, To Fulfill Requirements/Practical
description: The article identifies four participation styles formed by pairing each Why factor with its parallel How factor. The authors state: "The participation styles were accordingly defined as 'To Socialize/Connective,' 'To Get Information/Analytical,' 'To Discuss/Innovative,' and 'To Fulfill Requirements/Practical.'" Each style pairs a motivation (e.g., socializing, information seeking, discussing, fulfilling requirements) with a characteristic behavior pattern (connective, analytical, innovative, or practical participation). The styles are determined by the factor on which a student scores highest.
requirements: Scores are calculated per factor, and the predominant style is the one with the most points; when dimensions are used together, the predominant style is determined by averaging item points
constraints: The article notes there may be other styles beyond these four; the styles were validated with Turkish undergraduate and graduate student samples
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in online instructional discussions
target_learning_goals: categorizing learners' participation styles to guide discussion environment design and self-aware learning management
examples: Instructors and researchers can determine learners' participation styles before organizing discussion environments
key_sources: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x

article_title: Immersive virtual reality serious games for evacuation training and research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://www.scopus.com
title: Four narrative methods structure IVR serious game storylines: action-driven, instruction-driven, performance-driven, and surroundings-driven
description: The review identifies four narrative methods for encouraging participants to follow and complete IVR SG storylines: "there were four narrative methods recognized by this review, namely action-driven method (Chittaro & Buttussi, 2015) , instruction-driven method (Andrée et al., 2016; Aoki et al., 2007; Burigat & Chittaro, 2016; Cosma et al., 2016; Meng & Zhang, 2014; Smith & Ericson, 2009; Zou et al., 2016) , performance-driven method (Li et al., 2017), and surrounding -driven method". Action- and surroundings-driven methods restrict movement so participants must follow the storyline, while instruction- and performance-driven methods keep the open world, relying on participants' ability and willingness to complete the game.
requirements: A narrative method is needed because an IVR environment can often be simulated as an open world where participants may get lost or wander around out of curiosity
constraints: Narrative method choice should account for participants' background, expected outcomes, and the IVR environment
target_learners: building occupants training for indoor emergencies
target_learning_goals: following and completing evacuation training storylines
achieving expected learning and behavior outcomes
examples: Li et al. (2017) introduced a scoring system generating scores based on gaming performance; Duarte et al. (2014) and the Kinateder and Ronchi studies filled the environment with simulated hazards so participants had no choice but to follow the storyline pathway
key_sources: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.002

article_title: A framework to analyze argumentative knowledge construction in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Armin Weinberger, Frank Fischer. (2006). A Framework to Analyze Argumentative Knowledge Construction in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2005.04.003
title: Four process dimensions for analyzing argumentative knowledge construction in CSCL
description: The article proposes analyzing argumentative knowledge construction in CSCL along four process dimensions: participation, epistemic, argumentative, and social mode. The framework spans the whole analysis pipeline, "from sampling and segmentation of the discourse corpora to the analysis of four process dimensions". It is intended to refine process-oriented instructional support such as collaboration scripts by making specific discourse processes measurable.
requirements: Discourse corpora from CSCL settings must first be sampled and segmented before the four process dimensions can be analyzed.
constraints: The framework targets written argumentative discourse in CSCL, such as asynchronous discussion boards, rather than all forms of learning interaction.
target_learners: collaborative learners in computer-supported learning environments
target_learning_goals: argumentative knowledge construction
key_sources: Armin Weinberger, Frank Fischer. (2006). A Framework to Analyze Argumentative Knowledge Construction in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2005.04.003

article_title: Examining supervising field instructors’ reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement
citation: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753
title: Formalise school-university partnerships to align technology expectations on placement
description: The article argues that without formal school-university partnerships, pre-service teachers are caught between differing school and university expectations regarding technology use. It states that "Until stronger and more formalised school-university partnerships are achieved, this problem is unlikely to be addressed adequately, regardless of the level of professional mentoring provided to supervising field instructors." Formal partnerships would enable professional conversations between cooperating teachers and supervising field instructors, allowing both parties to interrogate dominant teacher-centred technology practices and align expectations for pre-service teachers.
requirements: Institutional policy commitment to developing formal school-university partnership structures
constraints: The article notes this applies to the Irish context where such partnerships are currently lacking and informal dialogue does not extend beyond conversations about how the pre-service teacher is getting on
target_learning_goals: developing student-centred technology-enhanced teaching practices
key_sources: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753

article_title: Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study
citation: Klassen, Robert Mark, Wang, Hui, Cutting, Joe, Thompson-Lee, Sophie, Snell, Rebecca J.S., See, Beng Huat, Saiger, Michael. (2025). Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105450
title: Four psychosocial dimensions of user experience in persuasive game design: meaning, immersion, mastery, and autonomy
description: The article draws on Abeele et al. (2020) to identify "four psychosocial dimensions related to user experience ... especially relevant in the design of persuasive games: meaning, immersion, mastery, and autonomy." Meaning connects to a game's purpose, immersion to cognitive absorption, mastery to competence-building from challenging experiences, and autonomy to perceived choice during gameplay. These dimensions were measured with the PXI and used as mediators in the study's latent change models.
requirements: Measured using the PXI user experience instrument with four 3-item domains rated 0–6
target_learning_goals: increase teaching interest
increase teaching self-efficacy
increase perceived person-vocation fit
key_sources: Klassen, Robert Mark, Wang, Hui, Cutting, Joe, Thompson-Lee, Sophie, Snell, Rebecca J.S., See, Beng Huat, Saiger, Michael. (2025). Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105450

article_title: Pixels and pedagogy: MISTT's insights into evolving teacher identities when technology comes to play
citation: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601
title: Four-context framing of teacher identity: personal, university, internship school, and school system
description: The article frames student-teachers' professional identities as spanning four contexts — "personal, university, internship school, and school system" — each perceivable with and without digital tools. This multi-context framing underpins the MISTT instrument's design and reflects the view that teacher identity is shaped by multiple nested environments rather than a single setting.
requirements: Perception of identity must be elicited separately for each of the four contexts and for with- and without-technology conditions
target_learning_goals: understanding professional identity formation across contexts

article_title: Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies: Principles and case studies
citation: Warin, B., Kolski, C., & Sagar, M. (2011). Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. Computers and Education, 57(2), 1595-1614. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.013
title: Analyzing pedagogical frameworks through four educational psychology paradigms
description: The article examines its framework in terms of the primary currents in educational psychology: behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism and social constructivism. This four-paradigm analysis serves as an organizing pattern for evaluating how a pedagogical design aligns with established learning theories. Each paradigm provides a different lens on how the framework supports knowledge acquisition and competency development.
requirements: The designer must be able to characterize the pedagogical design's mechanisms in terms of each paradigm's assumptions about learning
constraints: The analysis is limited to these four primary currents in educational psychology

professional competencies

article_title: Motivation and learning strategies in the use of ICTs among university students
citation: Valentín, A., Mateos, P. M., González-Tablas, M. M., Pérez, L., López, E., & García, I. (2013). Motivation and learning strategies in the use of ICTs among university students. Computers & Education, 61, 52–58. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2012.09.008
title: Four patterns of ICT use among university students: Social, Technical, Academic, and Educational Platform Use
description: The article proposes a taxonomy of four distinct patterns of ICT use derived from factor analysis. "Factor 1 ... was designated Social Use", covering communication (chats, forums) and reading newspapers; "Factor 2 ... was designated Technical Use", covering databases and web page design; "Factor 3 ... was designated Academic Use", covering office tools such as word processors and slide presentations; and "Factor 4 ... was designated Educational Platform Use (EPU)", covering e-learning platforms and e-mail. This taxonomy organizes how students' ICT engagement varies.
requirements: Requires survey data on the frequency of use of a range of ICT tools to be factor-analyzed.
constraints: Derived from a sample of first- and second-year undergraduates at a single Spanish university.
target_learning_goals: ICT use for learning
digital literacy
key_sources: Valentín, A., Mateos, P. M., González-Tablas, M. M., Pérez, L., López, E., & García, I. (2013). Motivation and learning strategies in the use of ICTs among university students. Computers & Education, 61, 52–58. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2012.09.008

article_title: Investigating L2 listening comprehension and experience in immersive and interactive virtual reality: An experimental study
citation: Liang, Y., & Hu, G. (2026). Investigating L2 listening comprehension and experience in immersive and interactive virtual reality: An experimental study. Computers & Education, 248, 105593. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105593
title: Four-dimensional flow model (Heutte et al., 2021) distinguishing cognitive and affective components
description: The article applies Heutte et al.'s (2021) refined four-dimensional flow model, restructured from Csikszentmihalyi's original dimensions because "not all original flow dimensions were consistently observed" in educational settings. The first three dimensions — cognitive control, immersion and time transformation, and loss of self-consciousness — collectively measure the cognitive component (absorption), while the fourth dimension, autotelic experience, measures the affective component. The study operationalizes listening experience as state flow using the EduFlow-2 scale based on this model.
requirements: Measured via the validated EduFlow-2 scale with 12 statements rated on a seven-point Likert scale
constraints: Developed specifically for educational settings where some original flow dimensions were not consistently observed
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
Flow experience during learning tasks

article_title: Formative e-assessment: Practitioner cases
citation: Norbert Pachler, Caroline Daly, Yishay Mor, Harvey Mellar. (2009). Formative e-assessment: practitioner cases. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00592754
title: Cases of formative e-assessment developed with practitioners
description: The project developed cases of formative e-assessment — accounts of practice where technologies play a key role in formative assessment of learning. The cases were developed collaboratively with practitioners and analysed with reference to key theoretical perspectives on formative assessment, particularly the work of Black and Wiliam (2009).
requirements: Development through a collaborative methodology involving practitioners
target_learning_goals: formative assessment of learning
examples: Cases developed during the JISC-funded project 'Scoping a vision of formative e-assessment' (June 2008 – January 2009)

article_title: Tracking e-learning through published papers: A systematic review
citation: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007
title: Four-dimension conceptual framework of e-learning research
description: The review organizes e-learning research into four dominant themes identified through Leximancer concept mapping: "education (314 hits)", "learning (208 hits)", "student (119 hits)" and "use (109 hits)". These dimensions group the literature's concepts into a holistic map that the authors argue outperforms other systematic reviews for understanding e-learning. The framework serves as the article's organizing taxonomy for the e-learning construct.
requirements: Requires a corpus of peer-reviewed articles on e-learning and education and qualitative text-analysis software such as Leximancer
constraints: Analysis is qualitative; the authors note limitations due to the qualitative nature of the analysis and propose meta-analysis with other databases as future work
target_learning_goals: understanding the e-learning construct across academic areas
examples: The concept map in Fig. 1 groups concepts (grey dots) into the four topics with hit counts

article_title: Comparing human-made and AI-generated teaching videos: An experimental study on learning effects
citation: Netland, Torbjörn; von Dzengelevski, Oliver; Tesch, Katalin. (2025). Comparing human-made and AI-generated teaching videos: An experimental study on learning effects. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105164
title: Four AI-generated short teaching videos for a management course
description: The study's materials are "four short teaching videos for a management course" developed with generative AI tools, compared against human-generated videos on the same subjects. Each video served as a treatment unit in the online experiment, with participants rating learning experiences after each video and completing a multiple-choice exam at the end.
requirements: Generative AI tools were used to develop the videos
target_learning_goals: management course content knowledge

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: Chilean EFL research areas organized into four groups: social-science studies, ELT/curriculum studies, community-attitude studies, and linguistically driven policy studies
description: The review organizes the retrieved EFL research into an organizing taxonomy of four groups. It states that "EFLresearch from various disciplines and perspectives can be grouped under various areas of knowledge that gofrom social sciences(economics and sociology)to education (curriculum,didactics, and methodology) and humanities(linguistics and appliedlinguistics)". The four printed groups are: (a) social-science studies of socio-economic factors, motivation and self-regulation; (b) works addressing Chilean ELT and the English curriculum including initial teacher education; (c) studies on factors impacting communities' attitudes toward learning; and (d) research emphasizing linguistic rationale with concerns about national language policy.
requirements: The taxonomy presupposes the 40-study retrieved corpus and thematic analysis of the selected articles
constraints: The grouping applies to research on English in Chile published 2011–2021 in the three databases used
target_learners: EFL learners and teachers in Chilean primary, secondary and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: Understanding the landscape of EFL teaching methodology research in Chile
examples: Group (a) is instantiated by Kormos & Kiddle (2013) and Yilorm & Acosta (2016) on socio-economic factors, motivation and self-regulation in Chile

article_title: Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/
title: Four overarching purposes of metacognitive regulation in PT clinical reasoning: pedagogical, clinical, professional developmental and sociopolitical
description: Beyond the expected learning and quality-of-care purposes, inductive analysis organized the reported purposes of metacognitive regulation into four categories. The article states: "This review identifies four primary purposes of MR engagement: pedagogical (learning and consolidation), clinical (adaptation and safety), professional developmental (identity and responsibility), and sociopolitical (emancipation and transformation)." The pedagogical purpose positions MR as "a lever for learning" supporting clinical reasoning development; the clinical purpose concerns adjusting reasoning in real time to improve safety, quality and equity of care; the professional developmental purpose links MR to identity formation and epistemic vigilance; and the sociopolitical purpose is framed as a "critical emancipatory function of MR". The data suggest the four purposes are not mutually exclusive but often interwoven.
requirements: Derived from synthesis of reported purposes in the included literature on PT clinical reasoning
constraints: The first two purposes were expected from prior codes; the sociopolitical purpose emerged inductively and the review is descriptive, not prescriptive
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development
Professional identity formation
Equity in care
examples: The article notes that metacognitive training may simultaneously reinforce professional identity and ethical sensitivity, and reflective peer interactions could contribute to all four purposes depending on context
key_sources: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/

article_title: Training interval, feedback, and retention in cardiopulmonary resuscitation education: a systematic review.
citation: Lee Hyeon-Ji. (2026). Training interval, feedback, and retention in cardiopulmonary resuscitation education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09538-4
title: Four-theme framework for retention-oriented CPR education design
description: The review organizes CPR education evidence into four a priori themes: "training interval and spaced practice; instructional modality and feedback mechanisms; cognitive, psychological, and team-based components; and target populations and educational delivery models." It uses this framework to structure its narrative synthesis of 20 studies, arguing effectiveness depends less on total training duration than on how training is structured, reinforced, and sustained. The framework integrates skill-retention outcomes with cognitive and delivery-model considerations.
requirements: Interventional studies (randomized, quasi-experimental, or other interventional designs) reporting CPR performance or skill-retention outcomes, published 2015 or later
constraints: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to substantial heterogeneity in designs, interventions, and outcome measures, so synthesis is narrative
target_learning_goals: CPR skill acquisition
long-term CPR skill retention
performance under stress
examples: The review applied the four themes to synthesize RCTs and quasi-experimental studies from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library
key_sources: Lee Hyeon-Ji. (2026). Training interval, feedback, and retention in cardiopulmonary resuscitation education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09538-4

article_title: A systematic review of the use of human body donor models for postgraduate laparoscopic surgical training.
citation: Pinar Sedat Alp, Morrow Joseph J., Kong Chia Yew. (2025). A systematic review of the use of human body donor models for postgraduate laparoscopic surgical training. Anatomical Science International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12565-025-00872-z
title: Four-type validity framework for evaluating surgical training models
description: The review organises its evaluation of body donor models around four validity types drawn from simulation literature: "face validity, construct validity, content validity, and predictive validity". Face validity concerns resemblance to a real-life procedure, construct validity the ability to distinguish experience levels, content validity the capacity to enhance knowledge and skills across settings, and predictive validity the translation of improved skills to real-life clinical settings. The review sorts its 55 included studies into groups by which validity type they assess, and uses this framework to diagnose where evidence is strongest (face validity) and weakest (predictive validity).
requirements: Studies must report an assessment of educational outcomes of postgraduate doctors on a body donor model for laparoscopic surgery to be classified within the framework
constraints: Only one included study assessed predictive validity, so the framework's highest-level evidence tier is nearly empty in this literature
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic surgical skills
anatomical knowledge
examples: The review categorised its 55 included studies into five discussion groups, including studies assessing content validity, construct validity, and comparative studies
key_sources: Pinar Sedat Alp, Morrow Joseph J., Kong Chia Yew. (2025). A systematic review of the use of human body donor models for postgraduate laparoscopic surgical training. Anatomical Science International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12565-025-00872-z

article_title: Competency-Based Simulation Training for Procedural Skills: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
citation: Vermylen JH, Cohen ER, Cook DA, McGaghie WC, Issenberg SB, Arnold J, Ballard H, Bayoumi M, Beestrum M, Bremner R, Crawford S, Einstein N, Mannarino C, Misra A, Tomita TM, Waldron H, Yanko F, Kessler DO. (2026). Competency-Based Simulation Training for Procedural Skills: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000895
title: Four-theme framework of instructional design variables for competency-based simulation research
description: The review inductively clusters the design variables compared across included studies into four main categories: "instructional strategies", "simulation models", "learner engagement", and "assessment models", each with named subdomains (e.g., feedback source, intensity, timing, automation; simulator type, cost, fidelity; stakes and motivation; minimum passing standards and validity). The authors recommend this framework, as presented in their Table 3, as a structure for future comparative efficacy studies of instructional design features.

constraints: Only 2 studies addressed the assessment theme and 3 the learner engagement theme, so several subdomains lack sufficient studies for pooled analysis

target_learning_goals: acquisition of psychomotor procedural skills to a defined competency threshold
examples: The review classified a study comparing a low-fidelity home model without an instructor against a high-fidelity simulation-center model with an instructor as spanning instructional strategies (feedback type and source) and simulation models (type, cost, fidelity)

article_title: Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review.

title: FourCe-PITO leadership framework for military medical leadership education
description: The "FourCe-PITO" model was created by the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences for its military medical leadership program. citation: Gonzalez-Garcia A., Marques-Sanchez P., Pinto-Carral A., Leiros-Rodriguez R., Perez-Rivera J., Perez-González S. (2025). Characterizing the Decision-Making Competency of Nurse Managers: A Scoping Review. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/2771210

The article states that "These dimensions are not isolated; they are interconnected components supporting informed, ethical, and strategic decisions in complex healthcare environments." article_title: Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report.
citation: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930
title: Four-module curriculum structure mapping learning objectives to systematic review competencies and SRSS skills
description: The course is organized into four modules that together cover the systematic review searching workflow: consultation and pre-searching, searching, search strategy peer review, and search reporting. Each module is mapped in Table 1 to the learning objectives set by the MLA SR Workgroup and to corresponding SRSS skills (8–14). As the article states, "Four modules were established that would meet the course objectives: Module 1, consultation and pre-searching, Module 2, searching, Module 3, search strategy peer review, and Module 4, search reporting." The pattern is reusable for librarian evidence-synthesis training.
requirements: Objectives must be defined in advance by a competency framework (here the Townsend et al. six competencies and the SRSS skills) so modules can be mapped to them
constraints: The pilot in-person offering was four hours and online offerings two 2.5-hour sessions; the article notes building a full systematic review search is not feasible in the course context
target_learners: health science librarians, both new and experienced searchers earning the SRSS specialization
target_learning_goals: systematic review searching skills: reference interviewing, preliminary searching, database selection, comprehensive search strategy building, search peer review, and search reporting
examples: Online offerings divided into two 2.5-hour sessions with a breakout-group activity constructing a search string for one of three concepts, followed by instructors live-testing the full three-concept search strategy in PubMed
