article_title: Determinants of academic achievement among higher education student found in low resource setting, A systematic review.
citation: Kassaw Chalachew, Demareva Valeriia. (2023). Determinants of academic achievement among higher education student found in low resource setting, A systematic review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294585
title: Four-category taxonomy of academic achievement determinants in low-resource higher education
description: The review organizes predictors of academic achievement into four operational categories: psychological factors ("mental pain, sleep quality, self-esteem, prosocial behavior, anxiety, depression, and suicidality"), biological factors (gender, age, and hormonal issues such as dysmenorrhea), facility-related factors (seating, lighting, technology, dormitories, and other physical conditions), and lifestyle factors (social media usage, premarital sex, sexual abstinence). Tables 1–4 map primary studies onto these categories, and Fig 2 summarizes the categorized factors associated with achievement in Ethiopian higher education.
requirements: Primary studies must report outcome variables and covariates with basic statistical analysis linking factors to academic performance
constraints: Limited to cross-sectional studies of Ethiopian higher education students published between 2013 and 2022
target_learners: higher education students in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: academic achievement as measured by GPA and performance indicators
examples: Tables 1–4 assign each primary study's findings to the psychological, biological, facility, or lifestyle category; Fig 2 summarizes the categories.
key_sources: Kassaw Chalachew, Demareva Valeriia. (2023). Determinants of academic achievement among higher education student found in low resource setting, A systematic review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294585

article_title: Learning outcomes for communication skills across the health professions: a systematic literature review and qualitative synthesis.
citation: Denniston C, Molloy E, Nestel D, Woodward-Kron R, Keating JL. (2017). Learning outcomes for communication skills across the health professions: a systematic literature review and qualitative synthesis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-014570
title: Four-domain taxonomy of communication skills learning outcomes: knowledge, content, process and perceptual skills
description: The review organises its final 205 learning outcomes into four themes, three of which derive from the seminal work of Kurtz, Silverman and Draper, with the research group adding a fourth theme, knowledge. Knowledge is defined as "An individual's understanding of information through which incoming data and/or experiences are processed and recorded"; content as what is communicated; process as how one communicates; and perceptual as awareness of self and others and how that impacts communication. The taxonomy structures the synthesised outcome list presented for educational design across the health professions.
requirements: Learning outcomes assigned to a theme must be judged against the theme definitions and the decision guide used in the qualitative synthesis
constraints: The authors present the list as a foundation for others to interpret rather than a prescriptive list, aligned with a social constructionist perspective
target_learners: health professionals across professions and levels of education, prequalification and postqualification
target_learning_goals: communication skills learning outcomes spanning knowledge, content, process and perceptual skills
examples: The final list presents content-domain outcomes in the chronological sequence of a healthcare interaction for ease of representation
key_sources: Denniston C, Molloy E, Nestel D, Woodward-Kron R, Keating JL. (2017). Learning outcomes for communication skills across the health professions: a systematic literature review and qualitative synthesis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-014570

article_title: Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation.
citation: Mak-van der Vossen M, van Mook W, van der Burgt S, Kors J, Ket JCF, Croiset G, Kusurkar R. (2017). Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0997-x
title: Four-theme taxonomy of unprofessional behaviours of medical students
description: The review organises real-life unprofessional behaviours of undergraduate medical students into four behavioural themes. The included articles yielded "205 different descriptions of unprofessional behaviours, which were coded into 30 different descriptors, and subsequently classified into four behavioural themes: failure to engage, dishonest behaviour, disrespectful behaviour, and poor self-awareness." Each theme is defined in behavioural terms: failure to engage is "insufficiently handling one's tasks", dishonest behaviour covers "cheating, lying, plagiarism and not obeying rules and regulations", disrespectful behaviour "has a negative effect on other people", and poor self-awareness is "inappropriately handling one's own performance". The framework is offered as a shared vocabulary for educators documenting lapses.
requirements: Behaviours must be witnessed by stakeholders or admitted by students themselves, within the educational context, to fall under the framework
constraints: Behaviours are specific to students in undergraduate education and not all guideline domains for physicians were found
What is seen as unprofessional is dependent on time and cultural context
target_learners: preclinical and clinical undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: professionalism
recognition and documentation of unprofessional behaviour
examples: The review mapped its findings to the GMC's domains of concern for medical students, finding many similarities plus some new descriptors
key_sources: Mak-van der Vossen M, van Mook W, van der Burgt S, Kors J, Ket JCF, Croiset G, Kusurkar R. (2017). Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0997-x

article_title: A systematic review of serious games in medical education: quality of evidence and pedagogical strategy.
citation: Gorbanev Iouri, Agudelo-Londoño Sandra, González Rafael A., Cortes Ariel, Pomares Alexandra, Delgadillo Vivian, Yepes Francisco J., Muñoz Óscar. (2018). A systematic review of serious games in medical education: quality of evidence and pedagogical strategy. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1438718
title: Four-perspective framework for classifying the pedagogical foundations of educational games
description: The review adopts Wu's classification of educational games by pedagogical perspective: behaviourism (learning as operant conditioning prioritizing knowledge transmission), cognitivism (learners as information processors), humanism (person-centred experiential learning), and constructivism (knowledge construction through problem-solving and social interaction). The authors used these definitions to classify each of the 21 reviewed games and to judge game/pedagogy coherence, arguing that "a selection of a pedagogical perspective would not be indifferent in this case since it mirrors the intentions of game authors and determines the architecture of the games".
requirements: Pedagogical strategy must be determinable from the article's stated views on medical education, student motivation, and game aims, as the review notes it was not always explicitly stated
constraints: The review notes the connection between pedagogical perspectives and serious games is weak, with developers emphasizing practicality over theoretical foundations
target_learning_goals: knowledge transmission and retention
skill development through repetition
problem-solving and knowledge construction
examples: Each of the 21 reviewed games was classified by reviewer pairs using Wu's definitions, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements; 76.2% of game designs were coherent with their pedagogical strategy
key_sources: Gorbanev Iouri, Agudelo-Londoño Sandra, González Rafael A., Cortes Ariel, Pomares Alexandra, Delgadillo Vivian, Yepes Francisco J., Muñoz Óscar. (2018). A systematic review of serious games in medical education: quality of evidence and pedagogical strategy. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1438718

article_title: The informal curriculum of family medicine - what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review.
citation: Rothlind Erica, Fors Uno, Salminen Helena, Wändell Per, Ekblad Solvig. (2020). The informal curriculum of family medicine – what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-020-01120-1
title: Formalize parts of the informal curriculum for Family Medicine residents to reduce dependency on individual supervisors and facilitate more retained learning
description: The review recommends complementing workplace-based experiential training with formalized training in aspects of the informal curriculum. It argues that 'formalizing parts of the informal curriculum would likely facilitate a shift from implicit or reactive informal learning to more deliberate forms, where a modification of skills and behaviors is also more probable to occur', and that this would reduce the dependency on the individual supervisor's interests or preferences by providing a more uniform base for all residents. The recommendation is grounded in the review's finding that formalized training currently appears lacking.
requirements: Awareness among supervisors of the areas in which they are likely to have great impact on their residents
Identification of gaps where formalized learning activities are needed
constraints: The review states the current literature is not sufficient to conclude how to best teach the informal curriculum
target_learning_goals: cultural competence
medical professionalism
dealing with uncertainty
examples: The review's 11 included interventions ranged from isolated workshops of 1–10 occasions to interventions integrated over at least 1 year, with small-group discussions the most common method
key_sources: Rothlind Erica, Fors Uno, Salminen Helena, Wändell Per, Ekblad Solvig. (2020). The informal curriculum of family medicine – what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-020-01120-1

article_title: The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century.
citation: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002
title: Four-level progression structure with indicative practice timeframes for competency development
description: The framework structures competence progression as four levels, each with an indicative timeframe in haemophilia practice: "beginner, in practice for 0‐6 months (level 1)" through competent (over 6 months), proficient (18–24 months) and expert (a minimum of 3 years). The timeframes were derived by consensus at the HNA annual meeting where delegates ranked their own competence alongside time in practice. Each level's indicators let nurses gauge progression and identify areas for further education.
requirements: Indicators at each level provide a standard against which nurses can measure their personal practice
constraints: The article states the timeframes "should be interpreted cautiously" because experience gain depends on centre activity level and prior roles
target_learners: Haemophilia nurse specialists progressing from novice to advanced practice
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of specialist haemophilia nursing competence
examples: The HNA annual meeting in 2018 asked delegates to rank their own level of competence alongside time in haemophilia practice, producing a consensus based on average time in practice.
key_sources: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002

article_title: Medical wikis dedicated to clinical practice: a systematic review.
citation: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/
title: Four information properties framework for assessing medical wiki relevancy for clinicians: accuracy, readability, reliability, and currency
description: The review proposes assessing the relevancy of medical wikis for clinicians according to four information properties: accuracy, readability, reliability, and currency. The authors state: "the relevancy for clinicians of the medical wikis can be discussed according to four information properties: accuracy, readability, reliability, and currency." Accuracy may be impaired in wikis not displaying a review policy; readability was assessed with the Flesch reading ease test; reliability through the 16-criterion information framework; and currency through editorial activity rates.
requirements: Assessment requires site disclosures, sampled articles, and activity data from the wikis themselves
constraints: No validated quality-assessment tool is currently fitted either to wikis or to a professional audience, per the review
target_learning_goals: evaluating the trustworthiness and usability of collaborative clinical knowledge resources
examples: The review applied the framework to conclude that no medical wiki meets all four information properties needed by clinicians
key_sources: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/

article_title: What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review.
citation: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461
title: Four latent classes characterize educational software in medical CBL research: multimedia, text, Web conference, and instructional
description: The review used latent class analysis on educational software variables from 251 articles, selecting four classes by best interpretability and lowest BIC. It reports: "We uncovered 4 latent classes for educational software, characteristically making use of multimedia (115/251, 45.8%), text (64/251, 25.5%), Web conferencing (54/251, 21.5%), and instructional design principles (18/251, 7.2%)." The multimedia class uses interactive websites with text, images, audio, and video plus quizzes and clinical cases; the instructional class is a small group of highly interactive multimedia apps built on multiple instructional design principles.
requirements: Class assignment requires software feature variables reported in at least 2% of studies; variables reported in <2% were excluded from the model
constraints: Classes describe the 2003–2013 medical education literature only; the instructional class contains just 18 studies (7.2%)
target_learning_goals: characterizing CBL software features in medical education research
key_sources: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461

article_title: The Effectiveness of Teamwork Training on Teamwork Behaviors and Team Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Interventions.
citation: McEwan D., Ruissen G.R., Eys M.A., Zumbo B.D., Beauchamp M.R. (2017). The Effectiveness of Teamwork Training on Teamwork Behaviors and Team Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Interventions. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169604
title: Four-dimension framework of teamwork: preparation, execution, reflection, and interpersonal dynamics
description: The article organizes teamwork into behaviors that regulate team performance and behaviors that keep the team together, following Lewin's locomotion and maintenance processes. Regulation spans behaviors "before/in preparation for team task performance," during execution (communication, coordination, cooperation), and after task completion (reflection, monitoring, adjustment), while a fourth dimension covers interpersonal dynamics such as conflict management and social support. The meta-analysis used these four dimensions to code targeted and measured dimensions of interventions.
requirements: Interventions and measures must be codable into the preparation, execution, reflection, and/or interpersonal-dynamics dimensions
constraints: The article notes 29 teamwork frameworks exist with differing numbers and labelling of dimensions; this framework reflects the generally agreed multi-behavior structure
target_learners: team members in health care, aviation, military, academic, industry, and laboratory settings
target_learning_goals: teamwork behaviors including goal setting, communication, coordination, reflection, conflict management, and social support
examples: Each included intervention was coded for which of the four dimensions it targeted and which were measured as outcomes
key_sources: McEwan D., Ruissen G.R., Eys M.A., Zumbo B.D., Beauchamp M.R. (2017). The Effectiveness of Teamwork Training on Teamwork Behaviors and Team Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Interventions. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169604

article_title: Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education
citation: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Four instructional strategy categories for web-based metacognitive skills training
description: The article integrates prior work into "four main categories, including advance organizer, concept map, scaffolding, and problem-solving strategies" for designing web-based metacognitive training. Advance organizers, drawn from Meaningful Learning Theory, help students integrate new knowledge with existing superordinate concepts; concept maps visualize relationships among concepts; scaffolding includes prompts, checklists, and procedural questions; and problem-solving strategies such as the IMPROVE method train students to raise metacognitive questions. The authors applied these categories in designing their website's four sections.
requirements: Instructors should investigate students' prerequisite knowledge first and design materials based on it, since meaningful learning occurs only when instructions comply with students' competencies and experiences
constraints: The authors note they applied only a portion of the design principles and did not further investigate applications of these principles
target_learning_goals: metacognitive skills: planning, monitoring, modifying, and evaluating learning
examples: Each website section began with an advance organizer, followed by a video-based case study and an exercise, with scaffolding tools such as summarization and self-evaluate checklists embedded in each section
key_sources: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932234

article_title: Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education
citation: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Four-section web-based metacognitive training website
description: The authors developed a website with four sections — self-plan, self-monitor, self-modify, and self-evaluate — each with stated learning objectives (e.g. "Make learning plans", "Identify the concepts learners do not understand"). Each section consisted of introduction, learning by case, exercises by case, and test, was expected to be completed in one hour, and integrated advance organizers, multimedia case studies, and exercises using concept maps, checklists, and the Creative Problem-Solving Model. Materials were also accessible from home after class.
requirements: Participants were given instructions on how to operate the website before the experiment to avoid time lost to unfamiliarity with the interface
constraints: Due to the limitation of time allowed for each section, the authors were unable to integrate training on self-judgment of performance and improvement of self-reaction into the instructions
target_learners: college students aged 19-22 in a private university in northern Taiwan
target_learning_goals: self-planning, self-monitoring, self-modifying, and self-evaluating one's learning
examples: In the self-plan section, students drew a concept map titled A day of an undergraduate, Chih-chun, then used concept map tools to draw a time allocation table for themselves
key_sources: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932234

article_title: Testing the Immediate and Long-Term Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention
citation: Ben Clarke, Christian Doabler, Keith Smolkowski, Evangeline Kurtz Nelson, Hank Fien, Scott K. Baker & Derek Kosty (2016). Testing the Immediate and Long-Term Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1116034
title: Tier 2 mathematics interventions should combine focused whole-number content with validated explicit instructional design principles
description: The article presents ROOTS as built on two key principles: focused whole-number content and the use of validated instructional design principles. ROOTS includes scripted guidelines facilitating "four essential features of explicit mathematics instruction: (a) teacher modeling, (b) deliberate practice, (c) visual representations of mathematics, and (d) academic feedback." The authors hypothesize that integrating these principles accelerates at-risk learners' mathematics learning.
requirements: Scripted guidelines for interventionists
Immediate and specific academic feedback tied to student errors
Systematically planned and scaffolded practice opportunities
constraints: Grounded in research on students with mathematics difficulties; the article cites rigorous experimental research supporting the explicit instructional approach
target_learners: Kindergarten students at risk for mathematics learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of whole numbers
Procedural fluency with whole-number skills
examples: ROOTS interventionists demonstrate cardinality by overtly counting objects in different configurations (line, array, circle, scattered) and use number lines and counting and place-value blocks as visual representations
key_sources: Ben Clarke, Christian Doabler, Keith Smolkowski, Evangeline Kurtz Nelson, Hank Fien, Scott K. Baker & Derek Kosty (2016). Testing the Immediate and Long-Term Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1116034

article_title: A Randomized Trial Examining the Effects of Conjoint Behavioral Consultation in Rural Schools: Student Outcomes and the Mediating Role of the Teacher-Parent Relationship
citation: Sheridan, S. M., Witte, A. L., Holmes, S. R., Coutts, M. J., Dent, A. L., Kunza, G. M., & Wu, C. (2017). A randomized trial examining the effects of conjoint behavioral consultation in rural schools: Student outcomes and the mediating role of the teacher-parent relationship. Journal of School Psychology, 61, 33-53. https://www.elsevier.com/journals/journal-of-school-psychology/0022-4405/guide-for-authors
title: Behavioral intervention plans built from four classes of research-based strategies plus home-school communication
description: In this pattern, each student's behavioral plan is assembled collaboratively from "four classes of intervention strategies documented empirically to reduce disruptive and promote prosocial behaviors": positive reinforcement/consequences, environmental structuring and antecedent control, skills training, and reductive techniques. All plans also promoted home-school communication through home-notes and other consistent means. Plan tactics preserved fundamental functional elements while allowing individuation in scheduling and delivery.
requirements: Plans developed in a student-specific manner based on the function of the behavior and teacher-parent preferences
target_learning_goals: reduction of disruptive behavior
prosocial classroom behavior
examples: Antecedent control strategies occurred in 89%, skill building in 25%, and reductive techniques in 11% of school-based intervention packages; the average plan had 8.67 steps (range 5-14)

A randomized trial examining the effects of conjoint behavioral consultation in rural schools: Student outcomes and the mediating role of the teacher-parent relationship. Journal of School Psychology, 61, 33-53. https://www.elsevier.com/journals/journal-of-school-psychology/0022-4405/guide-for-authors

article_title: The Effects of Planned Focus on Form on Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Accuracy
citation: Farahman Farrokhi, Mohammad Hassan Chehrazad. (2012). The Effects of Planned Focus on Form on Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Accuracy. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n1p70
title: Focus on form as a third option between synthetic and purely analytic instruction
description: The article presents focus on form, introduced by Long (1991), as an alternative that captures the strengths of analytic, meaning-focused approaches while addressing their limitations. It is distinguished by the requirement that it "involves learners briefly and simultaneously attending to form, meaning and use during one cognitive event". The article situates it against synthetic syllabi and strong and weak forms of communicative language teaching, and distinguishes planned versus incidental and reactive versus preemptive variants.
requirements: Occurs during meaning-focused classroom activity rather than in isolation from communication
Attention to form is triggered by perceived problems with comprehension or production
constraints: The article notes interpretations vary from a very narrow and implicit view to a general, liberal, and more explicit view
target_learners: low-intermediate adolescent and young adult EFL learners
target_learning_goals: grammatical accuracy in oral production, specifically simple past tense
examples: In the study, planned focus on form was operationalized as recasts during retelling and delayed explicit and metalinguistic feedback after retelling, targeting simple past tense errors
key_sources: Farahman Farrokhi, Mohammad Hassan Chehrazad. (2012). The Effects of Planned Focus on Form on Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Accuracy. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n1p70

article_title: Identifying Mechanisms of Change in the Early Grade Reading Study in South Africa
citation: Brahm Fleisch and Kerryn Dixon. (2019). Identifying mechanisms of change in the Early Grade Reading Study in South Africa. South African Journal of Education, Volume 39, Number 3, August 2019. https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v39n3a1696
title: Foucauldian mechanisms of change: time, space, and routines as disciplinary technologies
description: The article uses Michel Foucault's work as an analytical framework for identifying the interacting parts that constitute mechanisms of change in structured pedagogy programmes. Foucault examined "how people learn to behave in expected ways that are considered to be normal" through bodily training, standardisation of actions over time, and spatial control. The authors apply this lens to interpret how the EGRS's scripted lesson plans, classroom spatial arrangements, and mundane routines operate as mechanisms that both enable productive change and constrain it, since old embodied practices resist new ones.
requirements: A theoretical lens is needed because descriptive accounts alone cannot show how subtle social practices operate as interacting parts in a causal system
constraints: The article states mechanisms of change are interrelated and that it is not possible to identify all the causal processes of the interrelated parts; time and space are separated only for purposes of analysis
target_learners: Grade 1 and Grade 2 learners in South African Foundation Phase classrooms
target_learning_goals: Early grade reading in Home Language (Setswana) literacy instruction
examples: Analysis of time-based observation records, spatial movements triangulated from field notes, photographs and interviews, and patterns of routine practices cross-referenced to EGRS lesson plans and interview transcripts
key_sources: Brahm Fleisch and Kerryn Dixon. (2019). Identifying mechanisms of change in the Early Grade Reading Study in South Africa. South African Journal of Education, Volume 39, Number 3, August 2019. https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v39n3a1696

article_title: Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum
citation: Clinton, V. & Cooper, J.L. (2015, April). Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL.
title: Four instructional design principles for visuals: multimedia, signaling, contiguity, and coherence
description: The article applies four principles from Mayer (2009) and Sweller, Ayres, & Kalyuga (2011) to revise CMP2 visuals. The multimedia principle holds that "learning is greater when texts are accompanied by relevant visuals"; signaling says cues such as color coding improve learning by directing attention and connecting representations; contiguity requires relevant information across representations to be in close proximity; and coherence holds that "learning is improved when interesting, but irrelevant information is removed," tied to the seductive details effect.
requirements: Visuals must be integrated with lesson text so students can build both verbal and visual mental representations and connect them
constraints: The article notes removing representational visuals was supported by the coherence principle but not the multimedia principle, making that revision theoretically uncertain
target_learning_goals: mathematics comprehension and problem solving from curriculum materials
examples: Math-relevant visuals were added where appropriate; color coding and spatial reorganization were applied; decorative and some representational visuals were removed, while representational visuals critical to understanding lesson context were retained
key_sources: Clinton, V. & Cooper, J.L. (2015, April). Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574965

article_title: The Effect of Blackboard Collaborate-Based Instruction on Pre-Service Teachers' Achievement in the EFL Teaching Methods Course at Faculties of Education for Girls
citation: Hussein El-ghamry Mohammad Hussein. (2016). The Effect of Blackboard Collaborate-Based Instruction on Pre-service Teachers' Achievement in the EFL Teaching Methods Course at Faculties of Education for Girls. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p49
title: Fourteen-week blended course structure pairing weekly sessions with peer-teaching practice and staged assignments
description: The teaching methods course was organized as fourteen weeks of three contact hours each, pairing a first session of content (e.g., lesson planning, behavioral objectives, warming-up activities, questioning strategies) with a second session of peer teaching practice, plus weekly assignments such as formulating sample objectives and preparing practice activities. Student evaluation allocated 15 marks to attendance and in-class activities, 20 to the midterm exam, 15 to peer-teaching, and 50 to the final written exam. The course consisted of forty-two hours covering twenty-three items.
requirements: Course goals include recognizing and using error correction techniques, classroom management techniques, and planning and implementing a whole lesson
target_learners: seventh-level English Department pre-service EFL teachers
target_learning_goals: lesson planning, behavioral objectives, presentation and practice techniques, evaluation techniques, and whole-lesson implementation
examples: Week four covered warming-up activities in the first session and peer teaching practice of warming-up in the second, with preparing warming-up activities as the assignment
key_sources: Hussein El-ghamry Mohammad Hussein. (2016). The Effect of Blackboard Collaborate-Based Instruction on Pre-service Teachers' Achievement in the EFL Teaching Methods Course at Faculties of Education for Girls. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p49

article_title: The Impact of ICT on Pupils' Achievement and Attitudes in Social Studies
citation: Emin Cener, Ismail Acun & Gokhan Demirhan. (2015). The Impact of ICT on Pupils' Achievement and Attitudes in Social Studies. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 6(1), 190-207. http://www.sosyalbilgiler.org
title: Teachers should focus on achievement and subject attitudes rather than being misled by pupils' positive attitudes toward ICT
description: The article found that ICT-supported teaching raised pupils' attitudes toward ICT without improving their attitudes toward the subject, and warns that positive technology attitudes alone do not guarantee learning gains. It states that 'teachers' focus should not be misled by the positive attitudes towards ICT but they ought to really focus on achievement and attitudes towards subject matter.' The principle directs educators to treat ICT attitudes as at most a route to more frequent use, whose quality matters most.
requirements: Educators monitoring achievement and subject-matter attitudes as the primary outcomes of ICT integration
constraints: The article notes non-academic use of ICT may hinder learning, citing Ravizza, Hambrick & Fenn (2014)
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in social studies and positive attitudes toward the subject
examples: In the study, pupils formed positive attitudes toward ICT after realizing its potential in their learning, yet their social studies attitudes declined in both groups
key_sources: Emin Cener, Ismail Acun & Gokhan Demirhan. (2015). The Impact of ICT on Pupils' Achievement and Attitudes in Social Studies. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 6(1), 190-207. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105333

article_title: Effects of Experiential Learning Approach on Students' Mathematical Creativity among Secondary School Students of Kericho East Sub-County, Kenya
citation: Chesimet M. C, Githua B.N, Ng’eno, J. K. (2016). Effects of Experiential Learning Approach on Students’ Mathematical Creativity among Secondary School Students of Kericho East Sub-County, Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(23). http://www.iiste.org
title: Four-dimension characterisation of mathematical creativity: fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration
description: The article defines mathematical creativity as "a novel way of thinking characterised by fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration". Fluency is the number of relevant responses to a mathematical question; flexibility is the shift in categories or methods across responses; originality is statistical infrequency of responses compared with others; elaboration is building on ideas and producing detailed steps. The article uses these four dimensions as the construct measured by the Mathematical Creativity Test.
requirements: Measurement requires tasks allowing multiple responses, categories of ideas and detailed solution steps, as the article's definitions imply
target_learning_goals: mathematical creativity
examples: The study operationalised these dimensions in the MCT used to post-test all four groups
key_sources: Chesimet M. C, Githua B.N, Ng’eno, J. K. (2016). Effects of Experiential Learning Approach on Students’ Mathematical Creativity among Secondary School Students of Kericho East Sub-County, Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(23). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112801

article_title: Integrating Cognitive Linguistics Insights into Data-Driven Learning: Teaching Vertical Prepositions
citation: Kilimci, A. (2017). Integrating cognitive linguistics insights into data-driven learning: teaching vertical prepositions. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 13(2), 681-719. https://www.jlls.org
title: Four-step concordance procedure with a schema-activating pre-activity
description: The CPDL lesson pattern opened with a paired pre-activity in which "the activity aimed to activate the students’ pre -existing knowledge of over/above" by generating and comparing their own sentences, replicating a concordance task on their own output. The corpus work then followed four stages of Sinclair's procedure: "initiate, interpret, consolidate and report followed by a  classroom discussion to help the learners to uncover the contexts for the different uses of the vertical prepositions". The pattern interleaves metalinguistic cognitive explanation with hands-on corpus discovery.
requirements: Learners need prior DDL training in running and reading concordance queries
Polysemy network handouts are needed for the consolidation step
target_learners: second-year Turkish university students of English
target_learning_goals: distinguishing the prototypical and extended senses of polysemous prepositions
examples: In the initiate step students generated a 50-line KWIC concordance of over; in the interpret step they classified collocates and hypothesized the prototypical sense

article_title: A Game-Based Learning Approach to Improving Students' Learning Achievements in a Nutrition Course
citation: Jui-Mei Yien, Chun-Ming Hung, Gwo-Jen Hwang, Yueh-Chiao Lin. (2011). A Game-Based Learning Approach to Improving Students' Learning Achievements in a Nutrition Course. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Four-topic four-week nutrition unit pairing each weekly topic with purpose-built computer games
description: The teaching design organized nutrition education into four weekly 40-minute topics: 'Knowledge of eating functions,' 'Our eating,' 'Healthy eating habits' and 'Tracking eating habits,' each with stated purposes and an assigned game title. The same content was delivered to both groups, with only the medium differing, so the pattern isolates the game-based medium within a fixed curriculum sequence.
requirements: One class per week fitting the students' schedule; the same nutrition content across conditions so the medium is the only differing factor
constraints: Evaluated over four weeks with one 40-minute class per topic in a single elementary school
target_learning_goals: nutrition knowledge
healthy eating habits
food and drink habits
examples: Table 1 lists each topic's purposes, such as classifying the six types of food and comparing personal eating habits with standard healthy rules, alongside its game title

article_title: Factors Influencing Middle School Students' Spatial Mathematics Development While Participating in an Integrated STEM Unit
citation: Jennifer Wilhelm, Christa Jackson, Amber Sullivan, Ron Wilhelm. (2009). Factors Influencing Middle School Students' Spatial Mathematics Development While Participating in an Integrated STEM Unit. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Factors+Influencing+Middle+School+Students+Spatial+Mathematics+Development
title: Four spatial mathematical domains framework for astronomical understanding
description: The article claims lunar-related astronomical understanding rests on four spatial mathematical domains: Geometric Spatial Visualization ("9isXali]ing the geometric spatial featXres of a system as it appears above, beloZ, and Zithin the system's plane"), Spatial Projection, Cardinal Directions, and Periodic Patterns. The first two involve mental rotation, since visualizing the Moon-Earth-Sun system requires manipulating the system's motion and mentally maneuvering the sky through a day's viewing. The framework organizes the study's GSA and LPCI domain mapping (Table 3) and its interpretation of which domains each curriculum developed.
requirements: Assessment instruments must map items onto the four domains, as the LPCI and GSA do in Table 3
constraints: The article presents the framework as the authors' claim about astronomical concepts, illustrated by lunar phases; it is argued rather than independently validated
target_learning_goals: spatial reasoning in Earth/Space science
understanding lunar phases and Sun-Earth-Moon system motions
examples: The GSA assessed the same four spatial domains as the LPCI's spatial mapping, and domain-level gains were interpreted domain by domain against this framework

article_title: The Effect of Herrmann Whole Brain Teaching Method on Students' Understanding of Simple Electric Circuits
citation: Ali Khalid Ali Bawaneh, Ahmad Nurulazam Md Zain, & Salmiza Saleh. (2010). The Effect of Herrmann Whole Brain Teaching Method on Students' Understanding of Simple Electric Circuits. European Journal of Physics Education, Vol. 2 No. 2, ISSN 1309 7202. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/13097202
title: Fourteen-item multiple-choice conceptual test on simple electric circuits
description: The researchers developed a multiple-choice conceptual understanding test to measure misconceptions commonly held by eighth graders about simple electric circuits. "The final version of the test was a multiple -choice fourteen -item scale measuring misconceptions commonly held by students," with four alternatives per item and one correct answer. Items were derived from interviews about misconceptions limited to the eighth-grade textbook content, reviewed by a panel of six experts, and piloted with 39 ninth graders, yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.87 via Cronbach's alpha.
requirements: Expert panel review and pilot reliability testing as part of development
constraints: Content limited to concepts in the eighth-grade Jordanian science textbook for 2009-2010
target_learning_goals: diagnosing misconceptions about simple electric circuits
examples: Sample items in Appendix A ask about current at points in a circuit and the relation between current and voltage in a metallic conductor

article_title: Coaching Method in Teaching History of Visual Arts to Students
citation: Faizrakhmanova, A., Averianova, T., Aitov, V., Gibatova, G., & Lebedeva, I. (2018). Coaching Method in Teaching History of Visual Arts to Students. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 80-88. https://www.jsser.org
title: Four-stage coaching cycle applied to teaching history of visual arts
description: The article adopts the Parsloe and Wray conception of coaching as "a process furthering implementation of training and development and consequently improvement of the trainee's competence and professional skills", structured in four basic stages: goal setting, reality check, courses of action, and will to act. In History of Visual Arts classes, students set a goal such as mastering the historical periods of visual arts, assess their initial knowledge via questionnaires and self-study, seek courses of action in collaboration with the professor coach, and then carry out planned activities.
requirements: A professor acting as coach with whom students seek courses of action in collaboration
An initial knowledge assessment (questionnaires and self-study) to establish the reality check stage
constraints: The technology of its application in teaching is, per the authors' literature analysis, not sufficiently elaborated nor researched for efficiency
target_learners: higher education students in art and design programs
target_learning_goals: knowledge of historical periods of visual arts
representative artists of each period and their best-known works
examples: Students set the goal to master the basic knowledge of the historical periods of visual arts, each period's representative artists and their best-known works

citation: Mursalin. (2019). The Critical Thinking Abilities in Learning Using Elementary Algebra E-Books: A Case Study at Public Universities in Indonesia. Malikussaleh Journal of Mathematics Learning (MJML), 2(1), 29-33. https://doi.org/10.29103/mjml.v2i1.2292
title: Four-item essay test of mathematical critical thinking ability (pretest/post-test instrument)
description: The study measured mathematical critical thinking with a test of "4 items of essays given in the form of pretest and post-test". The instrument measures the abilities "to identify problems, take steps to solve, clarify a statement, and make conclusions", a critical-thinking operationalization the article notes was tested by Martiana (2015) in learning mathematics. Maximum score was 12.
requirements: Administered as both pretest and post-test to the same classes
target_learning_goals: mathematical critical thinking: problem identification, solution steps, clarifying statements, drawing conclusions
examples: Scores from this instrument produced the pretest, post-test, and N-gain data in Table 2

article_title: Extensions beyond Program Impacts: Conceptual and Methodological Considerations in Studying the Implementation of a Preschool Social Emotional Learning Program
citation: Choles JR, Roeser RW and Mashburn AJ (2022) Extensions beyond program impacts: Conceptual and methodological considerations in studying the implementation of a preschool social emotional learning program. Front. Educ. 7:1035730. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2022.1035730
title: Taxonomy of eight fidelity-of-implementation components: dosage, responsiveness, adherence, quality, differentiation, adaptations, program reach, and control-group monitoring
description: The article assembles a taxonomy of FOI components drawn from Dane and Schneider (1998) and Durlak and DuPre (2008). Common components "include the following: (1) Dosage, which describes the strength or quantity (in hours, sessions, etc.) of the program; (2) Responsiveness, which consists of the extent to which the program is engaging, interesting, and relevant to participants; (3) Adherence, which measures the extent to which the program is implemented as designed or planned; (4) Quality describes how well program components are delivered." The field has more recently added program adaptations, program reach, and, specifically for experimental studies, monitoring control group practices. The authors note these components are interrelated and that each affects the conclusions drawable about program impacts.
requirements: Measuring responsiveness alongside dosage, since participants learn when content is engaging, relevant, and interesting
Measuring quality alongside adherence to evaluate whether the program was engaging and relevant
constraints: Differentiation and program reach concern external validity and are outside the focus of this paper's framework application
In education interventions, measuring these components is complex because program components are diverse and span multiple levels
target_learners: preschool children and their teachers (as applied in this study)
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving implementation of SEL programs
examples: Table 1 of the article provides a glossary defining constructs such as FOI component, implementation level, program element, implementation agent, and intervention agent
key_sources: Choles JR, Roeser RW and Mashburn AJ (2022) Extensions beyond program impacts: Conceptual and methodological considerations in studying the implementation of a preschool social emotional learning program. Front. Educ. 7:1035730. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2022.1035730

article_title: Evaluation of the Effect of Mathematical Routines on the Development of Skills in Mathematical Problem Solving and School Motivation of Primary School Students in Abitibi-Témiscamingue
citation: Thomas Rajotte, Christine Marcotte, Lisa Bureau-Levasseur. (2016). Evaluation of the Effect of Mathematical Routines on the Development of Skills in Mathematical Problem Solving and School Motivation of Primary School Students in Abitibi-Témiscamingue. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(10): 2386-2391. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041017
title: Four-component model of school motivation (amotivation, intrinsic, identified extrinsic, introjected extrinsic)
description: The study operationalizes school motivation using the components identified by Vallerand and colleagues: "1) amotivation, which is a lack of motivation, 2) intrinsic motivation, which refers to the fact of undertaking an activity for the satisfaction and pleasure of doing so 3) the identified extrinsic motivation ... and 4) introjected extrinsic motivation, which involves behaviour regulation by internalized control sources". The article measures each component with a 12-question instrument (Cronbach's alpha 0,80) and analyzes each separately via ANCOVA.
requirements: Measurement requires a validated instrument covering all four components; the study used a tool developed by Vallerand et al.
target_learning_goals: school motivation
examples: The study's motivation variable had four distinct components, each tested with its own ANCOVA against the control group.

article_title: Active Learning and Flipped Classroom, Hand in Hand Approach to Improve Students Learning in Human Anatomy and Physiology
citation: Maria Entezari & Mohammad Javdan. (2016). Active Learning and Flipped Classroom, Hand in Hand Approach to Improve Students Learning in Human Anatomy and Physiology. International Journal of Higher Education, Vol. 5, No. 4. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n4p222
title: Four-activity active-learning package embedded in a flipped A&P lecture
description: The article designed four recurring in-class activities layered onto pre-posted flipped materials: a one-minute paper identifying the muddiest point, two to three group-based activities in groups of four, a partial outline completed in pairs after a ten-minute mini-lecture, and at least four clicker questions answered with colored response cards. The activities were "designed in a way to be suitable for all types of learning styles in order to increase the active participation of students in class". The instructor circulated, answered questions, and posted explanations for muddiest points on Blackboard the same day.
requirements: Course materials (outlines, notes, narrated PowerPoint slides, animations) posted on Blackboard one week before each class
Same instructor and same content coverage and exam schedule across conditions
constraints: Studied in a four-credit content-intensive A&P I course at a community college; the lab component was unchanged
target_learners: Community college allied health majors in Human Anatomy and Physiology I
target_learning_goals: Exam performance across Bloom difficulty levels
Conceptual understanding and misconception correction
Course satisfaction and retention
examples: One-minute papers were collected and read by the instructor, with explanations for muddiest points posted on Blackboard the same day
Students raised colored index cards marked A through D in response to clicker questions presented on PowerPoint slides

article_title: Evaluating Pedagogical Practices in Science Classrooms: A Randomized Controlled Trial Study on Teacher Virtual Professional Development with Virtual Mentoring and Coaching
citation: Lara-Alecio, R., Irby, B. J., Tong, F., Sutton-Jones, K. L., Guerrero, C. L., Tang, S., & Pang, H. (2024). Evaluating Pedagogical Practices in Science Classrooms: A Randomized Controlled Trial Study on Teacher Virtual Professional Development with Virtual Mentoring and Coaching. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 16(4), 479-494. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2024.347
title: Four-dimensional pedagogical classroom observation model
description: A classroom observation model integrating bilingual education theoretical principles, comprising "interrelated dimensions of language content, language of instruction, communication mode, and activity structures". Language content separates BICS and CALP into four levels (social routines, classroom routines, light cognitive, dense cognitive); language of instruction captures L1/L2 use patterns; communication mode classifies receptive and expressive modes; and activity structure records teacher pedagogical activities and student responses, grounded in Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development. It serves as the theoretical basis of the POP instrument used in this study.
requirements: Observation of classrooms with recorded lessons coded by trained raters using the derived POP rubric
constraints: Developed for observing classrooms with large numbers of emergent bilinguals
target_learners: Teachers of emergent bilingual and economically challenged students
target_learning_goals: Evaluating and improving science teachers' pedagogical practices in bilingual classrooms

article_title: Examining the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention
citation: Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Smolkowski, K., Baker, S. K., Fien, H., & Strand Cary, M. (2016). Examining the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 49(2), 152–165. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219414538514
title: Concentrate early mathematics intervention content on whole number understanding rather than broad coverage
description: Reviewing commonalities across promising early mathematics interventions, the article reports "a concentrated effort to reduce the amount of content coverage to provide a more in-depth and focused concentration on developing whole number understanding," citing programs that focused on a limited set of key topics. It states that this focused content design, combined with systematic and explicit instruction, corresponds with approaches advocated by prominent documents and national organizations, and suggests schools evaluate potential intervention programs with these parameters in mind.
requirements: Intervention content selected around critical whole number competencies aligned with standards such as the CCSS
constraints: The article presents this as guidance drawn from commonalities across programs, not as a directly tested design variable in this trial
target_learners: kindergarten and early elementary students at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: whole number understanding, including counting, number operations, and place value
examples: ROOTS exclusively focuses on whole number content across its 50 lessons, in contrast to the broader ELM core curriculum covering whole number, geometry, and measurement; cited programs focused on 17 key first-grade topics and critical kindergarten whole number competencies
key_sources: Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Smolkowski, K., Baker, S. K., Fien, H., & Strand Cary, M. (2016). Examining the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 49(2), 152–165. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219414538514

article_title: Effects of an Employer-Based Intervention on Employment Outcomes for Youth with Significant Support Needs Due to Autism
citation: Wehman P, Schall CM, McDonough J, Graham C, Brooke V, Riehle JE, Brooke A, Ham W, Lau S, Allen J, Avellone L. (2017). Effects of an employer-based intervention on employment outcomes for youth with significant support needs due to autism. Autism 21(3), 276–290. https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361316635826
title: Four-phase supported employment process
description: Supported employment, as used in PS-ASD internships, is "a four-phase process to assist job seekers with significant disabilities in achieving stability in competitive community-based employment." The phases are (1) job seeker profile, in which the individual works with a job coach on community-based assessments to set a personal job goal; (2) job development, applying for jobs and completing interviews; (3) job site training, until the employee is independent for 80% or more of work hours; and (4) long-term supports, entered when on-the-job coach support is 20% or less of work hours. It is a highly individualized approach based on ongoing data collection and on-site observation.
requirements: A trained job coach and long-term follow-along services in the fourth phase, which the article calls particularly important for youth with ASD who have significant support needs
constraints: All participants qualified for supported employment services due to significant support needs; long-term supports continued during employment
target_learners: Job seekers with significant disabilities, including youth with autism spectrum disorder
target_learning_goals: Securing and maintaining competitive community-based employment
Independence on the job
examples: Treatment participants received a mean of approximately 1 h weekly of long-term support hours (M = 0.91, SD = 0.43) after graduation
key_sources: Wehman P, Schall CM, McDonough J, Graham C, Brooke V, Riehle JE, Brooke A, Ham W, Lau S, Allen J, Avellone L. (2017). citation: Eldy, E.F., Chang, J.H.W., Butai, S.N., Basri, N.F., Awang. H., Din, W.A., & Arshad, S.E. (2019). Journal of Technology and Science Education, 9(3), 420-427. https://doi.org/10.3926/jotse.599

description: The article describes a four-step Physics PBL sequence used in both the inverted and traditional classrooms: students are presented with a real-life problem, understand and solve it in groups using an adaptation of the seven Maastricht steps, present and discuss their findings in a 10 to 15 minutes presentation, and finally reflect with facilitators on what they gained. It served as the end-of-module assessment format for both groups.
requirements: A facilitator to introduce and explain the problem scenario and guide group work
Group organisation of students for collaborative problem solving
constraints: Used as the assessment format at the end of every module in this pre-university physics course

problem-solving skills
application of mechanics concepts to real-life problems
examples: Groups gathered information from prior knowledge, online articles, videos and textbooks, then presented for 10 to 15 minutes per group before a reflection step

article_title: Empirical Study of Formative Evaluation in Adult ESL Teaching
citation: Qin Yi. (2012). Empirical Study of Formative Evaluation in Adult ESL Teaching. English Language Teaching, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n2p27
title: Five-step formative-evaluation teaching cycle for mastery learning in adult ESL units
description: The article implements formative evaluation as a recurring unit-level cycle: teaching, first formative evaluation with feedback, reflection/correction/supplementary instruction, a second formative evaluation, and summative evaluation. Unscored "formative assessment tests" diagnose learning, and students who master material move to enrichment or acceleration while others receive corrective instruction. The cycle repeats "till at least 80% to 90% students have fully mastered the given units" before a new unit begins.
requirements: The teacher defines learning units and mastery standards in advance and compiles definitive and corrective tests
A communication and feedback mechanism between teacher and students and among students is established
constraints: The article reports the cycle applied within one semester to one adult continuous-education class; mastery targets of 80–90% are the article's own stated working threshold, with a stated target rate of 100%
target_learners: adult part-time continuous-education ESL students in China
target_learning_goals: mastery of unit objectives in English vocabulary, grammar, and listening, speaking, reading, writing and translating skills
examples: The teaching material was divided into four units; after each unit's presentation, an assessment measured progress, feedback identified specific concepts needing more time, and corrective tests were given through group discussions or individual teaching
key_sources: Qin Yi. (2012). Empirical Study of Formative Evaluation in Adult ESL Teaching. English Language Teaching, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n2p27

article_title: Text-Based Vocabulary Intervention Training Study: Supporting Fourth Graders with Low Reading Comprehension and Learning Disabilities
citation: Solís, M., Scammacca, N., Barth, A. E., & Roberts, G. J. (2017). Text-based Vocabulary Intervention Training Study: Supporting Fourth Graders with Low Reading Comprehension and Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 15(1), 103-115.
title: Four-part small-group intervention session structure combining self-monitoring, vocabulary instruction, and text-based reading
description: Each of the eight 30-minute sessions was "organized according to four basic sections: introduction of self-monitoring (2-3 minutes), vocabulary instruction (10 minutes), text-based reading (15 minutes), and conclusion of self-monitoring (2-3 minutes)." The vocabulary routine introduced three new words and reviewed two previously taught words daily with simplified definitions, visuals, related words, and word-use discussion. The reading component had students re-read text to answer summarization, literal, and inferential questions, with instructors scaffolding down to paragraph, sentence, or word level.
requirements: Delivered in small groups of approximately two to three students by trained tutors
Grade-level expository texts modified for readability with a set of taught vocabulary words
target_learners: Fourth graders with low reading comprehension
Students at risk or with disabilities in tier 2 and tier 3 support
target_learning_goals: Content-area vocabulary acquisition
Reading comprehension of expository text
examples: Eight 30-minute sessions over two weeks in ten instructional groups of two to three students, five groups per tutor

article_title: Use of WebQuests in Mathematics Instruction: Academic Achievement, Teacher and Student Opinions
citation: Yenmez, A. A., Özpinar, İ., & Gökçe, S. (2017). Use of WebQuests in Mathematics Instruction: Academic Achievement, Teacher and Student Opinions. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(9). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050913
title: Four short-term WebQuest activities for ninth-grade data analysis and probability
description: The researchers developed four short-term WebQuests — two for data analysis (DAW1 pickle-making, DAW2 used-car selection) and two for probability (PW1 Turkish lottery, PW2 traffic accidents) — each designed to take about 3 class hours (135 minutes) and containing "introduction, task, process, resources, evaluation, and conclusion". Tasks were tied to daily-life situations, included open-ended questions requiring higher-order thinking, and specified curated internet resources so students would not waste time searching. Students accessed them at http://www.MathWebQuests.com and solved them in groups in a computer laboratory.
requirements: Schools need computer laboratories, internet networks and computers with necessary hardware
Teachers and students need sufficient computer-use skills
constraints: Teachers reported WebQuests on the internet are limited and inadequate and that preparing activities is difficult and time-consuming
target_learning_goals: data analysis and probability learning outcomes of the ninth-grade mathematics curriculum
examples: Experimental groups solved one WebQuest per week in elective courses, with the executive teacher acting as a guide and five teachers evaluating the solutions

article_title: Improving English Language Learners' Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role?
citation: Zainab Abolfazli Khonbi & Karim Sadeghi. (2017). Improving English Language Learners’ Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 5(3), 61-79. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: Four-mode idiom instruction package (movie clips, sentence-use, PowerPoint definitions, role-play)
description: The study’s treatment consisted of four ways of presenting the same 100 idioms over eight one-hour sessions, with 10 to 12 idioms taught per session per group. The Movie Group watched short clips from Everyday English Idioms on YouTube and guessed meanings; the Sentence-use Group wrote sentences with corrective feedback; the Definitions Group worked through 100 PowerPoint slides showing each idiom and its definition; the Role-play Group practiced and performed short conversational stories containing the idioms. All groups received the L1 (Persian) equivalent of each idiom.
requirements: The same idioms must be taught through each tool to keep conditions comparable; teaching/learning time was kept the same across groups.
constraints: Participants were 47 volunteers aged 15–22 from two language institutes, homogeneously upper-intermediate/advanced, all sharing Azeri L1 and Persian L2.
target_learners: upper-intermediate/advanced adolescent and young-adult EFL learners
target_learning_goals: idiomatic competence (comprehension and use of English idioms)
examples: The 45-item multiple-choice pretest/posttest, piloted and validated by expert professors, had a Cronbach reliability index of .84 and asked for Persian equivalents of the idioms.
key_sources: Zainab Abolfazli Khonbi & Karim Sadeghi. (2017). Improving English Language Learners’ Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 5(3), 61-79. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1156202

article_title: The Use of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) as a Teaching Method in Vocational Education and Training in Tourism
citation: Mocanu (Dedu) Elena Mădălina, Deaconu Alecxandrina. (2017). The use of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) as a teaching method in vocational education and training in tourism. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 10, Number 3. https://adn.teaching.ro
title: Four functional categories of ICT tools for teaching activities: information, location, knowledge-building, communication
description: Citing the Romanian Ministry of Communications and Information Society Teacher's Guide, the article classifies ICT tools for teaching into four functional categories: "a) Information ICT tools; b) Location ITC tools; c) ICT tools for building knowledge; d) Communication ICT tools." Information tools give access to information in multiple formats; location tools place students in virtual environments with simulated situations; knowledge-building tools support producing students' own materials such as portfolios; communication tools let students exchange educational messages across space and time. Each category is tied to named skills it develops.
requirements: Tools are chosen depending on the type and purpose of the training activities
target_learning_goals: searching, selecting and using information
experiential learning in simulated situations
building online learning portfolios
educational communication
examples: The article lists skills per category, e.g. identifying and collecting information on the Internet for information tools, and participating in online forum talks for communication tools

Combination of active teaching techniques
Personality-oriented interaction
Coordination of roles across teacher-student, student-student and teacher-teacher systems

title: Interconnectedness of experiential learning, active learning, flipped classroom and collaborative learning
description: The article argues (Figure 1) that "the four theories of learning are interconnected to form both theoretical and practical perspectives". It traces collaborative learning's antecedents to Kolb's experiential learning and Dewey, defines active learning through student activity and engagement, and defines collaborative learning as "an instruction method in which students work in groups toward a common academic goal". The flipped classroom supplies the technology tools through which students learn concepts before applying them collaboratively in real-world projects.

article_title: A Fitness Intervention Program within a Physical Education Class on Cardiovascular Endurance among Malaysia Secondary School Students
citation: Shabeshan Rengasamy, Subramaniam Raju, Wee Akina Sia Seng Lee, Ramachandran Roa. (2011). A Fitness Intervention Program within a Physical Education Class on Cardiovascular Endurance among Malaysia Secondary School Students. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(1). http://www.moj-es.net
title: Four-exercise circuit treatment embedded after the warm-up in physical education lessons
description: The treatment was a circuit of four exercises (Shuttle Run, Burpee, Jumping Jacks, and Modified Sit-up in pairs) performed immediately after the warm-up within the regular 40-minute physical education lesson. Students rotated through three stations, and "Each exercise was done for 30 seconds with a rest interval of 30 seconds." The rest interval was shortened after week five to apply the overload principle. The exercises were chosen because they "used large muscle groups and stressed the cardio respiratory chain".
requirements: Conducted within regular physical education classes twice a week for ten weeks, immediately after an eight-minute warm-up
Delivered by qualified physical education teachers following a researcher-prepared module followed strictly to avoid teacher effect
constraints: The rest interval reduction to 25 seconds after the fifth week was the article's stated overload adjustment
target_learners: Form Four Malaysian secondary school students (mean age about 16)
target_learning_goals: Health-related physical fitness, specifically cardiovascular endurance
examples: Experimental boys and girls performed the circuit for about four minutes within each 40-minute lesson, twice weekly, for ten weeks with no injuries reported

citation: Sakkarin Chattuchai, Adisak Singseewo and Paitool Suksringarm. (2015). Development of knowledge, awareness, global warming decreasing behavior and critical thinking of grade 11 students using the Four Noble Truths method with meta-cognitive techniques. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2360
title: The Four Noble Truths (FNT) method: a four-stage Buddhist-principled instruction method comparable to the scientific method
description: The FNT method, developed by Saroj Boasri, applies Buddhist principles for instruction with systematic thinking procedures the article describes as "comparable to the scientific method". It has four stages — suffering, cause of suffering, cessation of suffering, and the way to the cessation of suffering — emphasizing problem solving by oneself. In this study it structures environmental education lessons on global warming, with stages operationalized as setting the problem, formulating hypotheses, experimenting/collecting data, and discussing/concluding.
requirements: Instruction organized in the four FNT stages, with learners solving problems by themselves through searching data, processing data and drawing conclusions
target_learning_goals: environmental education knowledge
global warming awareness
global warming decreasing behavior
critical thinking
examples: Five lesson plans on global warming used the FNT stages with metacognitive questions added to the first and fourth stages

article_title: Mnemonic Aids during Tests: Worthless Frivolity or Effective Tool in Statistics Education?
citation: Karen H. Larwin, David A. Larwin, Jennifer Gorman. (2008). Mnemonic aids during tests: Worthless frivolity or effective tool in statistics education? Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mnemonic+aids+during+tests+statistics+education
title: Four-hypothesis framework for why in-test mnemonic aids may benefit performance
description: The article organizes competing accounts of why testing aids help into four hypotheses: the student engagement hypothesis (preparing aids fosters review, organization, and engagement with course material), the perception of control hypothesis (aids increase perceived control and reduce anxiety), the dependency hypothesis (students rely on the aid rather than learning), and a placebo effect hypothesis (belief in the aid's value, not learning, drives benefits). The study was designed to test all four simultaneously in a statistics course context.
requirements: Requires comparing conditions where aids are prepared by students, provided by instructors, replaced by an open textbook, or disallowed, so the accounts make divergent predictions
constraints: The article notes the placebo hypothesis had not been specifically examined before this study and that effects may vary across disciplines
target_learners: post-secondary students in required statistics courses
target_learning_goals: exam performance in applied statistics
understanding of core statistical concepts
examples: The study randomly assigned the four conditions across four exams in each of four course sections to test the divergent predictions
key_sources: Karen H. Larwin, David A. Larwin, Jennifer Gorman. (2008). Mnemonic aids during tests: Worthless frivolity or effective tool in statistics education? Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mnemonic+aids+during+tests+statistics+education

article_title: Effect of Motivational Scaffolding on E-Learning Environments: Self-Efficacy, Learning Achievement, and Cognitive Style
citation: Nilson Valencia-Vallejo, Omar López-Vargas, Luis Sanabria-Rodríguez. (2017). Effect of Motivational Scaffolding on E-Learning Environments: Self-Efficacy, Learning Achievement, and Cognitive Style. Journal of Educators Online. https://www.thejeo.com
title: Four-stage motivational scaffolding pattern for e-learning environments
description: A reusable instructional design pattern embedding motivation support into a computational environment across four stages: assessment, goal formulation and planning, learning execution and monitoring, and self-evaluation with final reflection. The scaffolding "promotes success experiences as the main activator of self-efficacy" through a self-evaluation module called "Supervise your knowledge," motivational messages attributing success to ability, effort, and persistence, and prompts for students to set goals, plan study time, and reflect on their learning process.
requirements: The environment must include a self-evaluation module with exercises equivalent to the final evaluation, goal-selection options, self-efficacy judgment scales, and motivational screen messages
constraints: The article states the results are inconclusive regarding cognitive-style equalization and recommends continuing experimental research on the scaffolding's design and implementation
target_learners: higher education students learning mathematical content in Web environments
field-dependent students with difficulties in mathematics
target_learning_goals: academic self-efficacy development
learning achievement in basic mathematics
examples: Students selected learning goals at basic, intermediate, or advanced levels, formulated self-efficacy judgments on a five-option scale, planned study time per lesson, and received messages such as "Very good! You have proven to have many abilities. Try to obtain better results"

article_title: The Effect of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) on Reading Comprehension in English for Specific Purposes Courses
citation: Fahimeh Farahani. (2018). The Effect of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) on Reading Comprehension in English for Specific Purposes Courses. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.1p.79
title: The four pillars of NLP as an operationalized framework for reading-task design
description: The study adopts "the 4 pillars of NLP" theory from Revell and Norman (1997) as its organizing framework, categorizing four key elements: outcome, rapport (maximizing similarities and minimizing differences among learners), sensory awareness (observing peers' reading techniques), and flexibility (moving between reading strategies until the desired outcome is achieved). The researcher operationalized these pillars in ten sessions of ESP reading tasks, making the task objective clear, conducting reading cooperatively, and briefing learners to switch strategies when a strategy proved ineffective.
requirements: Reading tasks must state the main objective (outcome) clearly
Tasks are conducted cooperatively to maximize similarities between learners
Learners observe peers' reading techniques as possible approaches
Learners are briefed to be flexible and move between strategies until the desired outcome is achieved
constraints: Operationalized here only for ESP reading comprehension with Iranian undergraduate medical-science learners
target_learners: Iranian undergraduate EFL learners in ESP courses
target_learning_goals: ESP reading comprehension
strategy flexibility in reading
examples: Ten treatment sessions covered NLP presuppositions, goal setting, sensory language, metaphor, emotion, belief, feedback, and finding the best strategy, each followed by reading a medical text and answering questions
