article_title: An Intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa
citation: Ona Janse van Rensburg. (2015). An intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, Vol. 4, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v4n2p110
title: Pedagogically justified principles framework for Foundation Phase intervention programmes
description: The article assembles a framework of principles that an intervention programme for young learners should rest on, arguing that "intervention programmes would only be effective if it is based on principles that can be pedagogically justified for young children". The framework spans nutrition and health, emotional factors, the teacher's role, language, culture, a constructivist approach to learning, perceptual abilities, motor development, learning through movement, concept forming, brain dominance, learning styles and multiple intelligences, music, memory, and television. It is used to design the ten-week Grade 1 intervention programme tested in the experiment.
requirements: Programme activities must be specially planned to stimulate learners with respect to each of the framework's factors
constraints: The framework was developed for learners in the first Grade of the Foundation Phase in the South African context
target_learners: Grade 1 learners (ages 6-7) in the Foundation Phase
target_learning_goals: School readiness
perceptual and motor development
concept forming
effective learning across Foundation Phase areas
examples: The researcher constructed an intervention programme based on these principles and tested it in a ten-week experiment with a multicultural Grade 1 class

article_title: On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context
citation: Mahnaz Saeidi, Elaheh Zaferanieh & Hafez Shatery. (2012). On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p72
title: Focus on Form instruction as a balance between Focus on Forms and Focus on Meaning
description: Focus on Form (FonF) is an instructional framework in which attention to linguistic code features occurs occasionally, within communicative activity, rather than through isolated discrete-item teaching or purely meaning-driven exposure. The article defines it as "an occasional shift of attention to linguistic code features—by the teacher and/or one or more students—triggered by perceived problems with comprehension or production" (Long & Robinson, 1998). It is learner-centered, responding to learners' perceived needs, and is presented as complementing rather than excluding Focus on Forms and Focus on Meaning.
requirements: A communicative classroom environment in which teachers and learners attend to form when necessary
constraints: The article distinguishes FonF from Focus on Forms (discrete items taught in separate lessons on a structural syllabus) and from Focus on Meaning (language experienced only as a medium of communication)
target_learners: Second/foreign language learners, including ESP university students
target_learning_goals: Second language vocabulary and grammatical form acquisition within communicative language use
examples: The study operationalized FonF as a dictogloss task in which students heard a short text twice, took notes, and reconstructed it in groups of three

article_title: On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context
citation: Mahnaz Saeidi, Elaheh Zaferanieh & Hafez Shatery. (2012). On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p72
title: Taxonomy of Focus on Form tasks and techniques ordered by degree of obtrusiveness
description: Doughty and Williams (1998) present a taxonomy of Focus on Form tasks and techniques arranged "as a continuum based on degree of obtrusiveness of Focus on Form," reflecting the degree to which the focus on form interrupts the flow of communication. Techniques range from unobtrusive (input flood, task-essential language, input enhancement, negotiation, recast) to obtrusive (output enhancement, interaction enhancement, dictogloss, CR tasks, input processing, garden path). Ellis (2003) additionally classifies focused-task design into structured-based production tasks (including dictogloss), comprehension tasks, and consciousness-raising tasks.
requirements: Tasks must be placeable along the unobtrusive-to-obtrusive continuum by how much they interrupt communication
constraints: The taxonomy is presented as a classification of tasks and techniques, not as a tested ranking of effectiveness
target_learners: Second language learners in communicative classrooms
target_learning_goals: Attention to linguistic form during meaning-focused activity
examples: The study used dictogloss, which the taxonomy places among the more obtrusive Focus on Form techniques

article_title: Development of Speaking Skills through Activity Based Learning at the Elementary Level
citation: Zahoor-UL-HAQ, Khurram, B. A., & Bangash, A. K. (2017). Development of Speaking Skills through Activity Based Learning at the Elementary Level. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 69, 241-252. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2017.69.13
title: Four p's lesson plan format for activity based language lessons
description: The experimental lessons were designed using "The four p's (preparation, presentation, practice, and production) lesson plan format". Lesson plans were consulted with a supervisor and language experts specializing in activity based learning and revised on their feedback. Activities were selected from the British Council's E.T.T.E project and the textbook, with the first two lessons consisting only of warm-up activities to motivate and engage students before other activities were introduced.
requirements: Lesson plans reviewed by a supervisor and language experts specializing in activity based learning
An ABL-trained teacher to deliver the lessons
constraints: Treatment lasted seven weeks with forty-minute lessons in a Pakistani public-sector elementary school
target_learners: 6th-grade elementary students learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Speaking skill development in English
examples: Activities used in the lessons included Simon Says, Chinese Whispers, Name Revision Ball Game, Action Song, Words, Role Play, and Dialogues

article_title: The Effects of Activities and Approachments Intended Performance Improvement on the Students' Performances in Mathematics
citation: Seval Deniz KILIÇ & Hüseyin ALKAN. (2018). The Effects of Activities and Approachments Intended Performance Improvement on the Students' Performances in Mathematics. Journal of Education and Learning, 7(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v7n5p146
title: Four-stage problem-solving performance rubric
description: The authors developed a rubric with four main stages for evaluating students' non-routine problem solutions, drawing on samples from Marzano, Pickering, & MCTighe (1993), Woodward, Monroe, & Baxter (2001) and Lianghuo (2011). Stage 1 assesses "Understanding the problem, determin ing its limitations and difficulties"; stage 2 presenting applicable and consistent ways of solution; stage 3 selecting solution ways and making adequate trials; stage 4 explaining and discussing why solution ways were selected. Each stage is scored 1–4 with descriptors.
requirements: Problems must be non-routine and open-ended so the four stages can be exhibited
Students were familiarized with the rubric stages via warm-up problems before scoring
constraints: Initially planned 8–10 question tests were reduced to 3 pretest and 4 posttest questions because students had difficulty completing questions on time
target_learning_goals: problem solving
reasoning
explaining and justifying solutions
examples: The rubric scored students' solutions to the 3-question pretest probing verbal, algebraic and geometric skills and the 4-question posttest on clusters, numbers, relations and functions

article_title: The Probability Approach to English If-Conditional Sentences
citation: Mei Wu. (2012). The Probability Approach to English If-conditional Sentences. English Language Teaching, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n5p37
title: Four-type probability-ordered classification of English conditionals
description: A lesson-level classification presenting conditionals in order of high-to-low probability of the result-clause event: factual (probability = 100%), predictive (~50%), hypothetical (~10%), and counterfactual (0%). Each type pairs a probability band with its verb-phrase structure, e.g. "If+past perfect→ would have+past participle" for counterfactuals. The article presents this ordering in Table 2 as the core instructional content of the Probability Approach.
requirements: Instruction must present the four types in probability order with example structures
constraints: Excludes mixed conditionals and non-standard conditional expressions
target_learning_goals: selecting the correct conditional type for a given meaning
examples: Table 2 lists factual, predictive, hypothetical and counterfactual conditionals with probability percentages and example structures

article_title: The Effect of Focused Communication Tasks on Instructed Acquisition of English Past Counterfactual Conditionals
citation: Broszkiewicz, A. (2011). The effect of focused communication tasks on instructed acquisition of English past counterfactual conditionals. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 335-363. http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: Focused communication tasks defined by the task-naturalness, task-utility and task-essentialness design criteria
description: Focused communication tasks are communicative tasks "designed to elicit production of a specific target feature in the context of performing a communicative task", also called structure-based communication tasks. The article adopts Loschky and Bley-Vroman's three design criteria: task-naturalness, where the construction may arise naturally but the task can be performed without it; task-utility, where the structure makes the task easier; and task-essentialness, where the task cannot be successfully performed unless the structure is used. The study's fourth treatment lesson applied these criteria to elicit the third conditional without telling learners which structure to use.
requirements: Tasks must be constructed to meet the three requirements of task-naturalness, task-utility and task-essentialness, which the article reports was a strenuous and demanding design process
constraints: If design procedures fail to elicit the target feature, methodological choices such as brief explicit instructions and clarification requests may be needed, which the article notes threatens the communicative nature of the task
target_learners: advanced (B2+) foreign language learners of English
target_learning_goals: implicit knowledge of specific grammatical structures, e.g. past unreal conditionals
examples: In the study's fourth lesson, FCT students exchanged information, opinions and experiences in pairs, small groups and a mingling activity, with the target structure highly desirable but never required

article_title: Advisor and Student Experiences of Summer Support for College-Intending, Low-Income High School Graduates
citation: Arnold, Karen D.; Chewning, Alexandra; Castleman, Benjamin; Page, Lindsay C. (2015). Advisor and Student Experiences of Summer Support for College-Intending, Low-Income High School Graduates. Journal of College Access. http://scholarworks.wmich.edu/jca/vol1/iss1/3
title: Four-task model of summer intervention: planning, financing, logistics/information, and anticipatory socialization
description: Figure 2 presents a model specifying the content of summer melt interventions, showing four major kinds of tasks required of college-intending graduates: postsecondary planning, financing, logistics/information, and anticipatory socialization. The model indicates interrelations among requirements: financing obstacles force students back into planning decisions, and informational barriers within logistics can likewise send students back to financing tasks. Very few low-income participants reached the anticipatory socialization level that higher-income students typically occupy.

constraints: Supports that help students actualize admission might have limited relevance to increasing their capacity to succeed academically once enrolled
target_learning_goals: completing pre-enrollment tasks and making an optimal transition into college
examples: Students fell from the anticipatory socialization level when unable to afford books, encountering racism during orientation, or facing uncertainty about acquiring a work-study job

article_title: Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners' Writing Ability: Teachers' Practices and Beliefs
citation: Hosseini, H., Chalak, A., & Biria, R. (2019). Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners’ Writing Ability: Teachers’ Practices and Beliefs. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 33-50. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.1223a
title: Forward design curriculum: content-first sequencing with assessment last
description: The article characterizes forward design as the traditional approach in which "input, process, and output are related in a linear fashion": content decisions precede methodology and assessment, described as a 'waterfall' model where each stage's output feeds the next. In a typical forward-design lesson the teacher chooses a topic, selects a resource, chooses instructional methods, and only then chooses essay questions to assess understanding. The article treats this as the conventional comparison condition against which backward design was evaluated.
requirements: Issues related to the content of instruction are resolved before decisions about methodology and output
constraints: The article states that in this approach "understanding does not play a pivotal role"
target_learners: EFL learners in institute-based language courses
target_learning_goals: Productive skills instruction (writing)
examples: The control group received writing instruction through a conventional method of forward design

article_title: Blended Learning Approach for Enhancing Students' Learning Experiences in a Knowledge Society
citation: Suprabha. K, & Subramonian, G. (2015). Blended learning approach for enhancing students learning experiences in a knowledge society. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 11(4). http://www.eric.ed.gov
title: Four-component blended learning instructional strategy: knowledge-, learner-, community-, and assessment-centred design
description: Attributed to the National Research Council as cited by Abdelaziz (2012), the article states that "blended learning instructional strategy consisted of four basic components": knowledge-centred, learner-centred, community-centred, and assessment-centred design. The knowledge-centred component emphasises understanding rather than remembering; the learner-centred component values learners' personal and cultural backgrounds and learning styles; the community-centred component makes learning activities collaborative; and the assessment-centred component uses formative assessment to make students' thinking visible with performance-oriented evaluations.
requirements: Knowledge-centred emphasis on understanding rather than remembering
Valuing individual learners' personal and cultural backgrounds and learning styles
Collaborative learning activities fostering a community of practice and inquiry
Formative assessment making students' thinking visible and performance-oriented evaluations
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
collaboration
self-regulated learning
examples: The article presents this four-component strategy as the basis of a framework for planning, developing and evaluating instruction based on learners' needs, content requirements and delivery methods.

article_title: Effects of an Informational Text Reading Comprehension Intervention for Fifth-Grade Students
citation: Kristen D. Ritchey, Kimberly Palombo, Rebecca D. Silverman, and Deborah L. Speece. (2017). Effects of an Informational Text Reading Comprehension Intervention for Fifth-Grade Students. Learning Disability Quarterly, 40(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948716682689
title: Four-day instructional cycle moving from explicit instruction to collaborative application
description: The intervention organized instruction into repeating 4-day cycles: "The intervention followed a specific sequence of instruction in 4-day instructional cycles." Day 1 provided explicit instruction and tutor modeling; Day 2 added supported and independent practice; Day 3 gave independent practice with trade books; Day 4 used a collaborative reading approach with student coaches applying the strategy to a biographical text. This sequence scaffolds learners from modeling toward peer-mediated application.
requirements: Tutors use scripted modeling language and prompts; a coach cue chart supports peer prompting on Day 4
target_learners: Upper elementary students with comprehension difficulties
target_learning_goals: Independent application of comprehension strategies across before, during, and after reading
examples: Day 4 coaches prompted peers with questions such as "What does this text remind you of?" using a cue chart on a coach's lanyard.

article_title: The Effect of Implementation of TBLT in Reading Comprehension Classes of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Mozhgan Madhkhan & Seyed Mojtaba Mousavi. (2017). The Effect of Implimentation of TBLT in Reading Comprehension Classes of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p119
title: Four task types for task-based reading instruction
description: The study designed four task types based on the students' book texts, identical for both groups in text but differing in activity. Task 1 was "Read and think" (deciding whether a visual aids comprehension), Task 2 "Read, note and discuss" (creating a visual to accompany a text), Task 3 "Read and discuss" (partner discussion of a visual's usefulness), and Task 4 "Read and write" (summarizing main points). Twenty tasks in four types were given across the sessions, one per session, and each performance was scored.
requirements: Tasks are designed based on the texts in the students' book that will be taught during the term
The same texts are used across comparison groups, with only the activities differing
constraints: Evaluated here only with intermediate-level Iranian EFL learners in institute settings
target_learning_goals: L2 reading comprehension
examples: In the experimental group, half an hour of the second part of each session reviewed prior vocabulary before the task was introduced with clear instructions and a model task
key_sources: Mozhgan Madhkhan & Seyed Mojtaba Mousavi. (2017). The Effect of Implimentation of TBLT in Reading Comprehension Classes of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p119

article_title: Designing University Courses to Improve Pre-Service Teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Evidence-Based Inclusive Practice
citation: Lancaster, J., & Bain, A. (2019). Designing University Courses to Improve Pre-Service Teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Evidence-Based Inclusive Practice. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 44(2). https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol44/iss2/4
title: Four-level embedding of target pedagogies within a course: knowledge, active experience, feedback, and personal impact
description: A course design pattern in which the pedagogies being taught are themselves used as the medium of instruction at four levels: "first introduced at a knowledge and awareness level, then in skill building through active experience, in 'real world' application with feedback, and then at a personal impact or consequential level as part of the course assessment". For example, pre-service teachers learned cooperative learning by experiencing Jigsaw II as the workshop medium, met in collaborative groups using each approach to prepare for quizzes, and used the practices in ways that affected their grades.
requirements: Common features such as self-questioning, peer mediation, structured collaborative problem solving, authentic assessment, advance organization and concept mapping are folded into a research-driven framework
Feedback mechanisms that let the schema evolve as participant capacity grows
constraints: Generalizability is limited to one university course, an available population, and a quasi-experimental design; instructor differences across sites could not be fully ruled out
target_learners: pre-service teachers in inclusive education coursework
target_learning_goals: mastery of evidence-based inclusive pedagogies including explicit teaching, cooperative learning and differentiation
examples: Five two-hour skill-building workshops in collaborative problem solving, explicit teaching and cooperative learning, each taught using the approach it taught; twenty-minute collaborative quiz preparation using the approach being learned
key_sources: Lancaster, J., & Bain, A. (2019). Designing University Courses to Improve Pre-Service Teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Evidence-Based Inclusive Practice. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 44(2). https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol44/iss2/4

article_title: Does Cognitive Strategy Training on Word Problems Compensate for Working Memory Capacity in Children with Math Difficulties?
citation: H. Lee Swanson, Michael J. Orosco, Cathy Lussier. (2013). Does Cognitive Strategy Training on Word Problems Compensate for Working Memory Capacity in Children with Math Difficulties? SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: Four prediction models of working memory capacity's role in strategy training outcomes
description: The article organizes its hypotheses around four models of how working memory capacity relates to strategy training outcomes for children with math difficulties: "(a) WMC as a limiting factor, (b) basic skills, (c) general resource, and (d) compensatory". The limiting model predicts low-WMC children benefit less; the basic-skills model predicts strategy instruction helps when declarative knowledge is intact without WMC demands; the resource model predicts a WMC main effect regardless of treatment; the compensatory model predicts low-WMC children rely more on strategy conditions. The results fit the limiting-type account, with high-WMC children showing strategy benefits.
requirements: Working memory capacity must be measured at pretest (composite of conceptual span, updating, digit/sentence span) to assign children to WMC levels
constraints: The article notes the moderating role of WMC may change with longer intervention periods as strategies become automatized, citing Ackerman (1988)
target_learning_goals: word problem solving accuracy
calculation accuracy
working memory span
examples: The study tested the four models in a 2 (MD vs. NMD) x 4 (treatment) ANCOVA with WMC as a covariate set at mean, low, and high levels
key_sources: H. Lee Swanson, Michael J. Orosco, Cathy Lussier. (2013). Does Cognitive Strategy Training on Word Problems Compensate for Working Memory Capacity in Children with Math Difficulties? SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563039

article_title: Effectiveness of Selected Supplemental Reading Comprehension Interventions: Findings from Two Student Cohorts. NCEE 2010-4015
citation: James-Burdumy, S., Deke, J., Lugo-Gil, J., Carey, N., Hershey, A., Gersten, R., Newman-Gonchar, R., Dimino, J., Haymond, K., and Faddis, B. (2010). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Four supplemental reading comprehension curricula evaluated in a school-randomized design
description: The element is the set of four fifth-grade supplemental reading comprehension curricula tested in the evaluation: Project CRISS, ReadAbout, Read for Real, and Reading for Knowledge. Schools were randomly assigned to use one of the four treatment curricula or to a control group, with teachers developing their own ways of fitting the assigned curriculum into daily schedules. The report states the curricula "were designed to supplement—not replace—the core curriculum being used by each teacher."
requirements: The curricula are supplemental and must be incorporated by teachers into their existing core reading instruction and daily schedules
constraints: Reading for Knowledge was not implemented with the second cohort because nine of its 18 assigned schools elected not to continue
target_learners: fifth-grade students in Title I schools
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of informational text in content areas such as science and social studies
examples: First year: 10 districts, 89 schools, 268 teachers, and 6,349 fifth-grade students; second-year fifth-grade component: 10 districts, 61 schools, 182 teachers, and 4,142 students

article_title: The Effectiveness of Peer Taught Group Sessions of Physiotherapy Students within the Clinical Setting: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Scott, D. and Jelsma, J. (2014). The effectiveness of peer taught group sessions of physiotherapy students within the clinical setting: A quasi-experimental study. Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 105-117. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/9
title: 40-question true/false end-of-block test with expert content validation for clinical group teaching outcomes
description: The outcome instrument was a test with 40 true or false questions devised by the clinical educator, composed of ten questions for each of four health conditions covered during the placement. It assessed students' ability to apply basic theoretical knowledge, clinical reasoning within the clinical context, and management of the health conditions presented. It was reviewed by three paediatric lecturers for content validity, piloted on an earlier cohort, judged to have face and content validity, and marked by a blinded third party.
requirements: Expert review by paediatric lecturers to establish content validity for the year level
Blinded third-party marking guided by an answer sheet
constraints: Designed for third-year physiotherapy level of learning in this specific paediatric placement context
target_learning_goals: application of theoretical knowledge
clinical reasoning in context
management of paediatric health conditions
examples: Ten questions per condition were included in a test at the end of each five-week block, totalling 40 questions

article_title: FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes
citation: Mireles, S. V., Acee, T. W., & Gerber, L. N. (2014). FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes. Journal of Developmental Education, 38(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=FOCUS+Intervention+College+Algebra+Mireles
title: The FOCUS model as a three-legged stool of interdependent program components
description: The FOCUS (Fundamentals of Conceptual Understanding and Success) model visualizes the credit-bearing course as the seat of a three-legged stool supported equally by developmental mathematics, learning support, and academic support services, with research-based best practices forming the rim. The article states "the credit-bearing course, is supported equally by Developmental Mathematics, Learning Support, and Academic Support Services". The model frames a co-requisite program in which components are interdependent rather than optional add-ons.
requirements: Concurrent enrollment in developmental mathematics and the credit-bearing course
Mandatory participation in academic support services such as tutoring
constraints: Developed and evaluated in the context of a single university's College Algebra and developmental education placement system
target_learners: College students placed into developmental mathematics
target_learning_goals: Completion of a credit-bearing College Algebra course
Increased mathematics proficiency
examples: The program was implemented across five semester/year administrations from Summer 2010 to Fall 2012 with 127 students
key_sources: Mireles, S. V., Acee, T. W., & Gerber, L. N. (2014). FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes. Journal of Developmental Education, 38(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1071436

article_title: FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes
citation: Mireles, S. V., Acee, T. W., & Gerber, L. N. (2014). FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes. Journal of Developmental Education, 38(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=FOCUS+Intervention+College+Algebra+Mireles
title: FOCUS curriculum design: backward design, just-in-time developmental sequencing, and deconstruct/reconstruct
description: The FOCUS curriculum pattern coordinates a credit-bearing course scope and sequence built by backward design from state and local objectives, a developmental course whose concepts are sequenced just-in-time to support the credit-bearing content, and a deconstruct/reconstruct approach that replaces memorized, context-bound rules with generalizable conceptual knowledge. The article notes "The notion of "deconstructing" misunderstanding and "reconstructing" conceptual knowledge was prevalent in the developmental mathematics curriculum". The developmental course extends an algebraic core to geometry, measurement, probability, and statistics.
requirements: Developmental concepts must be sequenced to support upcoming credit-bearing content, e.g., solving systems of equations before matrix methods
constraints: Some content, such as continuity and the logistic function, exceeded traditional College Algebra expectations
target_learners: Developmental mathematics students co-enrolled in College Algebra
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of functions and algebra beyond memorized procedures
examples: Students who used FOIL for multiplying binomials confronted its limitations and were taught the distributive property
key_sources: Mireles, S. V., Acee, T. W., & Gerber, L. N. (2014). FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes. Journal of Developmental Education, 38(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1071436

article_title: FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes
citation: Mireles, S. V., Acee, T. W., & Gerber, L. N. (2014). FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes. Journal of Developmental Education, 38(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=FOCUS+Intervention+College+Algebra+Mireles
title: FOCUS Intervention co-requisite program with wrap-around academic support services
description: The FOCUS Intervention is a comprehensive co-requisite program in which students placed into developmental mathematics bypass the traditional developmental sequence and enroll concurrently in a developmental mathematics course and the credit-bearing College Algebra course. The article states "Students enrolled in the FOCUS Intervention program were registered in a developmental mathematics course and credit-bearing mathematics course concurrently". Wrap-around services included weekly/monthly seminars, mentoring, and required tutoring; a faculty panel selected applicants based on criteria such as repeated developmental failure and first-generation status.
requirements: Faculty selection of candidates from the applicant pool
Mandatory pretest and posttest THEA assessment at the university testing center
Required participation in academic support services
constraints: Admission was selective rather than open; placement was based on university-defined cut-scores often higher than state standards
target_learners: Underprepared college students placed into developmental mathematics, including first-generation students and veterans
target_learning_goals: Completion of credit-bearing College Algebra
Reduced time to degree
examples: 127 students participated across Summer 2010, Summer 2011, Spring 2012, Summer 2012, and Fall 2012
key_sources: Mireles, S. V., Acee, T. W., & Gerber, L. N. (2014). FOCUS: Sustainable Mathematics Successes. Journal of Developmental Education, 38(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1071436

article_title: Game-Based Tasks for Foreign Language Instruction: Perspectives on Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Masoumeh Mehregan. (2014). Game-Based Tasks for Foreign Language Instruction: Perspectives on Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning. https://iafor.org/journal
title: Four-game vocabulary treatment sequence (hangman, flash card memory game, bingo, odd man out)
description: The treatment element is a sequence of four group-based vocabulary games adopted from "Games for Young Learners" and practiced in the last 20 minutes of each session: "New vocabulary items in "Happy Earth 1" (Bowler & Parminter, 2002) were taught and practiced via four games with the first group in the last 20 minutes of every session." Each game ran for five of the 20 total sessions, with learners arranged into small groups and the instructor monitoring and eliciting answers and reasons afterwards.
requirements: New vocabulary items from the course book Happy Earth 1 as the target content
Small-group arrangement and teacher monitoring during and after game play
constraints: Tested only with elementary-level learners aged 10 to 15 at one language institute
target_learners: young EFL learners at elementary proficiency level (ages 10-15)
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning and retention
examples: In hangman, groups guessed letters of new words; in bingo the teacher used 16 photo cards and a 16-space chart; in odd man out groups circled the unrelated word and justified their choice.
key_sources: Masoumeh Mehregan. (2014). Game-Based Tasks for Foreign Language Instruction: Perspectives on Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning. https://iafor.org/journal

article_title: Scenario-Based Case Study Method and the Functionality of the Section Called "From Production to Consumption" from the Perspective of Primary School Students
citation: Ahu TANERİ (2018). Scenario-Based Case Study Method and the Functionality of the Section Called 'from Production to Consumption' from the Perspective of Primary School Students. Asian Journal of Education and Training, 4(1): 56-61. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.522.2018.41.56.61
title: Four scenario-based lesson plans for the 'from Production to Consumption' unit
description: The researcher developed four lesson plans for the fourth-grade social studies learning field of production, distribution and consumption. Each plan pairs an unfinished case study with a finalized scenario script, open-ended questions, and digital and printed resources, so students work through a real-life case rather than a textbook. The plans were developed by the researcher and reviewed by surveying, Turkish and social sciences experts.
requirements: Scenario content must suit students' level of knowledge, make students act, and align with the teaching objectives with integrated concepts, as the article states for effective scenario-based learning
constraints: Developed and evaluated within one fourth-grade social studies classroom in a public school in Central District of Ankara
target_learning_goals: consumer behaviors, demands and needs
choosing and evaluating products
consumer rights
examples: Each lesson plan includes "a case study associated with the achievement but not finalized, a finalized scenario script covering the case study, open-ended questions, and digital and printed resources."
key_sources: Ahu TANERİ (2018). Scenario-Based Case Study Method and the Functionality of the Section Called 'from Production to Consumption' from the Perspective of Primary School Students. Asian Journal of Education and Training, 4(1): 56-61. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.522.2018.41.56.61

article_title: Forming Well Organized Writing Activities
citation: Irfan Tosuncuoğlu. (2018). Forming a Well Organized Writing Activities. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 6, No. 6. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i6.3111
title: Exercise set designed to form four writing abilities: chronological description, selecting main facts, causal relations, and forming conclusions
description: The article enumerates the abilities its exercise set was meant to form: describing events successively in chronological order, choosing main facts while describing things, characters and places, establishing causal relations in acts and events, and forming conclusions and summaries. This design pattern links each supplementary exercise to a target ability so students can "communicate their ideas in examinations, repo rts, etc."
requirements: Exercises must target the enumerated abilities rather than grammar drill alone
target_learning_goals: describing events in order
selecting main facts
establishing causal relations
forming conclusions and summaries
examples: The article lists forming conclusions and summaries among the abilities the exercises were meant to form
key_sources: Irfan Tosuncuoğlu. (2018). Forming a Well Organized Writing Activities. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 6, No. 6. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i6.3111

article_title: The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety
citation: Nihat BAYAT. (2014). The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.3.1720
title: Four-dimension expert rubric for evaluating academic essays
description: Writing success was measured by academic essays evaluated by two experts with doctorates in Turkish language teaching and more than five years of experience. "Four criteria were identified according to literature and expert opinion: the organization, content, word choice, and language use required for academic essays." A standardized checklist assigned each dimension a possible 25 points, with subsections worth 5 points each; the total score was the paper's score. Agreement between the two experts was 89% for the pretest and 91% for the posttest.
requirements: Two expert evaluators with relevant doctoral-level expertise and teaching experience
A standardized checklist with dimension and subsection point allocations
constraints: Topics were limited to academic essay writing on general concepts such as traditions, smoking, education, and politics
target_learning_goals: academic writing success in organization, content, word choice, and language use
examples: Pretest and posttest essays were written on participant-chosen topics such as communication problems among people, the effect of a life goal on the quality of life, and improper urbanization
key_sources: Nihat BAYAT. (2014). The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.3.1720

article_title: The Impact of Online Algorithm Visualization on ICT Students' Achievements in Introduction to Programming Course
citation: Fatih Saltan. (2017). The Impact of Online Algorithm Visualization on ICT Students' Achievements in Introduction to Programming Course. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p184
title: Four pedagogical approaches in algorithm visualization
description: Citing Hundhausen and colleagues' (2002) meta-analysis, the article describes four main pedagogical approaches in algorithm visualization: Epistemic Fidelity, Dual-coding, Individual Differences, and Cognitive Constructivism. Epistemic Fidelity "emphasizes encoding and transferring experts' mental model to learners through graphic illustration"; Dual-coding highlights verbal and non-verbal symbolic systems; the individual differences approach addresses learners' differing needs and abilities; and Cognitive Constructivism holds that each learner actively constructs knowledge. A game-based learning approach emphasizing goal-oriented, active and enjoyable learning is added as a more recent theoretical guide.
requirements: For Epistemic Fidelity, an excellent match between an expert's denotational semantics and the graphical representations
target_learning_goals: understanding how algorithms work
examples: The article frames OAV tools such as code.org within this lineage of AV environments from BALSA to Scratch and Greenfoot.
key_sources: Fatih Saltan. (2017). The Impact of Online Algorithm Visualization on ICT Students' Achievements in Introduction to Programming Course. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p184

article_title: The Effects of Learning Strategies Instruction on Metacognitive Knowledge, Using Metacognitive Skills and Academic Achievement (Primary Education Sixth Grade Turkish Course Sample)
citation: Muhittin ÇALIŞKAN & Ali Murat SÜNBÜL. (2011). The Effects of Learning Strategies Instruction on Metacognitive Knowledge, Using Metacognitive Skills and Academic Achievement (Primary Education Sixth Grade Turkish Course Sample). Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(1), 148-153. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ930514
title: Four-measure battery for assessing strategy awareness, metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive skill use, and achievement
description: The study collected four types of data using four instruments: the Learning Strategies Identification Scale (Güven, 2008) for strategy awareness, the Turkish Course Metacognitive Knowledge Interview Form, the Metacognitive Skills Standardized Open-Ended Interview Form, and a 28-item Turkish Course Achievement Test. The scale was re-administered to 424 students, yielding reliabilities of .75 for interpretation strategies, .67 for organization strategies, and .74 for repetition strategies; the interview form's alpha was .87 and the achievement test's KR-20 was .81.
requirements: Instruments validated and reliability-tested before use
Groups equalized on the basis of these measures and pre-test results
constraints: Reliability of the organization strategies sub-scale (.67) was the lowest of the three sub-scales
target_learning_goals: measuring strategy awareness, metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive skill use, and course achievement
examples: The achievement test had an average difficulty of .51 and an average distinctiveness of .41

article_title: Different Modes of Digital Learning Object Use in School Settings: Do We Design for Individual or Collaborative Learning?
citation: Akpinar, Y. (2014). Different modes of digital learning object use in school settings: Do we design for individual or collaborative learning? International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology, 10(3), 87-95. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu/viewarticle.php?id=1747
title: Four simulation-based learning objects with paired achievement tests and a usability questionnaire
description: The study used four LOs with simulation characteristics selected from a repository — Pressure/Buoyant force, Work and energy, and Electricity in daily life (seventh grade Science) and Map scales (ninth grade Geography). Tasks required solving contextualized problems using each LO's computational facilities. Two achievement tests per unit (pre and post, same number of multiple-choice items, different items) were developed, plus a 15-20 item three-point Likert usability questionnaire covering "system screen, terms and system information, learning to operate the system and system capabilities, and overall user reaction".
requirements: Tests targeted the same instructional objectives per unit; students answered test items on their own
constraints: The pre and post tests had not been pilot tested and their reliability was not statistically ensured; only expert opinion validated them, so results should be interpreted accordingly
target_learners: seventh and ninth grade state-school students in Turkey
target_learning_goals: unit content in science and geography deemed difficult to learn
examples: Sessions ran 30-70 minutes in school computer labs, with pretests lasting 10-20 minutes and posttests 8-20 minutes

International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology, 10(3), 87-95. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu/viewarticle.php?id=1747

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge
citation: Mathukorn Jingjit. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: Four-factor multimedia program design: segmentation, guidance, contiguity, and motivational appearance
description: The article's multimedia program embodied four design factors drawn from Mayer et al. (2002). Materials were delivered "through several learning units or modules in order to reduc e the complexity and difficulty level the materials"; written text and spoken instructions reduced external cognitive load; pictures and texts were placed to prevent split attention; and the appearance was made attractive to raise interest and engagement. This pattern operationalizes cognitive load management for young EFL vocabulary learning.
requirements: Materials segmented into modules to reduce internal cognitive load
Written text plus spoken instructions to reduce external cognitive load
Pictures and texts placed to prevent split attention
constraints: Requires adequate facilities such as computer rooms and computer availability
target_learners: third-grade primary pupils learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: size and depth of English vocabulary knowledge
examples: A researcher-designed multimedia program stored on CD delivered 52 word items from two Ministry-recommended English books over 8 weeks.
key_sources: Mathukorn Jingjit. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083500

article_title: Formation of Future Teachers' Professional Competence on the Basis of Polylingual Approach: The State Analysis
citation: Zhorabekova, A. N. (2015). Formation of Future Teachers' Professional Competence on the Basis of Polylingual Approach: The State Analysis. International Education Studies, 8(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n12p130
title: Four-level graduation of professional competence formation: low, medium, sufficient, high
description: Analysis of the criteria and indicators led to highlighting four levels: low, medium, sufficient and high. "At the heart of this graduation there is a certain amount available in the future teacher's formation: the fewer the indicators, the lower the level of formation" of professional competence on the basis of polylingual approach. Each level is described qualitatively, from indifferent interest and superficial knowledge (low) to firm conviction and deep knowledge with real educational experience (high).
requirements: Assessment of indicators across the motivational, cognitive and operational components
constraints: The level of formation describes readiness for professional activity and creative application of abilities in real teaching
target_learners: future teachers in university teacher training
target_learning_goals: readiness for polylingual professional teaching activity
examples: The high level reflects strong desire to develop general language and professional language skills and deep knowledge of polylingual approach essence
key_sources: Zhorabekova, A. N. (2015). Formation of Future Teachers' Professional Competence on the Basis of Polylingual Approach: The State Analysis. International Education Studies, 8(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n12p130

article_title: With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving
citation: Frederick, M. L., Courtney, S., & Caniglia, J. (2014). With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Four-square graphic organizer for non-routine mathematics tasks
description: A graphic organizer used by students to direct their thinking and promote metacognition while solving non-routine geometry tasks. It includes "the identification of critical components, strategy selection, computation, and analyses of answers". Each square was graded on a two-point scale, with daily-task scores computed by summing points across squares. It served as the base scaffolding intervention in both the control and experimental classes.
requirements: Tasks aligned to daily class objectives, drawn from previously released state assessment items
constraints: The article does not report its effect in isolation from the grouping scaffolds, since both classes used it
target_learning_goals: solving non-routine mathematics problems
conceptual knowledge of geometry
metacognition
examples: Students indicated that the daily task four-square format was helpful in analyzing and solving the problem

article_title: Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary
citation: Malik Behlol & Mohammad Munir Kaini. (2011). Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 4(1). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Four principles for personalizing word learning
description: Citing the author's 2010 work, the article enumerates four principles of vocabulary instruction for personalizing word learning: students decide what words to learn and how; students are immersed in vocabulary learning throughout the working day with language both exposed and explained; word building needs "multiple exposure of different intensity", with about 12 exposures cited for mastery; and students participate as active co-learners who connect new words to previous knowledge. The article also advises limiting the presentation of vocabulary in a lesson or academic year.
requirements: Ongoing commitment to vocabulary learning across the day; opportunities for students to generate new words and reflect on learnt items
constraints: Presentation of vocabulary must be limited, since massive exposure may confuse students in spoken and written use
target_learners: second language learners at secondary level
target_learning_goals: active vocabulary development and personalized word learning
examples: The article cites a need of 12 exposures for getting mastery and proper utilization of new lexical items
key_sources: Malik Behlol & Mohammad Munir Kaini. (2011). Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 4(1). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: The Effect of a Social-Emotional School-Based Intervention upon Social and Personal Skills in Children and Adolescents
citation: Tania Gaspar, Ana Cerqueira, Cátia Branquinho & Margarida G. Matos. (2018). The Effect of a Social-Emotional School-Based Intervention upon Social and Personal Skills in Children and Adolescents. Journal of Education and Learning, 7(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v7n6p57
title: "For me it's Easy" scale for personal and socio-emotional skills
description: A self-report evaluation tool of personal and socio-emotional skills for children and adolescents, built from the social skills checklist (Goldstein & McGinnis, 1997) and the emotional self-regulation questionnaire (Moilanen, 2007), with back translation of some items. The final version consists of 43 items "that include competencies from the simplest to the most complex", with several inverted items, and was used to assess the effect of the Social and Emotional Skills Promotion Program.
requirements: Self-fulfillment and voluntary participation with parental informed consent, as used in the study
constraints: The Goal Setting dimension shows the lowest internal consistency (α = 0.62 in Table 2)
Developed and validated in the Portuguese context (Gaspar & Matos, 2015)
target_learners: Portuguese children and adolescents aged 8 to 16+ in school settings
target_learning_goals: Personal and socio-emotional skills: problem solving, basic skills, emotional regulation, interpersonal relationships, defining goals
examples: Used pre and post to evaluate the ISC competences program in 4 schools in Lisbon, with a waiting-list comparison group

article_title: "Trees Have a Soul Too!" Developing Empathy and Environmental Values in Early Childhood
citation: Lithoxoidou, L. S., Georgopoulos, A. D., Dimitriou, A. Th., & Xenitidou, S. Ch. (2017). “Trees have a soul too!” Developing Empathy and Environmental Values in Early Childhood. International Journal of Early Childhood Environmental Education, 5(1). https://naaee.org
title: Forest-themed preschool environmental program integrating environmental ethics across four thematic units with empathy-building techniques
description: A semester-long interdisciplinary program (January to June 2002) comprising seventy five designed activities and fifteen emerging activities, organized in four units: Trees, Animals, Risks to the forest, and Protection of the forest. It aims at fostering environmentally friendly attitudes through knowledge acquisition, feelings of care and responsibility, forming values and rules of pro-environmental behaviour, and strengthening environmentally friendly action. Techniques include outdoor experiential games, literature and role-playing, inductive discussion, values-education strategies, and eco-management actions such as cleaning the forest and planting trees.
requirements: Children in direct contact with the natural environment
Techniques promoting feelings, especially empathy
Children playing an active role in creating behavior rules rather than rules stated as absolute truths
constraints: Implemented with a single convenience-sample kindergarten class; results not generalisable since the sample does not represent the population as a whole
target_learning_goals: environmental values
empathy for non-human beings
pro-environmental behavior rules and action
examples: Children participated in eco-management actions such as cleaning the forest, recycling at school and planting trees in a municipal park, and organized a protest in the school playground with placards

article_title: The Effect of Incidental Focus on Form on EFL Learners' Grammatical Accuracy
citation: Abdollahzadeh, S. (2015). The Effect of Incidental Focus on Form on EFL Learners’ Grammatical Accuracy. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.5p.40
title: Focus on form as a framework integrating attention to linguistic elements within meaning-based instruction
description: Focus on form is a framework from Long (1991) that draws learners' attention to linguistic elements as they arise incidentally in lessons whose primary focus is on meaning or communication. It differs from both focus on forms (isolated grammar teaching) and focus on meaning (no attention to form). The framework holds that learners benefit from attention to form during communicative interaction.
requirements: Instruction must maintain meaning or communication as the overriding focus while allowing attention to form to arise incidentally.
constraints: The framework assumes learners have limited processing capacities and cannot easily focus on both meaning and form simultaneously.
target_learning_goals: grammatical accuracy
communicative competence
examples: The study operationalized focus on form through recasting during jigsaw retelling tasks.

article_title: Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course
citation: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145
title: Nation's four strands principle as a framework for balancing ESP vocabulary programs
description: The article applies Nation's (2007) framework of four strands—"meaning-focused input, meaning-focused output, language-focused learning and fluency development"—as guidelines for combining subject matter and English learning in an ESP course. The framework holds that "learning from input alone is not enough" and that programs need "a balance of well proven learning activities across the four strands". The author uses it to evaluate both advantages and disadvantages of the vocabulary activities in students' evaluations.
requirements: The vocabulary program should balance activities across all four strands, with 95-98% of running words within learners' previous knowledge for meaning-focused input
constraints: The article notes more students favored a bilingual class over all-English teaching (38.30% commented positively on all-English class)
target_learners: accounting majors in an ESP course
target_learning_goals: technical vocabulary acquisition and retention
professional communication skills in accounting
examples: The journal entry practice activity was designed to cover meaning-focused output and language-focused learning strands

article_title: Design Experiments: Developing and Testing an Intervention for Elementary School-Age Students Who Use Non-Mainstream American English Dialects
citation: Shurita Thomas-Tate, Carol McDonald Connor, & Lakeisha Johnson. (2013). Design Experiments: Developing and Testing an Intervention for Elementary School-age Students who use Non-mainstream American English Dialects. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org/
title: Cyclical four-day instructional cycle: introduce forms, receptive practice, expressive practice, weekly writing or editing measure
description: Both intervention conditions used a weekly cycle teaching two dialect forms per week: "an introduction to the dialect forms of the day 1, receptive language activities on day 2 to build a foundation for the new knowledge, and expressive language activities on day 3 to practice using the forms". Day 4 provided a writing or sentence-editing task as a weekly measure. Activities included sentence sorts, cloze sentences, sentence completion, sentence generation, editing, puzzles, memory games, and bingo.
requirements: Both receptive and expressive tasks for each form
A weekly day-4 measure of understanding and usage
constraints: Implemented over a four-week period in 15–20 minute daily sessions
target_learners: Second through fourth grade students who use Non-mainstream American English
target_learning_goals: Producing School English grammatical forms (copula, plurals, past tense) in writing
examples: Small groups escorted to a quiet school area for daily 15–20 minute sessions across four weeks

article_title: The Beneficial Impacts of Applying Formative Assessment on Iranian University Students' Anxiety Reduction and Listening Efficacy
citation: Abbas Bayat, Ahmadreza Jamshidipour, Masoud Hashemi. (2017). THE BENEFICIAL IMPACTS OF APPLYING FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT ON IRANIAN UNIVERSITY STUDENTS' ANXIETY REDUCTION AND LISTENING EFFICACY. International Journal of Languages' Education and Teaching, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.18298/ijlet.1740
title: Formative assessment as continuous monitoring of learning with prompt feedback
description: The article frames formative assessment as evaluation woven through instruction rather than reserved for final exams: it is "a means to monitor and regulate learning process, features prompt feedback", administered "throughout the learning process as an effort to inform both teacher and learner". It cites the Assessment Reform Group definition of seeking and interpreting evidence about where learners are, where they need to go, and how best to get there, and presents weekly quizzes as its operational form in this study.
requirements: Administered during instruction, not only at the end of a course
Provides prompt feedback that informs both teacher and learner
target_learners: EFL learners in language institutes and universities
target_learning_goals: Listening comprehension
Anxiety reduction
Academic achievement in EFL
examples: In the study, the experimental group experienced one quiz per week during a two-month listening course, while the control group received only a summative post-test.

article_title: Generation of Student Interest in an Inquiry-Based Mobile Learning Environment
citation: Erkka Laine, Marjaana Veermans, Aleksi Lahti, Koen Veermans. (2017). Generation of student interest in an inquiry-based mobile learning environment. Frontline Learning Research Vol.5 No. 4 (2017) 42 - 60. https://doi.org/10.14786/flr.v5i4.306
title: Four-phase model of interest development
description: The article adopts the four-phase model of interest development (Hidi & Renninger, 2006; Renninger & Hidi, 2011), in which interest is "a multidimensional construct consisting of affect, knowledge, and value components". The model's four developmental phases — triggered situational interest, maintained situational interest, emerging individual interest, and well-developed individual interest — differ in how much weight the affect, knowledge, and value components receive. The article uses this framework to interpret how the learning environment's features might trigger situational interest and support its development toward individual interest.
requirements: Design should trigger interest in novice students and offer challenge and autonomy for more advanced ones, per the article's discussion of domain interest
constraints: The article notes single-item instruments measuring interest in the subject as a whole were arguably too broad, and future studies should consider how to reliably measure interest in its different developmental phases
target_learning_goals: Domain-specific interest development in STEM subjects
examples: The study measured domain-specific individual interest three times during the school year and interpreted interview data on interest generation against this model

article_title: The Effectiveness of Intercultural Sensitivity Development Activities Integrated with Scientific Research Methods Course
citation: Tuncel, İ. (2019). The effectiveness of intercultural sensitivity development activities integrated with scientific research methods course. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 301-312. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.301
title: Fogarty's nested integration model for embedding a second learning target within a single discipline
description: The nested model is one of Fogarty's models for integrating curriculum within a single discipline, in which a second set of objectives is nested inside an existing course. The article states that "The nested integration model monitors the training program with three -dimensional glasses and targets multiple dimensions of a course" and that attention is drawn to more than one area at the same time, providing enriched and improved learning paths. The study applied it by nesting intercultural sensitivity development activities inside a scientific research methods course.
requirements: A host discipline whose outcomes can accommodate activities serving the nested objective, as the scientific research methods course outcomes accommodated intercultural activities
constraints: The study applied the model within a single discipline (scientific research methods) in one English teacher education department, and the article limits its conclusions to activities integrable with that course's outcomes
target_learners: second-year pre-service English teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: intercultural sensitivity development
scientific research methods outcomes
examples: In the interview-method unit, students designed individual and focus group interviews with individuals from different cultures, contacted over social media and conducted on the internet

article_title: Research on the Boost of Development on Young Children's Fine Motor by Folk Games
citation: Xia Wei. (2016). Research on the Boost of Development on Young Children's Fine Motor by Folk Games. International Education Studies, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n9p111
title: Ten-week folk games teaching activity schedule for fine motor development in kindergarten A
description: The article's intervention artifact is a schedule of traditional folk game activities (Table 1) run three times weekly from April to June 2016, with topics such as Paper Folding Change, Cut Window, Cat's Cradle, Embroidery: Fan's Making and Making Zong Zi. The article states "There were three times of teaching intervention weekly and each intervention took 40 to 50 minutes", with actual interventions per child ranging from 26 to 30 due to attendance. Activities were revised by the kindergarten principal, teachers and university teachers, and practiced in two micro-teachings before classroom use.
requirements: Activities were applied only after revision by the kindergarten principal, kindergarten teachers and professional university teachers, and practiced by the team after two micro-teachings
constraints: Due to varying attendance, children received different actual interventions ranging from 26 to 30 times
target_learners: children aged 4 to 5 in middle classes of a public urban kindergarten
target_learning_goals: fine motor skills of pinching, touching, drawing, cutting, folding and stringing
examples: Week 7 included Pinching Clay Figurine, Cat's Cradle and Making Colorful Candy Wraps; Week 10 included Making Dragon Boat, Making Zong Zi and Pretty Embroidered Shoes

article_title: Research on the Boost of Development on Young Children's Fine Motor by Folk Games
citation: Xia Wei. (2016). Research on the Boost of Development on Young Children's Fine Motor by Folk Games. International Education Studies, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n9p111
title: Integrating multiple fine motor goals into a single folk game activity
description: Rather than drilling isolated skills, the research team embedded several fine motor goals into one culturally meaningful handwork activity. The article states the team began "to adjust overall curriculum goals and contents by integrating goals of different fine motor skills development into one teaching activity of folk games". For example, the Blue and White Porcelain Plate activity combined drawing, weaving, cutting and sticking, so children practiced drawing, cutting and pasting at a comprehensive level while experiencing traditional craft.
requirements: Activities must be designed so that one folk game carries several fine motor goals at once, integrating curriculum goals and contents
constraints: The article notes that targeting only coloring in the porcelain plate activity would have limited children to drawing practice alone, so integration required deliberate multi-goal design
target_learners: children aged 4 to 5 in kindergarten middle classes
target_learning_goals: combined drawing, cutting, folding, weaving and sticking skills within cultural craft activities
examples: In the Blue and White Porcelain Plate activity, children drew blue and white patterns on a plate, then cut and pasted corners to make a little fish, practicing drawing, cutting and pasting in one creation

article_title: Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner's Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary
citation: Chainikova, G.R., Zatonskiy, A.V., Mitiukov, N.W., Busygina, H.L. (2018). Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner’s Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.51
title: Four-stage model of lexical skill and speech ability development underlying the exercise complex
description: The exercise complex used with the thesaurus and dictionary rests on four interrelated stages of lexical skills and speech abilities development: 1) semantization and reproduction of lexical means; 2) stereotyping and varying of lexical means; 3) systematic application of FL lexical skills, their dynamic integration with other speech skills during oral and written communication; 4) synthesis and systematization of FL lexical skills at the stage of development of creative speech abilities. During the first two stages the Thesaurus and Dictionary serves as an external informative basis; at later stages it is used as a source of additional information. The stated purpose is developing the students' foreign language mental lexicon.
requirements: A special complex of exercises for developing foreign language lexical skills and speech abilities (informative reading, monological speaking) aligned to the four stages
target_learners: university students learning English for professional purposes
target_learning_goals: foreign language lexical skills
informative reading
monological speaking
examples: The experimental learning applied the complex across pre-test, mid-tests and post-test stages with 116 second-year students
key_sources: Chainikova, G.R., Zatonskiy, A.V., Mitiukov, N.W., Busygina, H.L. (2018). Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner’s Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.51

article_title: Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner's Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary
citation: Chainikova, G.R., Zatonskiy, A.V., Mitiukov, N.W., Busygina, H.L. (2018). Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner’s Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.51
title: Four-component learner's terminological thesaurus and dictionary structure
description: The article's reusable design pattern for a learner's terminological thesaurus and dictionary comprises four main components: 1) classification part, 2) ideographic part (thesaurus), 3) glossary, 4) bilingual dictionary. The classification part demonstrates the inner logic of the subject area; the glossary defines key terms; the thesaurus entry demonstrates paradigmatic and syntagmatic relations of the entry term; and the alphabetical bilingual dictionary contains all words from the ideographic part. The authors state its application makes it possible to develop subject-area knowledge, terminological competence, and demonstrate potential relations of key terms.
requirements: Logical and conceptual analysis of the subject area to sort out relations of key terms and determine their most important paradigmatic and syntagmatic relations
target_learners: students in occupational foreign language courses
target_learning_goals: development of foreign language professional mental lexicon
terminological competence
examples: The software-terms implementation grouped vocabulary around entry terms using relations such as action–agent, action–object, action–tool, and object–property/quality/quantitative characteristic, selected with a frequency criterion
key_sources: Chainikova, G.R., Zatonskiy, A.V., Mitiukov, N.W., Busygina, H.L. (2018). Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner’s Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.51

article_title: Didactic Model: Teaching the English Temporal System to Arabic Freshman Learners of English
citation: Hmidani, T. (2017). Didactic model: Teaching the English temporal system to Arabic freshman learners of English. Profile: Issues in Teachers' Professional Development, 19(Suppl. 1), 81-97. https://doi.org/10.15446/profile.v19n_sup1.68617
title: Four-phase eclectic didactic model for teaching the English temporal system
description: The article presents a didactic model that is "a selection of aspects from different methods combined" so that activities reinforce each other, aiming for higher linguistic competence. It consists of four phases adapted from Piaget's learning process and the researcher's own continuation: Reception and Assimilation (comprehension-based exercises), Accommodation (consciousness-raising and translation exercises), Production (reconstructive exercises and free writing), and Self-Assessment (an ongoing journal). The model transforms the grammar lesson into a language lesson integrating all skills.
requirements: Intensive instruction (20-30+ hours/week), large classes around 30 students, low-intermediate learner level, and teachers competent in managing time effectively
constraints: The teacher need not be highly proficient in speaking the L2 because comprehension questions can be supported by Arabic; the model was designed for and tested with Arabic-speaking learners
target_learners: Arabic-speaking freshman university students at low-intermediate English level
target_learning_goals: English tense and aspect system (temporal system)
language awareness
reading and writing skills
vocabulary building
examples: An appendix applies the model to teaching the past perfect using a reading passage about a dinner catastrophe, with translation exercises into Modern Standard Arabic (kaana + qad + perfective verb)

article_title: On the Communicative Functions of Context in Foreign Language Education
citation: Polok, K. (2021). On the Communicative Functions of Context in Foreign Language Education. International Journal of Instruction, 14(2), 1051-1072. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.14260a
title: Four-quadrant lesson design crossing context embeddedness with cognitive demand
description: The article proposes that juxtaposing context-embedded vs context-reduced communication with cognitively demanding vs undemanding talk yields 'four independent quadrants ready to contain any of the skill-practicing tasks'. Quadrant (a) is context-embedded, cognitively undemanding talk (e.g. informing learners of the lesson topic); (b) context-embedded, demanding talk (e.g. negotiating the term syllabus); (c) context-reduced, undemanding talk (e.g. oral task explanation); (d) context-reduced, demanding talk (e.g. discussion of a salient topic). Each quadrant trains a different context-searching technique.
requirements: Lesson design must contain both cognitively demanding and less demanding forms of communication, per Cummins (2008)
target_learners: Foreign language learners in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Context recognition and search skills
BICS and CALP development
examples: Informing learners which page to open (quadrant a); teacher-learner talk on term syllabus content (quadrant b)
key_sources: Polok, K. (2021). On the Communicative Functions of Context in Foreign Language Education. International Journal of Instruction, 14(2), 1051-1072. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.14260a

article_title: Effect of Feedback and Remediation on Students' Achievement in Junior Secondary School Mathematics
citation: Ajogbeje Oke James & Alonge Micheal Folorunso. (2012). Effect of Feedback and Remediation on Students’ Achievement in Junior Secondary School Mathematics. International Education Studies, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n5p153
title: Combine regular formative testing with prompt feedback and structured remediation to improve mathematics learning
description: The study recommends that mathematics teachers provide learners with regular diagnostic tests and adequate feedback with necessary remediation, rather than continuous testing without feedback or remediation, which the authors identify as a contributory factor to mass failure in external examinations.
requirements: Teachers must administer formative tests regularly and provide feedback promptly before the next unit begins
constraints: Effective feedback and remediation require extra effort and time, and large class populations may strain teacher capacity
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
examples: The remediation strategy involved dividing test items into sections, having high-scoring students lead class discussions, and allowing students to ask questions on difficult areas
