article_title: Children Literature Based Program for Developing EFL Primary Pupils' Life Skills and Language Learning Strategies
citation: Safaa M. Abdelhalim. (2015). Children Literature Based Program for Developing EFL Primary Pupils’ Life Skills and Language Learning Strategies. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p178
title: Teach life skills through children's literature using a four-phase lesson structure: pre-reading, during-reading, post-reading, and evaluation
description: The article presents "a detailed teaching strategy for teaching life skills through children literature" built on short stories and songs. Each lesson follows four phases: pre-reading activities that define and promote the targeted life skill, during-reading activities for skill acquisition and performance, post-reading activities fostering skill maintenance and generalization, and a formative evaluation phase involving parents. The program organized 16 short stories and 16 songs into four thematic units covering cognitive, personal, social, and linguistic life skills.
requirements: A criterion for selecting stories and songs suited to students' needs, attitudes, and the targeted life skills
A teacher's guide and students' booklet organized by life skill themes
constraints: Implemented in English language clubs held two hours weekly over eight weeks; teachers reported procedural difficulties with space and large class numbers
target_learning_goals: cognitive, personal, social, and linguistic life skills
language learning strategies
examples: Each lesson contains a short story and a song focusing on a life skills theme followed by interactive activities
Home activities with parental support included retelling stories, singing songs, and writing comments in learning logs
key_sources: Safaa M. Abdelhalim. (2015). Children Literature Based Program for Developing EFL Primary Pupils’ Life Skills and Language Learning Strategies. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p178

article_title: Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology
citation: Morris Siu-Yung Jong, Tom Chan, Vincent Tam and Ming-Tak Hue. (2017). Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology. International Conference Educational Technologies 2017.
title: Four-scaffold inquiry cycle delivered as context-aware game scaffolds
description: The app structures each inquiry spot around four scaffolds following Stripling's social inquiry model. The "Connection scaffold, which is in the form of voice navigation, will provide students with background information about the societal issue"; Investigation guides data collection; Construction supports "generalising the information on hand via mind-mapping and making an interim conclusion about the issue via audio-recording"; and Reflection uses video-blogging to set goals for the next spot.
requirements: Each inquiry spot must present all four scaffolds in sequence to complete the inquiry cycle
target_learning_goals: Inquiry into societal issues from multiple perspectives
key_sources: Morris Siu-Yung Jong, Tom Chan, Vincent Tam and Ming-Tak Hue. (2017). Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology. International Conference Educational Technologies 2017. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED579295

article_title: Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction versus Coursebook Instruction
citation: Le-Thi, D., Rodgers, M. P. H., & Pellicer-Sánchez, A. (2017). Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction Versus Coursebook Instruction. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 111–139. http://dx.doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1276
title: Formulaic sequences as prefabricated multiword units stored and retrieved whole from memory, with value for comprehension, fluency, and proficiency.
description: The article adopts Wray's (2002) definition of a formulaic sequence as "a sequence, continuous or discontinuous, of words or other meaning elements, which is, or appears to be, prefabricated: that is, stored and retrieved whole from memory at the time of use, rather than being subject to generation or analysis by the language grammar." The article describes how knowledge of formulaic sequences improves comprehension, contributes to smoothness in communication, and improves performance on proficiency tests. Formulaic sequences are considered an ideal unit for teaching, yet learners typically have limited knowledge of them.
requirements: Learners need sufficient encounters with formulaic sequences for them to become accessible as single units in the mental lexicon
constraints: Many learners have a limited command of formulaic sequences, particularly in EFL contexts, with studies showing knowledge of only 33% to 56.6% of tested collocations
target_learners: EFL learners, particularly those at low proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: Receptive knowledge of form and meaning of formulaic sequences
Improved comprehension and fluency through formulaic language
examples: The article notes formulaic sequences vary in fixedness: some are fixed groups of words (e.g., 'on the other hand') while others have slots filled by words with particular meaning senses (e.g., 'take __ for granted')
key_sources: Le-Thi, D., Rodgers, M. P. H., & Pellicer-Sánchez, A. (2017). Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction Versus Coursebook Instruction. article_title: Red Flags, Red Herrings, and Common Ground: An Expert Study in Response to State Reading Policy
citation: Collet, Vicki S.; Penaflorida, Jennifer; French, Seth; Allred, Jonathan; Greiner, Angelia; and Chen, Jingshu (2021) "Red Flags, Red Herrings, and Common Ground: An Expert Study in Response to State Reading Policy," Educational Considerations: Vol. 47: No. 1. https://doi.org/10.4148/0146-9282.2241
title: Four pattern codes organizing expert responses: reading instruction, reading purposes, sociocultural, and wording
description: This article contributes a qualitative coding framework derived from expert responses to statements about early reading instruction. Through open coding of survey comments and interview excerpts, the researchers identified nine initial codes which they narrowed into four pattern codes: "reading instruction, reading purposes, sociocultural, and wording." These codes organize the domains of expert concern, spanning instructional content such as phonics and needs-based teaching, the purposes reading serves including reading to learn and interdisciplinary reading, sociocultural influences such as home, culture, community, and discussion, and critiques of how policy statements are worded. The framework structures the article's findings about where the state literacy initiative aligned with expert knowledge and where it fell short.
requirements: A panel of recognized experts providing open-ended survey comments and follow-up interview responses about early literacy instruction statements
constraints: The codes were derived from a single expert panel of eight scholars responding to a specific state literacy initiative, so transferability to other policy contexts is not established by this study
target_learners: policymakers and educators implementing state reading initiatives
target_learning_goals: aligning early literacy policy and instruction with expert consensus on early reading instruction
examples: The researchers coded 124 expert comments and interview excerpts, with the Reading Instruction code containing 66 excerpts, the largest group, and 19 comments coded as sociocultural emphasis
key_sources: Collet, Vicki S.; Penaflorida, Jennifer; French, Seth; Allred, Jonathan; Greiner, Angelia; and Chen, Jingshu (2021) "Red Flags, Red Herrings, and Common Ground: An Expert Study in Response to State Reading Policy," Educational Considerations: Vol. 47: No. 1. https://doi.org/10.4148/0146-9282.2241

article_title: Effects of Focused Feedback on the Acquisition of Two English Articles
citation: Kao, C.-W. (2013). Effects of Focused Feedback on the Acquisition of Two English Articles. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 17(1). https://tesl-ej.org/
title: Focus corrective feedback on specific error types with communicative value embedded in writing tasks
description: The article recommends targeting corrections at specific language features that carry communicative value and occur naturally in writing tasks. It states that "when specific language features to be focused for corrections have communicative values, and are naturally embedded in writing tasks, correction improves not only students' written accuracy but also their communication." Picture description tasks in the reviewed studies naturally required definite and indefinite article use.
requirements: Feedback must target one or a few specific error types rather than all errors
constraints: Evidence limited to English article errors in picture description tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate use of English articles in writing
examples: Focused feedback studies in the meta-analysis corrected English article errors in picture descriptions where repeated description of objects required definite and indefinite articles
key_sources: Kao, C.-W. (2013). Effects of Focused Feedback on the Acquisition of Two English Articles. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1007571

article_title: Effects of Focused Feedback on the Acquisition of Two English Articles
citation: Kao, C.-W. (2013). Effects of Focused Feedback on the Acquisition of Two English Articles. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 17(1). https://tesl-ej.org/
title: Focused vs. unfocused written corrective feedback distinction
description: A taxonomy distinguishing written corrective feedback that targets "one or a few specific error types" (focused) from feedback that "does not specify specific error types but corrects grammar errors of all sorts" (unfocused). The meta-analysis applies this distinction to evaluate correction effects separately for direct correction and metalinguistic explanation types on English article errors.
requirements: Identification of specific error types to target for correction
constraints: Meta-analysis limited to focused feedback studies on English article errors
target_learning_goals: written grammatical accuracy
key_sources: Kao, C.-W. (2013). Effects of Focused Feedback on the Acquisition of Two English Articles. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1007571

article_title: Creative Thinking Ability to Increase Student Mathematical of Junior High School by Applying Models Numbered Heads Together
citation: Lince, R. (2016). Creative Thinking Ability to Increase Student Mathematical of Junior High School by Applying Models Numbered Heads Together. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(6), 206-212. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1098210
title: Four-aspect framework of mathematical creative thinking ability: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration
description: The article defines mathematical creative thinking ability (KBKM) through four aspects drawn from Munandar (2002) and Torrance: fluency (sparking ideas and providing many answers or examples), flexibility (generating varied answers and using multiple solution strategies), originality (producing new, unique, or unusual expressions and strategies), and elaboration (explaining in detail, enriching and developing an idea or product). The study measured these four aspects using a 10-item descriptive test, with items mapped to specific aspects. The author argues that if NHT is applied consistently, all four components can be improved optimally because each NHT stage elicits a different aspect.
requirements: Assessment instruments must include items targeting each of the four aspects separately
constraints: The study found students had not mastered all four aspects even after NHT instruction
target_learning_goals: mathematical creative thinking ability
examples: Question 1a, 8b and 10a measured fluency; Questions 2a, 3a, 3b, 7a, 7c and 9a measured flexibility; Question 6a measured originality; Questions 4b and 5a measured elaboration
key_sources: Lince, R. (2016). Creative Thinking Ability to Increase Student Mathematical of Junior High School by Applying Models Numbered Heads Together. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(6), 206-212. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1092494

article_title: The Effects of L1 and L2 Group Discussions on L2 Reading Comprehension
citation: Turnbull, B., & Sweetnam Evans, M. (2017). The effects of L1 and L2 group discussions on L2 reading comprehension. Reading in a Foreign Language, 29(1), 133–154. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Four-genre English text set for eliciting varied reading stances
description: The study used four English texts: an 88-word poem, a 606-word parody of Little Red Riding Hood, a 53-word joke with word-play, and a 910-word expository article on eating insects. The texts were selected for their range of genres and difficulty and for the likelihood they would elicit story-driven, information-driven, or point-driven reading stances from bilingual readers.
requirements: Texts spanning narrative and expository genres with discussion opportunities
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension across genres

article_title: Generative AI-Assisted Progressive-Disclosure Case-Based Learning for Clinical Reasoning in Occupational Medicine: Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Waseem J, Ritter Nicola L, McMordie J, Su P, Hu M, Chen C, Xu S. (2026). Generative AI–Assisted Progressive-Disclosure Case-Based Learning for Clinical Reasoning in Occupational Medicine: Quasi-Experimental Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/103584
title: 4-act progressive-disclosure case structure aligned with occupational poisoning workflow
description: A scripted 4-act CBL model that progressively releases key information with teacher-verified distractor cues. Act 1 focuses on problem framing and initial hypothesis generation; Act 2 on occupational history elicitation and laboratory cues; Act 3 on field investigation and exposure attribution; Act 4 on management and prevention decision-making.
requirements: Each act provides only the minimum information required for the current task, retaining other cues as to be elicited or verified
constraints: The intervention's scope is bounded by exploratory reasoning and should not be regarded as a general clinical-reasoning enhancer
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning, exposure assessment, and epidemiologic thinking in occupational medicine
examples: Applied to an occupational lead poisoning module at Chongqing Medical University using DeepSeek-V3 as the underlying generative model.

article_title: Acting It Out: A Classroom Activity to Improve Knowledge and Visualisation of Space Management Principles in Paediatric Dental Education.
citation: Speer Julie E., Rosel Mitzi M., Creech Joseph C. Jr., Williams Brittany L. (2026). Acting It Out: A Classroom Activity to Improve Knowledge and Visualisation of Space Management Principles in Paediatric Dental Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.70137
title: Foam-board dental models and MDF space maintenance appliances for role-playing space management scenarios
description: A set of physical learning materials for an active learning demonstration in paediatric dentistry. Dental models representing "the five primary teeth in each quadrant and the first permanent molars" were cut from ¼ inch white foam board using a CNC router based on SVG files. Space maintenance appliances (a unilateral band and loop and a distal shoe) were cut from ¼ inch MDF board. Students held tooth models, arranged themselves into a dental arch, and simulated tooth movement with and without appliances.
requirements: SVG files for guided cutting, a computer numerical control router, ¼ inch white foam board, and ¼ inch MDF board
target_learning_goals: space management and space maintenance in the developing occlusion
clinical decision making about space maintenance appliances
examples: Students arranged themselves to simulate a dental arch, discussed how teeth would move in given scenarios, and used appliance models to simulate how space could be maintained

article_title: Changes in Nursing Students' Clinical Handover Performance Following ISBAR-Structured Handover Simulation Teaching: A Mixed-Methods Study.
citation: Sun Jui-Chiung, Chang Min-Yu, Tsai Yi-Chun. (2026). Changes in Nursing Students' Clinical Handover Performance Following ISBAR-Structured Handover Simulation Teaching: A Mixed-Methods Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70955
title: Four-phase progressive ISBAR handover teaching design: didactic instruction, role-play, scenario simulation and OSCE
description: The article describes a four-phase intervention design for teaching ISBAR-structured handover in an obstetric simulation and practicum course. The phases progress from ISBAR-structured handover didactic instruction and expert modelling, through role-play with antenatal assessment and handover practice, to scenario simulation with standardized patients and video-assisted debriefing, and culminating in OSCE assessment. Within each scenario, students rotated through sender and receiver roles so that every student actively performed the ISBAR handover. The authors offer this sequence as a potentially useful educational strategy rather than a validated model.
requirements: Eight parallel practice groups each facilitated by one designated faculty facilitator, all registered nurses with a master's degree or above who completed an 8-h standardization workshop
constraints: The authors state the four-stage sequence is offered as a potentially useful educational strategy rather than a validated model, and its effectiveness warrants further evaluation across different settings and populations before broader adoption
target_learning_goals: structured clinical handover communication
clinical reasoning in obstetric contexts
examples: The 57 students were divided into eight practice groups of six to eight members each, with all eight groups practicing simultaneously at parallel simulation stations, each scenario comprising a 15-20-min pre-briefing, an 8-10-min scenario enactment, and a 20-30-min debriefing
key_sources: Sun Jui-Chiung, Chang Min-Yu, Tsai Yi-Chun. (2026). Changes in Nursing Students' Clinical Handover Performance Following ISBAR-Structured Handover Simulation Teaching: A Mixed-Methods Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70955

article_title: Simulation learning in the emergency department: Impact on VideoLaryngoscope Intubation Skills.
citation: Bahri Badra, Ghazali Hanene, Sedghiani Ines, Zoubli Aymen, Kilani Mohamed, Karraz Taycir, Belgacem Ines, Touj Hajer, El Hechmi Youssef Zied, Borsali-Falfoul Nebiha. (2025). Simulation learning in the emergency department: Impact on VideoLaryngoscope Intubation Skills. La Tunisie Médicale. https://doi.org/10.62438/tunismed.v103i8.5167
title: Four-step procedural simulation sequence for teaching videolaryngoscope intubation
description: The article structures procedural simulation learning as a graded four-step sequence: "1. The instructor performed the intubation by VL without commenting the different steps 2. The instructor performed the intubation by VL with a describing of the different steps 3. The learners described the different steps of the procedure, and the instructor performed the intubation 4. The learners performed the intubation individually, describing the different steps." Learners then practise until ready for a final evaluation with immediate debriefing, preceded by a 20-minute theoretical presentation and tutorial video.
requirements: Learners must be novices in direct laryngoscopy and never have intubated using a VL
A standardized simulator, evaluation grid, pre-test and post-test questionnaire, and an instructor are needed
constraints: Training mannequins do not accurately reproduce airway anatomy, muscle tone, or secretions, so results do not directly represent clinical practice
target_learners: medical residents novices in direct laryngoscopy
target_learning_goals: orotracheal intubation by videolaryngoscope
theoretical knowledge of airway anatomy and intubation procedure
examples: Residents in Tunis teaching hospitals completed the four-step session and were evaluated before and after on a standardized simulator
key_sources: Bahri Badra, Ghazali Hanene, Sedghiani Ines, Zoubli Aymen, Kilani Mohamed, Karraz Taycir, Belgacem Ines, Touj Hajer, El Hechmi Youssef Zied, Borsali-Falfoul Nebiha. (2025). Simulation learning in the emergency department: Impact on VideoLaryngoscope Intubation Skills. La Tunisie Médicale. https://doi.org/10.62438/tunismed.v103i8.5167

article_title: AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario-Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development.
citation: Kugler Maike, Aichroth Laura S. (2026). AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario‐Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development. New Directions for Student Leadership. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70067
title: Four‐scenario taxonomy of human–AI workplace constellations
description: The article develops four future workplace constellations using action‐based organizational learning scenario technique: "(1) AI as collaborative tool, (2) AI as delegated agent, (3) AI as team member, and (4) AI as autonomous partner." Each scenario is grounded in a distinct literature stream (Human‐AI Collaboration, AI Agents, Human‐AI Teaming, Human‐Autonomy Teaming) and analyzed for its implications for leading and following. The taxonomy organizes the article's gap analysis and educational recommendations.
requirements: Scenarios are derived from current literature via action‐based organizational learning scenario technique, requiring envisioning of multiple possible futures
constraints: The future AI scenarios only represent a limited number of options derived from today's knowledge
target_learners: higher education students in leadership and followership education
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI's evolving roles reshape leading and following
key_sources: Kugler Maike, Aichroth Laura S. (2026). AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario‐Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development. New Directions for Student Leadership. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70067

article_title: AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario-Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development.
citation: Kugler Maike, Aichroth Laura S. (2026). AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario‐Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development. New Directions for Student Leadership. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70067
title: Four‐level AI literacy scale (Informed, Empowered, Engaged, Active participant)
description: The article adopts MacCallum et al.'s (2023) four skill levels capturing the spread of digital and AI‐related competencies among students and educators in higher education: level 1 "Informed" (users with introductory awareness and essential, entry‐level understanding), level 2 "Empowered" (able to explore ideas and engage critically by reflecting on provided information), level 3 "Engaged" (able to co‐design and steer AI‐supported learning), and level 4 "Active participant" (able to design, adapt, and apply AI in ways that drive transformative change).
requirements: The levels are based on the analysis of differences in the maturity of AI competencies (MacCallum et al. 2023)
target_learners: students and educators in higher education
target_learning_goals: assessing and developing AI literacy levels
key_sources: Kugler Maike, Aichroth Laura S. (2026). AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario‐Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development. New Directions for Student Leadership. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70067

article_title: The digital transformation of clinical teaching: a review of AI and data-driven quality assurance systems in medical education.
citation: Zhao Kexin, Wang Ningning, Xie Zhicai. (2026). The digital transformation of clinical teaching: a review of AI and data-driven quality assurance systems in medical education. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1915158
title: Four-domain framework organizing AI applications in medical education: teaching, assessment, simulation, and data-based quality improvement
description: The review organizes synthesized evidence into four thematic domains: "AI in Clinical Education, Assessment, Simulation and Data-Based Quality Improvement". This taxonomy structures the narrative synthesis, mapping AI tools (ITS, adaptive platforms, NLP, computer vision, learning analytics) to educational functions and outcomes. It provides the organizing axis for the review's tables of applications, principles, competencies, and challenges.
requirements: Studies must specifically discuss AI implementation in clinical education, clinical competency assessment, or simulation to map onto the framework
constraints: Synthesis is narrative and descriptive rather than a quantitative meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: clinical competency
clinical reasoning
communication skills

article_title: Impact of SNAPPS-based teaching on diagnostic accuracy and academic achievement in pathology residents.
citation: Khanke Shraddha; Buch Pankti; Buch Archana; Gore Charusheela. (2026). Impact of SNAPPS-based teaching on diagnostic accuracy and academic achievement in pathology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09668-9
title: Four-phase SNAPPS implementation: preceptor sensitisation, traditional baseline, resident sensitisation, SNAPPS-guided presentation
description: The article structures its intervention as "four structured phases": sensitising preceptors with calibration exercises, baseline case writing by the traditional method with an MCQ pretest, sensitising residents to the six SNAPPS components, and SNAPPS-guided case presentation with checklist scoring, a post-test MCQ and a feedback survey. This phased design embeds the model in existing departmental activities rather than separate sessions.
requirements: Two trained preceptors supervising sessions
Standardized SNAPPS checklist with 5-point scoring per component
constraints: Single-centre, convenience-sampled cohort of 35 residents; same cases used in both phases, which the authors note as a performance-bias risk
target_learners: postgraduate pathology residents at three training levels
target_learning_goals: structured case presentation
diagnostic reasoning
clinicopathological correlation
examples: Each resident was assigned two cases appropriate to their level, e.g. JR-1: breast lump, appendix
key_sources: Khanke Shraddha; Buch Pankti; Buch Archana; Gore Charusheela. (2026). Impact of SNAPPS-based teaching on diagnostic accuracy and academic achievement in pathology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09668-9

article_title: Evidence to support integrating feedback best practice for computer-based assessment in pharmacology education.
citation: Hepburn CY. (2026). Evidence to support integrating feedback best practice for computer‐based assessment in pharmacology education. Br J Clin Pharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1002/bcp.70302
title: Four key components of effective feedback for computer-based assessment in pharmacology education
description: The review organizes effective computer-based assessment feedback around four elements, illustrated in Figure 1: "clear goals and standards, appreciating the needs of the intended audience, appropriate timing and supporting dialogue". Each component is elaborated in its own section: constructive alignment with outcomes tagging, audience-sensitive positively ideating feedback, context-informed timing, and curriculum-integrated dialogic feedback sessions. The framework is offered as an evidence-informed alternative to a universal feedback model, which the review says does not exist.
requirements: constructive alignment between taught outcomes and assessed standards
knowledge of student characteristics and feedback orientation
local-context-informed timing decisions
curriculum-level integration of dialogic feedback opportunities
constraints: no universal model of feedback design with consistently positive outcomes exists
target_learners: medical, biomedical sciences and pharmacy students
target_learning_goals: effective life-long learning
competent and safe prescribing practice
metacognitive skills development
examples: Figure 1 depicts the four components: clear goals and standards, dialogue opportunities with an academic, context-sensitive timing, and audience-appropriate feedback content
key_sources: Hepburn CY. (2026). Evidence to support integrating feedback best practice for computer‐based assessment in pharmacology education. Br J Clin Pharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1002/bcp.70302

article_title: Simulation-based and clinical training in undergraduate nuclear medicine education: evaluation of competency outcomes using a structured OSCE framework.
citation: Alyami Wadha, Alosaimi Manal H., Baeshen Arwa, Alghanimy Alaa, Salam Esra, Alhujaili Sultan, Alqahtani Mansour M., Saad Ibrahim E. (2026). Simulation-based and clinical training in undergraduate nuclear medicine education: evaluation of competency outcomes using a structured OSCE framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09443-w
title: Four-station OSCE framework for assessing nuclear medicine competency in a controlled hot lab environment
description: A structured four-station objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) assessing theoretical knowledge (station 1: hot lab instrument recognition), radiopharmaceutical dose preparation and generator handling (station 2), dose calibrator operation (station 3), and radiation safety management via simulated radioactive spill (station 4). Scoring ranges varied by station complexity: "station 1 (0–5 points), station 2 (0–8 points), station 3 (0–8 points), and station 4 (0–12 points)." Standardized scoring rubrics were applied across all stations with examiner orientation to enhance consistency.
requirements: Standardized scoring rubrics applied across all OSCE stations
Examiner orientation regarding scoring criteria to enhance consistency
A controlled clinical hot lab environment
constraints: Formal inter-rater reliability was not calculated
Examiners were not blinded to group allocation due to logistical constraints
target_learning_goals: Equipment recognition
Radiopharmaceutical preparation
Measurement accuracy
Radiation safety response behaviors
examples: Station 2 required students to elute a generator, prepare the required dose, and simulate administration into a phantom model, as hospital protocols in Saudi Arabia prohibit non-intern students from performing injections on real patients
key_sources: Alyami Wadha, Alosaimi Manal H., Baeshen Arwa, Alghanimy Alaa, Salam Esra, Alhujaili Sultan, Alqahtani Mansour M., Saad Ibrahim E. (2026). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09443-w

article_title: Student self-assessment: feasibility, advantages and limitations; example of a workshop for trainee surgeons using a suture score.
citation: Riquin Élise, Le Nerzé Thomas, Goulin Jeanne, Rony Louis, Boucher Sophie, Martin Ludovic, Schmitt Françoise. (2026). Student self-assessment: feasibility, advantages and limitations; example of a workshop for trainee surgeons using a suture score. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08223-2
title: Introduce formative self-assessment grids during medical studies to calibrate perceived technical skill
description: The article recommends that "formative self-reflection based on the use of SA grids should be introduced during medical studies so as to adjust the level of technical skill perceived by trainees and to make simulation-based training more effective". Self-assessment grids, particularly checklist-based tools, help medical trainees develop a more accurate perception of their technical skills and are especially suited for formative evaluation.
requirements: Self-assessment must follow on from mentoring to be valid and useful for learners
constraints: Self-assessment must be interpreted in light of the learner's previous experience and chosen specialty
target_learning_goals: accurate self-perception of technical skills
development of critical thinking
self-confidence
examples: A two-day seminar for trainee surgeons included a suture workshop where students filled out a self-assessment grid at the same time as expert evaluation

article_title: Exploration of an artificial intelligence-supported training mechanism for teaching competence development in graduate students of prosthodontics.
citation: Lei J, Weng X, Tong X, Zhang C, Chen R. (2026). Exploration of an artificial intelligence-supported training mechanism for teaching competence development in graduate students of prosthodontics. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09706-6
title: Four-stage AI-supported training framework for teaching competence development
description: The article proposes a structured framework comprising baseline assessment, AI platform training, AI-assisted cyclical teaching practice, and summative evaluation. DeepSeek served as the core AI tool for lesson preparation, lecture script drafting, concept map generation, and interactive teaching design. The framework was implemented over two semesters with five rounds of teaching practice, each lasting two weeks and organized around a unified teaching theme.
requirements: Faculty experienced in AI-assisted education to conduct training
A standardized scoring rubric with calibrated faculty evaluators
Different teaching topics assigned in each round to minimize practice effects
constraints: The study was designed to evaluate a pedagogical training framework centered on AI tools rather than to isolate the independent effect of a single AI system
target_learning_goals: Teaching competence development including course design, classroom organization, and reflective teaching practices
examples: Students used DeepSeek for rapid literature review, lesson plan generation, clinical case design, and language polishing; Doubao was used to enhance slide design and multimedia content production

article_title: Effect of humanistic care-integrated Mini-CEX teachingon nursing students' clinical competence: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Ding Yunxia, Tan Meichun, Xi Wenjuan, Zhang Hongyan, Ning Zhen, Hu Wei. (2026). Effect of humanistic care-integrated Mini-CEX teaching on nursing students' clinical competence: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09238-z
title: Integrate formative assessment tools as feedback engines within experiential learning cycles rather than using them solely for outcome evaluation
description: The article argues that assessment tools like Mini-CEX should serve dual roles: "Mini-CEX serves not only as an outcome evaluation tool but also as a structured feedback engine driving the entire experiential learning cycle". Embedding assessment indicators at each phase of the learning cycle ensures "feedback is timely, specific, and aligned with the learning phase", reinforcing practical experience accumulation and accelerating clinical competence development. This principle transforms what is tested into what is taught.
requirements: Assessment criteria must be defined as instructional dimensions across all phases of the learning cycle; feedback sessions must follow each assessment
constraints: In this study the approach improved soft skills but not procedural technical skills, suggesting differential effects across competency domains
target_learning_goals: clinical competence
reflective practice
self-directed learning
examples: Mini-CEX indicators were embedded in each phase of Kolb's cycle, with Sharing Insights feedback informing the next cycle of Concrete Experience
key_sources: Ding Yunxia, Tan Meichun, Xi Wenjuan, Zhang Hongyan, Ning Zhen, Hu Wei. (2026). Effect of humanistic care-integrated Mini-CEX teaching on nursing students' clinical competence: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09238-z

article_title: Structured phantom-assisted simulation for early abdominal ultrasound skill training in ultrasound medicine residents: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Wei Tianhong, Ke Mujing, Zhang Bo, He Zhiyou, Xie Xiuyun. (2026). Structured phantom-assisted simulation for early abdominal ultrasound skill training in ultrasound medicine residents: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09395-1
title: A four-step structured simulation session protocol: demonstration, deliberate practice, lesion identification, and immediate feedback
description: Each 90-minute training session followed "a standardized four-step protocol": faculty demonstration of standardized scanning procedures and acoustic window optimization, hands-on deliberate practice focused on mastering standard views, identification and localization of embedded simulated lesions (cystic lesions, solid masses, and stones), and immediate faculty feedback with real-time corrective guidance on probe manipulation and image optimization.
requirements: Faculty instructors followed a detailed training checklist to standardize intervention delivery
target_learners: Postgraduate year 2 residents in ultrasound medicine
target_learning_goals: Standard-view acquisition, probe handling, and image optimization
examples: The module was delivered over 4 consecutive weeks, comprising two 90-minute sessions per week for a total of 12 h of supervised simulation

article_title: In-Situ Simulation for Enhancing Safety in Outpatient Hysteroscopy: Development and Evaluation of a Crisis Resource Management-Based Training Package.
citation: Warshafsky C, Singh SS, Garber AB. (2026). In-Situ Simulation for Enhancing Safety in Outpatient Hysteroscopy: Development and Evaluation of a Crisis Resource Management-Based Training Package. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11604
title: Four-scenario in-situ simulation training package for outpatient hysteroscopy emergencies
description: A training package of four simulation scenarios targeting oversedation, hemorrhage, local anesthetic systemic toxicity, and vasovagal reaction in the outpatient hysteroscopy setting. Each scenario "was designed to resolve within 15 minutes, with up to 45 minutes for debriefing." The package includes appendices with case progression tables, debriefing materials, a CRM primer, and a latent safety threats template.
requirements: Minimum of 1 gynecologist and 1 nurse per scenario
Patient simulator (ACLS manikin), monitors, hysteroscopy tray, venous access supplies, oxygen supplies, and crash cart
constraints: Requires physical material resources, though low-fidelity alternatives are described
Small number of roles may restrict participant numbers, though actors and debriefers can be divided
target_learners: Interprofessional outpatient procedural teams including nurses, residents, and practicing gynecologists
target_learning_goals: Recognize presenting signs and symptoms of hysteroscopy complications
Initiate management of complications in an outpatient surgical suite
Apply crisis resource management principles
Identify latent safety threats
examples: Scenarios were run with 12 OHS staff across 4 sessions and implemented with practicing gynecologists at the CHyPS Course in 2022 and 2024
key_sources: Warshafsky C, Singh SS, Garber AB. (2026). In-Situ Simulation for Enhancing Safety in Outpatient Hysteroscopy: Development and Evaluation of a Crisis Resource Management-Based Training Package. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11604

article_title: Development and implementation of an ecological education model for evidence-based practice competency in undergraduate nursing students: A mixed-methods feasibility study.
citation: Li Xuejing, Meng Meiqi, Li Xiaohua, Wang Ziyan, Wang Letong, Han Liu, Hao Yufang, Shi Nannan. (2026). Development and implementation of an ecological education model for evidence-based practice competency in undergraduate nursing students: A mixed-methods feasibility study. International Journal of Nursing Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijnss.2026.04.002
title: Four-year progressive competency development pathway structures EBP learning from awareness to application
description: The model organizes evidence-based practice competency development across the full undergraduate program as a four-year progressive pathway. Year 1 establishes evidence-based awareness through a mandatory course introducing evidence-based practice concepts, literature retrieval, and critical thinking. Years 2-3 emphasize competency building through guideline-integrated courses and practice platforms, advancing to systematic review methods and critical appraisal. Year 4 concentrates on comprehensive application and outcome demonstration through an evidence-based nursing round practicum during clinical internships and evidence-based graduation thesis options.
requirements: Requires coordination of evidence-based content across all four years of the curriculum rather than isolated courses
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of evidence-based thinking, competency building, and comprehensive practice application
examples: Year 1 students formulated PICO questions and developed innovation project proposals; Year 4 students conducted bedside evidence-based nursing rounds during clinical internships

title: Foster non-cognitive skills—particularly motivation, curiosity, and self-perceived ability—to support long-term academic outcomes
description: Based on the finding that non-cognitive skills mediate genetic prediction of academic achievement across development, the article underscores "the importance of fostering non-cognitive skills to enhance students' long term academic outcomes". It cites evidence that interventions focusing on self-control and social skills at age 7 positively impacted academic achievement in early adulthood, and that early-life interventions targeting self-regulation and perseverance were associated with modest improvements in later-life academic outcomes. Because mediation effects increased developmentally and persisted longitudinally, cultivating these skills may be particularly valuable as students gain autonomy over their learning environments.

constraints: The article notes that the extant literature on non-cognitive skills and educational outcomes is characterised by inconsistencies, low-quality studies and publication bias

target_learning_goals: academic achievement across compulsory education

title: A bespoke one-on-one refresher training comprising four components aligned with Kolb's experiential learning cycle
description: The TCT refresher training was a bespoke two-hour, interactive refresher training delivered one-on-one, comprising four components: a semi-structured interview exploring teaching experiences, a joint review of key theoretical concepts, a hands-on session supervising a resident performing a colonoscopy on an actual patient, and a debriefing. The article states that "This iterative process of experience, reflection, conceptualization, and experimentation aligns with Kolb's experiential learning cycle [13] and supports both skill refinement and a deeper understanding of effective teaching behaviours." The one-on-one format enabled personalized feedback and goal setting.
requirements: Participants must have previously completed the original TCT course
constraints: The individualized format differs from the original TCT course, which is delivered in a group setting
target_learning_goals: Sustained retention and transfer of procedural teaching skills
examples: Between May 2022 and May 2023, four on-site refresher trainings were conducted at the participating hospitals, 6–9 months after the initial TCT courses.

Clinical decision points are embedded at key procedural steps, roles rotate systematically, and each simulation cycle is followed by peer feedback and facilitator-guided reflection. clinical reasoning and decision-making

title: Four-wave taxonomy of pre-licensure nursing informatics competency evolution
description: The review organizes the history of pre-licensure nursing informatics (NI) competencies into four thematic waves, each anchored by seminal frameworks. As the article states, "4 thematic 'waves' that characterize the evolution of NI competencies are evident (Figure 1)": a foundation wave of basic technical skills, a quality integration wave tied to safety initiatives, a global expansion wave of EHR adoption and contextual adaptation, and a maturity wave of full integration into core entry-level competencies.

constraints: The taxonomy is the product of a narrative, non-systematic review, not a systematic synthesis
target_learning_goals: nursing informatics competencies
examples: The review names the foundation, quality integration, global expansion, and maturity waves and anchors each to frameworks such as Staggers et al, the AACN Essentials, TIGER, QSEN, CASN, and the 2021 AACN Essentials

title: Four-module AI teaching platform for medical imaging
description: A closed-loop AI teaching system comprising four modules: (1) cognitive diagnosis using BKT (pyBKT) and DKT (custom LSTM in TensorFlow) for real-time mastery updates and misjudgment modeling; (2) case generation & selection from public image datasets with synthetic perturbations creating difficulty gradients and confusion pairs; (3) explainable guidance using Grad-CAM saliency maps and LLM-generated three-level cues; (4) adaptive scheduling via custom-coded PPO in PyTorch with a 15-feature state space and custom reward function.

Historical interaction sequences for DKT training (20 pilot learners)

Diagnostic accuracy
Reduction of systematic misjudgment errors

article_title: Interest and effort in learning and performance.
citation: Kehle, L., & Urhahne, D. (2025). Interest and effort in learning. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70040
title: Foster both interest and effort, cultivating effort by making learning goals explicit and guiding purposeful learning pathways
description: The article concludes that educators should support both motivational constructs rather than interest alone, because consistently high performance cannot be sustained by interest alone. It states that "While situational interest can be stimulated through novel stimuli, academic effort must also be cultivated by making learners aware of their learning goals and guiding them along purposeful learning pathways". Interest stimulates initial engagement, but effort is essential for sustained learning as tasks progress.
requirements: Awareness of learning goals and purposeful learning pathways to cultivate effort
constraints: Based on short-term laboratory tasks with university students; the authors note causal conclusions cannot be drawn from their modelling approach
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in learning
improved learning outcomes
examples: Across three tasks, actual effort was the only consistent significant predictor of test achievement, while triggered interest predicted achievement only for the familiar mental-arithmetic task

citation: Fox, K., Jarad, F. & Baaij, A. (2025). The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self‐efficacy and performance in endodontics. International Endodontic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14241
title: Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy — performance accomplishments, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional states — as levers in endodontic teaching
description: The article states that 'the development of self‐efficacy is influenced by four primary sources': performance accomplishments from successfully undertaking tasks, vicarious experience from observing others, verbal persuasion through positive feedback from a trusted credible source, and physiological and emotional states. It maps each source onto endodontic teaching events, from progression from simulation to complex patient care through to managing anxiety during invasive procedures.
requirements: Verbal persuasion is most effective when it comes from a trusted, credible source such as a respected teacher of endodontics
constraints: Stress and anxiety can undermine self-efficacy, so psychosocial stress management is proposed for dental curricula
target_learners: Undergraduate and postgraduate dental students learning endodontics

examples: Coaching conversations at the start of a session that prompt reflection on previous mastery successes and observed peer experiences
Acknowledging the stressful nature of invasive endodontic procedures and discussing where support may be required

article_title: Predictors of nurses' spiritual care competence: A replication study with Australian palliative care nurses.
citation: Mascio R, Lynch S, Phillips J, Best M. (2026). Predictors of nurses’ spiritual care competence: A replication study with Australian palliative care nurses. Palliative & Supportive Care. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1478951526102119
title: Four qualitatively different models of nurses' spiritual care arranged in order of increasing competence
description: The article organizes nurses' spiritual care into four models: A, active management of the patient experience; B, responsive facilitation of patients' wishes; C, accompanying the patient on the dying journey; and D, empowering co-action with the patient. It states that "Nurses understand spiritual care in 4 qualitatively different ways... each yoked with different bundles of spiritual care behaviors, and arranged in order of increasing competence." Each model bundles a meaning of spiritual care with characteristic behaviors, from unilateral comfort provision (A) to coaching and partnering (D). The study assigns survey respondents to these models and uses them as a competence proxy.
requirements: Respondents' open-ended descriptions of what spiritual care means and what they do must be codable into one of the four models
constraints: The models derive from prior studies of American nurses (Mascio et al. 2024b); Model D is described as the ideal but the article notes the actual proportions of palliative nurses subscribing to each model need further research
target_learners: nurses providing spiritual care to patients at end of life
target_learning_goals: spiritual care competence, defined as the ability to assess and care for a patient's spiritual needs
examples: Survey responses were coded to models, e.g., a Model C nurse wrote: "Mainly listen to what the patient has to say, show support by being present, not rushing things, prioritise conversation with patient over other things."

citation: Kubota Kazumi, Nishimura Ayako, Seto Ryoma, Li Liu. (2026). Trustworthy AI-Augmented Objective Structured Clinical Examinations in Nursing Education: Taiwan-Japan Viewpoint on 5 AI Roles, Governance, and Cross-Border Implementation. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/87830
title: Four governance pillars for trustworthy AI-augmented OSCEs
description: The article distills four cross-cutting governance pillars—human oversight, learning process transparency, ethics and safety, and traceability—that "translate international guidance into daily assessment practice." Human oversight keeps AI advisory with trained assessors making final judgments; transparency requires keeping "machine-readable blueprints, station rubrics, persona cards, and logs that capture who did what, when, and on which evidence"; ethics and safety demand deidentification, data minimization, and red teaming; traceability links scores to time-stamped evidence, raters, and model versions for audits, drift detection, and equity monitoring.
requirements: Standardized logs connecting scores to time-stamped utterances or actions, raters, and model versions; safety checklists and red teaming before deployment and after significant model updates
constraints: Explainability is judged by auditability rather than by opaque post hoc rationales; model retraining or fine-tuning is treated as a higher-risk intervention requiring explicit approval, revalidation, and a rollback plan
target_learning_goals: trustworthy, auditable high-stakes clinical competence assessment
examples: Raters label each AI suggestion as accept, modify, or reject with optional reason tags such as no supporting evidence or wrong rubric mapping, and these actions are logged alongside evidence links and model versions

title: Foster task-oriented coping and curb rumination-focused emotion-oriented coping to support teacher well-being
description: Based on the observed bidirectional relations, the article concludes that "fostering task‐oriented coping may be particularly beneficial for well‐being; at the same time, preventing negative consequences of rumination‐focused emotion‐oriented coping on well‐being seems warranted." Because well-being was both a product and a condition of productive coping, interventions aimed at fostering well-being may also help instructors adopt adaptive habitual coping via active problem solving, creating a reinforcing positive loop.

examples: The study found moderate to large positive reciprocal relations between task-oriented coping and positive affect over one semester, supporting the proposed reinforcing loop
