article_title: Short-term simulation training course improves basic obstetric ultrasound operational skills of residents: A multi-center study.
citation: Zhao Yongfeng, Zhou Ping, Tang Xiaohong, Zhu Wenhui, Liu Wengang, Zhou Jinguang, Wang Jie, Luo Yingchun, Zhang Junhui, Yang Lan, Xu Yan. (2025). Short-term simulation training course improves basic obstetric ultrasound operational skills of residents: A multi-center study. PLoS One 20(12): e0328122. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0328122
title: 4-hour modular simulation-based obstetric ultrasound training course (U/S Mentor, 123 core tasks, 4 modules)
description: A short-term simulation training course designed "to enable residents to conduct detailed mid-trimester obstetric ultrasound scans", built from 123 core tasks defined by ISUOG guidelines and organized into 4 task modules (head/face, fetal heart, neck/chest/abdomen, spine/limbs/placenta etc.). Trainees deliberately practice one hour per module on the U/S Mentor simulator in groups of 3–4 with instructor demonstration, on-demand feedback, and real-time 3D anatomical guidance and probe-orientation feedback. It can be introduced before clinical practice or as refresher training.
requirements: Uniform content across centers based on ISUOG guidelines; same simulator with uniform software versions and identical virtual patient cases; standardized didactic lecture (1 hour) and 30-minute online instructor training; supervised small groups of 3–4 with a standardized checklist covering all core tasks
constraints: Course focused on basic operational skills and excluded abnormal obstetric scenarios; class hours were allocated based on practicality rather than systematic difficulty assessment; findings limited to skill changes within simulated environment
target_learners: First-year residents without obstetric ultrasound training experience
Residents with more than one year of hands-on clinical training
target_learning_goals: Obtaining standardized mid-trimester obstetric ultrasound planes
Organized scanning thinking and basic probe-handling operational skills
examples: All centers used the same U/S Mentor simulator with a 20-week-gestation fetus with normal anatomy; trainees took 30-minute turns for repeated practice, 1 hour per module (4 hours overall); no concurrent training with real pregnant patients was allowed
key_sources: Zhao Yongfeng, Zhou Ping, Tang Xiaohong, Zhu Wenhui, Liu Wengang, Zhou Jinguang, Wang Jie, Luo Yingchun, Zhang Junhui, Yang Lan, Xu Yan. (2025). Short-term simulation training course improves basic obstetric ultrasound operational skills of residents: A multi-center study. PLoS One 20(12): e0328122. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0328122

article_title: Trends in the Japanese National Medical Licensing Examination: Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Morimoto Y, Shikino K, Nomura Y, Ito S. (2025). Trends in the Japanese National Medical Licensing Examination: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/78214
title: Modified four-tier taxonomy for medical licensing examination items subdividing Type III into IIIa (interpretation plus recall) and IIIb (interpretation plus interpretation)
description: The article introduces a refinement of Japan's traditional three-tier examination taxonomy, retaining Types I (recall) and II (interpretation) but subdividing Type III into IIIa and IIIb. Type IIIa covers "Items in which once the stem is correctly interpreted, the answer can be derived through a simple recall process", addressing a previously undefined region between Types II and III. Type IIIb requires interpreting both stem and answer choices, capturing context-sensitive decision making contingent on severity, comorbidities, or allergies. The framework was aligned with Revised Bloom's Taxonomy and ACGME Internal Medicine Milestones and applied to classify all 2880 sampled NMLE items.
requirements: A detailed classification manual, structured assessor training, calibration exercises, and interrater reliability testing with senior-physician adjudication, as the article states reliability "was ensured through the use of a detailed classification manual, structured assessor training, calibration exercises, and interrater reliability testing"
constraints: Developed and validated for Japanese NMLE multiple-choice items; the article does not report application beyond this examination context
target_learners: medical graduates preparing for licensing examinations
target_learning_goals: distinguishing recall-based from context-sensitive clinical problem-solving in assessment item design
examples: Applied to classify all 2880 items from six NMLE sessions (2001-2024), with Type IIIb items rising from 3.8% to 18.8%
key_sources: Morimoto Y, Shikino K, Nomura Y, Ito S. (2025). Trends in the Japanese National Medical Licensing Examination: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/78214

article_title: Student paramedic experiences of group-based simulation activities used in assessment: a qualitative UK study.
citation: Colthup Rebecca A, Johnson Gavin N, Jenkins Rebecca J, Runacres Jessica. (2025). Student paramedic experiences of group-based simulation activities used in assessment: a qualitative UK study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-101052
title: Four-phase group-based simulation assessment with teams of four demonstrating non-technical skills
description: A summative, 100% weighted module assessment in which first-year student paramedic teams managed "a clinical emergency with two patients" designed for their competence level. Students worked in "teams of four, demonstrating NTS (teamwork, decision-making, leadership, communication and reflection) and professional standards", with individual contributions assessed. The design ran through four phases: pre-briefing and role allocation, group management of the simulation, group reflection-on-action, and debriefing with the TALK tool.
requirements: Service users were employed to act in the role of patients during the simulation assessments, ensuring realistic interactions
Students used university tablets and a Microsoft Form for the reflection-on-action phase, submitting it within the 60-min period
constraints: Some students could hide in group simulation; this was mitigated by encouraging stronger team members to involve quieter members, with such contribution recognised within the marking
target_learners: first-year (level 4) student paramedics in UK higher education
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills including teamwork, decision-making, leadership, communication and reflection
safe and effective care delivery in simulated prehospital environments
examples: The 60-min simulation was a clinical emergency with two patients, with the TALK debriefing tool used for the final debriefing phase
key_sources: Colthup Rebecca A, Johnson Gavin N, Jenkins Rebecca J, Runacres Jessica. (2025). Student paramedic experiences of group-based simulation activities used in assessment: a qualitative UK study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-101052

article_title: The Future of Healthcare-Simulation-Based Learning Curricula and Preparing Future Midwives for Effective Rapport-Building in Telehealth Settings.
citation: Jones, C. and Cominos, N. (2025). The Future of Healthcare—Simulation‐Based Learning Curricula and Preparing Future Midwives for Effective Rapport‐Building in Telehealth Settings. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16927
title: Telehealth education needs standardised definitions, trained educators, standardised authentic scenarios and placement practice opportunities
description: This principle holds that telehealth rapport-building should be formalised, fully integrated and explicitly taught rather than left ad hoc, because the study found disparate definitions, untrained educators and inconsistent scenarios undermining graduate preparedness. The article argues "simulation‐based Learning curricula (SBLC) offer an effective means of delivering training", conditional on scenario choice, protocol standardisation and authentic modalities. Guidelines must balance institutional flexibility with specific competencies for midwives.
requirements: Standardised definitions of telehealth in midwifery care
Specific training for clinical educators
Focused scenario development and standardised educational resources
Skills training in rapport-building in digital environments
Opportunities to practise in clinical placements
constraints: Guidelines must balance flexibility for institutions to design context-suited curricula with directive detail on how telehealth encounters should be conducted
target_learning_goals: rapport-building in telehealth consultations
woman-centred communication in digital care settings
examples: The study's Bachelor of Midwifery program integrated simulation across Years 1 and 3, with a Year 1 telephone ward-enquiry scenario and a Year 3 abortion-care telehealth scenario, each structured as pre-brief, roleplay and debrief
key_sources: Jones, C. and Cominos, N. (2025). The Future of Healthcare—Simulation‐Based Learning Curricula and Preparing Future Midwives for Effective Rapport‐Building in Telehealth Settings. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16927

article_title: A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education.
citation: Rezaei-Zadeh M, Cerbin-Koczorowska M. (2025). A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education. BMC Medical Education 25:1653. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08078-7
title: Four-layer ISM interdependency model of AI assessment mega-opportunities
description: Using Interpretive Structural Modelling with a purposively selected panel of seven medical education experts, the article builds a hierarchical model of the seven mega-opportunities' cause-effect relationships. The article reports that "the ISM analysis produced a four-layered hierarchical model that illustrates the significant interdependencies among the seven identified mega-opportunities". Layers run from foundational root drivers through intermediate and connector opportunities to a highly dependent impact opportunity, read from left to right as a strategic sequencing lens for implementation.
requirements: Expert panel meeting stated criteria including at least five years of medical education experience and demonstrated AI integration experience; pairwise SSIM judgments achieved by facilitated consensus
constraints: The ISM method, per the article's own limitations, "identifies significant interdependencies but does not quantify their strength or intensity"; the model is based on a purposive sample of expert opinions and existing literature
target_learners: medical students assessed in undergraduate, postgraduate, or continuing medical education
target_learning_goals: strategic prioritisation and sequencing of AI adoption in student assessment
examples: Figure 2 of the article displays the interdependency digraph among the seven mega-opportunities across four layers
key_sources: Rezaei-Zadeh M, Cerbin-Koczorowska M. (2025). A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education. BMC Medical Education 25:1653. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08078-7

article_title: Engagement, self-efficacy and self-regulation as predictors of academic success in non-medical healthcare education.
citation: Martincová J, Staňková I, Snopek P, Zemánková L. (2025). Engagement, self-efficacy and self-regulation as predictors of academic success in non-medical healthcare education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08043-4
title: Four-part 80-item questionnaire measuring engagement, self-efficacy, self-regulation and academic success
description: A questionnaire developed for this study containing "a total of 80 items divided into four parts", rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Part one uses the 9-item UWES-9S engagement scale (vigour, dedication, absorption; α = 0.79); part two the 13-item Self-Efficacy Formative Questionnaire (α = 0.82); part three the 40-item DAUS1 self-regulation questionnaire (α = 0.89); part four measures academic success including GPA and subjective success items. Completion took approximately 20 minutes.
requirements: The revised questionnaire was pilot-tested on a smaller sample of students to ensure clarity of the items and verify reliability, and reliability was tested to ensure internal consistency before full-scale implementation.
constraints: The authors state the reliability of the self-constructed questionnaire may be influenced by social desirability bias and students' subjective perceptions, and self-reported data are susceptible to cognitive biases and variations in personal interpretation.
target_learners: non-medical healthcare students in Czech higher education
target_learning_goals: measuring engagement
measuring self-efficacy
measuring self-regulation of learning
measuring academic success
examples: Data were collected in 2022 via an anonymous online survey distributed in collaboration with the universities, yielding 540 responses with a response rate of 73%.
key_sources: Martincová J, Staňková I, Snopek P, Zemánková L. (2025). Engagement, self-efficacy and self-regulation as predictors of academic success in non-medical healthcare education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08043-4

article_title: Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students.
citation: Mehrdad M, Jambarsang S, Sadeghian H, Jabinian F, Keshmiri F. (2025). Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334545
title: Four-element framework of game-based pedagogy: cognitive, behavioral, social, and affective engagement
description: The article designs its game by observing four elements of game-based pedagogy. "Cognitive engagement encourages students to think analytically, apply their knowledge, and adapt to evolving situations in the game by stimulating cognitive processes through presenting challenging patient safety situations in the surgical unit." Behavioral engagement shapes active participation and problem-solving; social engagement operates through peer interaction, group play, and competition; and the affective element uses curiosity, excitement, points, and competition to make learning enjoyable and motivating.
requirements: Game scenarios presenting challenging patient safety situations
Group play structures enabling peer interaction and competition
Points and riddles to create curiosity and motivation
constraints: Described and applied in the context of surgical unit patient safety education
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and decision-making about patient safety risks
Engagement and collaboration in safety training
examples: The puzzle game operationalized each element: riddles for cognitive challenge, rotating roles for behavioral engagement, group competition for social engagement, and points for affective motivation
key_sources: Mehrdad M, Jambarsang S, Sadeghian H, Jabinian F, Keshmiri F. (2025). Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334545

article_title: Technical Skills Assessment in Robotic Surgery: A Review of Recent Methods.
citation: Laughlin Jacob L. BS, Johnson Lianne R. MS, Ghanekar Bhargav MS, O'Malley Marcia K. PhD. (2025). Technical Skills Assessment in Robotic Surgery: A Review of Recent Methods. Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular Journal. https://doi.org/10.14797/mdcvj.1667
title: Four-category taxonomy of robotic surgical skill assessment methods
description: The review organizes the landscape of robotic surgical technical skill assessment into four categories: "structured rubrics, skill-based metrics, crowd-sourcing techniques, and automated assessment models." Structured rubrics (OSATS, GEARS, GOALS and adaptations) use expert-rated grading categories; skill-based metrics capture completion time, kinematics, completion-based criteria, outcomes, robotic control, and precision errors; crowd-sourcing aggregates nonexpert rubric scores; and automated assessment uses supervised machine learning and deep learning on kinematic and video data. The taxonomy structures the survey of 61 da Vinci-focused studies and grounds the review's trend analysis.
requirements: Automated models require a training dataset of motion signals, task videos, and expert grading as ground truth
constraints: Kinematic data access is often limited due to proprietary restrictions
Crowd-sourced raters are limited to applications where visual cues are sufficient
target_learners: surgical trainees and surgeons learning robotic surgery
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill proficiency on robotic platforms
key_sources: Laughlin Jacob L. BS, Johnson Lianne R. MS, Ghanekar Bhargav MS, O'Malley Marcia K. PhD. (2025). Technical Skills Assessment in Robotic Surgery: A Review of Recent Methods. Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular Journal. https://doi.org/10.14797/mdcvj.1667

article_title: Do active learning techniques promote higher academic performance in an online graduate anatomy course?
citation: Bradley LJ, Meyer KE, Kerr MS, Maddux SD, Heck AJ, Reeves RE, Handler EK. (2025). Do active learning techniques promote higher academic performance in an online graduate anatomy course? Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70066
title: Four active learning techniques adapted for asynchronous online anatomy delivery via Canvas discussion boards
description: The course implemented four active learning techniques, each with a teaching phase and a learning phase, adapted for an asynchronous online format using the Canvas discussion board tool. As the article states, "The four active learning techniques implemented in the course were jigsaw, team‐learning module (TLM), concept mapping (CM), and question constructing (QC)." Jigsaw used recorded 3-minute PowerPoint presentations posted to shared boards; TLM used preparation, a five-question iRAT, and a shared 10-question tRAT worksheet; CM used concept-map creation with peer answering; QC used authoring two Bloom's-labeled multiple-choice questions and answering peers' questions.
requirements: Discussion board tool in the Canvas learning management system; students subdivided into subgroups of approximately 9-13 students each assigned a designated unit objective
constraints: Activities were supplemental and did not introduce new course material; all techniques were worth the same points within the course grading structure
target_learners: graduate health-professions students in a Master of Science in Medical Science program
target_learning_goals: human anatomy content across five body-region units
examples: Students created and recorded a single-slide, 3-minute presentation on their assigned subgroup objective for jigsaw; TLM used a five-question iRAT quiz secured with Respondus Lockdown Browser
key_sources: Bradley LJ, Meyer KE, Kerr MS, Maddux SD, Heck AJ, Reeves RE, Handler EK. (2025). Do active learning techniques promote higher academic performance in an online graduate anatomy course? Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70066

article_title: Evaluation of Paediatric Nursing Students' Medication Calculation Competence: An Observational Study Using a Gamified Contest.
citation: Sainz‐Rozas, P. B., Balaguer‐López, E., García‐Molina, P., and Martínez, P. G. (2025). Evaluation of Paediatric Nursing Students' Medication Calculation Competence: An Observational Study Using a Gamified Contest. Nursing Open 12(9): e70295. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70295
title: Four-phase gamified Medication Contest combining theory, escape room, online quiz and timed clinical simulation
description: The Medication Contest is a gamified educational innovation structured in four phases: a theoretical session with a practical medication preparation laboratory and an "Online Escape Room designed to simulate clinical scenarios interactively"; an online 30-question contest via a web platform from which the 50 best performers advanced; selection of the top nine students; and a final in-person competition with "advanced clinical simulations" under timed conditions assessing calculation, preparation and administration. The design follows principles of intelligent teaching based on prior knowledge, motivation, practical application and self-monitoring.
requirements: Completion as part of the subject's teaching guide evaluation
Faculty question-writing and validation for the assessment instrument
constraints: Scalability to other institutions may be influenced by curricular differences, available technological resources, and faculty training in gamified methodologies, per the authors
target_learning_goals: Medication management learning in paediatric patients
Engagement and motivation in medication calculation practice
examples: Phase 4 stations included medication preparation, mock patient administration, and evaluation panels (Figure 1)
key_sources: Sainz‐Rozas, P. B., Balaguer‐López, E., García‐Molina, P., and Martínez, P. G. (2025). Evaluation of Paediatric Nursing Students' Medication Calculation Competence: An Observational Study Using a Gamified Contest. Nursing Open 12(9): e70295. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70295

article_title: Students' motivation, study-effort and perceptions of teachers' goals when engaging in a learning design within the flipped classroom.
citation: Torbergsen HKS, Paulsby TE, Haugan G, Utvær BK. (2025). Students’ motivation, study-effort and perceptions of teachers’ goals when engaging in a learning design within the flipped classroom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07729-z
title: Four-activity flipped-classroom learning design for CPR in nursing education (MCQ, RQI skills training, TBL, simulation)
description: A longitudinal learning design in NTNU’s bachelor nursing program combining "two pre-class activities and two in-class activities": multiple-choice questions based on ERC guidelines, mannequin-based skills training with Resuscitation Quality Improvement providing real-time computer-generated feedback, facilitated team-based learning with case-based discussions, and low- to high-fidelity simulation in teams. Pre-class activities are non-mandatory and flexible; in-class activities are mandatory and scheduled. The design evolves across three study years, from basic CPR skills toward communication, teamwork and advanced techniques.
requirements: A structured design that helps students identify learning objectives and understand how to achieve them; teacher facilitation and justification of why the design was chosen
constraints: Pre-class activities are non-mandatory, and studies report challenges during pre-class activities including increased study-effort, unfamiliarity with the format, and lack of motivation among students
target_learners: Bachelor nursing students across three years of study
target_learning_goals: CPR theoretical knowledge, practical skills, assessment, decision-making, teamwork and competence in stressful cardiac-arrest situations
examples: MCQ available four weeks before in-class sessions and repeatable; RQI available three weeks ahead and mandatory to complete, usually about 30 minutes; TBL and simulation sessions each last approximately 2.5 hours within a two- to six-week window
key_sources: Torbergsen HKS, Paulsby TE, Haugan G, Utvær BK. (2025). Students’ motivation, study-effort and perceptions of teachers’ goals when engaging in a learning design within the flipped classroom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07729-z

article_title: Mediating role of online academic emotions between online presence and learning performance in blended learning environments.
citation: Li Xingqiao; Ye Yinghua. (2025). Mediating role of online academic emotions between online presence and learning performance in blended learning environments. Scientific Reports 15, 29875. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-15947-0
title: In blended course design, instructors should foster online presence to raise positive-low arousal emotions and thereby improve learning performance
description: Because online presence predicts positive-low arousal emotions, which partially mediate the presence–performance link, the article recommends that instructors attend to emotion in blended design: "Teachers need to focus on reducing negative academic emotions and increasing positive-low arousal academic emotions during students' online learning processes when implementing blended learning, which can improve learning performance." This implies designing interactive teaching, clear resources, and connected online/offline content that support teaching, social, and cognitive presence.
requirements: Deliberate pedagogical design integrating online and face-to-face modalities; sufficient, clearly explained course resources
constraints: The article warns that too much repetition or disconnection between online and offline content can make learners feel distracted and bored
target_learners: college and university students in blended learning
target_learning_goals: learning performance
positive academic emotions
reduced negative emotions
examples: The study surveyed 971 students across nine Hangzhou institutions and found presence predicted calmness/relaxation, which carried 20.57% of the total effect on performance
key_sources: Li Xingqiao; Ye Yinghua. (2025). Mediating role of online academic emotions between online presence and learning performance in blended learning environments. Scientific Reports 15, 29875. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-15947-0

article_title: Designing a cultivation model for top-notch students in basic medicine: a Delphi method.
citation: Geng N, Qin Y, Wang F, Huang J. (2025). Designing a cultivation model for top-notch students in basic medicine: a Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07347-9
title: Four-in-one course system for top-notch basic medicine curricula
description: The model's operational layer organizes the curriculum into four coordinated course categories. The article states: "At the operational layer, the focus is on implementing a four-in-one course system covering general education, professional integration, interdisciplinary research, and internationalized online learning." General education courses nurture analytical thinking and cultural awareness; professional integrated courses combine core biomedical knowledge with organ-system modules; interdisciplinary and research-oriented courses converge medicine, engineering and informatics; and international modules, MOOCs and top-university practice courses foster global outlook.
requirements: Alignment with the strategic layer's cultivation philosophy, standards and objectives
constraints: The interdisciplinary curriculum is described as a pilot innovation still in its early stages, lacking comprehensive statistical data on integration and outcome assessment
target_learners: top-notch basic medicine students in research-intensive universities
target_learning_goals: integrated biomedical and interdisciplinary knowledge
critical thinking and research methods
global competence
examples: Third-round expert scores in Table 2 rate course indicators such as Frontier Courses in Basic Medicine (mean 5.00) and Problem-Based Learning (mean 4.90)
key_sources: Geng N, Qin Y, Wang F, Huang J. (2025). Designing a cultivation model for top-notch students in basic medicine: a Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07347-9

article_title: The effectiveness of e-learning in focused cardiac ultrasound training: a prospective controlled study.
citation: Ruppert Johannes, Krüger Rebecca, Göbel Sebastian, Wolfhard Susanna, Lorenz Liv-Annebritt, Weimer Andreas Michael, Kloeckner Roman, Waezsada Elias, Buggenhagen Holger, Weinmann-Menke Julia, Weimer Johannes Matthias. (2025). The effectiveness of e-learning in focused cardiac ultrasound training: a prospective controlled study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07409-y
title: Web-based FOCUS e-learning module structured into basics and cardio-specific learning with interactive revision cards
description: A German-language, browser-based e-learning module designed by ultrasound experts, didactics, and IT specialists, developed following the waterfall model. It was "structured into two parts: 'basics', covering ultrasound physics, image production, and topographic anatomy; and 'cardio-specific learning'" with chapters on section planes, probe handling, sonoanatomy, and examination protocols. Individual revision cards formed its foundation, with interactive features such as fillable tables and labellable graphics; pathologies were not taught.
requirements: Access via internet browser; completion expected before the in-person FOCUS workshop
constraints: Pathologies were not taught in the module
target_learners: medical students in their clinical years
physicians preparing for certified FOCUS workshops
target_learning_goals: theoretical FOCUS competencies including ultrasound physics, anatomy, section planes, and examination protocols
examples: Students were given one to two weeks for digital preparation; most participants in both groups spent 2.5 to 4 hours on the e-learning

article_title: Exploring the Meta-debrief: Developing a Toolbox for Debriefing the Debrief.
citation: Kumar Prashant; Collins Kathleen; Oliver Nathan; Duys Rowan; Park-Ross Jocelyn Frances; Paton Catherine; Laws-Chapman Colette; Eppich Walter; McGowan Neil. (2024). Exploring the Meta-debrief: Developing a Toolbox for Debriefing the Debrief. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000830
title: Four pillars of meta-debriefing practice: theoretically driven, psychologically safe, context dependent, and formative in function
description: The article presents "4 fundamental pillars, which underpin the creation of an impactful meta-debriefing strategy: theoretically driven, psychologically safe, context dependent, and formative in function." Theoretically, meta-debriefing is rooted in constructionism and constructivist paradigms; psychologically, principles enabling learner psychological safety are applied to faculty; contextually, strategies must fit professional, cultural, and environmental settings; and functionally, meta-debriefing is formative, supporting growth toward adaptive expertise rather than summative assessment. These pillars form the basis of the implementation strategies the authors advocate.
requirements: Careful consideration of all four pillars in practice; the pillars underpin the toolbox of implementation strategies
constraints: The authors recognize that some recommendations may be better suited to certain cultural and socioeconomic contexts but less appropriate in others, and advocate a flexible approach; summative assessment of debriefers should be performed distinctly from meta-debriefing as defined
target_learning_goals: Designing impactful meta-debriefing strategies
Supporting debriefer professional development
examples: The authors, an intentionally diverse, multicultural, and international group, practice meta-debriefing across clinical settings, academic institutions, contrasting socioeconomic and cultural climates, and virtual venues
key_sources: Kumar Prashant; Collins Kathleen; Oliver Nathan; Duys Rowan; Park-Ross Jocelyn Frances; Paton Catherine; Laws-Chapman Colette; Eppich Walter; McGowan Neil. (2024). Exploring the Meta-debrief: Developing a Toolbox for Debriefing the Debrief. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000830

article_title: Exploring the Meta-debrief: Developing a Toolbox for Debriefing the Debrief.
citation: Kumar Prashant; Collins Kathleen; Oliver Nathan; Duys Rowan; Park-Ross Jocelyn Frances; Paton Catherine; Laws-Chapman Colette; Eppich Walter; McGowan Neil. (2024). Exploring the Meta-debrief: Developing a Toolbox for Debriefing the Debrief. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000830
title: Advocate formalized meta-debriefing training for faculty rather than relying purely on accumulated debriefing experience
description: The article observes that the transition from debriefer to meta-debriefer is ill-defined and, in the authors' experience, happens through "incremental time-based experience rather than via deliberate, intentional, or formal training." Because meta-debriefing challenges are inherently more complex—requiring advanced skills with assessment tools, faculty psychological safety, and adult educational theory—the authors "advocate for formalized meta-debriefing training activities rather than relying purely on previous debriefing experience," combining workshops and courses, self-assessment and coaching, and opportunities to conduct debriefings of the meta-debrief.
requirements: Training should combine meta-debriefing workshops and courses, self-assessment and coaching, and opportunities to conduct debriefings of the meta-debrief, embedded into formal faculty development processes
constraints: The absence of clear evidence-informed best practice may limit how local simulation centers can justify extra resources, time, and money; many practitioners are working clinicians, so strict mandatory faculty development requirements may lead to disengagement and adverse unintended consequences—suggesting a pragmatic rather than mandating approach
target_learners: Experienced debriefers transitioning to meta-debriefers; simulation faculty
target_learning_goals: Advanced meta-debriefing facilitation skills
Quality of meta-debriefing interactions
examples: The authors propose embedding such training activities into formal faculty development processes, which will likely improve the skills of meta-debriefers and thus the quality of meta-debriefing interactions
key_sources: Kumar Prashant; Collins Kathleen; Oliver Nathan; Duys Rowan; Park-Ross Jocelyn Frances; Paton Catherine; Laws-Chapman Colette; Eppich Walter; McGowan Neil. (2024). Exploring the Meta-debrief: Developing a Toolbox for Debriefing the Debrief. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000830

article_title: Evaluating construct validity of virtual osces in exceptional conditions.
citation: Asmar Nadia, Youssef Nazih Y., Malhab Sandrella Bou, Bahous Sola, Karam Vanda G. Yazbeck. (2025). Evaluating construct validity of virtual osces in exceptional conditions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07383-5
title: Four-dimension construct validity framework for virtual OSCEs (content, response process, internal structure, consequences)
description: The article organises its validity evaluation around "the framework described in the Standards of Educational and Psychological Testing", examining "four aspects of construct validity": content, response process, internal structure, and consequences of testing. Content was addressed via blueprint alignment and expert scenario review; response process via training and calibration of examiners, SPs and students; internal structure via six psychometric metrics; and consequences via BRM and Angoff standard setting. The framework structures both the methods and the discussion of the virtual OSCE.
requirements: Alignment of stations with a predefined blueprint and expert review of scenarios
Training and calibration of physician examiners, simulated patients, and students on the platform and checklists
Psychometric metrics computed from completed checklists reviewed for accuracy

citation: Korteland, R.-J., Kok, E., Hulshof, C., & van Gog, T. (2024). Teaching through their eyes: effects on optometry teachers’ adaptivity and students’ learning when teachers see students’ gaze. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 29(5), 1735–1748. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10325-3
title: Four-facet taxonomy of (non)adaptive teacher support
description: The article adopts Van de Pol et al.'s distinction between four facets of (non)adaptive support, operationalized in the QTSA. "Adaptive support means increasing teacher regulation upon low student understanding" (A+) and decreasing regulation upon high understanding (A-), while non-adaptive behavior is increasing regulation upon higher understanding (NA+) or decreasing regulation upon lower understanding (NA-). Providing adaptive support requires accurately judging students' understanding and adjusting regulation accordingly, which is difficult because teachers often overestimate students' understanding.
requirements: Teachers must accurately judge the student's current level of understanding before increasing or decreasing regulation
constraints: Teachers often overestimate students' understanding, so provided support is not always tailored to student needs
target_learners: optometry students learning OCT interpretation in one-to-one sessions
target_learning_goals: interpretation of optical coherence tomography images
examples: The QTSA measured all four facets on 5-point Likert scales after the teaching session; students in both conditions perceived that support was very often increased when they did not understand (A+) and decreased when they did (A-)

article_title: Teaching conflict management to medical students: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Mohseni Fatemeh, Mohammadi Aeen, Khabaz Mafinejad Mahboobeh, Khajavirad Nasim, Basiri Kamal, Gruppen Larry D. (2024). Teaching conflict management to medical students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06514-8
title: Fogg Behavior Model (FBM) as a framework for designing conflict-management e-learning
description: The Fogg Behavior Model explains behavior change through three factors — motivation, ability and prompt — with motivation and ability able to "reinforce and compensate for each other". Prompts are delivered as a spark (motivational initiation), a facilitator (emphasizing ease), or a signal (a simple reminder). In education, FBM helps planners "think systematically about motivational elements, simplicity, and strategies used to change student performance". This trial operationalized FBM as motivation (attractive infographics, motivational mini-lectures, evidence-based statistics), ability (animated clips, completed negotiation worksheets), and prompts (polling, immediate feedback, educational SMS on WhatsApp).
requirements: Learners must have motivation and commitment to learning goals as prerequisites to developing new behaviors
An e-learning platform and delivery channel (e.g., messaging apps) able to send prompts at specified intervals
constraints: The article notes not all individuals successfully modify their behavior during the learning process despite motivation
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes toward conflict management in healthcare teams
conflict management behavior change
examples: The trial delivered asynchronous infographics, animations, worksheets and WhatsApp SMS prompts between two synchronous sessions over four weeks

title: A four-phase conceptual framework of intervention reasoning: generating, selecting, implementing, and evaluating interventions
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework for intervention reasoning comprising four phases. As the authors state, "In this commentary, we present a conceptual framework for intervention reasoning that includes four phases: generating, selecting, implementing, and evaluating interventions." The framework describes cognitive activities in each phase, such as developing interventions from a patient's diagnosis and symptoms, contrasting and prioritizing options by feasibility and effectiveness, planning and executing treatments, and monitoring outcomes. It is intended as a foundation for research and training in medical education and potentially beyond.
requirements: The framework is preliminary and requires validation studies, such as observational or interview studies, before it can guide practice
constraints: The article presents it as a conceptualization based on limited existing literature, not as an empirically validated model
target_learning_goals: intervention reasoning skills
clinical reasoning
key_sources: Richters C, Schmidmaier R, Popov V, Schredelseker J, Fischer F, Fischer MR. (2024). Intervention skills – a neglected field of research in medical education and beyond. GMS Journal for Medical Education 41(4):Doc48. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2024-41/zma001703.shtml

article_title: Laparoscopic training workshop to assess medical students' skill acquisition and interest in surgical careers.
citation: Chen Pin-Chun, Yang Po-Wen, Kao Yi-Kai, Chen Chia-Hung, Tsai Chih-Jong, Chen Yi-Chieh, Song Ling-Chiao, Tsai Kai Lung, Wu Richard C., Chen Chih-I. (2024). Laparoscopic training workshop to assess medical students' skill acquisition and interest in surgical careers. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05708-4
title: Four-task laparoscopic training box module (Precision Bead Placement, Beads Transfer, Precision Balloon Cutting, Intracorporeal Suturing)
description: The article's training module comprises four distinct tasks performed in a training box containing laparoscopic instruments (graspers, scissors, needle holders), a camera system, and materials such as beads, balloons, and sutures. Each task targets a specific skill set: bead placement emphasizes "precision and dexterity", bead transfer focuses on instrument coordination, balloon cutting requires peeling an outer balloon without puncturing the inner water-filled balloon, and intracorporeal suturing demands suturing within a confined space mirroring actual surgical conditions. Task completion times with task-specific penalties served as the skill measure.
requirements: A training box with laparoscopic instruments, a camera system, and materials for practicing skills
constraints: The advanced live tissue techniques (endoGIA staplers, intestinal anastomosis) were not assessed as part of the outcomes
target_learners: Medical students with varied laparoscopic experience, from novices to clinically experienced
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic precision, instrument coordination and handling, control, and intracorporeal suturing technique
examples: The workshop also included a live tissue training component using pig intestines, providing introductory exposure to endoGIA staplers and intestinal anastomosis
key_sources: Chen Pin-Chun, Yang Po-Wen, Kao Yi-Kai, Chen Chia-Hung, Tsai Chih-Jong, Chen Yi-Chieh, Song Ling-Chiao, Tsai Kai Lung, Wu Richard C., Chen Chih-I. (2024). Laparoscopic training workshop to assess medical students' skill acquisition and interest in surgical careers. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05708-4

article_title: Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses.
citation: Meszaros Mariana de Jesus; de Almeida Angélica Olivetto; da Silva Ruana Luiz Ferreira; Eduardo Aline Helena Appoloni; Lima Maria Helena de Melo; Oliveira-Kumakura Ana Railka de Souza. (2023). Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2023-0019
title: Debriefing pattern combining formative debriefing during the simulation and summative debriefing afterwards
description: The scenarios embed a two-part debriefing pattern based on the Three Stages of Efficient Focused/Formative/Summative Debriefing guide for instructors. The article reports that "the formative debriefing took place during this same period during the practical experience and the summative debriefing in 30 minutes after the simulated experience," with the model chosen "for allowing a formative and summative approach and being directed to the performance of nurse educators." Debriefing is facilitated and aims to help participants reflect on the simulated experience, learning acquired and transfer to clinical practice.
requirements: A facilitator mediating reflection and the instructor debriefing guide as theoretical reference
constraints: Debriefing time bounded by the 15-minute scenario and 30-minute post-experience period as applied in this study
target_learners: Nurses participating in simulation-based continuing education
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking, integration of learning with practice, and improved future clinical performance
examples: Checklists formulated for each scenario served to examine participants' performance and guide the subsequent debriefing stage

article_title: Enhancing proficiency in ascites puncture through procedural simulation: an audit type study investigating medium-term skill retention.
citation: Hammami Aya, Ghali Hela, Elleuch Nour, Ben Saad Omar Khalil, Jaziri Hanen, Ksiaa Mehdi, Ali Habiba Sik. (2024). Enhancing proficiency in ascites puncture through procedural simulation: an audit type study investigating medium-term skill retention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05063-4
title: Four-stage learning sequence for procedural simulation: demonstration without comment, commented demonstration, learner explanation, then learner performance with real-time feedback
description: The session used the "four-stage learning" approach, in which responsibility for explaining the procedure progressively shifts from trainer to learner. The trainer first demonstrates the ascites puncture sequence in real time without comment, then demonstrates while describing each step, then performs while learners explain the techniques, and finally each candidate completes the sequence receiving feedback in real time. The article pairs this with a 10-minute pre-briefing, real-time analytical debriefing, and a 20-minute summary debriefing.
requirements: A trained trainer providing supervision and real-time feedback, and a pre-briefing presenting the educational objectives and familiarizing learners with the dummy and equipment
constraints: The article applied this sequence to a single 90-minute procedural session on ascites puncture with groups of about six learners; it does not claim the sequence generalizes beyond such procedural sessions
target_learners: third-year medical students (DCEM1) on gastroenterology placement
target_learning_goals: performing an ascites puncture correctly according to a ten-step technical checklist
examples: In this study the four-stage sequence was embedded in a 90-minute session preceded by a self-learning module and video, with a five-MCQ pre-test and identical post-test

citation: Peña-Jorquera Humberto, Martínez-Flores Ricardo, Espinoza-Puelles Juan Pablo, López-Gil José Francisco, Ferrari Gerson, Zapata-Lamana Rafael, Lofrano-Prado Mara Cristina, Landaeta-Díaz Leslie, Cigarroa Igor, Durán-Agüero Samuel, Cristi-Montero Carlos. title: Four Mediterranean-style-based dietary patterns in Chilean adolescents identified by latent class analysis
description: The article identifies four distinct eating-pattern groups among Chilean adolescents using latent class analysis on nine KIDMED questionnaire items. As the Results state, "we identified four distinct clusters: WD (4.3%), LFV-HSD (28.2%), LFV-LSD (42.2%), and MED-DIET (25.3%)". The clusters differ mainly in fruit and vegetable intake, sugar and junk-food consumption, breakfast omission, and fish consumption, and serve as the grouping variable for all cognitive and academic comparisons in the study.
requirements: Latent class analysis on KIDMED dietary items after a sensitivity analysis with elbow plot and fit indicators (AIC, BIC, ABIC, CAIC)
constraints: Patterns were derived from a dichotomous nine-item questionnaire in a single cross-sectional sample of 10–14-year-olds from Valparaíso, Chile
target_learning_goals: Characterizing dietary patterns linked to cognitive and academic achievement
examples: Cluster sizes in the sample: WD n = 56, LFV-HSD n = 365, LFV-LSD n = 547, MED-DIET n = 328 (Table 1)

article_title: Barriers to implementing problem-based learning at the school of medicine of Debre Berhan University, Ethiopia.
citation: Tefera Aklile Semu, Melaku Ermiyas Endewunet, Urgie Besufekad Mulugeta, Hassen Erzik Muhammed, Tamene Tilahun Deresse, Gebeyaw Enguday Demeke. (2024). Barriers to implementing problem-based learning at the school of medicine of Debre Berhan University, Ethiopia. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05252-1
title: Four-category taxonomy of PBL implementation barriers: student-related, tutor-related, case scenario-related, and assessment-related
description: The article organizes the barriers to implementing problem-based learning at Debre Berhan University medical school into four main themes derived from Spradley's four-step qualitative analysis (domain, taxonomic, componential, and theme analysis). As the authors state, "The study identified student-related, tutor-related, case scenario-related, and assessment-related barriers as the most significant obstacles to implementing problem-based learning." Each category contains subthemes: student resistance, workload, dominance, expectations and communication skills; tutor motivation, overload, training and orientation; case ambiguity, time allocation and delivery timing; and assessment subjectivity and lack of ongoing evaluation.
requirements: Derived from qualitative interview and focus group data at a single institution; applying it elsewhere requires local barrier exploration
constraints: The study was carried out in a single medical school, so findings may not reflect comprehensive national barriers
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of problem-based learning in undergraduate medical education
examples: The taxonomy was built from semi-structured interviews with 15 academic staff, including the PBL coordinator and school dean, and focus group discussions with 16 students.

article_title: Obstetric simulation for undergraduate medical education: how to improve students' self-confidence and expectation according to gender.
citation: Nomura Roseli Mieko Yamamoto, Reis Fabiana Medeiros D., Gonçalves Amanda Menezes, de Proença Carolina Matos. (2023). Obstetric simulation for undergraduate medical education: how to improve students’ self-confidence and expectation according to gender. Revista da Associação Médica Brasileira. https://doi.org/10.1590/1806-9282.20221625
title: Four-scenario obstetric simulation course with a full-sized birth simulator, standardized speeches, and debriefing
description: A 2-week simulation course embedded in the fifth-year 4-week obstetric clerkship, run in groups of 5–6 students across 3–4 sessions of approximately 3 h. Each session followed three steps: orientation, simulation, and debriefing. "In the simulation-training sessions, a NoelleS575, a full-sized female anthropomorphic birth simulator, and models of cervical dilation and pelvis were used." The four scenarios covered childbirth stages, partograph analysis and pelvimetry, premature rupture of membranes at term, and third-trimester bleeding.
requirements: Sessions include orientation to learning objectives, case management by students, and debriefing
Standardized speeches and role-played patient dialogue prepared for admission scenarios
constraints: Designed for fifth-year undergraduate medical students during their obstetrics clerkship rotation
target_learning_goals: self-confidence in obstetric procedures and skills
childbirth care management
clinical reasoning in obstetric scenarios
examples: Scenery 1 had each student individually assist a simulated primiparous labor lasting about 20 min, performing vaginal exam, perineal protection, delayed cord clamping, and third-stage management

article_title: Force-based assessment of tissue handling skills in simulation training for robot-assisted surgery.
citation: Rahimi A. Masie, Hardon Sem F., Willuth E., Lang F., Haney Caelan M., Felinska Eleni A., Kowalewski Karl-Friedrich, Müller-Stich Beat P., Horeman Tim, Nickel F., Daams Freek. (2023). Force-based assessment of tissue handling skills in simulation training for robot-assisted surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-023-09905-y
title: ForceSense objective force and time measuring system for surgical simulation training
description: The ForceSense system (Medishield, Delft) is an objective measuring system used to assess tissue handling during simulated surgical tasks. It "provided feedback regarding maximum force, mean force, max impulse, force volume and time", and in this study assessed robotic suturing trials on the da Vinci Si system, with all trials recorded and uploaded to an online database. Its five force-based parameters were used to distinguish experience groups and plot learning curves.
requirements: Requires instrumented training hardware (box trainer with suture pad) connected to the measuring system, and trials recorded to an online database for analysis.
constraints: In this study no motion parameters could be measured, due to the discrepancies of trocar instrument and da Vinci instrument diameter.
target_learners: Surgical trainees (junior residents, senior residents, young surgeons, robot experts) in robotic surgery simulation training
target_learning_goals: Tissue manipulation and force control in robot-assisted suturing and knot tying
examples: Used to assess six trials of an interrupted robotic suture and knot tying task performed by 60 participants across three experience groups.
key_sources: Rahimi A. Masie, Hardon Sem F., Willuth E., Lang F., Haney Caelan M., Felinska Eleni A., Kowalewski Karl-Friedrich, Müller-Stich Beat P., Horeman Tim, Nickel F., Daams Freek. (2023). Force-based assessment of tissue handling skills in simulation training for robot-assisted surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-023-09905-y

article_title: Force-based assessment of tissue handling skills in simulation training for robot-assisted surgery.
citation: Rahimi A. Masie, Hardon Sem F., Willuth E., Lang F., Haney Caelan M., Felinska Eleni A., Kowalewski Karl-Friedrich, Müller-Stich Beat P., Horeman Tim, Nickel F., Daams Freek. (2023). Force-based assessment of tissue handling skills in simulation training for robot-assisted surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-023-09905-y
title: Incorporate objective force-based assessment and feedback into robot-assisted surgery training programs
description: Because current robotic training curricula with VR and box training lack the ability to train and assess tissue manipulation and force application, the article advises trainers to incorporate force-based assessment into robotic surgery training systems. Objective force parameters can determine technical proficiency and, potentially, help prevent tissue trauma, and repetitive assessment shows learning curves over time.
requirements: Access to an objective force and time measuring system such as ForceSense integrated with a simulation trainer.
constraints: Most robotic platforms lack direct force feedback, so ex vivo training is of paramount importance; VR simulator force metrics do not translate to force exerted on tissue by instruments.
target_learning_goals: Safe tissue manipulation, force control, and technical proficiency in robotic suturing
examples: The study used ForceSense-derived force parameters to distinguish novices, intermediates and experts and to demonstrate learning curves over six suturing trials.

article_title: Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population.
citation: Mayer Anja, Da Silva Domingues Vital, Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Larrosa Marcos, Martínez-Jarreta Begoña, Rodriguez-Molina Daloha, Sousa-Pinto Bernardo, Sudacka Małgorzata, Morin Luc. (2022). Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19106175
title: Four-step blueprinting process for planning a representative virtual patient collection
description: The article proposes a replicable planning process for VP collections, run by an interdisciplinary partnership across five European countries. Criteria are first defined and categorized, then data sources for representativeness checks are identified, the blueprint is populated, and consensus is reached. As the authors state, partners "developed a blueprint for a collection of 200 VPs in four steps: (1) Defining the criteria (e.g., key symptoms, age, sex) and categorizing them into disease-, patient-, encounter- and learner-related, (2) Identifying data sources for assessing the representativeness of the collection, (3) Populating the blueprint, and (4) Refining and reaching consensus." The process was motivated by the lack of guidance for designing VP collections rather than individual VPs.
requirements: An international, interdisciplinary partnership able to reach consensus, plus identified external data sources (WHO, EUROSTAT, national competency frameworks) against which representativeness is assessed
constraints: The article notes the approach was "challenging and time-consuming" and that no Scandinavian or Balkan country was represented in the consortium, so Northern or Southeastern European perspectives may be missing
target_learners: medical students in European higher education
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning through deliberate practice with virtual patient cases
examples: The iCoViP consortium mapped 75 existing VPs into the blueprint and asked each partner institution to add 25 VPs based on curricular needs, then refined distributions against literature and statistics
key_sources: Mayer Anja, Da Silva Domingues Vital, Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Larrosa Marcos, Martínez-Jarreta Begoña, Rodriguez-Molina Daloha, Sousa-Pinto Bernardo, Sudacka Małgorzata, Morin Luc. citation: Kaneko Regina Mayumi Utiyama, Monteiro Inês, Lopes Maria Helena Baena de Moraes. (2022). Form for planning and elaborating high fidelity simulation scenarios: A validation study. PLoS ONE 17(9): e0274239. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0274239
title: ForPEC (Healthcare Simulation Scenario Planning and Elaboration Form) version 1.3
description: ForPEC is a structured form for planning and elaborating high-fidelity healthcare simulation scenarios, based on best-practice references [21–26]. It "contains 10 sections in a total of 91 sub-items", covering general planning, minimum requirements, learning and results, references and pre/post-simulation reading, simulation center logistics, full case description, laboratory and imaging test results, debriefing, checklist, and case reading. Participants used it to build technical, behavioral, and combined scenarios.
requirements: To be completed with its Operational Manual, which presents the 91 items with descriptions and guidelines
constraints: The article states one limitation was that it "was only available on paper, which limited the registration space"
target_learners: health professionals in simulation facilitation roles
students and health professionals in training
target_learning_goals: planning and elaborating high-fidelity simulation scenarios
developing technical and non-technical skills
examples: In the test, most scenarios developed by participants (75%) were aimed at developing technical skills, including chest tube care, cardiopulmonary arrest, and septic shock; five were behavioral (e.g., communicating bad news) and two combined technical and behavioral objectives.
key_sources: Kaneko Regina Mayumi Utiyama, Monteiro Inês, Lopes Maria Helena Baena de Moraes. (2022). Form for planning and elaborating high fidelity simulation scenarios: A validation study. PLoS ONE 17(9): e0274239. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0274239

building simulation scenarios

citation: Padilla L, Meleski WB, Dominick C, Athing C, Jones CL, Burns D, Cathers LA, Fields EC. (2022). Introductory patient communication training for medical physics graduate students: Pilot experience. Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics. https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.13449

description: A four-part experiential training sequence in which learners meet a simulated patient before instruction, receive a didactic lecture, apply the strategies in a second encounter, and close with written reflection. The curriculum was "designed following Kolb's experiential learning theory", moving from a new experience to reflection, conceptualization, and application in a new situation. The article reports the sequence increased both participant confidence and competence.

Simulated patient actors trained in their role and a rubric for assessing communication behaviors

target_learning_goals: effective patient communication skills

description: The LAPSTAR box trainer used in the study was equipped with the ForceSense measuring system, which "provides force-, motion- and time parameter outcomes used for objective assessment of laparoscopic performance". article_title: A Health eLearning Ontology and Procedural Reasoning Approach for Developing Personalized Courses to Teach Patients about Their Medical Condition and Treatment.
citation: Michalowski Martin, Wilk Szymon, Michalowski Wojtek, O'Sullivan Dympna, Bonaccio Silvia, Parimbelli Enea, Carrier Marc, Le Gal Grégoire, Kingwell Stephen, Peleg Mor. (2021). A Health eLearning Ontology and Procedural Reasoning Approach for Developing Personalized Courses to Teach Patients about Their Medical Condition and Treatment. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18147355
title: Personalization of patient courses across four axes
description: The framework's course-level design pattern personalizes educational materials along four patient axes. As the article states, "The resulting courses generated by the framework are personalized across four patient axes—condition and treatment, comprehension level, learning style based on the VARK (Visual, Aural, Read/write, Kinesthetic) presentation model, and the level of understanding of specific course content according to Bloom's taxonomy." Courses progress from lower-order remembering lessons to higher-order understanding and applying lessons only after several correct answers, and BUK presentation modality follows the patient's preferred VARK style with a K → V → R → A fallback sequence.
requirements: A patient's comprehension level must be known in advance, currently proxied by education level or physician judgement
constraints: The structure of a course is fixed and progression through a course is linear; a patient's learning style is set to a default and not determined a priori
target_learners: outpatients newly diagnosed with a condition and starting a prescribed treatment
target_learning_goals: understanding of condition, treatment options, dosage, monitoring, side effects, and coping with missed doses
examples: For fictional patient Mario (V and R styles) the framework generated an anticoagulation course; for Anne (V and K styles) a lower back pain course with NSAID and exercise therapy

article_title: Learning outcomes of a flipped classroom teaching approach in an adult-health nursing course: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Fan Jun-Yu, Tseng Ying-Jung, Chao Li-Fen, Chen Shiah-Lian, Jane Sui-Whi. (2020). Learning outcomes of a flipped classroom teaching approach in an adult-health nursing course: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02240-z
title: Four-phase flipped classroom cycle for a nursing course: online self-directed pre-class learning, face-to-face team-based learning, simulation, and post-class assignments
description: This pattern structures each course topic as a recurring four-phase cycle. The first phase is "an online self-directed learning pre-class phase in which students reviewed assigned reading materials via the online e-campus platform"; the second is a face-to-face TBL activity beginning with an individual quiz, followed by group discussion and an appeal process; the third is a face-to-face simulation exercise based on an actual clinical case; the last phase involves completing post-class assignments, reflection reports, and evaluations on the platform. In the study, this cycle was applied to five adult-health nursing topics over 36 course hours.
requirements: Instructors upload pre-class reading materials, case descriptions, assignments, and evaluation forms on an online platform two weeks before the course begins, and faculty training sessions are held to ensure consistency of content and materials.
constraints: The pattern was implemented in a classroom-based two-year RN-to-BSN program at a single private university with two campuses; students were not monitored for whether they actually reviewed the online materials.
target_learners: Registered nurses in a two-year RN-to-BSN bridge program
target_learning_goals: Adult-health nursing competencies including pathophysiology, physical assessment, nursing care, and psychosocial issues for leading causes of death
examples: The 36-hour course was divided into five blocks on diabetes mellitus, COPD, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, and cancer, each addressed through the four phases.
key_sources: Fan Jun-Yu, Tseng Ying-Jung, Chao Li-Fen, Chen Shiah-Lian, Jane Sui-Whi. (2020). Learning outcomes of a flipped classroom teaching approach in an adult-health nursing course: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02240-z

article_title: Tips for teaching procedural skills.
citation: Burgess A, van Diggele C, Roberts C, Mellis C. (2020). Tips for teaching procedural skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02284-1
title: Four-stage development of competency: unconsciously incompetent to unconsciously competent
description: The article describes a four-level model of skill acquisition adapted from Peyton (1998): "1) Unconsciously incompetent, 2) Consciously incompetent, 3) Consciously competent, 4) Unconsciously competent." Learners progress through these stages, illustrated by the everyday example of learning to drive. The article adds a caution that experts may regress to being unconsciously incompetent over the long term, for example by over-estimating their ability or not staying up to date.
requirements: Reflection on performance to recognise one's stage and avoid regression to unconscious incompetence
constraints: The article notes experts may again become unconsciously incompetent over time
target_learners: Novice health professionals learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: Understanding progression toward competency in clinical skills
key_sources: Burgess A, van Diggele C, Roberts C, Mellis C. (2020). Tips for teaching procedural skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02284-1

article_title: Developing an Evidence-Based Technical Assistance Model: a Process Evaluation of the National Training and Technical Assistance Center for Child, Youth, and Family Mental Health.
citation: Olson Jonathan R., Coldiron Jennifer Schurer, Parigoris Ryan M., Zabel Michelle D., Matarese Marlene, Bruns Eric J. (2020). Developing an Evidence-Based Technical Assistance Model: a Process Evaluation of the National Training and Technical Assistance Center for Child, Youth, and Family Mental Health. The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11414-020-09686-5
title: Four dimensions of high-quality technical assistance: dosage, intensive-plus-light-touch mix, collaboration, and proactivity
description: The article enumerates four dimensions of effective TA drawn from the literature. First, TA must be of sufficient dosage, with "long-term, ongoing TA is associated with better outcomes than one-shot, time-limited efforts." Second, TA should mix intensive supports such as on-site consultation and learning communities with frequent, low-cost off-site check-ins, plus individualized and tailored feedback. Third, a collaborative approach builds "trust, positive communication, and empathy." Fourth, proactive TA providers anticipate stakeholder needs and respond in a timely, positive, and ongoing way, building on stakeholder strengths toward improved systems-level capacity.
requirements: TA providers must form working relationships with policy-makers, program administrators, implementers, and service recipients
constraints: the relation between dosage and outcomes is moderated by task difficulty, being weaker for tasks that are very easy or very difficult
target_learners: TA recipients implementing youth-focused behavioral health programs and systems
target_learning_goals: successful implementation and sustainability of evidence-based practices and systems change
examples: peer-to-peer learning communities have been found associated with implementation fidelity and sustainability of evidence-based practices over time

Developing an Evidence-Based Technical Assistance Model: a Process Evaluation of the National Training and Technical Assistance Center for Child, Youth, and Family Mental Health. The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11414-020-09686-5

article_title: Formative assessment of practical skills with peer-assessors: quality features of an OSCE in general medicine at the Heidelberg Medical Faculty.
citation: Möltner Andreas, Lehmann Mirijam, Wachter Cornelia, Kurczyk Sonia, Schwill Simon, Loukanova Svetla. (2020). Formative assessment of practical skills with peer-assessors: quality features of an OSCE in general medicine at the Heidelberg Medical Faculty. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(4), Doc42. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001335.shtml
title: Formative OSCE General Medicine program at Heidelberg Medical Faculty with peer tutors as examiners
description: A formative OSCE program of the Department of General Practice and Implementation Research, conducted and evaluated by peer tutors since 2013 within the AaLPLUS pre-clinical courses. In May 2018 it was attended by 300 fourth-semester students over two days with four testing stations of eight minutes each (5 minutes per task and 3 minutes feedback), assessed with checklists by 32 students with basic didactic training who were at least in their sixth semester, using tablet computers. Five supervisors carried out random second evaluations (135 evaluations in total) as quality assurance.
requirements: Trained student examiners with basic didactic training who are at least in their sixth semester
Checklists with essential evaluation criteria known to students from previous tutorials
Supervisors to monitor quality of implementation and evaluation
constraints: The article states the small number of four stations does not provide measurement reliability meeting the requirements of high-quality examinations
Generalization to other institutions or conditions is not possible from this individual case
target_learning_goals: Practical clinical skills and anamnesis techniques in general medicine
examples: The May 2018 OSCE used 11 different clinical examination tasks and three anamnesis stations with trained acting patients, with 25 points per station (30 at anamnesis stations)

Formative assessment of practical skills with peer-assessors: quality features of an OSCE in general medicine at the Heidelberg Medical Faculty.
